methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. We aim for benchmarks of 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. All three use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The possible 1,000-problem expansion has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The targets are 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. Top 100, Top 500 and the possible Top 1000 use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.

cards.title: Does P equal NP?
cards.formal: Does every language with polynomially bounded, polynomial-time verifiable certificates admit a deterministic polynomial-time decision algorithm? Equivalently, do there exist a deterministic Turing machine A and constants C,k such that, for every encoded Boolean formula F of bit length n, A decides whether F has a satisfying assignment and halts within $C(n+1)^k$ steps? The algorithm must give the correct answer on every input.
cards.definitions: A language is a subset of the finite binary strings. P consists of languages decided by one deterministic multitape Turing machine with worst-case running time C(n+1)^k for some constants C,k. NP consists of languages L for which there are a deterministic polynomial-time verifier V and a polynomial p satisfying $x\in L\iff\exists y\in\{0,1\}^{\le p(|x|)}:V(x,y)=1$. The verifier's time is polynomial in the combined input length. SAT is the language of well-formed Boolean formulas with at least one satisfying assignment; malformed encodings are rejected. Fix any ordinary explicit binary encoding of formulas using AND, OR, and NOT. The question concerns uniform deterministic computation, with no advice, oracle, or error probability. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove P=NP or P≠NP in the deterministic uniform model defined here. Equality requires that every NP language have a polynomial-time decision algorithm; inequality requires that at least one NP language have none.
cards.why: This is the basic test of whether efficient verification entails efficient solution. It organizes the complexity of optimization, search, logical reasoning, and many graph problems, while motivating the development of general algorithmic lower-bound techniques.

importance.reason: The central boundary between efficient verification and efficient computation, with implications throughout TCS. It is the highest-priority landmark in the complexity category.

progress.text: The Cook–Levin completeness theorem identifies Boolean satisfiability as NP-complete; Karp reductions connect it to many standard combinatorial problems. This establishes equivalent targets, rather than a separation.

Relativization and subsequent natural-proofs and algebrization barriers delimit broad approaches to separation. The natural-proofs obstruction to general circuit lower bounds is conditional on sufficiently strong pseudorandomness assumptions.

Williams proves that NEXP is not contained in polynomial-size nonuniform ACC circuits, using faster satisfiability algorithms to obtain lower bounds. ACC has constant depth and modular counting gates. Both the larger language class and the restricted circuit model matter; this does not prove P≠NP.
The Clay Mathematics Institute continues to list P versus NP among its unsolved Millennium Prize Problems.

context_blocks.text: A proposed assignment to a Boolean formula is easy to check: evaluate the formula under that assignment. Finding a satisfying assignment seems to demand a different kind of work because the assignment is missing. The question asks whether this difference can always be overcome with only polynomial computation. It is a worst-case statement about arbitrarily long inputs, so extensive experiments on current SAT solvers cannot settle it.

NP-completeness makes SAT a representative of an entire class. A polynomial-time reduction converts any NP verification problem into a satisfiability instance while preserving its answer. Consequently, one polynomial-time SAT algorithm would supply polynomial-time decision procedures for all NP languages. It would also allow witnesses to be recovered by asking a sequence of decision questions about their successive bits.

The two possible answers have different practical limits. P=NP would not by itself give a small polynomial exponent or an implementation useful at realistic sizes. P≠NP would establish some worst-case superpolynomial difficulty, but would not imply an exponential lower bound, hardness of typical instances, or the existence of secure cryptography. Those are stronger or differently quantified claims.

Many successful lower bounds impose restrictions on the competing computations, such as bounded circuit depth or the absence of negation. Removing those restrictions is a central obstacle. Conversely, theorems about relativization, natural proofs, and algebrization identify limitations of particular proof methods. These results do not decide P versus NP.

cards.title: Does P equal PSPACE?
cards.formal: Does every language decidable by a deterministic Turing machine using polynomial working space have a deterministic polynomial-time decision algorithm? Equivalently, do there exist a machine A and constants C,k such that A decides truth of every closed quantified Boolean formula of encoded length n in at most $C(n+1)^k$ steps?
cards.definitions: P consists of languages decided by one deterministic multitape Turing machine with a fixed polynomial worst-case time bound. PSPACE consists of languages decided by one deterministic Turing machine which halts on every input and visits at most C(n+1)^k work-tape cells, for some constants C,k, on inputs of length n. The input is read-only and is not charged as work space; a fixed finite tape alphabet is used. PSPACE imposes no polynomial time bound. A closed quantified Boolean formula has the form Q₁x₁⋯Qₘxₘ φ(x₁,…,xₘ), where each Qᵢ is ∃ or ∀, quantified variables are distinct, and φ is an explicitly encoded Boolean formula using AND, OR, and NOT, with no free variables. Every quantifier ranges over {0,1}. The number of quantifiers and their alternations may grow with n; the input is not restricted to a fixed number of blocks. Use any standard explicit binary encoding, reject malformed inputs, and count its full bit length n. Truth means the usual nested Boolean quantifier semantics. This language, TQBF, is PSPACE-complete under polynomial-time many-one reductions. No oracle, advice, randomization, or promise is allowed. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove P=PSPACE or P≠PSPACE. The first outcome asserts a deterministic polynomial-time decision procedure for every polynomial-space language; the second asserts a polynomial-space language with no deterministic polynomial-time decision procedure.
cards.why: This asks whether reusing a feasible amount of memory can provide computational power beyond feasible running time. It is a central unresolved separation even when the allowed language class is enlarged from NP to all of PSPACE, and it organizes the complexity of quantified reasoning, games, and verification.

importance.reason: A defining question about the relationship between the two basic computational resources, time and working memory. It is a top-priority foundational class separation.

progress.text: Quantified Boolean formulas provide a PSPACE-complete target. Chandra, Kozen, and Stockmeyer characterize deterministic polynomial space as alternating polynomial time.
Shamir proves IP=PSPACE, giving an interactive-proof characterization without resolving deterministic polynomial-time computation.
Williams proves the O(sqrt(t log t)) space simulation of time-t multitape machines, improving the decades-old O(t/log t) bound. It yields fixed-exponent time lower bounds for linear-space languages.
Williams’ MFCS invited survey discusses this simulation and further space-complexity developments. It supplies no separation of the unions P and PSPACE.

cards.status_note: Primary-source review and a search for subsequent results on 11 September 2026 found no resolution. Williams’ 2025 simulation and August 2026 MFCS survey concern time-space bounds; neither states an equality or separation of P and PSPACE.

context_blocks.text: Time measures the total number of computation steps; space measures how much information the machine retains at once. Space can be reused. For example, a machine can evaluate a quantified formula by recursively exploring possible choices and reusing its work area when it returns from a branch. The resulting computation may inspect exponentially many choices while keeping only a polynomial amount of information.

Alternating quantifiers express a finite game of choices: existential moves try to make the final formula true, and universal moves challenge them. For example, ∀x∃y (y=x) is true because y may depend on x, whereas ∃y∀x (y=x) is false. Both variables range over {0,1}. A winning strategy for a longer formula can have exponentially many branches even though each play has polynomial length. Polynomial-time alternation captures exactly PSPACE.

The inclusion P⊆PSPACE is immediate, but its strictness is unknown. P≠NP would imply P≠PSPACE because NP⊆PSPACE. A proof of P=NP, however, would collapse the polynomial hierarchy without automatically giving a polynomial-time algorithm for formulas with an unbounded number of quantifier alternations. This separates the present question from merely solving satisfiability.

The theorem IP=PSPACE characterizes the same space class through interaction: a polynomial-time randomized verifier can check claims from an unbounded prover using a bounded-error interactive protocol. The prover’s assistance is a resource. Removing the prover to obtain an ordinary deterministic polynomial-time algorithm is not a consequence of that characterization.

Williams’ time-to-space simulation gives a concrete advance in the comparison of these resources. For time bounds t(n)≥n, a time-t multitape computation can be simulated in O(√(t log t)) working space. A consequence is that some linear-space languages require time n^(2−ε) for every ε>0. The lower-bound exponent remains bounded: the result does not exhibit a polynomial-space language outside every polynomial time bound.

cards.title: Can every polynomial-time decision problem be solved in logarithmic space?
cards.formal: Is L=P? Equivalently, does the Circuit Value Problem have a deterministic algorithm that always halts and uses O(log(n+2)) bits of working memory on an input of binary encoding length n?
cards.definitions: L consists of total decision languages recognized by a fixed deterministic Turing machine with a read-only input tape and a fixed finite number of initially blank read/write work tapes over fixed finite alphabets. The input can be revisited freely; all visited work-tape cells count toward space, but the read-only input itself does not. For each language there must be a constant C such that every n-bit input uses at most C log₂(n+2) work bits and the machine halts. Acceptance is a final state, not a long output tape usable as memory. A halting machine in this model has only polynomially many possible configurations on a fixed input, so its time is automatically polynomial. P is the class of languages decided by uniform deterministic Turing machines in O((n+2)ᶜ) time for some fixed c. Circuit Value receives an explicit topologically ordered DAG of AND, OR, and NOT gates, Boolean input values, and one designated output gate, and asks whether its value is 1. The entire gate and input encoding counts toward n; malformed encodings are rejected. There are no random bits, oracle, advice, auxiliary catalytic tape, or restrictions on circuit depth. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove L=P or L≠P in the read-only-input model defined here. Equality means that every polynomial-time decision language admits a halting deterministic logarithmic-space machine; inequality means that at least one such language admits none.
cards.why: This is a fundamental question about how much memory efficient computation needs. It asks whether all of polynomial-time reasoning can be reorganized around logarithmic working storage, and connects circuit evaluation, graph reachability, recomputation, and the structure of space-bounded complexity.

importance.reason: A canonical unresolved boundary between time and memory, asking whether any polynomial-time decision problem intrinsically needs more than logarithmic workspace.

progress.text: Ladner’s logspace completeness theorem for Circuit Value supplies a universal P-complete problem for the question.
Reingold proves undirected connectivity is in L. This resolves a major special case of low-memory graph computation without handling all directed reachability or P-complete problems.
Williams obtains the O(√(t log t)) deterministic space simulation and square-root-type circuit-evaluation space bounds. These remain far above logarithmic space in the general case.
Blais’s logarithmic-space notes explicitly state that strictness between these basic classes remains unknown and fix the read-only-input convention needed to formulate the question.

cards.status_note: The Winter 2026 logarithmic-space notes explicitly leave the basic containments unresolved. A primary-source and later-result search on 11 September 2026 found no resolution of L versus P. The square-root-space simulation remains above logarithmic space for general polynomial-time computations.

context_blocks.text: A polynomial-time algorithm may keep a large table of intermediate results. A logarithmic-space algorithm has room for a fixed number of indices into its input: one position among n symbols needs about log₂ n bits. It can revisit the read-only input and recompute intermediate values, but it cannot retain an arbitrary n-bit table. The question asks whether this severe memory restriction still permits every polynomial-time decision task.

Circuit Value is a concrete complete problem for P under logarithmic-space reductions. Evaluating gates in topological order uses polynomial time and readily stores their values. An alternative may recompute gate values, but shared dependencies make naive recursive expansion expensive in both stack space and repeated work. Completeness says that a logarithmic-space solution to this one task would extend to all polynomial-time decision problems.

Logarithmic workspace already forces polynomial time for a halting deterministic machine: revisiting the same full configuration would produce an infinite loop. Consequently the question does not grant unlimited superpolynomial recomputation while retaining membership in L. The polynomial time exponent can nevertheless depend on the machine, so lower bounds for one fixed time budget are insufficient.

L⊆NL⊆P, where NL allows nondeterministic logarithmic-space computation. A proof that L≠NL would therefore separate L from P, but L=NL would not itself settle L=P. Reingold resolves undirected reachability in logarithmic space; directed reachability remains a separate NL-complete target, and Circuit Value represents the potentially larger class P.

Recent time-to-space simulation substantially improves general upper bounds without reaching logarithmic space. Williams simulates time t in O(√(t log t)) space and obtains an analogous square-root-type space bound for Boolean circuit evaluation. With polynomial t, the guarantee is still polynomial space. This advances the tradeoff while leaving the much smaller O(log n) target unresolved.

cards.title: Is nonuniform TC⁰ strictly smaller than nonuniform NC¹?
cards.formal: Is TC⁰⊊NC¹ for the nonuniform circuit classes defined below? Equivalently, does there exist a Boolean function family f=(f_n:{0,1}^n→{0,1}) in NC¹ such that for every fixed depth d≥1, exponent k≥1, and constant M≥1, there is an n for which every depth-at-most-d majority circuit computing f_n exactly has size greater than M(n+1)^k?
cards.definitions: A circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with input nodes x_1,…,x_n, optional constants 0,1, and one output. Depth is the maximum number of gates on an input-to-output path. Size is the number of gates plus the number of wires; if an input is repeated at a gate, each occurrence counts as a wire. A majority circuit has AND and OR gates of arbitrary positive fan-in, NOT gates of fan-in one, and MAJ gates of arbitrary positive fan-in m, with output 1 exactly when strictly more than m/2 inputs equal 1. TC⁰ consists of all families with such circuits of size M(n+1)^k and depth at most d for every n, for some constants M,k,d depending on the family. NC¹ consists of families with circuits over AND, OR, NOT, with fan-in at most two (one for NOT), size M(n+1)^k, and depth at most b log_2(n+1), for fixed M,k,b. Circuits may share intermediate gates. Both classes are nonuniform: an arbitrary separate circuit may be chosen for each input length, without any requirement to compute its description. The output must be correct on every input; no randomness, approximation, promise, or distributional error is allowed.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove TC⁰⊊NC¹ or TC⁰=NC¹ for the nonuniform families defined here. Strictness requires a single NC¹ family with no polynomial-size constant-depth majority-circuit family; equality requires that every NC¹ family admit such a family.
cards.why: One of the central small-circuit questions: whether a constant number of counting layers can perform every logarithmic-depth Boolean computation. A resolution would clarify the power of threshold circuits, finite-group computation, and the role of sequential dependence in parallel computation.

importance.reason: A flagship unresolved containment between basic circuit classes, with explicit complete problems and connections to arithmetic, algebraic automata theory, and lower-bound amplification.

cards.status_note: The source and subsequent-work checks on 11 September 2026 found no equality or separation of these nonuniform classes. The 2026 depth-two result concerns a function in E^NP and polynomial circuit size; the typed-monoid result concerns uniform classes. context_blocks.text: The two models trade different resources. A majority gate can aggregate arbitrarily many bits in one step, whereas a binary Boolean gate sees only two. NC¹ permits logarithmically many layers of binary computation. A majority of polynomially many bits can itself be computed by a polynomial-size logarithmic-depth Boolean circuit, so a constant number of majority layers gives TC⁰⊆NC¹. The open issue is whether counting in a fixed number of layers can also replace every logarithmic-depth computation.

Arithmetic tasks are an instructive warning against judging depth from familiar sequential algorithms. Hesse, Allender, and Barrington prove that integer division and iterated multiplication have even DLOGTIME-uniform TC⁰ circuits. A binary long-division procedure takes many dependent steps, but that procedure does not establish a lower bound on all circuits for division. These arithmetic problems therefore cannot serve as the missing separation.

There are concrete complete problems on the NC¹ side. Evaluating a Boolean formula, and evaluating a product of elements of the fixed permutation group S_5, capture NC¹ under very simple reductions. S_5 consists of the 120 permutations of five objects, with permutation composition as its operation. Chen and Tell study these complete problems in their lower-bound amplification results.

Chen and Tell prove a conditional amplification theorem connecting certain mildly superlinear wire lower bounds to a separation of the full classes. Its hypothesis imposes a specific quantitative dependence on circuit depth. Thus a lower bound proved only at one fixed depth, or with an insufficient exponent at growing constant depths, is a different statement from their theorem’s hypothesis and from the conjecture here.

Dawar and Evans give an algebraic characterization of uniform NC¹ using typed monoids in FSTTCS 2025, extending earlier work on uniform TC⁰. Typed monoids allow infinite algebraic structures while restricting recognition through finitely many types. This supplies another mathematical language in which to compare the classes. Their theorem is a characterization, not a separation, and its uniform scope must be kept distinct from this card’s formulation.

Chen, Tal, and Wang’s 2026 preprint proves n^(2.5−ε) gate lower bounds for depth-two linear-threshold circuits computing a function in E^NP. Here E^NP allows deterministic time 2^{O(n)} with an NP oracle. A linear-threshold gate tests a weighted sum, while this card fixes unweighted majority gates. More decisively, the result treats one depth, a polynomial size bound, and a hard function not shown to belong to NC¹. The target here concerns an NC¹ family against every fixed depth and every polynomial size bound.

cards.title: The Berman–Hartmanis isomorphism conjecture
cards.formal: For every pair of languages A,B⊆{0,1}* that are NP-complete under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions, does there exist a bijection f:{0,1}*→{0,1}* such that f and f⁻¹ are computable in deterministic polynomial time and, for every string x, x∈A if and only if f(x)∈B?
cards.definitions: A language is a set of finite binary strings, including a specified membership decision for every string; malformed encodings are therefore part of the language convention. NP consists of languages L for which x∈L exactly when some witness of length polynomial in |x| is accepted by a deterministic polynomial-time verifier. A many-one reduction from L to A is a total deterministic polynomial-time function g with x∈L iff g(x)∈A. A is NP-complete if A∈NP and every L∈NP reduces to A in this sense. The desired f is a permutation of all finite binary strings, taking members to members and nonmembers to nonmembers. Its running time is polynomial in its input length, and its inverse has a polynomial bound in the inverse input length. The algorithms and polynomial bounds may depend on the fixed pair A,B, but not on the particular input string. No advice, oracle, randomness or length-preservation requirement is allowed. This is the unconditional conjecture; P≠NP is not an assumption.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that every pair of polynomial-time many-one NP-complete languages is polynomial-time isomorphic, or prove that some pair has no bijection with both directions computable in polynomial time. The statement is unconditional: P≠NP is not an added hypothesis.
cards.why: A fundamental test of what NP-completeness means beyond mutual reducibility: does it impose one efficiently reversible structure on all complete decision problems? It links padding, cryptographic inversion, uniformity and the limitations of relativizing methods.

importance.reason: A defining structural-complexity conjecture about the entire NP-complete degree, stronger than P≠NP and supported by substantial restricted-model theorems and oracle barriers.

cards.status_note: The 2022 primary-author problem column states that the full conjecture is open. A later-source search on 11 September 2026 located the 2025 recovery-reduction preprint, which still uses it as a conjectural hypothesis, and found no resolution. Its truth-table recovery consequence is conditional.

context_blocks.text: NP-completeness normally identifies problems by their ability to simulate one another. A reduction may map many distinct instances to the same target instance, leave most target strings unused, and erase information that would be needed to reconstruct its input. The isomorphism conjecture asks for a much more rigid relationship: an efficiently reversible relabelling of the entire instance space. Its claim includes every artificially constructed NP-complete language, not only the familiar examples used in applications.

The distinction is visible in the quantifiers. Choosing one clever reduction from SAT to another problem and discovering that it is many-to-one says nothing decisive about whether some other reduction could be a bijection. Conversely, an abstract bijection between two infinite sets is not enough: it might take exponential time to compute or invert. The conjecture requires both computations to be efficient, while allowing a polynomial change in the lengths of instances.

Padding supplies the strongest classical evidence. A paddable language has an efficient injective way to append arbitrary recoverable auxiliary information without changing the answer. For satisfiability, fresh variables and a suitably delimited formula encoding can carry extra bits while preserving whether the original formula has a satisfying assignment. Berman and Hartmanis used padding to show that the standard NP-complete examples known at the time are polynomial-time isomorphic. The unresolved step is proving that arbitrary complete languages possess enough recoverable structure.

The conjecture implies P≠NP, but its negation does not automatically imply P≠NP. To see the first point, suppose P=NP. Then the nontrivial languages {0} and 0{0,1}* would both be NP-complete: decide the source problem and output a fixed yes string or no string. Yet a bijection preserving membership cannot map a one-element yes-set onto an infinite yes-set. This elementary obstruction also explains why the unconditional conjecture must be distinguished from its version conditional on P≠NP.

The connection with one-way functions depends on more than difficulty inverting a particular reduction. An NP-complete language can have many reductions from SAT, and invertibility of one map does not determine whether a different efficient isomorphism exists. The Hartmanis problem column distinguishes one-way functions, scrambling functions and easy-cylinder hypotheses; these additional structural conditions are not interchangeable.

Oracle results go in both directions. Kurtz, Mahaney and Royer construct random-oracle counterexamples using scrambling functions. Fenner, Fortnow and Kurtz construct a different oracle setting in which the conjecture holds. These are results about relativized computation, where the algorithms can query a supplied set. They do not settle the ordinary conjecture, but they show that an argument valid uniformly across all such oracle settings cannot choose its truth value.

Restricting the completeness reductions can produce affirmative theorems. Agrawal, Allender and Rudich prove an isomorphism theorem for sets complete under nonuniform AC⁰ reductions, with nonuniform depth-three AC⁰ circuits computing the isomorphisms and their inverses. Here AC⁰ means polynomial-size Boolean circuits of constant depth with unbounded-fan-in AND and OR gates and negations. Both the restricted completeness hypothesis and the availability of nonuniform circuits matter; dropping them would be a stronger statement.

Agrawal and Watanabe further relate structural assumptions about one-way functions to nonuniform isomorphisms. Under their stated hypotheses they obtain P/poly isomorphisms, permitting polynomial advice that depends on input length. This does not provide the uniform polynomial-time algorithms demanded here. The broad question remains whether NP-completeness itself forces reversible structure, or whether some complete languages have an intrinsically different organization of their yes and no instances.

Nareddy and Mishra’s 2025 preprint studies recovery of Boolean truth tables after random corruptions. It states the Berman–Hartmanis conjecture explicitly and derives, conditionally on it, recovery guarantees for every NP-complete language after partitioning instances by the length of their image under an isomorphism. This is an application of the conjecture as a hypothesis, not a proof of it.

cards.title: Is the polynomial hierarchy strict at every finite level?
cards.formal: Is $\Sigma_k^{\mathrm P}\subsetneq\Sigma_{k+1}^{\mathrm P}$ for every integer k≥0? Here Σ₀^P=P, and Σₖ^P for k≥1 consists of languages definable by k alternating blocks of polynomially bounded Boolean quantifiers, beginning existentially, followed by a deterministic polynomial-time predicate.
cards.definitions: A language L is in Σₖ^P if there exist a polynomial p and a deterministic polynomial-time predicate R such that, for every binary input x, $x\in L\iff\exists y_1\in\{0,1\}^{p(|x|)}\ \forall y_2\in\{0,1\}^{p(|x|)}\cdots Q_k y_k\in\{0,1\}^{p(|x|)}:R(x,y_1,\ldots,y_k)=1$, where Qₖ is existential for odd k and universal for even k. Each yᵢ is an entire string, so k counts quantifier blocks, not individual bits. The predicate is polynomial-time in the combined input length. k is fixed for a class membership claim and cannot grow with |x|; p and R may depend on k and L. Let Πₖ^P consist of complements of Σₖ^P languages, and let PH=⋃ₖ≥0Σₖ^P. In particular Σ₁^P=NP and Π₁^P=coNP. These are uniform, unrelativized classes of total decision languages. Strictness at level k means that some language in Σₖ₊₁^P is absent from Σₖ^P. The separating language may depend on k. All classes use ordinary Turing computation with no advice or external oracle.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove strict containment at every finite level, or prove equality Σₖ^P=Σₖ₊₁^P for some fixed k. Equality at any adjacent pair collapses all higher levels to that level, so a collapse at even one finite level answers no. Proving strictness for finitely many levels or relative to an oracle does not answer yes.
cards.why: This is the organizing conjecture behind the computational cost of alternating existential and universal reasoning. It strengthens the basic P-versus-NP distinction across all fixed quantifier depths and underlies many conditional lower bounds in complexity, verification, and graph problems with nested solution requirements.

importance.reason: A foundational conjecture asserting that every further alternation increases computational power. It governs a large family of complexity classifications and has major circuit-lower-bound consequences.

progress.text: Meyer and Stockmeyer introduce the hierarchy; Stockmeyer develops its structural properties and complete problems.
Oracle constructions show that all levels can be distinct in a relativized world. Karp–Lipton-type theorems connect small circuits for NP to a collapse of the unrelativized hierarchy.
Rossman, Servedio, and Tan establish infinitude relative to a random oracle with probability one. Their proof comes from an average-case lower bound separating consecutive constant circuit depths.

Hirsch and Volkovich study the Linear Ordering Principle, related small complexity classes, and Karp–Lipton-style conditional collapses. These are implications under hypotheses, not an unconditional collapse or separation of PH.

cards.status_note: Explicitly conjectured in the primary-source survey and Wigderson’s hierarchy discussion. Research through 10 September 2026 yielded no unrelativized proof of infinitude or finite collapse. Random-oracle infinitude and conditional Karp–Lipton collapses are not recorded as resolutions.

context_blocks.text: NP captures a single existential choice of a certificate. A second block permits a statement of the form “there is a candidate that survives every challenge”; a third permits a response to every challenge. Polynomially many bits may be chosen at each stage. The question is whether every additional fixed stage enables some decision problem that cannot be expressed with fewer stages and a polynomial-time final check.

The hierarchy is monotone because unused quantifier blocks can be inserted. Its collapse property is much stronger: if two neighboring levels coincide, all later alternations can be eliminated down to that level. Consequently the target is a single binary statement, not a request to classify an unspecified collection of logical formulas.

Strictness includes P≠NP at its first step, but P≠NP alone would leave the possibility of a later collapse. The conjecture also implies that PH is a proper subclass of PSPACE: if TQBF belonged to PH, it would belong to one fixed level, and PSPACE-completeness would force the whole hierarchy into that level. Allowing arbitrarily many quantifier alternations in the input is therefore a separate issue from allowing any fixed number.

The Karp–Lipton implication connects this conjecture to circuit complexity. Polynomial-size circuits for NP would collapse PH, so an infinite hierarchy would imply an NP language without polynomial-size circuits. Conditional collapse arguments are useful precisely because they can turn an assumption about nonuniform circuits into a conclusion about uniform classes; the conditional conclusion is not an established collapse.

Rossman, Servedio, and Tan prove that PH is infinite relative to a random oracle with probability one, through an average-case circuit-depth hierarchy theorem. Random membership bits supplied by an oracle are an extra computational resource. The result shows that strictness is compatible with, and typical in, that oracle model; it leaves the unrelativized hierarchy open.

cards.context:
NP captures a single existential choice of a certificate. A second block permits a statement of the form “there is a candidate that survives every challenge”; a third permits a response to every challenge. Polynomially many bits may be chosen at each stage. The question is whether every additional fixed stage enables some decision problem that cannot be expressed with fewer stages and a polynomial-time final check.

The hierarchy is monotone because unused quantifier blocks can be inserted. Its collapse property is much stronger: if two neighboring levels coincide, all later alternations can be eliminated down to that level. Consequently the target is a single binary statement, not a request to classify an unspecified collection of logical formulas.

Strictness includes P≠NP at its first step, but P≠NP alone would leave the possibility of a later collapse. The conjecture also implies that PH is a proper subclass of PSPACE: if TQBF belonged to PH, it would belong to one fixed level, and PSPACE-completeness would force the whole hierarchy into that level. Allowing arbitrarily many quantifier alternations in the input is therefore a separate issue from allowing any fixed number.

The Karp–Lipton implication connects this conjecture to circuit complexity. Polynomial-size circuits for NP would collapse PH, so an infinite hierarchy would imply an NP language without polynomial-size circuits. Conditional collapse arguments are useful precisely because they can turn an assumption about nonuniform circuits into a conclusion about uniform classes; the conditional conclusion is not an established collapse.

Rossman, Servedio, and Tan prove that PH is infinite relative to a random oracle with probability one, through an average-case circuit-depth hierarchy theorem. Random membership bits supplied by an oracle are an extra computational resource. The result shows that strictness is compatible with, and typical in, that oracle model; it leaves the unrelativized hierarchy open.

cards.title: Does NP contain a language without polynomial-size Boolean circuits?
cards.formal: Is $\mathrm{NP}\nsubseteq\mathrm{P/poly}$? Precisely, does there exist one language L∈NP such that, for every integer k≥1, real C>0, and integer N≥1, some n≥N satisfies $\operatorname{CC}(L_n)>C(n+1)^k$, where Lₙ is the characteristic function of L on n-bit inputs and CC is minimum Boolean circuit size?
cards.definitions: A Boolean circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with n input bits, binary AND and OR gates, unary NOT gates, constants 0 and 1, and one output bit. There are no depth or fan-out restrictions; a gate output may be reused arbitrarily. Size counts AND, OR, and NOT gates. Lₙ must be computed exactly on every n-bit string. A family {Cₙ} is nonuniform: no algorithm is required to construct Cₙ from n, and the circuit may depend arbitrarily on the input length, but not on the particular input of that length. P/poly consists of languages having circuits of size at most C(n+1)^k for some fixed constants C,k and every n. NP consists of languages L with a deterministic polynomial-time verifier V and polynomial p such that x∈L iff some y of length at most p(|x|) satisfies V(x,y)=1. The existentially chosen language L is the same for every exponent k. The lower bound need only hold at arbitrarily large lengths for each k; an eventual bound at every sufficiently large length would be stronger. Equivalently, ask whether the NP-complete language SAT has no polynomial-size circuit family under an ordinary explicit binary formula encoding.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove NP is not contained in P/poly, or prove the containment. A positive separation requires one NP language escaping every polynomial circuit-size bound. Proving that, for each exponent k, a possibly different language requires more than n^k gates does not suffice. Containment can be established by giving polynomial-size circuits for SAT at every input length; an efficient uniform circuit generator is not required.
cards.why: This is the main unrestricted Boolean circuit lower-bound conjecture for efficiently verifiable problems. Circuits remove issues of uniform program construction and expose a finite combinatorial object, making the problem a central route toward unconditional computational lower bounds. It connects complexity classes, pseudorandomness, learning, and limitations of proof techniques.

importance.reason: A foundational strengthening of P≠NP and the central target of general Boolean circuit lower bounds. Its consequences and methods reach across complexity, derandomization, learning, and cryptography.

progress.text: The Karp–Lipton theorem shows NP⊆P/poly implies PH=Σ₂^P. Wigderson’s Theorem 5.5 records this consequence next to Conjecture 5.4.
Razborov and Rudich prove the natural-proofs barrier under a strong cryptographic hardness assumption. This does not establish the desired circuit lower bound or its impossibility.
Williams proves that NEXP lacks polynomial-size nonuniform ACC circuits. ACC has fixed depth and allows modular counting gates; the result does not handle unrestricted circuits for an NP language.

Chen, Tal, and Wang obtain n^(2.5−ε) gate lower bounds against depth-two linear-threshold circuits for a function in E^NP, for every ε>0. Their introduction identifies NP⊄P/poly as the flagship open target.

context_blocks.text: A polynomial-time algorithm yields a polynomial-size circuit for each input length by unrolling its computation. The converse fails because a different circuit may be selected for every length without any effective way to generate those circuits. The conjecture asks whether NP retains hard problems even after granting this substantial extra freedom. A separation would imply P≠NP, while P≠NP alone does not establish the circuit claim.

Counting arguments show that most truth tables need exponentially many gates. They do not produce the required language in NP: an arbitrary sequence of hard truth tables need not have efficiently verifiable membership certificates. This is the central explicitness difficulty. It is also why enumerating hard functions at a few fixed lengths cannot satisfy the quantified statement on this card.

The Karp–Lipton theorem gives a consequence of the opposite outcome: if NP has polynomial-size circuits, the polynomial hierarchy collapses to its second level. This is evidence linking nonuniform algorithms to uniform complexity, but it is not a contradiction because the hierarchy is not known to be infinite.

The natural-proofs theorem identifies a conditional obstacle to a broad family of circuit lower-bound techniques. Under sufficiently strong pseudorandom-function assumptions, a property of truth tables that is both efficiently recognizable and sufficiently common cannot distinguish all hard functions from polynomial-size circuits in the required way. The theorem constrains a method, not every possible proof.

Williams’ separation for nondeterministic exponential time and constant-depth modular circuits demonstrates that faster satisfiability algorithms can yield nonuniform lower bounds. It leaves two restrictions relative to this target: the hard language may lie above NP, and the competing circuits have constant depth.

cards.title: Does every unsatisfiable Boolean formula have a short efficiently checkable certificate?
cards.formal: Do there exist a deterministic polynomial-time verifier V and a fixed polynomial p such that, for every Boolean CNF formula F, $F\text{ is unsatisfiable}\iff\exists\pi\in\{0,1\}^{\le p(|F|)}:V(F,\pi)=1$, with V never accepting a certificate for a satisfiable formula? Equivalently, is NP=coNP? The verification algorithm and polynomial are fixed for all formulas.
cards.definitions: A CNF formula is a conjunction of clauses, each a disjunction of literals x or NOT x. Variables take values in {0,1}; unsatisfiable means that no assignment makes all clauses true. The formula is encoded explicitly in binary, and |F| is its total bit length, including variable names and all literal occurrences. Empty clauses and an empty conjunction have their usual false and true meanings. V halts in time polynomial in |F|+|pi| on every pair of strings and rejects malformed formula encodings. Certificates may be arbitrary binary strings; they are not restricted to any particular inference calculus. NP is the class of languages with polynomial-length certificates checked in deterministic polynomial time. coNP consists of complements of NP languages. No randomization, oracle, advice, or interaction with a prover is allowed.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct a sound verifier and one polynomial length bound covering every unsatisfiable formula, or prove that no such verifier and bound exist. Equivalently, prove NP=coNP or NP≠coNP. A lower bound for a particular proof system is insufficient for separation, and an efficient algorithm for finding certificates is not required for equality.
cards.why: This asks whether every nonexistence claim with an efficiently verifiable positive counterpart also has concise evidence. It is a central bridge between computational complexity, the length of mathematical proofs, and the limits of automated reasoning.

importance.reason: A fundamental certificate-complexity question that implies P≠NP in the separation direction and motivates the entire general proof-complexity lower-bound program.

progress.text: Cook and Reckhow establish the equivalence between NP=coNP and the existence of a polynomially bounded propositional proof system. This turns a complexity-class question into a precise proof-length target.

Haken proves an exponential resolution lower bound for pigeonhole formulas; Buss gives polynomial-size Frege proofs of the pigeonhole principle. These results demonstrate why lower bounds must account for the chosen proof system.

The ICTS program Circuits, Communication, and Proofs continues to present separation of NP from coNP as the goal of the Cook–Reckhow program. It describes current connections with circuit lower bounds and communication complexity; it announces no resolution of this question.

cards.status_note: The unrestricted certificate question remains a research target in the August 2026 primary workshop description. Searches through 10 September 2026 did not locate a resolution. Lower bounds for individual proof systems do not establish the universal separation.

context_blocks.text: A satisfiable formula has a direct certificate: a satisfying assignment. For an unsatisfiable formula, one must explain why every possible assignment fails. Listing all assignments and a violated clause for each gives a checkable certificate, but its length can be exponential. The question asks whether some fixed verification scheme can always compress this explanation to polynomial length.

Simple contradictions already have short certificates. For instance, the conjunction of the one-literal clauses x and NOT x has no satisfying assignment, which can be checked immediately. The difficulty is a universal guarantee over all formulas, including large contradictions whose structure does not reveal such a local conflict. The verifier must be sound even on adversarially chosen purported proofs.

Cook and Reckhow formalized proof systems by requiring efficient verification, soundness, and completeness. Their connection with complexity theory says that a polynomially bounded propositional proof system exists exactly when NP=coNP. The theorem permits any efficiently checked proof format. Restricting the allowed inference rules changes the problem to one about the power of that particular system.

This also distinguishes the question from P versus NP. If NP differs from coNP, then P differs from NP because deterministic polynomial time is closed under complement. The converse implication is not known. Equal certificate classes would still leave open whether those certificates can be found efficiently. Thus the target is symmetry between short evidence for yes and no answers, rather than an algorithm for deciding every NP problem.

Restricted lower bounds are nevertheless instructive. The pigeonhole principle has exponentially long resolution refutations in its usual encoding, while stronger Frege reasoning has polynomial-size proofs of the same principle. A formula family hard for one proof language therefore need not be hard for another.

cards.title: An explicit function with no linear-size Boolean circuits
cards.formal: Does there exist a total function F:{0,1}*→{0,1}*, computable by one deterministic polynomial-time algorithm and satisfying |F(x)|=|x|, such that its unrestricted Boolean circuit complexity is not O(n)? Explicitly, for every C>0 and N≥1, must some n≥N satisfy CC(Fₙ)>Cn?
cards.definitions: Fₙ is the restriction of F to n-bit inputs, with n output bits. CC(Fₙ) is the least number of gates in a directed acyclic Boolean circuit computing all these outputs exactly on every input. Each gate may compute any Boolean function of at most two input bits: the full B₂ basis, including AND, OR, XOR and negation. Input nodes, constants 0 and 1, and designated output wires are free; gates have unrestricted fan-out and there is no depth bound. Gates may be shared among outputs. The family of competing circuits is nonuniform: the circuit at one input length need have no effective relationship to circuits at other lengths. In contrast, explicitness of F means a single deterministic Turing machine outputs F(x) in at most p(|x|) steps for one fixed polynomial p, with no advice. The empty input has empty output. This card fixes a polynomial-time interpretation of the source’s broader word “explicit” and preserves its allowance of n output bits. Changing between B₂ and the usual bounded-fan-in AND/OR/NOT basis changes size by at most a constant factor.
cards.answer_criterion: Exhibit one such polynomial-time function and prove that CC(Fₙ)/n is unbounded along arbitrarily large input lengths, or prove that every polynomial-time length-preserving function has O(n)-size nonuniform circuits, with the hidden constant allowed to depend on the function. A fixed bound such as 10n is insufficient. The precise target is not O(n); it does not additionally require the ratio to tend to infinity at every sufficiently large length. A superlinear single-output example would also settle the question after padding the output with zeros.
cards.why: This asks for the first unbounded improvement over linear size for an efficiently computable unrestricted circuit task. It isolates a basic gap between knowing that hard functions abound and proving hardness for one explicitly computable function.

importance.reason: A fundamental lower-bound milestone for unrestricted computation, with connections to matrix complexity, proof techniques and the limitations of nonuniform algorithms.

cards.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. No superlinear unrestricted Boolean circuit lower bound for a polynomial-time length-preserving function was located. The question fixes the source’s explicitness convention; recent gate-simplification, covering and conditional natural-proofs results do not furnish such an example.

context_blocks.text: A circuit is a finite computation with a separate design for each input length. Intermediate results can be used many times, and different output bits can share the same work. This sharing is a central source of power: a lower bound for formulas, which cannot freely reuse intermediate results, need not hold for circuits. The target here leaves depth, fan-out and Boolean operations unrestricted apart from the two-input gate bound.

The explicitness requirement prevents a counting argument from solving the problem. There are vastly more Boolean functions than small circuits, so most functions require exponentially many gates. But describing one by its entire truth table takes exponential space, and selecting the first hard truth table by exhaustive search need not yield a polynomial-time function. We need an efficiently specified computation and a proof that every circuit for it exceeds every fixed linear bound.

Multi-output functions make the question especially concrete. A fixed, efficiently constructible binary matrix Aₙ defines Fₙ(x)=Aₙx over the two-element field. Its n outputs are parity sums of selected inputs. Computing every output separately can cost Θ(n²), yet a clever circuit may share partial sums across rows. Counting proves that some matrices need Ω(n²/log n) gates, but an explicit superlinear lower bound remains unknown even for this linear-algebra setting. A lower bound against XOR-only circuits would not automatically rule out smaller circuits that use nonlinear Boolean gates.

The polynomial-time convention also separates this question from NP versus P/poly. The desired F already has polynomial-size circuits because its algorithm can be simulated by circuits. Showing that it lacks linear-size circuits would separate two size scales within efficient nonuniform computation; it would not establish P≠NP. Conversely, proving superpolynomial circuit lower bounds for an NP language would address a stronger resource barrier but would not by itself make that language a polynomial-time example for this card.

For one output bit, Li and Yang obtain a 3.1n−o(n) lower bound over the full two-input basis. Their functions are affine dispersers, meaning that they remain nonconstant on every sufficiently large affine subspace of the Boolean cube, and suitable examples are polynomial-time computable. The proof refines gate elimination: restrict inputs so that gates disappear while retaining enough difficulty in the restricted function. Raising the constant was a substantial advance, but any fixed constant still falls short of the present target.

Cavalar and Oliveira’s 2025 work develops another route through the fusion method and combinatorial covering problems. It translates circuit lower-bound questions into suitably defined two-dimensional covers and proves strong bounds for random graphs. The remaining challenge is obtaining the necessary explicit cover lower bounds. A reformulation that can express the desired hardness is valuable, but does not yet provide the hard polynomial-time function.

Two 2026 developments clarify proof techniques. Carmosino, Dang and Jackman formalize convergent gate simplification in selected bases and construct efficient refuters for a classical parity lower bound. Their constructive proof notion concerns finding errors in proposed small circuits; it is additional structure on a lower-bound proof, rather than a superlinear size bound.

Raz’s July 2026 revision studies natural proofs specifically for linear maps represented by matrices. Under the stated cryptographic assumptions, pseudorandom matrices with unusually small circuits obstruct large, efficiently recognizable classes of hard matrices. Different constructions yield barriers above near-linear or linear size. These are conditional restrictions on a defined proof strategy, not an impossibility theorem for proving the desired lower bound by other means.

cards.title: Exponential circuit lower bounds for 3-SAT
cards.formal: For the explicitly encoded n-variable 3-SAT function SATₙ defined below, do there exist constants c>0 and n₀ such that CC(SATₙ)≥2^{cn} for every n≥n₀?
cards.definitions: For each n≥1, enumerate all clauses on variables x₁,…,xₙ containing zero, one, two or three distinct variables, each with either sign. A zero-literal clause is false. There are M(n)=Σⱼ₌₀³2ʲ·binom(n,j) such clauses, with binom(n,j)=0 when j>n. Order them first by length, then by the increasing tuple of variable indices, then by their sign bits, with 0 meaning positive and 1 negated. The input is b∈{0,1}^{M(n)}; its jth bit says whether clause j is included. Let Φ_b be the conjunction of included clauses, with an empty conjunction true, and define SATₙ(b)=1 iff some assignment in {0,1}ⁿ satisfies Φ_b. Thus every input is valid. CC counts gates in a directed acyclic circuit with one output, arbitrary Boolean gates of at most two inputs, constants 0 and 1, unrestricted depth and fan-out, and exact correctness on every b. Inputs, constants and output wires are not gates. Circuits may be chosen nonuniformly for each n. The exponential parameter is the number n of variables, while the circuit has M(n)=Θ(n³) input bits. This fixed encoding and the restriction to 3-CNF are an editorial variable-parameter formulation of the source’s exponential SAT circuit question.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the displayed eventual exponential lower bound for unrestricted circuits, or prove its negation: for every c>0 and N≥1 there exists n≥N with CC(SATₙ)<2^{cn}. A circuit family of size 2^{o(n)} at all lengths would suffice for the negative direction, but that is stronger than the exact negation. A lower bound only against bounded-depth, monotone, formula, uniform or proof-system models does not settle the question. A circuit upper bound 2^{αn} for one fixed α>0 remains compatible with a smaller positive lower-bound exponent.

cards.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. No unconditional exponential lower bound for unrestricted circuits deciding variable-parameterized 3-SAT was located. The card specifies an almost-everywhere bound, an explicit total clause-incidence encoding, and n as the variable count; it does not assert exponential hardness in the Θ(n³) encoding length.

context_blocks.text: SAT asks whether a collection of local constraints admits a simultaneous Boolean assignment. Here each selected clause prohibits one pattern on at most three variables. An assignment can be checked efficiently, but the conjecture says that deciding whether any assignment works requires exponentially many gates even when a different circuit may be designed separately for every n. It is a quantitative strengthening of the question whether NP has polynomial-size circuits.

Fixing the representation is essential. An n-variable 3-CNF can have Θ(n³) distinct clauses; writing a list of literals instead introduces binary variable names and a different bit length. These encodings are polynomially interconvertible, but a claim exponential in the literal number of input bits is not invariant under polynomial changes of encoding. This card therefore fixes both the representation and the variable parameter. The target is 2^{Ω(n)}, which is 2^{Ω(M^{1/3})} in the number M of circuit inputs.

There is a simple matching exponential scale for an upper bound. For each of the 2ⁿ assignments, form an AND requiring bⱼ=0 for every clause that assignment would falsify. OR these tests over all assignments. The resulting circuit decides SATₙ and has O(M(n)2ⁿ) gates. This is an explicit construction showing what exhaustive search means in the chosen nonuniform model. The conjecture allows substantial improvements in the exponential constant, while ruling out the absence of every positive eventual exponential lower bound.

The Exponential Time Hypothesis concerns uniform algorithms and the number of variables. Impagliazzo, Paturi and Zane’s sparsification lemma relates general fixed-width CNFs to disjunctions of sparse CNFs, with at most 2^{εn} branches for each fixed ε>0. This explains why variable and clause parameters are closely connected in exponential-time reductions. It does not automatically turn a uniform hypothesis into a lower bound against arbitrary circuits, and the precise almost-everywhere quantifiers on this card are part of its target.

Even much weaker general-circuit lower bounds remain elusive. Li and Yang prove 3.1N−o(N) gates for particular explicit single-output functions of N input bits. That is a theorem about carefully chosen affine dispersers, not an exponential lower bound for SAT. A counting argument can prove that most truth tables are exponentially hard, but it cannot identify SAT among those hard functions.

There has been important progress by linking faster satisfiability algorithms to lower bounds for other circuit classes. Williams proves that nondeterministic exponential time has languages without polynomial-size ACC circuits. ACC restricts depth while allowing unbounded-fan-in Boolean and modular gates. The distinction matters in two places: the hard language need not be in NP, and the competing circuits are not unrestricted. This theorem demonstrates a powerful strategy without resolving this card.

Algorithmic progress continues within the exponential regime. Jiang and Cai’s July 2026 preprint refines the analysis of the existing PPSZ algorithm, reporting a randomized general-3-SAT running-time base of 1.307031578 and a slightly smaller base under uniqueness. The authors retain the same algorithm and unique-to-general lifting theorem; their improvement comes from a sharper combination of inequalities with rational certificates. These are upper bounds, with randomness and success guarantees, rather than lower bounds for exact circuits. A constant base above one remains compatible with the target.

A positive answer would rule out polynomial-size circuits for this NP decision problem and therefore imply P≠NP. A negative answer would not imply P=NP: circuits of size 2^{√n}, for example, would refute an eventual exponential bound while still being superpolynomial in the input size, and a nonuniform circuit family need not be constructible by one efficient algorithm.

cards.definitions: Languages are subsets of {0,1}*. PSPACE contains the languages decided by deterministic Turing machines that halt on every input of length n while using at most C(n+1)^a work-tape cells, for constants C,a depending on the machine. The read-only input tape is not charged, and there is no polynomial time limit. Set Σᵖ₀=P, the deterministic polynomial-time languages. For k≥1, a language L lies in Σᵖ_k if there are a deterministic polynomial-time predicate R and a polynomial p such that x∈L exactly when ∃y₁∀y₂∃y₃⋯Q_k y_k R(x,y₁,…,y_k)=1, where each y_i ranges over {0,1}^{p(|x|)} and Q_k is existential for odd k and universal for even k. Set PH=⋃_{k≥0}Σᵖ_k. The integer k is fixed for an entire language; it cannot grow with an input. Machines and predicates are uniform and have no advice or oracle. A fully quantified Boolean formula is an explicit Boolean formula using AND, OR and NOT, preceded by quantifiers binding every variable exactly once; variable names and the entire formula are binary encoded. Its truth uses the ordinary successive quantifier semantics over {0,1}. The language TQBF consists of its true well-formed encodings; malformed strings are rejected. The number of quantifier blocks in TQBF inputs is unrestricted.
cards.answer_criterion: A positive resolution proves PSPACE⊆PH; the reverse inclusion is already known. Equivalently it places TQBF in one fixed Σᵖ_k, which would put every PSPACE language in that same level by polynomial-time reductions. A negative resolution proves that some PSPACE language, equivalently TQBF, is outside every fixed level. A separation at one fixed level or an oracle-relative result alone does not answer the question.

context_blocks.title: What is being compared?
context_blocks.text: Polynomial space lets a computation reuse a bounded amount of memory for a potentially very long time. The polynomial hierarchy instead organizes efficiently checked conditions by a fixed number of alternating existential and universal choices. For example, an existential block asks for a witness, a following universal block checks every challenge to it, and another existential block can give a response depending on that challenge. The question asks whether any polynomial-space computation can be expressed with a fixed number of such blocks.

context_blocks.title: Order of choices matters
context_blocks.text: The formula ∀x∃y (x=y) is true: after the value of x is fixed, y can take the same value. The formula ∃y∀x (x=y) is false because one bit cannot equal both possible values of x. Thus replacing a sequence of dependent choices by one initial guess changes the problem. A formula with arbitrarily many alternating choices describes a potentially long strategy, even though testing its final Boolean condition is straightforward.

context_blocks.title: Why polynomial space is enough
context_blocks.text: A quantified formula can be evaluated by recursively trying the two values of each variable and combining the answers according to its quantifier. The procedure reuses memory after finishing each branch; it need not store the exponentially large game tree. TQBF is PSPACE-complete. The standard alternation theorem also identifies polynomial-time alternating computation, with no fixed bound on its number of alternations, with PSPACE. Neither characterization shows that an arbitrary number of rounds compresses to a constant.

context_blocks.title: A union of levels has a subtle consequence
context_blocks.text: The definition of PH initially lets different languages use different fixed numbers of blocks. Nevertheless, equality with PSPACE would imply one common finite level containing all of PSPACE: TQBF would belong to some Σᵖ_k and every PSPACE language reduces to it. Therefore PH=PSPACE would collapse the hierarchy. Conversely, proving that the hierarchy has infinitely many distinct levels would separate it from PSPACE. A separation PH≠PSPACE alone does not establish that every hierarchy level is distinct; this is why the card differs from the non-collapse question.

context_blocks.title: What later results do and do not show
context_blocks.text: Grüne, Johannes, Orlin and Wulf’s February 2026 results make many multilevel optimization problems complete for individual hierarchy levels or for PSPACE. Completeness locates the problems within the classes; it does not prove the classes different. Egidy’s 2026 oracle construction illustrates another distinction: relative to that oracle, PH collapses while remaining strictly below PSPACE. This is a statement in a model with an additional oracle, rather than a resolution for ordinary machines. Historical preprints claim equality or non-collapse, but the sources checked here do not establish either as a settled theorem. The review did not independently audit those claimed proofs.

cards.definitions: NEXP=⋃_{a≥1}NTIME(2^{n^a}): a language is accepted by one nondeterministic Turing machine whose every computation branch halts within exponential time 2^{n^a}, up to a constant factor, for some fixed a. An input is in the language exactly when at least one branch accepts. A circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with n Boolean inputs, constants 0 and 1 and one output. AND and OR may have any positive fan-in; NOT has one input. A majority gate on m inputs outputs 1 when at least ⌈m/2⌉ of them are 1, including a tie when m is even. Fan-out is unrestricted. Size is the number of operation gates plus wires. Repeated connections count individually, so their multiplicities cannot encode uncharged weights. Depth is the maximum number of operation gates on an input-to-output path. All circuits compute exactly on every input; no average-case correctness or randomness is allowed. TC⁰ consists of languages having one fixed depth bound and one polynomial size bound across all input lengths. The family may be nonuniform: no algorithm is required to construct its nth circuit. NEXP machines are uniform and have no oracle or advice. The formal quantifiers permit the lower bound to be witnessed at infinitely many input lengths, rather than requiring failure at every sufficiently large length.
cards.answer_criterion: A positive resolution proves that one language in NEXP has no polynomial-size constant-depth majority-circuit family, with depth and polynomial exponent both unrestricted constants. A negative resolution proves NEXP⊆TC⁰. A bound ruling out only n^k gates for one fixed k, or only one fixed circuit depth, does not by itself establish the displayed separation.

context_blocks.title: Small depth still permits powerful gates
context_blocks.text: A constant-depth circuit applies only a bounded number of layers, but a majority gate can inspect many inputs at once. For three bits it returns 1 on 110 and 111, while returning 0 on 100. Thus majority is not a bounded-fan-in local operation. TC⁰ permits many such gates in parallel and lets their outputs feed later layers. The depth bound stays fixed as input length grows, while the number of gates and wires may be any fixed polynomial.

context_blocks.title: Why parity is not enough
context_blocks.text: Parity is difficult for constant-depth circuits using only AND, OR and NOT, but it is easy for majority circuits. A threshold test for whether an n-bit input has at least t ones is implementable with a majority gate and suitable constants. Two adjacent threshold tests identify an exact number of ones, and taking an OR over odd counts gives parity with a polynomial number of gates in constant depth. This example shows why a lower bound for the weaker gate set cannot simply be reused after majority is added.

context_blocks.title: What NEXP contributes
context_blocks.text: The hard language need only have a nondeterministic exponential-time algorithm; it need not be in P or NP. That is a generous uniform computation budget, making the lack of a known separation striking. Nevertheless, counting the truth tables that have no small circuits does not automatically identify one language within this budget. The assertion requires one language that defeats every fixed polynomial size and every fixed depth, rather than a different unrestricted truth table for each desired bound.

context_blocks.title: The established nearby separation
context_blocks.text: Williams proves that NEXP does not have polynomial-size ACC circuits. ACC allows constant-depth Boolean circuits with gates testing the number of 1 inputs modulo a fixed integer. TC⁰ can implement these modular tests by combining threshold comparisons. It is therefore a more permissive class, and excluding ACC does not exclude TC⁰. The original 2011 reference supports this nearby theorem, not the stronger conclusion asked here.

context_blocks.title: The 2026 results retain important restrictions
context_blocks.text: Chen, Tal and Wang prove super-quadratic gate lower bounds for depth-two linear-threshold circuits, with a hard function in E^NP, exponential time with an NP oracle. Their n^(2.5−ε) bound is still a fixed polynomial and addresses depth two. A September preprint claims near-cubic wire bounds in that setting; its source also carries a critical comment, and it is not independently verified here. Wire counts and gate counts are different quantitative parameters. Ren and Williams obtain near-maximum general circuit bounds with a promise-Merlin–Arthur oracle and one bit of advice. None of these statements supplies the required ordinary NEXP language outside all of nonuniform TC⁰.

The hard language need only have a nondeterministic exponential-time algorithm; it need not be in P or NP. That is a generous uniform computation budget, making the lack of a known separation striking. Nevertheless, counting the truth tables that have no small circuits does not automatically identify one language within this budget. The assertion requires one language that defeats every fixed polynomial size and every fixed depth, rather than a different unrestricted truth table for each desired bound.

Williams proves that NEXP does not have polynomial-size ACC circuits. ACC allows constant-depth Boolean circuits with gates testing the number of 1 inputs modulo a fixed integer. TC⁰ can implement these modular tests by combining threshold comparisons. It is therefore a more permissive class, and excluding ACC does not exclude TC⁰. The original 2011 reference supports this nearby theorem, not the stronger conclusion asked here.

Chen, Tal and Wang prove super-quadratic gate lower bounds for depth-two linear-threshold circuits, with a hard function in E^NP, exponential time with an NP oracle. Their n^(2.5−ε) bound is still a fixed polynomial and addresses depth two. A September preprint claims near-cubic wire bounds in that setting; its source also carries a critical comment, and it is not independently verified here. Wire counts and gate counts are different quantitative parameters. Ren and Williams obtain near-maximum general circuit bounds with a promise-Merlin–Arthur oracle and one bit of advice. None of these statements supplies the required ordinary NEXP language outside all of nonuniform TC⁰.

cards.title: NL versus UL
cards.formal: Is NL=UL? Equivalently, is there a single nondeterministic Turing machine that decides directed s–t reachability using O(log N) work space and polynomial time, has exactly one accepting computation on every reachable instance, and has no accepting computation on every unreachable instance, where N is the explicit input length?
cards.definitions: An input consists of a finite directed graph with labelled vertices and explicitly listed edges, together with vertices s,t. Reachability asks whether a directed path from s to t exists; the length-zero path is allowed when s=t. A machine has a read-only two-way input tape, O(log(N+2)) read/write work-tape cells over a fixed finite alphabet, and a fixed finite nondeterministic transition relation. Every computation branch must halt within a polynomial in N. NL permits any positive number of accepting branches on yes inputs; UL permits exactly one. On no inputs both classes require zero accepting branches. A branch is a sequence of transition choices, not merely its endpoint or output. Rejecting branches need not be unique. Machines are uniform finite programs without advice, randomness, oracle access or additional catalytic storage. The equality asks whether every NL language has some equivalent UL machine; it does not require a computable compiler converting descriptions of arbitrary machines. Directed reachability is NL-complete under deterministic logspace reductions, so its UL membership suffices.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove a uniform O(log N)-space unambiguous algorithm for all directed reachability inputs, or prove that some NL language is not in UL. Any positive construction must remain unambiguous on every input without assuming that the supplied graph itself has a unique path. A polynomial-time algorithm using O((log N)^{3/2}) space, nonuniform advice, catalytic memory, or an unproved hardness hypothesis is progress rather than a solution.
cards.why: Determine whether the multiplicity of accepting computations adds power to logarithmic-space computation.

importance.reason: A basic class equality tying directed reachability, isolation, pseudorandomness and the structure of low-memory witnesses.

progress.text: Reinhardt–Allender show that min-isolation supports unambiguous reachability and prove the nonuniform equality NL/poly=UL/poly.

context_blocks.text: A nondeterministic reachability algorithm can guess the next vertex of a path, checking each edge as it goes. It needs only a current vertex and a step counter, so logarithmic memory suffices. The difficulty is that a graph can offer many successful sequences of guesses. An unambiguous algorithm must retain the ability to recognize a path while allowing only one successful computation.

This restriction is weaker than determinism. The machine may still branch many times and have many rejecting computations. On a reachable graph, only one complete branch may accept. Consequently, NL=UL would explain something about the source of nondeterministic power without establishing L=NL. A proof that NL≠UL would, however, also separate deterministic and nondeterministic logspace, since L⊆UL⊆NL.

One approach is to assign positive integer weights to edges so that every reachable ordered pair has a unique minimum-weight path. Reinhardt and Allender show how such min-isolating weights support an unambiguous reachability algorithm. If the weights are polynomially bounded and can be generated in deterministic logspace from the graph, the resulting memory use remains logarithmic. Randomly choosing suitable weights can give isolation, but does not provide a uniform deterministic construction.

Reinhardt and Allender also prove NL/poly=UL/poly. Here a polynomial-length advice string may depend on the input length and be shared by every input of that length, without any requirement that the string be generated efficiently. This is evidence that isolation is possible in a broad nonuniform sense. Removing the advice is essential to the ordinary NL=UL question.

The strongest checked unconditional general simulation uses more than logarithmic memory. Van Melkebeek and Prakriya give an unambiguous polynomial-time simulation of NL using O((log N)^{3/2}) space. Their work reduces the randomness and weight-description costs of isolation. The remaining square-root-of-logarithm factor is small numerically, but it is an unbounded factor in the resource defining the target class.

The inherited 2025 paper by Doron, Pyne, Tell and Williams develops new hardness-versus-randomness tools for isolation. Its main conditional unambiguity theorem concerns the linear-space analogue NSPACE[n]⊆USPACE[O(n)], under uniform circuit lower bounds with specified oracle access. The March 2026 Pyne–Tell survey gives a refined version. These assumptions are unproved, and the linear-space conclusion should not be reported as an unconditional logspace equality.

A February 2026 revision by Arvind, Chakraborty and Datta gives reachability algorithms in a catalytic model with UL oracle access. Catalytic computation permits extra memory initially containing arbitrary data, provided that the data are restored at the end. This is an interesting way to use storage, but it supplies resources absent from a plain UL machine. The headline about derandomizing isolation therefore does not resolve this card.

Hoza proves a new limitation in July 2026. Suppose one weight assignment must work for every layered graph of given width w and length ℓ, without examining which edges are actually present. Such an oblivious min-isolating assignment requires weights of magnitude 2^{Ω(log w·log ℓ)}, so polynomially bounded universal weights cannot solve the general problem by this route. This restriction does not cover assignments that depend on the actual graph or other unambiguous algorithms.

A solution would determine whether many successful paths are ever intrinsically necessary when computation has only logarithmic memory. It would also clarify how much information must be retained to select a unique witness from a large implicitly represented family. The challenge is not to name a canonical path mathematically, but to recognize one with the required uniqueness guarantee and very little working storage.
