context_blocks.text: A processor that sees far through a narrow part of a graph can inspect much less information than one that explores an entire ball of the same radius. The VOLUME model measures that inspected information. Its adaptive exploration captures a central feature of answering a query about a huge graph without first constructing an entire solution.

Correctness still couples the answers. Independently determining the color or matching status of one vertex must agree with the answers obtained for every other vertex. The algorithm cannot save previous answers and use their accumulated state as a growing global solution. This makes a low-volume construction substantially stronger than an arbitrary sequential greedy algorithm.

Rosenbaum and Suomela ask whether there is any deterministic volume complexity strictly between iterated logarithmic and linear, and conjecture there is none. Their model supplies exact graph size and polynomially bounded identifiers. Removing these conventions changes the indistinguishability arguments, so the card keeps them explicit.

The known small-complexity gaps leave the central interval unresolved. Randomized examples inhabit many intermediate scales, but an algorithm that follows a favorable random exploration does not automatically give a deterministic procedure that succeeds on every labeled graph. A deterministic counterexample to the proposed collapse would establish a new basic behavior.

July 2026 work constructs additional randomized polylogarithmic and polynomial volume complexities. Its introduction explicitly separates those results from the still-open deterministic question. The increased richness on the randomized side makes the contrast sharper while supplying no deterministic intermediate example.

cards.title: Quadratic expected message complexity for asynchronous crash consensus
cards.formal: Does a randomized asynchronous binary consensus protocol exist with expected O(n²) messages against a strong adaptive adversary, tolerating every t<n/2 crash failures?
cards.definitions: The n processes communicate by reliable asynchronous point-to-point messages and start with binary inputs. A crashed process takes no further steps. Every process that does not crash must eventually decide with probability one under fair scheduling; all decisions agree, and when all initial inputs are b every decision is b. A strong adversary observes past states, messages and revealed random outcomes and chooses subsequent process steps, message deliveries and crashes without seeing future coins. The bound counts all messages sent before protocol termination and must hold in expectation for every admissible adversary. It does not impose a bit bound on each message.

cards.title: Is two-dimensional single-grain sandpile prediction in NC?
cards.formal: Is the following decision problem in logspace-uniform NC? An input gives positive integers W,H, an explicit W-by-H array c with entries in {0,1,2,3}, and two cells p,q in that rectangle. Extend c by zero to the whole integer square lattice and add one grain at p. Answer YES exactly when q eventually topples under the four-neighbor parallel sandpile dynamics defined below. The input length N includes every array entry, not a compressed representation.
cards.definitions: The four neighbor displacements are E={(1,0),(-1,0),(0,1),(0,-1)}. Set c_0(v)=c(v)+1 if v=p, and c_0(v)=c(v) otherwise. At each integer time t>=0 every vertex v with c_t(v)>=4 topples once, losing four grains and sending one to each neighbor. Equivalently, c_{t+1}(v)=c_t(v)-4 I[c_t(v)>=4]+sum_{e in E} I[c_t(v-e)>=4], where I is the indicator. The question is whether c_t(q)>=4 for some t>=0. The array is row-major with binary dimensions and cell coordinates; invalid encodings are rejected. The zero extension is an infinite lattice, not a periodic boundary or a boundary that absorbs grains. A supplied rectangle may contain extra zero rows or columns to include p and q. Finite initial mass eventually stabilizes. NC here means that for some fixed integers a,k the decision has Boolean circuits of size O(N^a) and depth O((log N)^k), with fan-in at most two, whose description is generated from 1^N in O(log N) work space. There is no requested time t in the input and the answer is exact, without random error.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove or refute membership of the specified language in logspace-uniform NC. Any complexity assumption used in a negative result must be stated explicitly.
cards.why: A local deterministic physical process can have a long cascade after a single perturbation. This problem asks whether its outcome permits an efficient parallel computation, addressing the boundary between prediction and sequential evolution.

importance.reason: A canonical unresolved parallel-complexity question for a simple two-dimensional dynamical system, connecting computational prediction with statistical physics.

context_blocks.text: The initial configuration is stable, so all activity comes from the extra grain. The requested output is a single eventual-toppling bit; computing the entire final configuration or a toppling at a specified time are related but different tasks.
The classical dimension-dependent results provide efficient parallel prediction in one dimension and P-completeness in dimensions at least three. They leave the planar case as a distinct question.

Recent work still separates the standard four-neighbor lattice from weighted or nonuniform grids. NC membership and P-completeness are not an unconditional exclusive dichotomy: a P-completeness result rules out NC only under NC != P.

progress.text: Moore and Nilsson obtain NC^3 prediction in one dimension and P-completeness in dimensions at least three, leaving dimension two open.
Concha-Vega and Perrot explicitly define single-grain eventual prediction on the infinite lattice and retain the von Neumann-neighborhood problem as open.

cards.title: What is the deterministic round complexity of maximum independent set in the congested clique?
cards.formal: Determine, up to constant factors as n grows, the optimal worst-case number $T_{\mathrm{MIS}}(n)$ of synchronous communication rounds needed to output an exact maximum independent set of an arbitrary simple undirected n-vertex graph in the deterministic unicast congested-clique model below. For every vertex v, its processor must output one bit indicating whether v belongs to the chosen set. Local computation and local storage are unrestricted; only communication rounds are charged. Here maximum means largest cardinality, not merely inclusion-wise maximal.
cards.definitions: There is one processor for each vertex in {1,...,n}. Initially every processor knows n, all processor identifiers, its own identifier, and exactly the edges incident to its vertex. The communication network is the complete graph regardless of which input edges exist. In each synchronous round, each processor may send a different message of at most $b=\max\{1,\lceil\log_2 n\rceil\}$ bits to each other processor; messages sent in a round become available at its end. Protocols are deterministic and must terminate correctly on every input. An independent set S contains no edge with both endpoints in S; maximum requires |S| >= |I| for every independent set I of the input graph. Define T_MIS(n) as the minimum round bound among protocols for n processors in this model. No polynomial bound is imposed on the computation between rounds. The deterministic and fixed-bandwidth conventions specialize the broader seminar question.
cards.answer_criterion: Give asymptotically matching upper and lower bounds: identify an explicit asymptotic function f(n), construct protocols taking O(f(n)) rounds on every graph, and prove that every correct deterministic protocol requires Omega(f(n)) rounds on some n-vertex graph for all sufficiently large n. Bounds separated by a logarithmic factor or a result only for maximal independent sets do not settle this target.
cards.why: This places a canonical exact graph optimization problem in a model where computation is free but communication is limited. Understanding its round complexity would help distinguish the benefit of distributing information from merely gathering the graph at one processor.

importance.reason: A canonical exact optimization task testing the communication power of the congested clique. Its relevance extends beyond symmetry breaking, although the chosen deterministic model is one specific frontier.

progress.text: Drucker, Kuhn, and Oshman establish circuit-simulation connections and distinguish unicast from broadcast congested cliques. Their work supplies model context, not a tight bound for the present task.
Chechik explicitly asks for the communication rounds necessary to compute a maximum independent set in the congested clique.

cards.status_note: The 2025 seminar source asks for the optimal round complexity. Searches through 10 September 2026 did not locate matching bounds for this exact task. Randomness and bandwidth are fixed explicitly here; results for maximal MIS, broadcast cliques, or edge-restricted CONGEST do not resolve this formulation.

context_blocks.text: The graph being optimized and the network carrying messages are different objects. Two vertices that are not adjacent in the input can still communicate directly. This removes distance as an obstacle while retaining a limit on how much information a processor can receive in one round. The task asks how much this distributed information limits exact optimization.

A simple baseline is to collect the entire graph at processor 1. Each other processor sends its n-bit adjacency row along its direct link, in blocks of b bits. These transmissions happen simultaneously and take O(n / log n) rounds for n >= 2. Processor 1 then enumerates subsets locally, chooses a largest independent set, and sends each processor its membership bit. This is an elementary upper bound for the stated model, rather than a claim that centralizing the graph is optimal.

The unlimited local computation is essential to interpreting this baseline. The exponential subset enumeration has no communication cost. Conversely, a faster centralized algorithm does not by itself reduce the number of rounds needed to assemble the input. The question isolates information movement from the ordinary running-time difficulty of exact independent set.

Lower bounds are especially delicate in the unicast clique. Drucker, Kuhn, and Oshman relate this model to powerful circuit computations, explaining why familiar sparse-network bottleneck arguments do not transfer directly. Chechik nevertheless identifies exact maximum independent set as a concrete round-complexity question. The catalogue has a separate constant-round question for a maximal independent set; that weaker output requirement must not be substituted here.

cards.title: Bipartite maximal matching with polynomial-in-degree volume
cards.formal: Do there exist constants C>0 and k≥1 and one deterministic VOLUME algorithm that computes a maximal matching on every bipartite graph of maximum degree at most Δ, inspecting at most C(Δ+1)^k distinct vertices per queried vertex, independently of the number n of graph vertices? A proper input two-coloring specifying the bipartition is supplied. Answers to all vertex queries must describe the same matching.
cards.definitions: The input is a finite simple undirected graph, arbitrary local port orders, a supplied proper two-coloring, distinct identifiers in [n²], and known integers n and Δ≥1 bounding its size and degrees as stated. A query at v must output either ⊥ for unmatched or the local port of its matching edge. If v names u then u must name v. Every edge must have at least one matched endpoint, which is equivalent to maximality by inclusion. Initially the algorithm sees only v’s identifier, degree, color, ports, n, and Δ. It may adaptively follow a port at any already visited vertex; doing so reveals the neighbor’s identifier, degree, color, and reciprocal port. Count all distinct visited vertices, including v. The explored set is connected: arbitrary jumps to identifiers are forbidden. Each query starts afresh, with no preprocessing or memory retained between queries. Repeating a query must give the same answer regardless of other queries or their order. Local computation and temporary memory are unrestricted but finite, and only the number of distinct visited vertices is charged. One finite deterministic program must work for all n, Δ, graphs, identifiers, and port orders; the constants C,k are universal. There is no additional log n or log* n term in the allowed volume.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct the uniform polynomial-in-Δ algorithm with globally consistent matching answers, or prove that every correct deterministic algorithm violates every such polynomial bound on some valid input and query. A randomized bound, expected volume, an approximation to maximum matching that need not be maximal, or a polynomial bound containing a factor depending on n does not settle this formulation.
cards.why: This is a basic test of whether a fast distributed symmetry-breaking algorithm can be evaluated locally without exploring an exponentially branching dependency structure. A polynomial bound would give a small deterministic oracle for a fundamental graph primitive; a superpolynomial lower bound would expose an information cost that round complexity alone does not capture.

importance.reason: A fundamental maximal-matching oracle question that isolates degree dependence and the difference between distance and volume. It asks for a qualitative polynomial-versus-superpolynomial classification with no network-size term.

progress.text: Brandt and Olivetti sharpen the degree dependence of bipartite maximal matching in LOCAL. In the identifier model, the deterministic Ω(min{Δ,log n/log log n}) lower bound gives an Ω(Δ) obstruction to any degree-only volume bound by choosing sufficiently large n.

Rosenbaum and Suomela formalize connected adaptive exploration and explain why an f-round LOCAL algorithm gives a Δ^O(f)-volume algorithm. Combining this with the bipartite O(Δ)-round procedure gives the baseline Δ^O(Δ) volume.
Suomela explicitly asks whether bipartite maximal matching admits polynomial volume in Δ, and conjectures 2^Θ(Δ) as the correct dependence. The conjecture is not a proved lower bound.

context_blocks.text: A matching is maximal when there is no edge that can be added while keeping its endpoints disjoint from the current matching. It can be much smaller than a maximum matching. The local output is only one port or an unmatched symbol, so the difficulty is the information needed to make this small answer consistent with answers elsewhere.

The supplied bipartition lets the two sides play different roles. A simple distributed procedure has unmatched vertices on one side propose along a new incident edge, while vertices on the other side accept at most one proposal and remain matched thereafter. After O(Δ) rounds this yields a maximal matching. Gathering a whole neighborhood to simulate those rounds can inspect Δ raised to a linear-in-Δ power many vertices.

Volume asks whether that exploration can be made much narrower. A vertex may follow a few carefully chosen dependencies far into the graph, instead of collecting every branch of a large ball. But it cannot simply choose a convenient partner in isolation: when that partner is queried separately, the answers must agree. The lack of shared mutable query state makes this coordination part of the algorithm itself.

The independence from n is essential. For each fixed Δ, even an enormous function such as Δ^(2Δ) is constant as n grows. This question compares those constants uniformly as Δ grows, asking for a single polynomial. It is therefore different from obtaining logarithmic dependence on n for fixed degree or from studying only a single fixed-degree LCL.

Known round lower bounds force at least linear dependence on Δ when n is sufficiently large. They leave a large interval between that obstruction and full-neighborhood simulation. Suomela conjectures an exponential degree dependence for volume, so even deciding whether a polynomial is possible would determine which side of that major gap is achievable.

cards.title: Can bipartite 3-coloring be maintained with logarithmic recoloring radius?
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic algorithm and a universal constant C such that, for every n and every adversarial sequence of edge insertions into an initially edgeless graph on [n], with every intermediate graph bipartite, the algorithm maintains a proper coloring with colors {1,2,3} while changing colors only within distance C log₂(n+2) of an endpoint of the newly inserted edge? Distance is measured in the graph immediately after that insertion. The algorithm sees the entire current graph and may retain arbitrary state, but has no knowledge of future insertions.
cards.definitions: The vertex set [n] and n are supplied initially. The graphs are finite, simple and undirected, and maximum degree is unrestricted. An insertion adds one previously absent edge {u,v}; no edge deletions or supplied bipartition are included. The adversary may select its next insertion after inspecting the algorithm’s previous colors. Before any insertion the algorithm chooses a color for each isolated vertex. After update i it must output c_i:[n]→{1,2,3} with c_i(x)≠c_i(y) for every edge {x,y} of G_i. If min(dist_G_i(w,u),dist_G_i(w,v))>⌈C log₂(n+2)⌉, then c_i(w)=c_{i−1}(w); vertices in other components have infinite distance. All colors must be valid after every update. One computable program works for all n and terminates on every update. Global reading, computation time, memory and the number of recolorings inside the permitted neighborhood are unrestricted. The resource being bounded is the worst-case spatial radius of changed output, not amortized update time or communication rounds. This fixes the incremental edge-update convention of dynamic-LOCAL.
cards.answer_criterion: Give such an algorithm with a proof valid for every bipartite insertion sequence, or prove that no deterministic algorithm has an O(log n) worst-case recoloring radius. A bound only for trees, only on the number of recolored vertices, or for a model with advance access to future edges does not settle this formulation.
cards.why: Bipartite 3-coloring is a simple test of whether global information and local repairs can match the power of online lookaround. A tight answer would clarify a basic separation between dynamic and online computation without hiding the issue in expensive local processing.

importance.reason: A canonical coloring task that tests the power of maintaining solutions under local changes. The logarithmic target matches a known lower bound, and its resolution would clarify the relationship between two general locality models.

progress.text: Akbari and coauthors define incremental dynamic-LOCAL and give an O(log n)-locality online-LOCAL algorithm for 3-coloring bipartite graphs. The online algorithm is not a dynamic repair algorithm.

Chang, Mishra, Nguyen, Yang, and Yeh establish an Ω(log n) deterministic online-LOCAL lower bound even for grids. Together with the model simulation, this supplies the same lower bound for dynamic-LOCAL.

The corrected v4 of Online Locality Meets Distributed Quantum Computing retains Õ(√n) versus Ω(log n) in the dynamic-LOCAL entry of Table 1. Its corrections section withdraws a claimed general dynamic derandomization theorem from earlier versions.
Suomela’s updated open-problem page explicitly asks whether dynamic-LOCAL can 3-color bipartite graphs with O(log n) locality.

context_blocks.text: Every intermediate graph has a two-coloring, but a maintained coloring commits to choices before future edges are known. Two separately colored components may later be joined with incompatible parities. With only two colors, repairing that conflict can force a change across a large component. A third color offers additional ways to create a local transition between regions.

The question measures where a repair spreads. It does not limit how much of the graph the algorithm may inspect to decide on that repair. In particular, an algorithm could perform expensive global computation and still have small dynamic locality if only nearby output labels change. Conversely, a fast data structure could recolor a distant vertex and violate the radius bound.

The online-LOCAL model has a different source of power: when a vertex must be colored, a neighborhood in the eventual input graph is revealed. The ICALP 2023 algorithm uses logarithmic visibility to 3-color bipartite graphs. That result is a useful benchmark, but does not provide a logarithmic repair radius when edges themselves arrive without such advance visibility.

The later logarithmic lower bound for online-LOCAL already holds on grids and transfers to the weaker dynamic-LOCAL setting. Therefore an affirmative answer here would attain the correct asymptotic order. It remains possible that repairing a sequence of past commitments requires a substantially larger radius than choosing a color with a view into the eventual graph.

The corrected February 2026 comparison paper still lists a logarithmic lower bound and a roughly square-root upper bound for dynamic-LOCAL bipartite 3-coloring. It also withdraws an earlier general claim about derandomizing LOCAL in dynamic-LOCAL. The card uses the corrected version when describing the relationship between the models.

cards.title: How many rounds does triangle detection require in CONGEST?
cards.formal: For arbitrary simple undirected n-vertex networks, determine the optimal worst-case randomized round complexity of triangle detection in CONGEST, up to constant factors. Each vertex initially knows its distinct O(log n)-bit identifier and its neighbors, and may send a separate O(log n)-bit message in each direction of every incident edge per synchronous round. On a triangle-free graph all vertices must output NO; otherwise at least one must output YES. The joint answer must be correct with probability at least 2/3 on every input and identifier assignment. The algorithm is uniform, has private random bits, and may know n. The currently established bounds are $\Omega(\log\log n)$ and $\widetilde O(n^{1/3})$.
cards.why: I include this because it isolates the cost of learning one local pattern under network bandwidth constraints. A sharp answer would distinguish the communication needed for deciding existence from the communication needed for distributing all witnesses, and would test how far current lower-bound methods reach.
cards.definitions: $\widetilde O$ suppresses polylogarithmic factors. Local computation is unrestricted, vertex identifiers have $O(\log n)$ bits, and the communication graph is exactly $G$, not an all-to-all overlay. Nodes may know $n$. The output convention avoids charging the graph diameter merely to inform every vertex of a remote triangle. The triangle is a subgraph on three distinct mutually adjacent vertices.

progress.text: Chang, Pettie, Saranurak, and Zhang give $\widetilde O(n^{1/3})$-round algorithms for triangle enumeration, counting, and detection. The matching enumeration lower bound does not establish the same detection lower bound.

context_blocks.text: Every vertex knows two of the three edges of a triangle containing it. The missing information is whether two of its neighbors are adjacent. If messages had unlimited length, neighbors could exchange their complete adjacency lists in one round. The difficulty comes from fitting the relevant information through bounded-capacity edges.

For example, a vertex with many neighbors cannot simply send its entire neighborhood to every neighbor in one short message. On the other hand, most pairs of its neighbors may be irrelevant, so transmitting every adjacency list can be wasteful. An algorithm must exploit the topology to decide which information needs to move and where it can be combined.

Detection asks for one bit of global evidence, whereas listing requires the network collectively to output every triangle. A graph can contain a cubic number of triangles. Consequently, a lower bound driven by the volume of listed output does not automatically apply to detection. The near-optimal listing algorithm supplies a detection upper bound, but leaves this distinction unresolved.

The 2025 lower bound rules out every fixed number of rounds, including randomized protocols. It changes the old question of whether even two rounds are necessary into a quantitative gap. Conventional two-party communication reductions encounter barriers here, making stronger lower bounds a problem about proof techniques as well as about graph algorithms.

cards.title: Can a congested clique find a maximal independent set in constant rounds?
cards.formal: Is there a randomized algorithm that, on every n-vertex simple input graph, finds a maximal independent set in O(1) rounds in the Congested Clique model, with success probability at least $1-n^{-c}$ for every requested fixed $c>0$? Processor v initially knows its identifier and incident input edges. Every ordered pair of processors may exchange an O(log n)-bit message per synchronous round, whether or not the input edge exists. Each processor outputs whether it belongs to an independent set that dominates every vertex outside it. The algorithm must be uniform across inputs; it cannot be chosen after seeing the graph.
cards.why: I include this beside the LOCAL MIS problem because it tests a different limitation of distributed computation: restricted bandwidth despite universal communication. A constant-round algorithm would show that exact local domination needs only a bounded number of global exchanges. A lower bound would have to explain why distributed processing cannot avoid the bottleneck.
cards.definitions: Here $\Delta$ is the maximum degree of the input graph, not of the communication network. Messages to different recipients may differ. Local computation is unrestricted. $O(1)$ means independent of both $n$ and $\Delta$, with constants allowed to depend on the requested failure exponent. This is the unicast Congested Clique, rather than the weaker broadcast variant.

progress.text: Ghaffari, Gouleakis, Konrad, Mitrović, and Rubinfeld obtain the $O(\log\log\Delta)$-round MIS bound using sparsification.
Cambus, Kuhn, Pai, and Uitto obtain constant rounds for the 2-ruling-set relaxation.

Censor-Hillel, Even, Flin, and Halldórsson obtain constant rounds, for example, when average degree is at most $2^{O(\sqrt{\log n})}$. They also identify graph families on which existing sparsification methods require $\Omega(\log\log n)$ iterations. That restriction applies to those methods, not to all Congested Clique algorithms.

context_blocks.text: This changes the communication network while leaving the graph problem unchanged. A vertex can contact a distant processor immediately, so graph distance no longer limits the spread of information. Bandwidth still matters: one processor can receive only $O(n\log n)$ bits per round, whereas a general graph can contain $\Theta(n^2)$ independently specified edges. Sending the entire input to one leader is therefore not a constant-round solution.

That bottleneck is not itself a lower bound for MIS. A complete graph has many edges but is easy: a designated vertex can join the independent set and all others can stay out. The sought algorithm only needs enough information to coordinate a valid answer; it need not reconstruct every edge in one place.

Known algorithms exploit this by solving suitably sparse sampled subgraphs and reducing the remaining degrees. The general upper bound is $O(\log\log\Delta)$ rounds. The central question is whether a bounded number of communication phases can remove the need for repeated sparsification.

A closely related relaxation is already possible in constant rounds: a 2-ruling set remains independent but only has to put every vertex within distance two of a selected vertex. MIS requires distance one. This supplies a precise nearby success case against which to assess the unresolved target.

cards.title: Can deterministic (Delta+1)-coloring beat square-root dependence on degree?
cards.formal: Is there one deterministic LOCAL algorithm that properly colors every simple n-vertex graph of maximum degree $\Delta\ge2$ with colors in $\{1,\ldots,\Delta+1\}$ in $O(\Delta^{0.499}+\log^* n)$ synchronous rounds? Vertices have arbitrary distinct O(log n)-bit identifiers and know n and Delta. Messages along input edges and local computation are unbounded. The constant in the round bound must be independent of both n and Delta.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct an algorithm with the specified uniform round bound, or prove that no deterministic LOCAL algorithm attains it. Improving a logarithmic factor while retaining degree exponent one-half does not meet the target.
cards.why: I include this because the familiar greedy palette bound hides a distinct distributed coordination problem. A fixed improvement in the degree exponent would reveal new ways to resolve local conflicts, while an impossibility result would explain why the square-root dependence persists across different coloring methods.
cards.definitions: Proper coloring means adjacent vertices receive different output colors. Delta denotes a supplied upper bound on degree, and the guarantee holds for every such valid bound. The algorithm is uniform over n, Delta, and identifier assignments. Log-star n is the number of repeated base-two logarithms needed to reach at most one. Elapsed synchronous rounds are measured; this is not a sequential running-time or message-count target.

progress.text: Maus and Tonoyan obtain $O(\sqrt{\Delta\log\Delta}+\log^*n)$ deterministic rounds for the more general degree-plus-one list-coloring task. Ordinary coloring follows by using a common palette.
Suomela’s updated open-problem list explicitly asks whether the exponent 0.499 is attainable with Delta+1 colors and only an additive log-star n dependence.

The SODA 2026 discussion records a separate deterministic $\widetilde O(\log^{5/3}n)$ upper bound for Delta+1 coloring. That bound is independent of degree but does not provide the two-parameter guarantee asked here.

cards.status_note: Reviewed 10 September 2026. The target is deterministic and uniform in both degree and graph size; fast randomized coloring is not a resolution.

context_blocks.text: A sequential greedy algorithm needs only one more color than the maximum degree: when processing a vertex, at most Delta colors have already been used by its neighbors. In a distributed algorithm many adjacent vertices act simultaneously, so they can choose conflicting colors unless their decisions are coordinated.

Unique identifiers break perfect symmetry, but treating every identifier as a color starts with far too many colors. Color reduction has to compress this large palette while preserving a distinction across every edge. The degree controls how many simultaneous conflicts a vertex may need to avoid.

The two parameters in the target play different roles. Even when degree is fixed, the network can have arbitrarily many vertices, and iterated logarithmic time captures the unavoidable symmetry-breaking dependence on that size. An algorithm taking a power of log n cannot simply replace this term: for sufficiently large n, it exceeds every bound depending only on Delta plus log-star n.

The target chooses a specific exponent strictly below one-half, as in Suomela’s list. The numerical improvement is small; its purpose is to cross the apparent degree barrier while keeping the optimal-size palette. Allowing more colors, randomness, or a larger n-dependent term gives separate questions.

cards.title: Can deterministic LOCAL coloring use a near-linear palette in log-star n rounds?
cards.formal: Do there exist absolute constants K,C and one deterministic LOCAL algorithm that, for every simple n-vertex graph and supplied maximum-degree bound $\Delta\ge2$, outputs a proper coloring with at most $\lceil K\Delta^{1.001}\rceil$ colors in at most $C(1+\log^*n)$ rounds? Vertices know n and Delta and have arbitrary distinct O(log n)-bit identifiers. Messages along input edges and local computation are unbounded. Neither K nor C may depend on Delta or n.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove existence of the uniform algorithm and constants, or prove that no such constants and algorithm exist. A log-star n bound with a degree-dependent hidden constant does not settle this proposition.
cards.why: I include this because it separates the cost of symmetry breaking from the number of colors used to absorb local conflicts. A solution would clarify whether the quadratic palette in a foundational distributed primitive reflects an intrinsic limitation or merely the current method of reducing identifiers to colors.
cards.definitions: Proper means that every input edge has differently colored endpoints. Colors are integers from one shared palette. The identifier bound has a fixed polynomial range in n. Log-star uses base two. The target is deterministic worst-case elapsed rounds over graphs and valid identifier assignments. Delta is not treated as a fixed constant outside the asymptotic bound.

progress.text: Linial’s color reduction gives an $O(\Delta^2)$-coloring in $O(\log^*n)$ rounds. Symmetry-breaking lower bounds also show that the graph-size dependence cannot in general become o(log-star n) when degree is fixed.
Maus and Tonoyan revisit the local color-reduction method and extend it to list and conflict constraints. Their result does not establish the near-linear palette at the requested uniform round bound.
Suomela explicitly lists the Delta-to-the-1.001 palette target within O(log-star n) deterministic rounds.

context_blocks.text: A fast coloring algorithm can allow itself more colors than a sequential greedy algorithm. The extra palette gives neighboring vertices more room to make independent choices. This question fixes an extremely short round budget and asks how much extra palette is actually necessary.

The exponent 1.001 makes the requested palette slightly superlinear in maximum degree. It is still much smaller than a quadratic palette for sufficiently large degree. Because the graph family ranges over every degree, hiding a large degree-dependent factor in the running time would erase the intended tradeoff.

For example, fixing degree first and then saying that an algorithm takes a constant number of rounds is insufficient: that constant might grow as the degree squared. The question instead requires one numerical multiplier on log-star n that works as both graph size and degree grow. This is why all the constants are quantified explicitly.

Classical color reduction reaches a quadratic-degree palette in iterated-logarithmic time. The source lists reducing the palette below that quadratic scale, and in particular to degree raised to 1.001, as unresolved. The card focuses on that one concrete target; optimal Delta+1 coloring with a larger degree-dependent round budget is a separate question.

cards.title: Is the known exponent for distributed even-cycle detection optimal?
cards.formal: For every fixed integer $k\ge3$, is $\widetilde\Omega(n^{1-1/k})$ a worst-case round lower bound for randomized detection of a simple cycle of length exactly 2k in the CONGEST model? The network is an arbitrary simple undirected n-vertex graph. Each vertex initially knows n, its distinct O(log n)-bit identifier, and its incident edges; each edge carries O(log n) bits per direction per synchronous round. If a cycle exists at least one vertex must output YES, and otherwise all must output NO. Require the joint answer to be correct with probability at least 2/3 on every input.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the stated lower bound for every fixed k at least three, or refute it for at least one fixed k. A randomized algorithm with a fixed improvement in the exponent for one such k would refute the conjecture. The k=2 case is already known and is not the open target.
cards.why: I include this because it asks whether a simple pattern parameter determines a precise hierarchy of communication costs. The gap is not merely about derandomizing an algorithm: the upper bound is already deterministic, while the missing lower bound must exclude every randomized protocol in the stronger unicast model.
cards.definitions: The cycle need not be induced: additional edges between its vertices are allowed. Local computation is unrestricted and random bits are private. Here $\widetilde\Omega(n^a)$ means a lower bound $\Omega(n^a/(\log n)^b)$ for some fixed b; constants may depend on k and the algorithm, but not n. A worst-case bound ranges over input graphs and identifier assignments. k is known to all vertices and is fixed before n grows.

progress.text: Censor-Hillel and coauthors give improved algorithms for small even cycles and show that, already for six-cycles, a lower bound $\Omega(n^{1/2+\alpha})$ for fixed positive alpha would imply major circuit lower bounds.
Fraigniaud, Luce, Magniez, and Todinca obtain randomized $O(n^{1-1/k})$-round detection for every fixed k.
The same authors obtain deterministic $O(n^{1-1/k})$ rounds in Broadcast CONGEST. Their conclusion explicitly leaves optimality open for every k>2.

context_blocks.text: Cycle detection asks whether information about a bounded number of vertices can be assembled somewhere in the network. With unbounded messages, a constant-radius neighborhood suffices for a fixed cycle length. With limited messages, a vertex may learn that there are many short paths without having enough information to combine compatible paths into a cycle.

A simple six-cycle uses six distinct vertices. Walking across one edge and back three times is also a closed walk of length six, but is not a valid witness. Conversely, a graph containing a six-cycle may also contain triangles or four-cycles. Computing only the shortest cycle length would therefore not answer the exact-length existence question.

The algorithmic exponent changes with the fixed requested length. The conjecture predicts two-thirds for six-cycles, three-quarters for eight-cycles, and progressively larger exponents for longer fixed even cycles. Constants may depend on the length; the question is about how the communication cost grows with network size.

The best known upper bound already works deterministically even when each vertex must broadcast the same message to all its neighbors. The proposed lower bound concerns the stronger model allowing different messages to different neighbors. Establishing it would show that neither private randomness nor this extra communication flexibility improves the exponent.

Conversely, a graph containing a six-cycle may also contain triangles or four-cycles. Computing only the shortest cycle length would therefore not answer the exact-length existence question.

The algorithmic exponent changes with the fixed requested length. The conjecture predicts two-thirds for six-cycles, three-quarters for eight-cycles, and progressively larger exponents for longer fixed even cycles. Constants may depend on the length; the question is about how the communication cost grows with network size.

The best known upper bound already works deterministically even when each vertex must broadcast the same message to all its neighbors. The proposed lower bound concerns the stronger model allowing different messages to different neighbors. Establishing it would show that neither private randomness nor this extra communication flexibility improves the exponent.

cards.title: Can bipartite maximal fractional matching be found in sublinear-in-degree rounds?
cards.formal:
Is there a deterministic LOCAL algorithm and a function $f(\Delta)=o(\Delta)$ that, on every simple bipartite graph of maximum degree at most Delta, outputs a maximal fractional matching within f(Delta) rounds, independently of n? Each edge e receives a nonnegative rational weight x_e, agreed upon by its endpoints. Require $\sum_{e
i v}x_e\le1$ for every vertex v, and for every edge uv require $\sum_{e
i u}x_e=1$ or $\sum_{e
i v}x_e=1$. The bipartition is supplied as an input two-coloring, nodes know n and Delta, and identifiers are distinct O(log n)-bit integers.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct a uniform algorithm with a degree-only bound whose ratio to Delta tends to zero, or prove that no such deterministic algorithm exists. An additive log-star n term, an almost-maximal solution, or a lower bound only for nonbipartite graphs does not settle this target.
cards.why: I include this because it asks whether relaxing discrete choices to fractional ones changes the intrinsic time needed for local coordination, once a bipartition is available. The constraints are simple, but exact maximality makes the question stronger than approximately solving a packing problem.
cards.definitions: LOCAL uses synchronous rounds with unbounded messages along input edges and unrestricted local computation. Rational weights have finite encodings; there is no imposed output-bit bound. The algorithm must work for every identifier assignment and every valid supplied degree bound. The little-o statement concerns Delta tending to infinity and must hold uniformly over all graph sizes. Vertices output weights for all incident edges, with exact endpoint agreement.

progress.text: Åstrand and Suomela give local algorithms for approximating covering and packing problems, including the linear-degree maximal-fractional-matching upper bound used in subsequent work.
Göös, Hirvonen, and Suomela prove that o(Delta) rounds are impossible for maximal fractional matching on general graphs. This does not resolve the bipartite question as stated.
Suomela’s open-problem list explicitly asks for o(Delta) rounds on bipartite graphs and conjectures that the answer is negative.

context_blocks.text: A fractional matching divides one unit of capacity at each vertex among its incident edges. Maximality means that no single edge can have its weight increased without exceeding an endpoint’s capacity. It does not mean that the total edge weight is as large as possible.

For example, on a star one can place the entire unit on a single leaf edge or divide it equally among all leaf edges. Both assignments saturate the center and are maximal, even though many leaves are unsaturated. Allowing fractions gives the algorithm ways to share capacity that do not exist for ordinary integral matching.

Bipartiteness supplies a globally consistent division into two sides, and the card gives that division to the algorithm. This can remove symmetry obstacles that occur when a vertex does not know which role it should play. Nevertheless, neighboring choices still have to agree on edge weights and achieve exact saturation somewhere along every edge.

Approximate saturation is a different requirement: leaving a small amount of unused capacity at both endpoints violates the condition on that edge. The known linear-degree lower bound on general graphs therefore cannot simply be combined with an approximation algorithm or transferred to the supplied-bipartition setting. The source specifically leaves this bipartite case open.

sentences: Submodular matching maximization chooses disjoint graph edges to maximize a monotone submodular objective on the selected set.
The objective can express diminishing returns and therefore generalizes additive edge weights.
The source asks for stronger one-pass streaming lower bounds than those inherited from ordinary maximum weighted matching.

sentences: Weighted all-pairs shortest paths requires every vertex to learn exact distances to all others in an edge-weighted network.
The 2017 source asks whether this can be done in a linear number of CONGEST communication rounds.
Straightforward repeated distance propagation is slower, while subquadratic algorithms suggest room for improvement.
The paper also shows that a standard two-party communication framework cannot establish a superlinear lower bound for this task.
The question therefore seeks either an algorithm coordinating many weighted searches within linear time or a different explanation of why their shared communication demands prevent it.

cards.title: Does general rational linear programming have a strongly polynomial algorithm?
cards.formal: Does there exist a deterministic algorithm, with fixed polynomials p and q, that solves every rational linear program $\min\{c^Tx:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}$, where A has m rows and n columns, using at most p(m+n) elementary arithmetic, comparison, and data-transfer operations, while every intermediate rational number has binary encoding length at most q(N)? Here N is the total input bit length. Solving means returning an exact optimal rational solution if one exists, or correctly reporting infeasibility or an objective unbounded below.
cards.definitions: A is in Q^(m by n), b in Q^m, and c in Q^n, with m,n>=1. All coefficients are supplied explicitly as binary signed numerators and positive denominators. No full-rank, nondegeneracy, strict-feasibility, coefficient-size, or conditioning promise is made. Elementary scalar operations are addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by a nonzero quantity, comparisons, and transfers of stored values. The program is fixed and finite; no oracle, advice, randomization, floor operation, or uncharged access to binary digits is allowed. Rational encoding length means the bit length of a numerator-denominator representation. The polynomial p is independent of N and of every coefficient magnitude; q may depend on N. Consequently the algorithm must also admit a polynomial-time bit implementation. The output is a solution vector, not a required optimal basis. Infeasible means that the feasible set is empty; unbounded means it is nonempty and the infimum of c^T x is minus infinity. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: This isolates whether the combinatorial dimensions of a linear program suffice to control its arithmetic complexity. A resolution would clarify the relation between numerical precision, polyhedral structure, and the complexity of one of optimization’s basic models.

importance.reason: A leading open question in optimization, separating ordinary polynomial-time solvability from a dimension-only arithmetic bound. Its reach includes general linear programming and many combinatorial optimization problems.

progress.text: The ellipsoid method and early interior-point algorithms establish polynomial-time solvability in the total input bit length. They do not provide a general strongly polynomial operation bound.

Tardos gives an algorithm whose arithmetic count is independent of the right-hand side and objective magnitudes, with remaining dependence on the constraint matrix. Small integer entries in that matrix give important strongly polynomial special cases.

Allamigeon, Gaubert, and Vandame construct LP families forcing exponentially many iterations for the self-concordant-barrier path-following methods covered by their theorem. This restricts a route to solving the problem; it is not an unrestricted LP lower bound.

Dadush, Koh, Natura, Olver, and Végh solve minimum-cost generalized flow and LPs with at most two nonzeros per row or column in strongly polynomial time. Their analysis also controls intermediate bit lengths.

Dadush, Ma, Natura, and Végh improve interior-point bounds in terms of straight-line complexity and give strongly polynomial trust-region subroutines. Straight-line complexity can itself be large, so these are not dimension-only bounds for arbitrary LPs.

Version 10 of Awoniyi’s preprint claims at most 2(m+n) complementary-pivot iterations for general LP. This review has not validated the termination/correctness argument and complete bit-complexity guarantee, and found no independent primary confirmation. The claim is not promoted to an established resolution.

context_blocks.text: Linear programming is already solvable in polynomial time when input length includes the bits used to write its coefficients. The unresolved issue is whether the number of arithmetic decisions can depend only on the number of constraints and variables. Very large capacities, costs, or denominators may require long arithmetic operands, but the question asks whether they must also force more arithmetic steps.

Both requirements in the definition are essential. Bounding the number of steps while allowing intermediate integers with exponentially many bits could hide enormous computation inside single arithmetic operations. Bounding only total bit time gives ordinary polynomial-time linear programming, which is already known. The strongly polynomial target combines a dimension-only operation count with controlled numerical representation.

Combinatorial optimization supplies positive examples. Tardos’s method removes dependence on the magnitudes of the right-hand side and objective, and yields strongly polynomial bounds for suitable small-coefficient constraint matrices. More recently, a strongly polynomial algorithm was obtained when each row, or each column, has at most two nonzero entries. These cases show that large numerical data alone need not force many arithmetic steps.

For unrestricted matrices, an algorithm may need a different way to navigate the feasible region. Long central paths can defeat broad classes of path-following methods, even though other approaches remain possible. A separate status issue is a 2025 preprint, revised in July 2026, claiming a general solution. Its claim is recorded below, but this review has not established its correctness or found independent validation.

cards.title: Is exact semidefinite feasibility in polynomial time?
cards.formal: Is the following language in P in the ordinary Turing model: all lists of symmetric rational matrices A_0,A_1,…,A_m∈Q^{n×n} for which there exists a real vector x∈R^m satisfying A_0+sum_{i=1}^m x_i A_i⪰0? Both m and n are unbounded parts of the input, and the algorithm must decide exact nonemptiness in time polynomial in the total binary encoding length.
cards.definitions: Every matrix entry is an explicitly supplied rational number, with signed binary numerator and positive binary denominator; all matrices have the same size n≥1. A symmetric matrix M is positive semidefinite, written M⪰0, when zᵀMz≥0 for every real vector z, equivalently when all eigenvalues are nonnegative. The unknown x ranges over all real vectors, not just rational vectors. Singular feasible matrices count as YES. There is no strict-feasibility, boundedness, conditioning, rank, or distance-to-infeasibility promise, and no radius or accuracy parameter is supplied. The output is one bit specifying whether any feasible x exists; an explicit feasible point is not required. An affine subspace given by rational linear equations can be parametrized by rational Gaussian elimination, so this is also the rational-affine-subspace intersection formulation. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: A basic boundary between numerical convex optimization and exact efficient computation. Resolving it would clarify what semidefinite programming can guarantee without hidden regularity or witness-size assumptions, with consequences for optimization relaxations, algebraic certificates and verification.

importance.reason: A foundational complexity gap in a widely used convex optimization model; exact decision remains open despite powerful approximation algorithms, exact duality and symbolic decidability.

cards.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The primary literature retains general exact SDP feasibility as an open polynomial-time problem. Ramana’s dual does not establish NP∩coNP membership in the Turing model, and recent convex-polynomial optimization results address a different constraint family. This card permits real witnesses, singular feasible points, weak infeasibility and unbounded feasible regions.

context_blocks.text: Semidefinite constraints replace scalar nonnegativity by nonnegativity of a quadratic form in every direction. They include linear inequalities as the diagonal-matrix special case and support powerful relaxations in combinatorial optimization. Approximation algorithms are well developed, but their guarantees require attention to input geometry and numerical precision. De Klerk and Vallentin establish polynomial bit complexity for a short-step interior-point method under appropriate assumptions; their theorem is about controlled approximation, not arbitrary exact feasibility.

The unrestricted problem is decidable. Introduce a real n×n matrix Y and impose A_0+sum_i x_i A_i=YYᵀ. These are finitely many polynomial equations of degree at most two, and a real symmetric matrix is positive semidefinite exactly when such a factor exists. General real-algebraic decision procedures therefore apply. Henrion, Naldi and Safey El Din develop more specialized symbolic algorithms, including treatment of degenerate feasible sets. None of this supplies polynomial time when both input dimensions vary.

Exact feasibility can differ even from arbitrarily close approximation. The matrix M(t) with rows (0,1) and (1,t) has determinant −1, so it is never positive semidefinite. Yet as t tends to positive infinity, its negative eigenvalue (t−√(t²+4))/2 tends to zero. Thus these infeasible matrices approach the positive semidefinite cone arbitrarily closely. A numerical tolerance alone cannot distinguish this situation from a singular feasible matrix.

Rational input also need not admit a rational witness. Consider a block diagonal matrix with blocks [[x,2],[2,2x]] and [[2,x],[x,1]]. The first block is positive semidefinite exactly when x≥√2, and the second when |x|≤√2. The whole matrix is therefore feasible exactly at x=√2. All coefficient matrices are rational, but searching only rational substitutions would miss the solution. This example explains why the domain of the unknowns is part of the formal question.

Even rational feasible points can be enormous. Conditions x_1≥2 and [[x_{i+1},x_i],[x_i,1]]⪰0 force x_{i+1}≥x_i², hence x_k≥2^{2^{k−1}}. A block diagonal LMI encodes the chain compactly, while writing its final coordinate in ordinary binary needs exponentially many digits in k. Pataki and Touzov analyze how such growth arises beyond isolated examples, including connections to singularity degree. Large explicit witnesses obstruct a naive search algorithm; they do not prove that deciding existence is hard.

Ramana’s exact dual provides an alternative feasibility system of polynomial description size without regularity assumptions. In the Turing model, it implies that semidefinite feasibility belongs to NP if and only if it belongs to coNP. It does not establish either membership individually. The corresponding NP∩coNP theorem over exact real-number machines belongs to a different computational model. This distinction prevents a common overstatement of what SDP duality proves about bit complexity.
Pataki’s October 2025 work gives a new derivation and a fuller description of the feasible set of Ramana’s dual using facial reduction.

A separate STOC 2026 result by Slot, Steurer and Wiedmer obtains small approximate solutions for minimizing convex polynomials over polyhedra. That result concerns polynomial objectives with linear constraints; the authors explicitly contrast it with the large-solution obstacle for semidefinite programs. It does not settle general exact semidefinite feasibility.

cards.title: Does the packing property imply the max-flow min-cut property?
cards.formal: Does every finite clutter with the packing property have the max-flow min-cut property? Equivalently, if every deletion/contraction minor satisfies unweighted integral packing–covering equality, must weighted integral packing–covering equality hold for every nonnegative integer weight vector?
cards.definitions: A clutter C on a finite ground set E is a family of subsets of E, no one properly containing another. In the original instance all members are nonempty; the empty family is allowed. A cover T⊆E meets every member, and τ(C) is the smallest cover size. A packing is a family of pairwise disjoint members, with maximum size ν(C). Deleting e removes e from the ground set and discards all members containing e. Contracting e removes it from the ground set and from every member, and retains only inclusion-minimal resulting members. A minor results from any sequence of these operations. The packing property means τ(C′)=ν(C′) for every minor C′. For the empty family both values are zero; for a minor containing the empty set both are defined as +∞, with the empty member permitted arbitrarily many times in a packing. For w∈ℤ_{≥0}^E, let τ_w(C)=min{Σ_{e∈T}w_e:T covers C}. Let ν_w(C) be the maximum of Σ_{F∈C}y_F over nonnegative integers y_F satisfying Σ_{F∋e}y_F≤w_e for every e∈E. Thus a weighted packing may use a member repeatedly, subject to capacities w. The max-flow min-cut property is τ_w(C)=ν_w(C) for every such w. The original nonempty-member assumption makes these weighted optima finite.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that the packing property implies τ_w=ν_w for every finite clutter and every nonnegative integer weight vector, or give a finite clutter and weight vector with the packing property and τ_w>ν_w. A counterexample must verify equality for all minors, not merely for the original unweighted clutter. Finite searches, proofs for a proper subclass, or fractional optimality alone do not resolve the universal statement.

context_blocks.text: Packing and covering often give two descriptions of the same combinatorial optimum. In a clutter, the unweighted equality can fail. Requiring equality after every deletion and contraction removes many such obstructions. The Conforti–Cornuéjols conjecture asks whether this local robustness already guarantees equality for every integer capacity vector.

For a concrete example, take E as the vertices of a bipartite graph and the clutter members as its edges. Covers are vertex covers and packings are matchings. This illustrates the familiar kind of min–max equality that the general conjecture seeks to characterize, without restricting its input to graph edge families.

If A is the member-by-element incidence matrix, the associated linear programs are min wᵀx subject to Ax≥1 and x≥0, and max 1ᵀy subject to Aᵀy≤w and y≥0. Equality of the two integer optima forces their values to agree with the fractional optimum by weak and strong duality. This is the standard MFMC integrality requirement.

Schrijver’s Survey Question 68 calls the target the assertion that every packing hypergraph is Mengerian. The terminology differs, but its packing property includes all minors and its conclusion includes arbitrary nonnegative integer weights. Checking only the all-ones weight on the original instance would yield a much weaker, insufficient hypothesis.

Abdi and Schwarcz’s July 2026 manuscript calls the statement the replication conjecture and explicitly retains it as open. It reports verification for clutters on at most ten elements and for a specified bounded-degree family of cuboids. These are finite or restricted confirmations, not a proof for arbitrary ground-set size.

The same work gives a finite set of weight vectors sufficient to test the MFMC property of a fixed clutter, with an improved bound on their entries. This makes checking individual instances more effective. The number and size of possible clutters still grow without bound, so instance-wise testability does not prove the universal implication.

cards.why: Identify whether all obstructions to weighted integral packing–covering duality are already visible as unweighted failures in minors, a central issue in integer programming and combinatorial optimization.

importance.reason: A central conjecture connecting minor obstructions, integral linear programming and packing–covering duality. Schrijver treats it as a major survey question, and a July 2026 primary paper develops both theoretical and computational methods around it.

cards.title: Nearly linear-time solution of general sparse linear systems
cards.formal: For every fixed integer c≥1, does there exist a uniform randomized classical algorithm A_c with the following guarantee? Given n≥2, a nonsingular rational n×n matrix A with m nonzero entries, a nonzero rational vector b, and an integer 1≤p≤c·ceil(log_2 n), output a rational vector x̂ such that ||Ax̂−b||_2≤2^(−p)||b||_2 with probability at least 2/3. Each numerator and positive denominator of A and b has at most c·ceil(log_2 n) binary digits, and the spectral condition number κ_2(A) is promised at most n^c. The worst-case running time must be O_c(m log^(d_c)n) for some constant d_c independent of the input.
cards.definitions: The input lists the row index, column index and rational value of each nonzero coefficient, without duplicate positions, together with the n entries of b; hence n≤m≤n². The Euclidean norm is ||v||_2=(Σ_i v_i²)^(1/2), and κ_2(A)=σ_max(A)/σ_min(A), the ratio of its largest and smallest singular values. Nonsingularity makes the denominator positive. A may be nonsymmetric, indefinite and unrelated to a graph Laplacian. The algorithm need only meet its guarantee on promised inputs; it is not asked to certify the condition-number promise. Computation uses a word RAM with Θ(log n)-bit words, conventional arithmetic, comparison, bit operations and memory access; all operations on longer numbers, preprocessing, random-bit generation and writing the output are charged. No operation on an arbitrary real number has unit cost. Converting word operations to bit operations changes only polylogarithmic factors. Constants and the fixed program may depend on c, but neither nonuniform advice depending on n nor a supplied inverse or preconditioner is allowed. Here ε=2^(−p); this is the polynomial-condition, inverse-polynomial-accuracy regime of the near-input-size target. The output is the full list of n rational coordinates, each as a signed binary numerator and positive binary denominator; every output bit is charged. The word instructions are random-access reads/writes, comparisons, conditional branches, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo 2^w, integer quotient/remainder with nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, and shifts of a w-bit word; shifts by at least w yield zero. The constant in word length w=Θ(log n) (or Θ(log N) when N is the stated input size) is fixed with the algorithm. Address arithmetic has the same cost, larger integers occupy multiple words, and no instruction performs arbitrary-precision arithmetic in one step. When randomization is allowed, a fresh independent uniform w-bit word costs one operation.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: This tests whether sparsity and moderate conditioning suffice for solving linear equations at essentially the cost of reading them. A resolution would clarify the limits of graph-based solvers, preconditioning and numerical subroutines used throughout algorithms and optimization.

importance.reason: A fundamental input-size complexity question for one of the most widely used computational primitives, with meaningful positive results for structured classes and general reductions from apparently special systems.

cards.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. This is an editorial, fully specified near-linear target in the polynomial-conditioning and precision regime, not a named positive conjecture. The faster-than-matrix-multiplication problem has already been solved. The August 2026 report discusses broader scalable solvers but does not claim this universal guarantee; the simplicial-Laplacian reduction is not a general running-time lower bound.

context_blocks.text: Solving Ax=b is a basic operation inside scientific simulation, optimization and data analysis. A sparse input can be read and multiplied by a vector without scanning all n² matrix positions. The question is whether solving one system can always be comparably inexpensive, up to powers of logarithms. Peng and Vempala frame the general complexity problem around exploiting sparsity while also controlling numerical precision, rather than treating arithmetic on exact real numbers as free.

The target fixes a residual norm because different meanings of approximate solution can conceal different costs. If x*=A^(-1)b, the elementary inequality ||x̂−x*||_2/||x*||_2≤κ_2(A)·||Ax̂−b||_2/||b||_2 relates residual error to forward error. Thus a tiny residual need not mean an equally tiny solution error. For instance, A=diag(1,δ), b=(1,δ) and x̂=(1,0) have residual δ while the second solution coordinate is wrong by one. The condition promise and requested accuracy make this dependence explicit.

Nearly linear solvers already exist for major structured families. Spielman and Teng establish such algorithms for symmetric diagonally dominant systems using preconditioning and graph structure. Their guarantee is naturally expressed in the matrix energy norm. For positive-definite systems, norm comparisons relate this guarantee to residual accuracy, with conditioning affecting the required tolerance. An arbitrary sparse matrix lacks the diagonal-dominance structure that supports this machinery.

Peng and Vempala’s SODA 2021 result breaks the matrix-multiplication barrier for sufficiently sparse, polynomially conditioned systems. They implement a randomized block Krylov approach using structured factorizations and a numerical-stability analysis. This is why merely asking for a sparse solver faster than matrix multiplication would be an obsolete open question. The stronger near-input-size target remains far beyond that theorem.

Nie improves the required anti-concentration bounds for random Krylov matrices. His STOC 2022 result yields a bound of Õ(m^((ω−2)/(ω−1))n²) in the polynomial-conditioning and precision regime. The paper’s numerical exponent 2.2716 uses the matrix-multiplication bound available at that time; it is not a claim about today’s best numerical value of ω. Either expression remains far above linear for very sparse inputs.

The distinction between a sparse matrix and a structurally easy sparse matrix is sharpened by Ding, Kyng, Probst Gutenberg and Zhang. They reduce general linear equations with polynomially bounded integer coefficients and conditioning to Laplacians of two-dimensional simplicial complexes while preserving sparsity up to logarithmic factors. Consequently, extending graph-Laplacian techniques to those higher-dimensional Laplacians would already have general consequences. This is a completeness reduction, not an unconditional proof that a near-linear solver cannot exist.

The Simons workshop report, revised in August 2026, calls for broader classes of scalably solvable systems and studies the finite-precision behavior of iterative methods. Its benchmark questions are more focused than a universal worst-case solver, and its discussion of preconditioning makes clear that constructing a useful preconditioner is itself part of the computational task. The present card is an explicit editorial formulation of the general complexity target; it is not attributed to a numbered conjecture in that report.

The output requirement also matters. An explicit n-vector is compatible with nearly linear time because a nonsingular n×n input has at least n nonzeros. Returning only access to a vector, a few observables, or a quantum state encoding its normalized coordinates changes the task. Conversely, demanding an exact rational solution could introduce much larger output encodings; the specified numerical approximation avoids building that extra requirement into the question.

cards.definitions: S²={x∈ℝ³: x₁²+x₂²+x₃²=1}. The energy is E_N(x₁,…,x_N)=Σ_{i≠j}−ln‖x_i−x_j‖₂, counting ordered pairs; collisions have energy +∞. E_N* is the infimum over all N-tuples on S². ln is the natural logarithm and ‖·‖₂ is Euclidean distance. The algorithm is one finite real-arithmetic program with a fixed finite list of real constants, independent of N. It has exact real registers and a finite-control tape machine with register copying, addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by a nonzero register, and branching on the sign of a register. Tape movements and each scalar arithmetic, comparison or copy operation have unit cost. Input is the integer N as an exact real value; output is a list of 3N real coordinates. Any finite tape/register storage used by the program is charged through its operations. There is no primitive logarithm, square root, floor, random sample or minimization oracle. Polynomial time is in N, not in log N. The inequality is a mathematical condition on the output; the algorithm need not evaluate the energy. This specifies the real-number computation convention in Smale’s problem; coordinates need not be rational and no bit-cost bound is asserted.
cards.answer_criterion: A positive answer supplies one permitted real-arithmetic program and constants C,K,k, fixed independently of N, with the stated running time and total-energy guarantee for every integer N≥2. A negative answer proves that no such program and constants exist. Failure of one construction, a lower bound for a restricted method, or energy estimates for finitely many cardinalities do not establish the negation.

context_blocks.text: Imagine placing mutually repelling particles on a sphere. For this problem, a pair contributes minus the logarithm of its straight-line distance through three-dimensional space. Bringing two points together sends their contribution to positive infinity. Spreading points lowers the energy, but the question asks for a guarantee against the best configuration of the entire collection, rather than against a locally stable arrangement. Exact minimizers are called elliptic Fekete configurations.

For two points the answer is concrete: opposite poles have distance 2, the largest possible distance on the unit sphere, and ordered-pair energy −2 ln 2. For general N an optimum still exists: the sphere is compact, collisions have infinite energy, and some distinct configuration has finite energy. Existence therefore is not the open part. The unresolved requirement is one fixed algorithm with a polynomial operation bound for every N.

The tolerance C ln N is an additive error in the total energy. It is small compared with its known expansion E_N*=(1/2−ln 2)N²−(N/2)ln N+aN+o(N), where a is a universal constant. Matching only the leading N² term, or even allowing a linear error, leaves far more uncertainty than the target permits. Uniform-looking points and good numerical values for finitely many N do not establish this error bound.

Smale’s original statement counts each unordered pair once. This card counts each pair twice, as in much subsequent literature. Both the optimum and excess energy are doubled, so the existence of a universal logarithmic-error constant is unchanged. The real-arithmetic model also comes from Smale’s formulation: a step manipulates an exact real value. A polynomial number of such steps does not assert polynomial bit complexity, and the output inequality does not give the program a free logarithm or minimization instruction.

The generalized Diamond ensemble supplies configurations for every N with a precisely analyzed expected energy: the two leading terms above plus a specified linear term and an O(√N ln N) remainder. These constructions quantify how well a structured distribution spreads points. That estimate is not a deterministic C ln N excess guarantee relative to the unknown optimum.

Beltrán and Hardy obtain the required logarithmic excess for a low-temperature Coulomb-gas distribution: at inverse temperature N, the mean excess is at most 9 ln N, and excess at most 10 ln N holds with probability at least 1−exp(−N ln N). The theorem analyzes the distribution, while polynomial-time sampling from it remains an additional computational issue. A probabilistic existence statement also differs from the deterministic algorithm asked for here.

Michelen and Yakir prove a central limit theorem for the energy of zeros of a rotationally invariant random polynomial, with fluctuations on the √N scale. This measures variation around that ensemble’s mean, not error from the global minimum.

Recent exact algebraic work by Armentano and coauthors classifies critical configurations with at most six points, and treats seven points under an antipodal-pair restriction. Such finite classifications do not supply a uniform algorithm for arbitrary N.

The original motivation connects low-energy spherical points, through stereographic projection, to well-conditioned polynomials and the complexity of finding polynomial roots. The energy question has its own stronger output guarantee; progress on polynomial conditioning or on a different Smale problem does not automatically resolve it. It also asks a basic algorithmic question in discrete potential theory: how cheaply can globally near-equilibrium configurations be constructed?

cards.title: Is there a polynomial-time simplex pivot rule?
cards.formal: Does there exist a uniform deterministic primal-simplex pivot algorithm and a polynomial p such that, for every rational linear program max{cᵀx: Ax=b, x≥0} with A of full row rank, a finite optimum, and any supplied feasible basis B_0, the algorithm reaches a basis whose reduced costs are all nonpositive using at most p(L) bit operations in total? Here L is the binary input length of A,b,c and B_0, and every basis change must be a legal improving simplex pivot as defined below.
cards.definitions: A has m rows and n columns with 1≤m≤n; all rational numerators and positive denominators are explicit binary integers. A basis B is a set of m columns with invertible A_B. Its basic solution is x_B=A_B^{-1}b and x_j=0 for j∉B, and feasibility means x_B≥0. An entering column j∉B must have reduced cost r_j=c_j−c_BᵀA_B^{-1}A_j>0. Put a=A_B^{-1}A_j. Choose a leaving basic index i attaining θ=min_{k∈B:a_k>0}x_k/a_k, and replace i by j in the basis. The finite-optimum promise ensures that this minimum exists for an improving column. Ties may be resolved by the rule; θ=0 is an allowed degenerate pivot and counts toward the bound. The rule may inspect the whole input and maintain history, with all preprocessing, pivot selection, exact arithmetic, helper computations and memory operations charged to p(L). It must follow these basis exchanges on the supplied LP from B_0: it may not jump to another feasible basis or replace the feasible region by an extended formulation. The required terminal condition r_j≤0 for all j∉B certifies optimality. This is the supplied-feasible-basis optimization version; phase-I feasibility construction is not part of this card.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct such a rule and prove its total polynomial bit complexity for every promised input and initial feasible basis, or prove that no such rule exists. Merely bounding the number of pivots while leaving their selection computationally unbounded is insufficient. A lower bound for a prescribed family of rules, or for nonlinear objectives, does not establish the negative answer for all rules here.
cards.why: A fundamental question about whether local, improving basis exchanges can support efficient global optimization. It would explain a central practical algorithm and sharpen the relationship between polyhedral geometry, degeneracy and algorithmic access to an optimum.

importance.reason: A longstanding foundational problem about one of the most important optimization algorithms; the existence and efficient discovery of short improving basis paths remain unresolved even though LP itself is polynomial-time solvable.
