context_blocks.text: A junta is a model of prediction with many irrelevant features. The target may use only a small hidden subset of a very long input, but its behaviour on those relevant features is unrestricted. The goal is accurate prediction on a new uniform input. Identifying the support exactly is not required: variables that affect too little probability mass may be ignored at the requested accuracy.

The allowance of 2^k is deliberate. An arbitrary function on the relevant coordinates can have a truth table with 2^k entries, so a polynomial dependence on that quantity accommodates the complexity of the target itself. The desired improvement is in locating useful coordinates among n possibilities. For k proportional to log n, the proposed bound would give polynomial-time learning. Brute-force support enumeration has about n^k possibilities and becomes quasipolynomial in that regime.

The sample requirement already fits the target. There are at most (k+1)n^k·2^{2^k} juntas on n variables. A union bound shows that O((2^k+k log(n+1)+log(k+1)+1)/ε) independent examples suffice for every consistent hypothesis in this finite class to have error at most ε, with constant confidence. Such a hypothesis exists because the labels come from a junta. The difficulty is finding it efficiently; enumerating supports and filling their truth tables gives a direct but expensive method.

Mossel, O’Donnell and Servedio obtained the first constant-factor improvement in the exponent of this search. Their algorithm combines structural information about Boolean functions with algebraic computation and learns exactly in approximately n^{0.704k}·poly(n,2^k) time at the matrix-multiplication exponent used in the paper. This is an algorithm for arbitrary juntas from uniform random examples, so it addresses the same access model.

Gregory Valiant subsequently improved the exponent to below 0.6k, with polynomial factors in n and 2^k, through algorithms for finding correlations and learning sparse parities with noise. His argument combines a noise-robust parity learner with the junta structure used in earlier work. The approximately n^{0.6k} benchmark is still stated in Servedio’s November 2025 survey. It is a major improvement over exhaustive search, but the exponent on the ambient dimension still grows with k.

Simple correlation screening is insufficient. For example, f(x)=x₁ XOR x₂ XOR x₃ is independent of each individual input bit under the uniform distribution, although all three are relevant. This does not make noiseless parity computationally hard: one can learn an unknown parity by solving linear equations over the two-element field. It explains why a limitation of low-order correlations or statistical queries cannot automatically be converted into a lower bound for every algorithm using actual examples.

Membership queries change the task substantially. They allow the learner to choose an input and ask for its label, making it possible to isolate relevant variables by carefully comparing nearby points. Learning juntas in polynomial time in n and 2^k is known with this additional access. Servedio’s survey also notes that monotone juntas admit the desired bound from ordinary uniform examples; arbitrary juntas need not expose their variables through such first-order information.

The phrase “learning junta distributions” describes another problem: recovering a probability mass function that depends on a small coordinate set. Beretta’s RANDOM 2025 paper relates that distribution-learning task to learning sparse parities with noise. Its introduction explicitly distinguishes noiseless Boolean junta learning and reports the existing n^{0.6k} benchmark. An equivalence for distribution learning is not an unconditional lower bound for the noiseless prediction task here.

Cornacchia, Mikulincer and Mossel show in May 2026 that a suitable neural-network training procedure can learn juntas efficiently from a lazy random walk on the hypercube, with essentially linear sample complexity in ambient dimension for each fixed k. Their loss uses differences between consecutive samples. Even if each sample has a uniform marginal distribution, consecutive samples are correlated; an independent-example oracle does not provide those labelled neighbouring points. This result therefore leaves the present question intact.

The problem is a gateway to learning richer representations. A k-junta has both a decision tree and a DNF representation of size at most 2^k. Efficient uniform-example learners for those general classes would consequently learn juntas within the requested resource bound. A positive result here would solve a central obstacle, while a negative result for unrestricted learners would explain a computational limitation of feature selection even under a particularly simple input distribution.

Wigderson’s Open Problem 17.9, the source inherited as TCS-0023, concerns the class F_k of functions depending on at most k input bits. The old catalogue title incorrectly described it as growing-size DNF learning. Its challenge is to go beyond constant support size with polynomial-time learning, or justify a hardness assumption. This card retains the precise stronger target poly(n,2^k,1/ε) for every k. A positive answer supplies polynomial time when k=O(log n); a learner for only one slower-growing support regime need not meet the full target. sentences: A Boolean junta depends on only k coordinates even though its input contains n possible features.
The project asks whether it can be learned from uniformly random labeled examples in time polynomial in n, the size of its k-variable truth table, and the inverse error tolerance.
The allowed exponential dependence on k accommodates an arbitrary function of the relevant coordinates.
The difficult step is locating useful coordinates without enumerating all possible subsets of the n features.
A learner with this guarantee would turn hidden low-dimensional structure into efficient prediction even when the number of relevant variables grows logarithmically with n.

cards.context:
A junta is a model of prediction with many irrelevant features. The target may use only a small hidden subset of a very long input, but its behaviour on those relevant features is unrestricted. The goal is accurate prediction on a new uniform input. Identifying the support exactly is not required: variables that affect too little probability mass may be ignored at the requested accuracy.

The allowance of 2^k is deliberate. An arbitrary function on the relevant coordinates can have a truth table with 2^k entries, so a polynomial dependence on that quantity accommodates the complexity of the target itself. The desired improvement is in locating useful coordinates among n possibilities. For k proportional to log n, the proposed bound would give polynomial-time learning. Brute-force support enumeration has about n^k possibilities and becomes quasipolynomial in that regime.

The sample requirement already fits the target. There are at most (k+1)n^k·2^{2^k} juntas on n variables. A union bound shows that O((2^k+k log(n+1)+log(k+1)+1)/ε) independent examples suffice for every consistent hypothesis in this finite class to have error at most ε, with constant confidence. Such a hypothesis exists because the labels come from a junta. The difficulty is finding it efficiently; enumerating supports and filling their truth tables gives a direct but expensive method.

Mossel, O’Donnell and Servedio obtained the first constant-factor improvement in the exponent of this search. Their algorithm combines structural information about Boolean functions with algebraic computation and learns exactly in approximately n^{0.704k}·poly(n,2^k) time at the matrix-multiplication exponent used in the paper. This is an algorithm for arbitrary juntas from uniform random examples, so it addresses the same access model.

Gregory Valiant subsequently improved the exponent to below 0.6k, with polynomial factors in n and 2^k, through algorithms for finding correlations and learning sparse parities with noise. His argument combines a noise-robust parity learner with the junta structure used in earlier work. The approximately n^{0.6k} benchmark is still stated in Servedio’s November 2025 survey. It is a major improvement over exhaustive search, but the exponent on the ambient dimension still grows with k.

Simple correlation screening is insufficient. For example, f(x)=x₁ XOR x₂ XOR x₃ is independent of each individual input bit under the uniform distribution, although all three are relevant. This does not make noiseless parity computationally hard: one can learn an unknown parity by solving linear equations over the two-element field. It explains why a limitation of low-order correlations or statistical queries cannot automatically be converted into a lower bound for every algorithm using actual examples.

Membership queries change the task substantially. They allow the learner to choose an input and ask for its label, making it possible to isolate relevant variables by carefully comparing nearby points. Learning juntas in polynomial time in n and 2^k is known with this additional access. Servedio’s survey also notes that monotone juntas admit the desired bound from ordinary uniform examples; arbitrary juntas need not expose their variables through such first-order information.

The phrase “learning junta distributions” describes another problem: recovering a probability mass function that depends on a small coordinate set. Beretta’s RANDOM 2025 paper relates that distribution-learning task to learning sparse parities with noise. Its introduction explicitly distinguishes noiseless Boolean junta learning and reports the existing n^{0.6k} benchmark. An equivalence for distribution learning is not an unconditional lower bound for the noiseless prediction task here.

Cornacchia, Mikulincer and Mossel show in May 2026 that a suitable neural-network training procedure can learn juntas efficiently from a lazy random walk on the hypercube, with essentially linear sample complexity in ambient dimension for each fixed k. Their loss uses differences between consecutive samples. Even if each sample has a uniform marginal distribution, consecutive samples are correlated; an independent-example oracle does not provide those labelled neighbouring points. This result therefore leaves the present question intact.

The problem is a gateway to learning richer representations. A k-junta has both a decision tree and a DNF representation of size at most 2^k. Efficient uniform-example learners for those general classes would consequently learn juntas within the requested resource bound. A positive result here would solve a central obstacle, while a negative result for unrestricted learners would explain a computational limitation of feature selection even under a particularly simple input distribution.

Wigderson’s Open Problem 17.9, the source inherited as TCS-0023, concerns the class F_k of functions depending on at most k input bits. The old catalogue title incorrectly described it as growing-size DNF learning. Its challenge is to go beyond constant support size with polynomial-time learning, or justify a hardness assumption. This card retains the precise stronger target poly(n,2^k,1/ε) for every k. A positive answer supplies polynomial time when k=O(log n); a learner for only one slower-growing support regime need not meet the full target. Conditional hardness allowed as an outcome in the source is also weaker than an unconditional negative answer here. The source record is consolidated as a related milestone, not asserted to be an equivalent formulation; The removed TCS-0023 keeps its reserved ID and deletion reason; its bibliography and weaker milestone are preserved here.

cards.title: Polynomial-time distribution-free PAC learning of DNF
cards.formal: Is there a uniform classical randomized algorithm that, for every n,s≥1, every Boolean function f representable by a DNF with at most s terms on n variables, every distribution D on {0,1}ⁿ, and all accuracy and confidence parameters ε,δ∈(0,1), PAC learns f from independent D-distributed labelled examples in time polynomial in n,s,1/ε and log(1/δ)? The output may be any efficiently evaluable Boolean hypothesis; membership queries are not allowed.
cards.definitions: A literal is a variable x_i or its negation. A term is a conjunction of literals, and a disjunctive normal form (DNF) is an OR of terms. Terms may have arbitrary width up to n after simplification. The size parameter s bounds the number of terms; counting literal occurrences instead changes polynomial bounds by at most a factor n. The target DNF is unknown: the learner is supplied only n, the upper bound s, and learning parameters. For an exact encoding, supply integers t,b≥2 and set ε=1/t and δ=2^(−b). One fixed probabilistic Turing machine must use at most p(n,s,t,b) steps for one fixed polynomial p, on every sequence of sample and random outcomes. Each example-oracle request supplies a fresh pair (x,f(x)) with x drawn independently from the same arbitrary unknown D; the learner cannot select x. Receiving and reading the n-bit sample counts toward the time bound. Samples are noiseless and realizable by the promised target. The output is an explicitly written deterministic Boolean circuit h on n input bits, not necessarily a DNF. With probability at least 1−δ over the examples and internal randomness, Pr_{x drawn from D}[h(x)≠f(x)]≤ε. Writing and evaluating this circuit have polynomial cost. Reciprocal-integer accuracy and dyadic confidence suffice for the usual general parameters by rounding toward stronger guarantees. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.

context_blocks.text: A DNF represents a union of rule-defined regions: an example is accepted when it satisfies at least one conjunction of feature conditions. The task is to infer accurate predictions from observations, without being given those rules. Feldman’s introduction identifies the general distribution-free question before studying more structured input distributions; that introductory question is the source of this catalogue record.

There is no information-theoretic obstacle to using polynomially many examples. There are at most 3ⁿ simplified conjunctions, since each variable is absent, positive or negative. Padding a DNF with empty slots bounds the number of candidate formulas by (3ⁿ+1)^s. The finite-class union bound therefore gives O((ns+log(1/δ))/ε) samples sufficient for every consistent DNF in this class to generalize. Exhaustively finding such a DNF may still take enormous time. The question asks whether that computational search can be avoided, even by outputting a different representation.

The distinction between a constant and a growing number of terms is essential. The classical n^{O(s)} algorithm is polynomial for each fixed s, but does not provide a single polynomial in n and s. Servedio’s 2025 survey records the longstanding goal and the subexponential distribution-free upper bound 2^{Õ(n^{1/3} log s)}. For polynomially many terms and fixed learning accuracy, this still leaves a substantial gap to polynomial time.

A distribution-free learner must handle probability concentrated on any subset of the Boolean cube. An argument that a long conjunction rarely holds under independent uniform coordinates need not survive such a distribution. Feldman’s Fourier-based work uses uniform or product structure and, in some settings, additional query access. Its positive results should not be read as a solution from arbitrary-distribution random examples alone.

Allowing hypotheses outside the target class is substantive. A hardness proof for producing another DNF can leave open an efficient learner that outputs a Boolean circuit or a polynomial threshold function. Daniely and Shalev-Shwartz obtain hardness that also covers improper learning, under their assumption about refuting random K-SAT. The assumption is part of that theorem, so it supplies evidence against efficient learning without deciding the unconditional question posed here.

Daniely and Vardi later derive hardness for DNF with a growing number of terms from an assumption about local pseudorandom generators. This gives a second precise route connecting the computational difficulty of learning compact rules to average-case complexity. Neither theorem should be abbreviated to an unconditional assertion that DNF cannot be learned.

The May 2026 Iterative Chow Filtering paper obtains quasipolynomial-time DNF learning under a uniform training distribution in a framework permitting abstention under distribution shift. Those distribution, output and runtime guarantees differ from the present target. This recent result was included in the status check and does not supply the required polynomial-time distribution-free learner.

A positive resolution would also give the learner sought in TCS-6543: every k-junta can be written as a DNF with at most 2^k terms, and the uniform distribution is one allowed choice of D. This implication goes from general DNF learning to junta learning; learning juntas alone does not supply an algorithm for general DNF targets. The two cards retain distinct targets. The mislabelled legacy record TCS-0023 is consolidated with the junta card because its actual cited problem concerns growing junta support.

cards.why: Determine whether compact Boolean rules that need only polynomially many observations can also be learned with polynomial computation, without assumptions on the input distribution. A positive result would cover decision trees and uniform-example juntas; a negative result would identify a fundamental computational barrier in realizable learning even when the output representation is unrestricted.

cards.definitions: H is a nonempty set of functions X→{0,1}; a finite subset B⊆X is shattered when all its binary labelings are restrictions of functions in H. Its VC dimension is the maximum shattered cardinality. Proper means that every output belongs to H. For z=((x_i,y_i))_{i=1}^n, loss(h,z)=(1/n)Σ_i 1[h(x_i)≠y_i]. To define CMI_D, draw a supersample Z̃=(Z̃_i,0,Z̃_i,1)_{i=1}^n with 2n independent draws from D, and independent fair bits S=(S₁,…,S_n); feed the selected sample (Z̃_i,S_i)_i to A with independent randomness. Put W=A((Z̃_i,S_i)_i). CMI_D(A)=I(W;S|Z̃)=H(S|Z̃)−H(S|W,Z̃), with base-two conditional Shannon entropy of the finite random variable S. The learner may depend on H,n, but not on D. The source does not specify sigma algebras for arbitrary X,H, measurability of evaluation, or admissibility of learners and distributions; those choices affect the quantified statement. No domain restriction is silently added here.

sentences: Conditional mutual information measures what a learner’s output reveals about which examples were selected from an independent supersample.
The target is the proper agnostic-learning Conjecture 6 of Steinke and Zakynthinou: information O(d) and expected empirical excess loss O(√(d/n)).
Here d is the VC dimension, n is sample size, and the learner must work for every data distribution.
The paper’s separate proper realizable Conjectures 7 and 8 were refuted by Haghifam, Dziugaite, Moran and Roy in 2020.
Measurability conventions for the arbitrary-domain question remain to be specified, so this formulation is still marked unfinished.

context_blocks.text: A learner can fit its observed labels while retaining information that is irrelevant to future prediction. Conditional mutual information measures one aspect of this dependence: after revealing a pool of two candidate examples for each position, how much does the output reveal about which member of each pair was actually used? The hidden selection consists of n fair bits, so this information is between zero and n bits. The conjecture asks whether dependence can be limited by the class complexity d while retaining near-best training accuracy.

For a one-pair illustration, fix two different candidate observations. An output that identifies the selected observation reveals the selector bit completely; an output independent of that choice reveals nothing. This describes the information experiment, not a proposed learning algorithm. The conditioning removes uncertainty about the observations themselves, so even an observation with an arbitrarily long numerical description need not reveal more than that one selection bit.

Agnostic means that observed labels need not agree with any hypothesis in the class. The empirical comparison is therefore with the best in-class training loss, rather than with zero. Properness requires the output to remain in that same class. The learner may vary with the class and sample size but must be chosen before the data distribution; otherwise the distribution-free claim changes.

The source gives an empirical-risk minimizer with CMI at most d log n+2. Its question is whether the logarithmic dependence on sample size can be removed if expected empirical excess loss of order √(d/n) is allowed. The significance is that the ordinary CMI generalization inequality would then recover a dimension-dependent √(d/n) scale without an extra logarithmic loss.

The paper’s Conjectures 7 and 8 instead ask for proper realizable learners with expected empirical loss O(d/n), or zero. Haghifam, Dziugaite, Moran and Roy refute those claims in Theorem 4.2. Their negative theorem assumes that sharper empirical-loss requirement. Since d/n can be much smaller than √(d/n), it cannot simply be substituted for a refutation of the agnostic Conjecture 6 retained here.

Hafez-Kolahi and coauthors recover tighter VC generalization estimates through chained conditional mutual information. This shows that an information-theoretic analysis can eliminate the extra logarithmic factor by changing the bound being analyzed. It does not supply a proper learner whose unmodified output CMI obeys the conjectured O(d) bound. A statement about a successful analysis and a statement about how much information the learner itself retains are different.

One formulation issue remains explicit. On arbitrary domains, the probability distributions, hypothesis-valued random output and evaluation map require compatible measurable structures. Those conventions are not specified in the cited conjecture. This card preserves that gap instead of silently restricting the question to a finite domain. Its content and source distinction have been improved, but it is still an unfinished benchmark formulation.

cards.title: Learning decision trees from uniform random examples in polynomial time
cards.formal: Is there a uniform randomized learner which, for all n,s≥1 and rational ε∈(0,1), learns every size-at-most-s Boolean decision tree on n variables from uniform random labeled examples in time poly(n,s,1/ε), with error at most ε and success probability at least 2/3?
cards.definitions: A decision tree has internal nodes querying one input coordinate, two outgoing edges labeled zero and one, and leaves labeled zero or one. Size counts all nodes. Samples are independent uniform x∈{0,1}^n labeled by the unknown target f. The learner receives n,s,ε and may draw samples but cannot request labels at chosen inputs. It outputs a Boolean circuit h of polynomial size, with Pr_{x uniform}[h(x)≠f(x)]≤ε on at least two thirds of runs. All sampling, computation, circuit writing and evaluation costs use classical bit operations; the total worst-case learning time has one polynomial bound.

context_blocks.text: Decision trees are an elementary representation for Boolean classification. Uniform data removes distributional pathologies but still leaves open whether random examples suffice for fully polynomial learning.

Kalai and Teng contrast the unresolved uniform-distribution problem with their positive result for most perturbed product distributions. Chosen-input queries can provide information unavailable from examples alone. The existing proper-learning card allows membership queries and requires a tree output. This target permits improper output but removes that query access.

cards.title: Distribution-free improper learning of two unrestricted halfspaces
cards.formal: Can intersections of two halfspaces on {0,1}^n be PAC learned, with an arbitrary efficiently evaluable hypothesis, in time polynomial in n, the target description length and inverse accuracy?
cards.definitions: Each target is the conjunction of two integer-weight linear threshold functions on the Boolean cube; threshold weights and offsets use binary encoding. Samples are independent labeled examples from an arbitrary distribution on the cube, with realizable labels. The intended guarantee is error at most ε with success probability at least 2/3 using polynomial time in n, target encoding length and 1/ε. Membership queries are unavailable. There is no margin or factorization promise.

context_blocks.text: A single halfspace is efficiently learnable, but combining only two thresholds introduces a longstanding computational obstacle. Allowing an arbitrary output representation avoids the known hardness of proper learning.

The existing TCS-6544 explicitly assumes a positive margin and polynomial dependence on its reciprocal. This candidate instead concerns unrestricted integer-weight thresholds on the Boolean cube. The distinction affects the running time and cannot be hidden behind their similar titles.

cards.title: Statistically optimal sparse robust Gaussian mean estimation in polynomial time
cards.formal: Is there a polynomial-time algorithm for ε-contaminated N(μ,I_d) samples, with k-sparse μ, achieving Euclidean error O(ε) from Õ(k log d/ε²) samples?
cards.definitions: The clean samples are independent draws from a d-dimensional Gaussian with identity covariance; at most an ε fraction may be replaced adversarially after observing them. A k-sparse mean has at most k nonzero coordinates. Success is intended with probability at least 2/3 over clean samples and algorithm coins for every such contamination. Runtime must be polynomial jointly in d,k and 1/ε, rather than having an exponent depending on k.

context_blocks.text: Sparsity reduces the number of samples statistically needed to estimate a high-dimensional mean. Adversarial corruption creates a gap between that sample advantage and the guarantees of polynomial-time estimators.

The cited work develops sum-of-squares algorithms and lower-bound evidence for this gap. Their resource tradeoffs do not establish a universal polynomial-time algorithm at the stated statistical scale. The goal is distributional robustness, not a particular estimator or proof technique.

cards.title: Do one-way functions imply public-key encryption in the standard model?
cards.formal: Does the existence of a classical cryptographic one-way function imply the existence of a classical public-key encryption scheme with negligible correctness error and security against uniform probabilistic polynomial-time chosen-plaintext adversaries? General constructions and security proofs may use the code of the one-way function; they need not be black-box.
cards.definitions: A one-way function is a deterministic polynomial-time map f:{0,1}*→{0,1}* such that every uniform classical PPT inverter I has negligible probability, for x uniform in {0,1}ⁿ, of outputting z∈{0,1}ⁿ with f(z)=f(x) on input (1ⁿ,f(x)). A function ν(n) is negligible if for every d>0 it is eventually at most n^{−d}. The scheme comprises uniform classical polynomial-time algorithms Gen, Enc, Dec. Gen(1ⁿ) randomly outputs public and secret bit strings (pk,sk); Enc(1ⁿ,pk,b) randomly encrypts a bit b; Dec(1ⁿ,sk,c) deterministically outputs a bit or failure. For each b, the probability over honest generation and encryption that decryption is wrong is negligible. Security means that for every uniform classical PPT adversary A, in the experiment (pk,sk)←Gen(1ⁿ), b←{0,1}, c←Enc(1ⁿ,pk,b), the advantage |Pr[A(1ⁿ,pk,c)=b]−1/2| is negligible. The adversary knows all algorithms and can encrypt arbitrary chosen bits itself with fresh randomness. This bit-message formulation extends to polynomially long messages by independent bit encryption and a hybrid argument. All runtime bounds are worst-case polynomial in the security parameter and appropriate input lengths. There is no shared secret before key generation, trusted setup, random oracle, quantum state, or auxiliary hardness assumption. Security is eventually negligible at all sufficiently large parameters, not merely infinitely often.

context_blocks.text: A one-way function creates an asymmetry between evaluating a map and finding a preimage of a random image. Public-key encryption needs a different asymmetry: anyone holding the public information can produce ciphertexts, yet a receiver possessing related secret information can recover their messages. The question is whether this additional structure is implicit in every possible source of one-wayness.

One-way functions already suffice for pseudorandom generators and, through the standard chain of constructions, private-key encryption. There the honest parties initially share a secret. Public-key encryption removes that initial shared secret, so the existence of symmetric cryptography is not already a construction of the desired public-key primitive.

The classical obstacle is the Impagliazzo–Rudich black-box separation. Roughly, an idealized one-way-function oracle can supply private-key cryptographic hardness without enabling the necessary key agreement. A construction allowed to inspect and reason about a concrete function’s program lies outside the oracle interface, which is why the general implication remains open despite this barrier.

Public-key encryption would give a two-message key-agreement protocol: send a public key, then send an encryption of a freshly chosen shared secret. Barak and Mahmoody show a quadratic-query attack on key agreement built from a random oracle, matching the limited query advantage of Merkle puzzles. The theorem counts oracle queries and allows extensive other computation; it is not an unconditional attack on every standard-model encryption scheme.

New constructions continue to broaden the available assumptions. Chatterjee, Mu, and Vasudevan base public-key encryption on a planted MinRank problem over random instances, equivalently a rank-metric decoding assumption, rather than hiding a specially structured efficiently decodable code. This is progress in the choice of concrete hardness assumptions. It still assumes that specific problem is hard, a property not supplied merely by the existence of some arbitrary OWF.

cards.title: Does P≠NP imply the existence of one-way functions?
cards.formal: Does P≠NP imply that there exists a deterministic polynomial-time computable function f:{0,1}*→{0,1}* such that, for every uniform probabilistic polynomial-time algorithm I and every constant c>0, all sufficiently large n satisfy $\Pr_{x\sim U_n,\,I}[\,|z|=n\ \land\ f(z)=f(x)\,]\le n^{-c}$, where $z\leftarrow I(1^n,f(x))$?
cards.definitions: Uₙ is the uniform distribution on n-bit strings. The function f is computed by one deterministic Turing machine in worst-case polynomial time; in particular its output length is polynomially bounded in n. The inverter receives n in unary and the output f(x), uses independent unbiased random bits, and runs in worst-case polynomial time in the length of its input on every random tape. Its output may be an n-bit candidate or failure. Finding any n-bit preimage counts as success, not only recovering the original x. The probability includes both the choice of x and the inverter’s coins. Formally, for every fixed inverter I and real c>0 there exists N(I,c) such that the inequality holds for every n≥N(I,c). This is eventual negligible inversion probability, not security only at infinitely many lengths. Algorithms have no oracle, nonuniform advice, trapdoor, or quantum computation. The premise P≠NP concerns ordinary uniform deterministic polynomial-time decision versus polynomial-time verification. The task is an existence implication and does not require a black-box construction or a particular proof method.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: A positive answer would base fundamental cryptographic hardness on the best-known general conjecture about efficient computation. A negative answer would demonstrate that efficient verification and worst-case intractability can coexist without this basic form of usable secrecy. The problem identifies the gap between computational difficulty and adversarial security.

progress.text: The theory of computational cryptography develops reductions from one-way functions. Håstad, Impagliazzo, Levin, and Luby establish equivalence between existence of one-way functions and pseudorandom generators.

Wigderson’s Open Problem 4.9 explicitly asks whether P≠NP implies one-way functions, and separately asks about stronger average-case premises and trapdoor conclusions. This card fixes the basic one-way-function implication.

Liu and Pass strengthen characterizations using boundary hardness of randomized time-bounded Kolmogorov complexity. Their ordinary deterministic K^t consequence assumes exponential circuit hardness for derandomization; it does not derive one-way functions from P≠NP alone.

context_blocks.text: If P=NP, an inverter can search for a preimage one bit at a time. At each step, it asks whether the current prefix can be extended to an n-bit string mapping to the given output. That is an NP question because a full preimage is a short efficiently checked certificate. Thus one-way functions imply P≠NP. The missing direction is whether worst-case difficulty alone supplies the required average-case inversion hardness.

A hard instance somewhere is insufficient for security. A polynomial-time inverter might succeed on nearly every output generated from a uniform input and fail only on an extremely rare set. One-wayness must rule out even inverse-polynomial overall success. The distribution is induced by evaluating f on uniform x; requiring hardness on uniformly random output strings would be a different condition, particularly when f has uneven preimage sizes.

One-way functions have unusually broad consequences despite their simple definition. Håstad, Impagliazzo, Levin, and Luby prove that they suffice for pseudorandom generators, with the converse also holding. This makes the question a foundation for computational pseudorandomness and basic cryptographic constructions. Public-key encryption or a trapdoor for inversion would impose additional requirements beyond the target here.

Known barriers constrain certain attempts to turn an arbitrary NP-hard problem into a secure function by oracle reductions. They do not rule out constructions that use more structure or different proof methods. Separating a limitation of a reduction from a negative answer to the mathematical implication is essential.

The 2026 work of Liu and Pass relates one-way functions to boundary hardness of time-bounded description complexity. For the ordinary deterministic description-length formulation, their characterization retains an exponential circuit-hardness derandomization assumption. This is progress on specific sources of cryptographic hardness, but the premise is not merely P≠NP.

cards.title: Does ordinary polynomial-hard LWE suffice for circuit obfuscation?
cards.formal: Does the decisional LWE assumption with the fixed polynomial parameters below imply the existence of indistinguishability obfuscation for all polynomial-size Boolean circuits, with no additional hardness, leakage-resilience, or circular-security assumption? The target is a classical polynomial-time obfuscator secure against classical polynomial-size adversaries.
cards.definitions: Fix q(n) to be the least prime at least n^4 for every integer n≥2. Let χ_n be the discrete Gaussian on Z with probability of e proportional to exp(−πe²/n²). The assumed LWE statement is: for every polynomial m(n), the ensembles (A,A s+e mod q) and (A,u) are computationally indistinguishable, where A is uniform in Z_q^(m×n), s is uniform in Z_q^n, the m coordinates of e are independent χ_n samples, and u is independent uniform in Z_q^m. Indistinguishable means every polynomial-size classical circuit family has negligible advantage in n; negligible means smaller than n^(−c) eventually for every constant c>0. No secret-dependent leakage is supplied. An obfuscator O is a uniform probabilistic algorithm running in time polynomial in λ+|C| that outputs a Boolean circuit O(1^λ,C) of polynomial size. Circuits are finite acyclic AND/OR/NOT circuits with fan-in at most two, a specified list of input and output bits, and explicit binary descriptions; |C| is description length. For every polynomial p, there is negligible μ_p such that for every |C|≤p(λ), with probability at least 1−μ_p(λ) over the obfuscator’s coins the output circuit agrees with C on ALL inputs. For every pair of circuit sequences C_0,λ and C_1,λ with polynomially bounded, equal description lengths, the same input/output lengths and identical functions, their obfuscations are computationally indistinguishable against all polynomial-size circuit families. Both functionality and security quantify over all such circuits, without requiring an efficiently checkable proof of equivalence. There is no oracle, trusted setup, quantum state, or restriction to a special circuit family. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.

cards.why: Asks whether a single basic noisy-linear-equation assumption supports general program obfuscation. Resolving the implication would clarify the strength of LWE and the assumption cost of a broad family of cryptographic constructions that currently use iO as a separate resource.

cards.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. No construction from the plain polynomial-hard decisional-LWE assumption fixed here was identified. Existing multi-assumption and circular-security constructions do not settle it. Polynomial hardness, polynomial modulus/noise ratio, classical adversaries, arbitrary circuits and no auxiliary leakage are explicit choices that make the broad LWE-alone question unambiguous.

context_blocks.text: Indistinguishability obfuscation compares two implementations of exactly the same function. After obfuscation, an efficient observer should not tell which implementation was used. Equality of size prevents a trivial distinction from the amount of code supplied; padding can put implementations under a common size bound. This definition does not say that every secret written into an arbitrary program is hidden. A secret that the function itself reveals through its outputs remains visible.

That distinction is necessary. Barak and coauthors rule out general obfuscation under the stronger virtual-black-box requirement, which would make code reveal no more than oracle access to its function. Their impossibility theorem does not rule out indistinguishability obfuscation. The weaker comparison between equivalent implementations has therefore become a central target, rather than an informal promise to make arbitrary software unreadable.

LWE supplies a particularly concrete potential foundation. Its samples are linear equations modulo a public integer, perturbed by small independent errors. Exact equations would reveal the secret by linear algebra; the errors obstruct that approach. Regev introduced reductions connecting LWE to worst-case lattice problems and used it to build public-key encryption. This card fixes a particular ordinary decisional-LWE ensemble so that the noise distribution, modulus, number of samples, and adversarial resources cannot vary silently.

Jain, Lin, and Sahai established general-circuit iO from a combination of four assumptions: LWE, LPN over large fields, a local Boolean pseudorandom generator, and a bilinear-group assumption. Their theorem uses stronger quantitative security than mere polynomial hardness. Its Journal of the ACM version appeared in February 2026, following the STOC 2021 work. That publication is an important foundation for iO, but is not a 2026 construction from plain LWE alone.

A follow-up by the same authors removes LWE from that combination, leaving the other three assumptions. Eliminating LWE from a sufficient set is logically different from eliminating all the other assumptions while retaining LWE. The follow-up explicitly poses the possibility that LWE alone might suffice, without claiming a resolution.

Brakerski, Döttling, Garg, and Malavolta give another route using LWE-based encryption with circular randomness-leakage resilience. The construction uses that stronger assumption. Its security experiment exposes structured information related to keys and encryption randomness, whereas ordinary LWE supplies only the noisy linear samples defined above. Calling the construction LWE-based therefore does not remove the extra security hypothesis.

A solution would unify the assumptions behind many uses of obfuscation with an established lattice-learning problem. The specific target here is deliberately demanding: ordinary polynomial security and a polynomial modulus-to-noise ratio. Even a construction from plain LWE with stronger quantitative hardness would be substantial progress, but the security loss would still need attention before it established this exact implication. The question concerns mathematical feasibility; it does not impose practical code size or execution speed.

cards.title: Unleveled fully homomorphic encryption from LWE alone
cards.formal: Does ordinary polynomial-modulus decisional LWE, with the parameter convention below, imply a classical compact fully homomorphic encryption scheme whose keys are generated without an evaluation-depth bound, secure against nonuniform polynomial-size adversaries without any additional circular-security or key-dependent-message assumption?
cards.definitions: Fix the following ordinary LWE assumption: for every fixed integer c≥3 and polynomial sample count M(d), let q(d) be the least prime at least d^c, let s be uniform in Z_q^d, let A be uniform in Z_q^{M(d)×d}, and let the coordinates of e be independent integers with probability proportional to exp(−πz²/(4d)), reduced modulo q. The ensembles (A,As+e mod q) and (A,u), for independent uniform u∈Z_q^{M(d)}, are computationally indistinguishable against nonuniform classical circuits of size polynomial in d. Thus the error distribution is the discrete Gaussian D_{Z,2√d}; only ordinary independently generated LWE samples are assumed hard. The FHE scheme has uniform classical polynomial-time algorithms Gen(1^λ)→(pk,evk,sk), Enc(pk,b), Eval(evk,C,c₁,…,c_t), and Dec(sk,c), with bit plaintexts and Boolean circuits over AND, OR and NOT. Gen takes no circuit-size or depth bound. There is one fixed polynomial P such that keys, fresh bit ciphertexts, evaluated one-bit ciphertexts and the time to decrypt a valid output are bounded by P(λ), independently of C and t. Evaluation is polynomial-time in λ and its total input length. For every polynomial p, uniformly over all circuits C of size and input count at most p(λ) and all input bits b₁,…,b_t, decrypting Eval on independent encryptions of these bits equals C(b₁,…,b_t), except with negligible probability over generation, encryption and evaluation. Ordinary decryption is correct with negligible error. Given both pk and evk, every nonuniform polynomial-size classical adversary has negligible advantage in distinguishing an encryption of 0 from one of 1. Negligible means smaller than λ^{-a} eventually for every a>0. This fixes a polynomial-modulus version of “standard LWE”; it does not assume any encryptions of secrets or correlated hints are secure.

cards.status_note: No classical unleveled compact FHE construction from the specified ordinary LWE assumption alone was found through 11 September 2026. Functional-encryption constructions use additional assumptions. The inspected February and April 2026 no-circularity proposals retain explicit level bounds; the latter also uses quantum evaluation. This card fixes polynomial-modulus LWE, nonuniform classical security and fresh-input FHE correctness.

context_blocks.text: Homomorphic encryption lets a server compute on encrypted data and return an encrypted answer. Compactness makes this substantive: the client should decrypt a short answer, rather than receive the original ciphertexts together with the whole circuit and perform the computation itself. Here all four algorithms are classical, and the ciphertext for one output bit remains bounded by a fixed polynomial in the security parameter.

The order of choices is the heart of the problem. In a leveled scheme, the user first chooses a maximum depth L and generates keys suitable for that level. This can support every circuit up to L without revealing the data. The present question asks for one key-generation algorithm that receives only the security parameter and supports every polynomial-depth circuit later supplied to the evaluator. Choosing L=λ¹⁰ during setup still leaves deeper polynomial computations outside the guarantee.

Lattice ciphertexts generally include small errors that hide the plaintext. Homomorphic operations transform the desired message and these errors together. Once the error exceeds the decryption tolerance, the output may no longer decode correctly. Gentry’s bootstrapping idea refreshes a ciphertext by homomorphically evaluating a decryption circuit, with the secret key itself provided in encrypted form. Micciancio’s teaching slides explain both this noise issue and the associated circular-security question.

A chain of independent keys avoids the immediate circularity. Encrypt the secret key at level i under the public key at level i+1, then use the next level to refresh the current ciphertext. The usual hybrid proof can replace those encryptions in reverse order because the chain has an endpoint. But the public material grows with the number of refreshes planned in advance. Closing the chain into a cycle reuses a bounded collection of keys and changes the security argument.

Brakerski and Vaikuntanathan’s construction makes the distinction explicit in its journal abstract: ordinary LWE gives leveled FHE, while removing the depth restriction uses an additional weak circular-security assumption. Later bootstrapping work supports polynomial-modulus parameters and polynomial lattice approximation factors. Improvements in error growth and efficiency do not themselves justify exposing the secret-key encryptions needed to reuse the keys.

The requested proof need not avoid bootstrapping, or even avoid encrypted keys. It must justify the actual public evaluation information using ordinary LWE alone. Conversely, it is not enough to prove that some artificially designed CPA-secure encryption scheme becomes insecure when encrypting its own key. Such a counterexample refutes an automatic upgrade for every scheme; it does not rule out designing a particular FHE scheme with a valid ordinary-LWE proof.

Bitansky and Solomon obtain FHE without circular-security assumptions using functional encryption, under polynomial hardness assumptions. This is a significant positive result for a broader assumption set. In their ITCS 2023 construction, the available functional-encryption instantiation uses assumptions including LPN, bilinear SXDH and shallow pseudorandom generators, in addition to the LWE-based homomorphic component. The basic theorem protects against uniform adversaries; their nonuniform extension requires an additional worst-case complexity assumption. Neither version establishes LWE alone under the convention here.

Recent claims also require checking the formal setup. Wang, Huang and Tang’s February 2026 dynamic multi-key scheme advertises avoiding a common reference string and circular security. Definition 2.2 nevertheless gives Setup the depth parameter L, and the construction chooses its dimension and modulus using L. Its stated compactness also permits dependence on L. This is a leveled guarantee, even though the number of participating keys can change dynamically.

Liu and coauthors’ April 2026 quantum homomorphic proposal also advertises classical LWE and no circular-security assumption. Its Section 3.4 uses L+1 independent key layers; a later discussion explicitly preallocates L evaluation gadgets. It therefore retains a level bound, and its evaluator performs quantum operations. These scope differences already prevent it from settling the classical, depth-independent target; this review does not validate its separate efficiency or quantum-security claims.

There is a further definitional distinction between evaluating one arbitrary circuit on fresh ciphertexts and repeatedly evaluating new circuits on the resulting ciphertexts. Micciancio’s slides show that correctness for the first task does not automatically imply correctness for the second. This card asks for the usual fresh-input FHE guarantee. Establishing full composability would be an additional accomplishment, rather than an implicit condition that makes the target harder.

A solution would remove a central gap between the clean assumption used to prove the security of leveled lattice encryption and the extra assumption used to reuse a fixed key set indefinitely over polynomial computations. It would clarify the foundation of FHE independently of practical parameter optimization, and could improve the assumptions of constructions that use unrestricted encrypted computation as a component.

cards.title: Can every perfect secret-sharing access structure use shares below exponent one half?
cards.formal: Do there exist real constants K>0 and 0<c<1/2 such that, for every n≥1 and every monotone access structure Γ on [n] with ∅∉Γ and [n]∈Γ, there exists a perfect secret-sharing scheme for a uniform one-bit secret with max_i log₂|S_i|≤K·2^(cn), where S_i is the finite alphabet of participant i’s share?
cards.why: A worst-case storage benchmark for information-theoretic access control, separating the power of general secret sharing from linear schemes. The newly reported bound directly addresses its strict exponential threshold.

cards.definitions: [n]={1,…,n}. An access structure Γ⊆2^[n] is monotone when A∈Γ and A⊆B⊆[n] imply B∈Γ. A scheme is a joint probability distribution of a secret B uniform on {0,1} and shares X_i∈S_i, where each S_i is a finite nonempty set. For each A∈Γ there is a deterministic map r_A:∏_{i∈A}S_i→{0,1} such that r_A((X_i)_{i∈A})=B with probability one. For each A∉Γ, the conditional distributions of (X_i)_{i∈A} given B=0 and B=1 are identical. This is exact reconstruction and perfect information-theoretic privacy, with arbitrary collusion within A. Share size is the base-two logarithm of its alphabet cardinality, not its Shannon entropy or the sum over participants. It is normalized by the secret size of one bit. There is no linearity, field, threshold, computation-time or uniform construction requirement. The scheme may depend on the whole finite access structure. K,c must be universal. Rounding log₂|S_i| up to an integer encoding length changes K only by an absolute factor.
cards.answer_criterion: Establish universal K>0 and 0<c<1/2 with the stated guarantee for every n and every monotone access structure, or prove that no such constants exist. A refutation must rule out all permitted schemes, including nonlinear ones. An upper bound with exponent exactly 1/2 or a lower bound confined to linear schemes does not resolve the target.

context_blocks.text: Status update: Nir’s August 2026 preprint states a directly matching positive result. Theorem 1.5 gives every n-party access structure a scheme for a one-bit secret with maximal share size 2^{0.496n+o(n)}. Taking any fixed c between 0.496 and 1/2 absorbs the sublinear exponent for large n; a universal K covers the finitely many smaller sizes. The proof has not been independently verified here, so the card records an uncertain claimed resolution.

An access structure describes which groups may reconstruct a secret. It need not depend only on group size: a designated participant may be essential, or several different combinations may be authorized. Monotonicity means that an authorized group stays authorized when more participants join. Perfect privacy requires even an unlimited observer holding every share of an unauthorized group to see the same distribution for either secret value.

For example, suppose participant 1 together with either participant 2 or participant 3 may reconstruct a bit B. Choose an independent uniform bit R and give shares R, B XOR R, B XOR R respectively. Either authorized pair recovers B by XOR. Participants 2 and 3 together see two copies of a uniform masked bit and learn nothing about B; participant 1 alone sees independent randomness. This simple access structure needs only one bit per share, but arbitrary patterns can be much harder.

The question concerns the largest participant’s stored alphabet, measured in bits. A share with M possible values costs log₂ M, even if its probability distribution has smaller entropy. The total share size is between the largest share and n times that share; these measures have the same leading exponential rate. None of these conventions permits replacing perfect privacy by computational secrecy or small statistical leakage.

The classical construction treats authorized sets separately and can use exponentially large shares. Successive results reduced the exponent; Applebaum and Nir’s 2021 bound is 1.5^{n+o(n)}, equivalently 2^{0.58496…n+o(n)}. This remains above the half exponent requested in the seminar question. The seminar list prints a different earlier upper exponent; the primary construction is used for the historical bound recorded here.

Linearity is a real restriction: shares are linear combinations of the secret and random field elements. Known exponential lower bounds for linear schemes do not apply to all joint distributions allowed in this card. Likewise, lower bounds for particular reconstruction degrees or graph access structures need their own hypotheses. A general upper bound must handle every monotone authorized-group pattern, with one universal exponent.

The same 2026 preprint gives a half-exponent linear construction and a strictly smaller nonlinear exponent. Its nonlinear theorem is the part relevant to this card; the linear theorem alone would not satisfy c<1/2.

cards.definitions: The security parameter n≥1 is given in unary as 1ⁿ. A single deterministic Turing machine computes f on every finite binary string in time polynomial in its input length. Each inverter I is one classical randomized Turing machine with a worst-case polynomial running-time bound; its input contains 1ⁿ, so its running time and output length are polynomial in n. It receives f(X), not X, and has no advice, oracle or secret information. An output Y succeeds exactly when f(Y)=f(X); any preimage is accepted, even one of a different length from X. An explicit failure output is unsuccessful. No injectivity, permutation property or length preservation is imposed. A probability function is negligible if it is eventually at most n⁻ᵈ for each integer d≥1. The threshold n₀ can depend on I and d. Security is averaged over the uniformly sampled input and the inverter’s coins, and must hold for all sufficiently large n, not merely an infinite subsequence.
cards.answer_criterion: A positive resolution proves, without an unproved computational hardness assumption, that at least one f satisfies the stated efficiency and inversion bound. A negative resolution proves that every polynomial-time f has a polynomial-time inverter whose success is non-negligible: for some d≥1 it exceeds n⁻ᵈ for infinitely many n. A conditional construction or a failure of one particular candidate does not decide existence.

context_blocks.title: What must be hard
context_blocks.text: Computing an output and finding an input that produces it are different tasks. The experiment first generates an ordinary random input, computes its image, and asks an efficient algorithm for any matching input. The difficulty must survive every polynomial-time inverter on this distribution. A few exceptional hard inputs, or a single unsuccessful attack, do not establish this average-case guarantee.

context_blocks.title: Forgetting information is not enough
context_blocks.text: Suppose f keeps the first ⌈n/2⌉ bits of an n-bit input and discards the rest. Recovering the exact original random string would usually be impossible because the discarded bits are missing. Inversion as defined here is easy: append enough zero bits to obtain an n-bit string with the given prefix. Its image is the required value. This example explains why the success condition accepts any preimage and why simple information loss is not cryptographic hardness.

context_blocks.title: How strong is negligible success?
context_blocks.text: An inverter that succeeds with probability 1/n¹⁰ still violates the requirement. A probability such as 2⁻ⁿ is negligible, while 1/n¹⁰ is not. The quantifiers allow a different eventual threshold for each algorithm and each requested exponent. They do not ask for a single finite input length at which every conceivable polynomial-time program is already defeated. The forward computation and all adversaries here are classical; a quantum primitive with different inputs or outputs is a separate model.

context_blocks.title: Relation to other open questions
context_blocks.text: One-way functions would imply P≠NP, since P=NP would permit efficient search for a polynomial-length preimage. Whether P≠NP alone implies their existence is separately recorded in TCS-0022. One-way functions are equivalent to several basic cryptographic primitives, including pseudorandom generators and suitable private-key encryption, but it is not known whether they suffice for public-key encryption; that implication is TCS-6545. cards.context:
Computing an output and finding an input that produces it are different tasks. The experiment first generates an ordinary random input, computes its image, and asks an efficient algorithm for any matching input. The difficulty must survive every polynomial-time inverter on this distribution. A few exceptional hard inputs, or a single unsuccessful attack, do not establish this average-case guarantee.

Suppose f keeps the first ⌈n/2⌉ bits of an n-bit input and discards the rest. Recovering the exact original random string would usually be impossible because the discarded bits are missing. Inversion as defined here is easy: append enough zero bits to obtain an n-bit string with the given prefix. Its image is the required value. This example explains why the success condition accepts any preimage and why simple information loss is not cryptographic hardness.

An inverter that succeeds with probability 1/n¹⁰ still violates the requirement. A probability such as 2⁻ⁿ is negligible, while 1/n¹⁰ is not. The quantifiers allow a different eventual threshold for each algorithm and each requested exponent. They do not ask for a single finite input length at which every conceivable polynomial-time program is already defeated. The forward computation and all adversaries here are classical; a quantum primitive with different inputs or outputs is a separate model.

cards.definitions: For security parameter n≥1, Gen(1ⁿ) samples a public key pk and a secret key sk. Enc(1ⁿ,pk,m) takes a bit m∈{0,1} and fresh independent coins and outputs a binary ciphertext; Dec(1ⁿ,sk,c) returns a bit or failure. All three algorithms have worst-case polynomial running time in their input length. Correctness means that max over m∈{0,1} of Pr[Dec(1ⁿ,sk,Enc(1ⁿ,pk,m))≠m] is negligible in n, with probability over key generation, encryption and any decryption coins. For IND-CPA, Gen runs first, and a uniform PPT adversary A₁ receives (1ⁿ,pk) and outputs bits m₀,m₁ and a state z. Independently choose a uniform bit b, generate c=Enc(1ⁿ,pk,m_b), and give (1ⁿ,pk,z,c) to its second stage A₂, which outputs a bit b′. For every pair (A₁,A₂), |Pr[b′=b]−1/2| must be negligible. A function η(n) is negligible if, for every integer d≥1, η(n)≤n⁻ᵈ for all sufficiently large n. Adversaries may run the public encryption algorithm themselves polynomially many times before and after seeing c; there is no decryption oracle. The model has no trusted correlated setup, ideal oracle, secret advice or quantum algorithms. The receiver’s public key is given authentically; its replacement by an active attacker is outside this confidentiality experiment. One-bit message space fixes an equivalent existence question: independent bit encryptions and the standard hybrid argument extend IND-CPA security to every polynomial message length.
cards.answer_criterion: A positive resolution proves existence of a scheme satisfying the stated correctness and computational indistinguishability bounds with no unproved computational assumption. A negative resolution proves that every efficient correct scheme fails that security requirement. An assumed-hardness construction, experimental resistance to attacks, or an impossibility theorem only for unbounded attackers does not settle this question.

context_blocks.title: Public information, private recovery
context_blocks.text: A sender receives the public key and can encrypt a message without knowing the secret key. The receiver can decrypt with that secret key. An observer has the same public encryption capability as the sender, so secrecy must come from a limitation on computation rather than from hiding the encryption algorithm. The question asks whether such a limitation can be proved to exist for some efficient scheme.

context_blocks.title: Why the challenge compares two messages
context_blocks.text: The adversary chooses two messages after seeing the public key, then receives an encryption of a fair random choice between them. Guessing always gives success 1/2. Security requires every efficient adversary’s additional advantage to be negligible. This is stronger than merely failing to recover a long message exactly: learning one distinguishing bit can already violate the requirement. Restricting the displayed experiment to message bits keeps the existence question concrete without requiring a particular practical ciphertext format.

context_blocks.title: A simple failure of deterministic encryption
context_blocks.text: Imagine that encryption uses no fresh randomness and the two possible messages are 0 and 1. Anyone with the public key can compute both ciphertexts and compare the challenge with them. On keys for which both messages decrypt correctly, the two ciphertexts must differ, so the comparison reveals the challenge bit. Randomized encryption avoids this immediate comparison attack, but randomness by itself is not a proof of security.

context_blocks.title: Which assumptions are still missing?
context_blocks.text: Regev’s lattice-based construction gives classical public-key encryption from learning-with-errors hardness. This is a theorem relating two computational tasks; it does not prove the assumed task hard. In March 2026, Lu, Poremba, Quek and Ramkumar gave another conditional route based on average-case hardness of quantum stabilizer decoding, with classical cryptographic algorithms. A new candidate assumption broadens the foundations available for constructions while leaving unconditional existence unresolved. The word quantum in the underlying decoding problem does not itself make the encryption algorithms quantum.

context_blocks.title: The boundary of the question
context_blocks.text: Secure public-key encryption implies one-way functions and hence P≠NP. The converse implication from arbitrary one-way functions is a separate open question, TCS-6545; proving that implication alone would still leave their existence unproved. Computational security here permits an unbounded adversary to succeed. Consequently, the impossibility of information-theoretic secrecy from only public information does not answer the present question. Chosen-ciphertext security adds access to a decryption oracle and is also a different requirement. The requested theorem concerns precisely efficient classical attackers in the stated chosen-plaintext experiment.

cards.title: Do one-way functions imply classical key agreement?
cards.formal: Does the existence of a classical one-way function imply the existence of a classical two-party key-agreement protocol with negligible disagreement and computationally secret shared keys, against passive probabilistic polynomial-time eavesdroppers, in the plain public-channel model defined below?
cards.definitions: All algorithms are uniform classical probabilistic Turing machines; security parameter λ is supplied in unary. A one-way function is a deterministic polynomial-time f:{0,1}*→{0,1}* such that, for every probabilistic polynomial-time I, Pr[f(Y)=f(X) and |Y|=λ] is negligible in λ, where X is uniform in {0,1}^λ and Y is the single output of I(1^λ,f(X)); probability also includes I’s private coins. A function μ:N→[0,1] is negligible if for every integer d≥1 there is λ₀ such that μ(λ)≤λ^(−d) for all λ≥λ₀. The protocol consists of two interactive machines A,B with independent private fair coins and total worst-case computation and communication polynomial in λ. They exchange classical messages on a noiseless public channel, with no correlated initial secrets, trusted setup, random oracle or quantum communication. At termination each outputs a λ-bit string K_A,K_B. Correctness requires Pr[K_A≠K_B] to be negligible. Let T be the full public transcript, and let U_λ be an independent uniform λ-bit string. For every probabilistic polynomial-time distinguisher D, |Pr[D(1^λ,T,K_A)=1]−Pr[D(1^λ,T,U_λ)=1]| must be negligible, over the honest coins, D’s coins and U_λ. The eavesdropper observes T but does not alter the messages. The target is the unrelativized existence implication; neither the construction nor its proof is required to treat f as a black box. Both premise and conclusion use the same uniform adversary convention.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation, with all definitions, promises, resource bounds and quantifiers as stated. A conditional result establishes only the explicitly conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-verified proof of the full target.

context_blocks.text: A one-way function supplies a computational asymmetry: evaluating it is easy, while recovering a preimage of a random image is hard. Key agreement asks for a different capability. Two parties begin without a common secret and exchange visible messages, yet their final common key must remain hidden from an observer. The question is whether the first kind of asymmetry always suffices for the second.

The security definition concerns the entire transcript. Merely showing that a transcript has many possible explanations is insufficient if an efficient observer can identify the common key. Likewise, keeping each party’s private randomness hidden is weaker than hiding the particular string on which both parties agree. Comparing the actual key with an independent uniform key makes the secrecy requirement explicit.

Impagliazzo and Rudich established a black-box barrier between one-way functions and key agreement. Couteau, Farshim and Mahmoody’s 2021 work studies stronger notions of black-box uselessness and proves results for specified restricted settings. Such results delimit families of constructions; they do not refute the unrestricted existence implication on this card.

The existing TCS-6545 asks for public-key encryption from one-way functions. Public-key encryption would yield a key-agreement protocol by sending a fresh random key under the published encryption key. General interactive key agreement is a separate, weaker desired primitive. A negative conclusion about a restricted encryption construction cannot by itself rule out all interactive protocols.

The classical and passive conventions matter. Quantum key distribution uses an additional communication resource, while protection against an active man-in-the-middle requires an authentication model. Neither is part of this target. The card isolates the foundational question of creating a secret by classical public interaction from the minimal generic computational assumption.

cards.title: Does public-key encryption imply oblivious transfer?
cards.formal: In the classical plain model, does the existence of an IND-CPA-secure public-key encryption scheme for bits imply the existence of a polynomial-time 1-out-of-2 bit oblivious-transfer protocol secure against static semi-honest corruption of either party? Both primitives have negligible error and computational security as defined below. The implication may use arbitrary non-black-box techniques and a polynomial number of communication rounds.
cards.definitions: The security parameter is λ, supplied in unary. Honest algorithms are uniform probabilistic polynomial-time Turing machines; adversarial distinguishers are polynomial-size classical circuit families. A function μ is negligible if for every c>0, μ(λ)<λ^(−c) for all sufficiently large λ. Public-key encryption consists of KeyGen(1^λ)=(pk,sk), Enc(pk,m;r), and Dec(sk,c), for m∈{0,1}; decryption fails with negligible probability over key generation and encryption coins, for each m. IND-CPA means that no such adversary given pk distinguishes Enc(pk,0) from Enc(pk,1) with nonnegligible advantage; public encryption is available to it. In OT, sender S has bits (m_0,m_1), receiver R has a choice bit c, and R must output m_c except with negligible probability for every input triple; S has no output. The parties follow their prescribed algorithms but keep their entire views, including inputs, random tapes, and messages. There must be uniform probabilistic polynomial-time simulators Sim_S(1^λ,m_0,m_1) and Sim_R(1^λ,c,m_c) whose outputs are computationally indistinguishable from the corresponding real views for every sequence of input triples. Thus S learns nothing about c and R learns nothing beyond (c,m_c). The parties have independent private randomness and exchange classical messages directly. There is no trusted setup, common reference string, random oracle, pre-shared correlated randomness, trusted hardware, or quantum resource.
cards.answer_criterion: Establish the stated existence implication without a second unproved hardness assumption, or refute that unrelativized implication. A construction may inspect and use the code of the encryption algorithms and use non-black-box security arguments. An oracle separation or a lower bound restricted to black-box reductions is a barrier, not a negative resolution of this question. A construction requiring an additional property of encryption must also derive that property from arbitrary IND-CPA encryption to settle the card.
cards.why: Determines whether the ability to send secrets to a designated receiver already suffices for general private computation between mutually distrustful parties. It is a basic boundary in the hierarchy of cryptographic assumptions, with a longstanding black-box barrier and no known unrestricted implication.

importance.reason: A foundational comparison between ordinary public-key confidentiality and a primitive complete for secure computation; resolving it would change which assumptions suffice for a broad range of protocols.

progress.text: Gertner and coauthors prove an oracle with PKE but no semi-honest OT, and give positive constructions when PKE has specified extra properties. Their oracle separations use uniform adversaries.
Haitner and coauthors give a fully black-box compiler from semi-honest to malicious OT and general secure computation, establishing the strength of even the passive-security target.
Maji and Wang prove limitations on optimal fair coin tossing from black-box PKE or key agreement; this is further evidence about restricted constructions, not an unrestricted separation.
Li, Zhang, and Lin construct OT from rerandomizable PKE, replacing oblivious sampling with a public ciphertext-rerandomization requirement.
The journal version of Tanishita and coauthors’ work derives OT from updatable encryption with additional sampling properties. It does not remove all extra assumptions on the starting primitive.

cards.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. No unrestricted classical implication from arbitrary IND-CPA public-key encryption to OT was identified. Known oracle/black-box separations and positive results for rerandomizable or suitably samplable encryption do not settle this formulation. The card fixes semi-honest standalone security with classical communication and no setup.

context_blocks.text: Ordinary encryption protects a message from someone who lacks the secret key. Oblivious transfer must arrange a more selective situation: the receiver can read one of two messages, cannot read the other, and does not disclose which one it selected. This combines privacy for both participants. Merely encrypting both messages under a key generated by the receiver fails, because that receiver can decrypt both ciphertexts. Asking the receiver to reveal which key it can decrypt would instead reveal its choice.

Some encryption schemes offer the missing structure. If a receiver can create two indistinguishable-looking public keys while knowing a decryption key for just one, it can place the decryptable key in position c. The sender encrypts the two messages under the corresponding keys. Such an argument needs a suitable oblivious-sampling property, including security even given the sampler’s retained randomness. Gertner and coauthors identify sufficient properties and also prove an oracle separation between general PKE and even semi-honest OT. Their historical separation uses uniform adversaries.

That result constrains a style of construction, rather than deciding the unrestricted implication. In an oracle argument all algorithms are given access to an additional idealized operation. A construction based on the actual implementation of an encryption scheme may use features that do not survive replacement by an arbitrary oracle. Consequently, the qualifier allowing non-black-box techniques is substantive; removing it would turn the card into a question already addressed by known barriers.

The semi-honest target is already powerful. Haitner, Ishai, Kushilevitz, Lindell, and Petrank show how to transform semi-honest OT into OT secure against malicious parties, and obtain general secure computation without an honest majority. Their result fixes static corruption and standalone security; it does not promise fairness or guaranteed output delivery against a party that aborts. This explains why the basic passive-security implication matters without building stronger composition or fairness requirements into the question.

Progress continues through additional algebraic or sampling structure. Li, Zhang, and Lin construct OT from rerandomizable PKE: anyone with the public key can turn a ciphertext into a fresh encryption of the same plaintext. This avoids their predecessors’ oblivious-sampling requirement but introduces a different hypothesis. Ordinary IND-CPA security alone does not include a public rerandomization algorithm.

A 2026 journal paper by Tanishita and coauthors studies updatable encryption, where update tokens let a third party transform ciphertexts across keys. With specified oblivious-sampling properties, it derives two- or three-round OT. Those theorems refine the boundary for a structured encryption primitive. They do not give a transformation starting with an arbitrary public-key encryption scheme.

A related barrier concerns fair coin tossing. Maji and Wang show limits for protocols using public-key encryption or key agreement as black boxes, whereas OT supports optimally fair constructions. This gives another operational way to see the distinction between ordinary encrypted communication and primitives complete for secure computation. The fairness result has its own model and does not constitute a proof against all non-black-box OT constructions.
