If a receiver can create two indistinguishable-looking public keys while knowing a decryption key for just one, it can place the decryptable key in position c. The sender encrypts the two messages under the corresponding keys. Such an argument needs a suitable oblivious-sampling property, including security even given the sampler’s retained randomness. Gertner and coauthors identify sufficient properties and also prove an oracle separation between general PKE and even semi-honest OT. Their historical separation uses uniform adversaries.

That result constrains a style of construction, rather than deciding the unrestricted implication. In an oracle argument all algorithms are given access to an additional idealized operation. A construction based on the actual implementation of an encryption scheme may use features that do not survive replacement by an arbitrary oracle. Consequently, the qualifier allowing non-black-box techniques is substantive; removing it would turn the card into a question already addressed by known barriers.

The semi-honest target is already powerful. Haitner, Ishai, Kushilevitz, Lindell, and Petrank show how to transform semi-honest OT into OT secure against malicious parties, and obtain general secure computation without an honest majority. Their result fixes static corruption and standalone security; it does not promise fairness or guaranteed output delivery against a party that aborts. This explains why the basic passive-security implication matters without building stronger composition or fairness requirements into the question.

Progress continues through additional algebraic or sampling structure. Li, Zhang, and Lin construct OT from rerandomizable PKE: anyone with the public key can turn a ciphertext into a fresh encryption of the same plaintext. This avoids their predecessors’ oblivious-sampling requirement but introduces a different hypothesis. Ordinary IND-CPA security alone does not include a public rerandomization algorithm.

A 2026 journal paper by Tanishita and coauthors studies updatable encryption, where update tokens let a third party transform ciphertexts across keys. With specified oblivious-sampling properties, it derives two- or three-round OT. Those theorems refine the boundary for a structured encryption primitive. They do not give a transformation starting with an arbitrary public-key encryption scheme.

A related barrier concerns fair coin tossing. Maji and Wang show limits for protocols using public-key encryption or key agreement as black boxes, whereas OT supports optimally fair constructions. This gives another operational way to see the distinction between ordinary encrypted communication and primitives complete for secure computation. The fairness result has its own model and does not constitute a proof against all non-black-box OT constructions.

cards.title: Does one-wayness suffice for collision-resistant hashing?
cards.formal: In the ordinary classical computational model, does the existence of a polynomial-time computable one-way function secure against all polynomial-size circuit families imply the existence of a publicly keyed collision-resistant hash family H_k:{0,1}^{2λ}→{0,1}^λ secure against all polynomial-size circuit families?
cards.definitions: A one-way function is a deterministic uniformly polynomial-time computable map f on finite binary strings, with output length bounded by a polynomial in the input length, such that for every family of possibly randomized Boolean circuits A_n of size polynomial in n, Pr[f(A_n(1^n,f(X)))=f(X) and |A_n(1^n,f(X))|=n] is negligible in n, where X is uniform on {0,1}^n. The same invocation of A_n supplies the candidate preimage in both parts of this event. A function μ is negligible if for every c>0 there is N_c such that μ(n)≤n^{-c} for all n≥N_c. A hash family consists of a uniform probabilistic polynomial-time key generator Gen(1^λ) producing a polynomial-length public key k, and a uniform deterministic polynomial-time evaluator H(1^λ,k,x). For every key in the generator’s support, H_k maps every 2λ-bit input to a λ-bit output. Collision resistance means that for every polynomial-size possibly randomized circuit family B_λ, the probability that B_λ(1^λ,k) outputs distinct x,x′∈{0,1}^{2λ} with H_k(x)=H_k(x′) is negligible in λ, over k←Gen(1^λ) and the attacker’s coins. Both messages may be chosen after the attacker sees k. Circuit descriptions may depend on the security parameter, but not on the freshly sampled key. The implication permits arbitrary use of the description of f and arbitrary proof techniques; no random oracle, additional setup assumption, quantum resource, trapdoor, or stronger quantitative hardness assumption is supplied.
cards.answer_criterion: Establish the stated existence implication without additional assumptions, or refute it in the ordinary unrelativized model. A positive result may use non-black-box techniques. An oracle world where one-way functions exist but collision-resistant hashing fails proves only a relativizing barrier. Failure of a particular construction, even for a specific one-way function, is also insufficient to refute the existence implication. Producing only target-collision resistance, noncompressing injective functions, or a construction from stronger product-hardness assumptions does not settle the proposition.

Existing black-box separations do not settle this ordinary-model existence statement. The definitions explicitly use uniform honest algorithms, nonuniform classical adversaries, public fresh keys and factor-two compression.

context_blocks.text: A collision-resistant hash compresses its input while making it computationally difficult to find two distinct messages with the same digest. Collisions must exist by the pigeonhole principle: there are 2^{2λ} possible inputs and only 2^λ outputs. Security is therefore not a claim that collisions never occur, or that a digest uniquely identifies a message. It is a claim about what an efficient adversary can construct after learning the hash key.

A one-way function poses a different challenge. The attacker receives the image of a random input and must find any preimage. An injective one-way function can have no collisions at all, yet it is not a compressing hash. Conversely, a compressing map may have easily found collisions even if some inversion tasks look difficult. The question asks whether the minimal assumption of computationally hard inversion can always supply the more structured difficulty of finding collisions.

The public key matters to the asymptotic definition. If a single compressing function were fixed at each security parameter and security were required against nonuniform circuits, an attacker could hard-code one collision for each parameter. A fresh polynomial-length key prevents that pair from being selected in advance for the actual function used. The key is not secret: the adversary sees it before choosing either colliding message.

Target-collision resistance changes the order of moves. An attacker first commits to one message, then sees a random key and seeks a second message colliding with its committed target. Rompel constructs universal one-way hash functions of this kind from arbitrary one-way functions, as part of the route to secure signatures. That theorem does not give the present game, where both messages are chosen after the key is known. The order difference is small syntactically but central to the unresolved assumption gap.

Simon constructs an oracle setting with one-way permutations but no collision-resistant hash functions in the relevant relativized sense. It rules out building and proving the desired primitive by treating the assumed function purely as an oracle in the separated framework. The theorem does not rule out exploiting a function’s implementation or a proof that fails to relativize. The ordinary mathematical implication in this card therefore remains stronger than the black-box construction question already answered negatively.

Holmgren and Lombardi give a positive route under stronger assumptions about simultaneously inverting independent challenges. Their one-way product functions require quantitative batch hardness beyond ordinary one-wayness. They construct collision-resistant hashing from suitable such functions and connect the missing assumption to unusually strong parallel repetition. This identifies a concrete intermediate target without showing that every ordinary one-way function possesses the required batch security.

The separation also connects hashing to total search problems. Given a circuit for a compressing map, a collision is guaranteed to exist and can be checked efficiently. Folwarczný and coauthors study whether one-way functions can establish hardness for total NP search more generally, extending limitations for a class of single-query reductions. These are restrictions on reductions, not an unconditional proof that collision-resistant families cannot follow from one-wayness by any method.

Applications can sometimes avoid the full primitive. Rothblum’s July 2026 work constructs efficient interactive arguments for bounded-space computations from one-way functions. Communication depends on the space bound times a polynomial in log T and the security parameter, and the security loss depends polynomially on the computation time T. This weakens assumptions for that interactive application; it does not construct a publicly evaluable compressing hash that withstands arbitrary key-dependent collision attempts.

A resolution would clarify the foundations of many protocols that use short commitments to large data. It would either place full collision resistance on the same assumption level as ordinary one-wayness, or demonstrate a separation that survives beyond black-box barriers. The card asks for polynomial security only; requiring near-optimal exponential security or resistance to quantum attacks would introduce additional questions.

cards.title: One-way permutations from one-way functions
cards.formal: Does the existence of classical one-way functions secure against nonuniform polynomial-size adversaries imply the existence of a classical, efficiently generated family of full-domain one-way permutations with the same security convention?
cards.definitions: A one-way function is a uniformly polynomial-time computable family f_n:{0,1}ⁿ→{0,1}^{ℓ(n)}, for a polynomially bounded, computable output length ℓ, such that for every randomized polynomial-size circuit family A_n, Pr[f_n(A_n(1ⁿ,f_n(X)))=f_n(X)] is negligible in n for uniform X∈{0,1}ⁿ; outputs outside {0,1}ⁿ fail. A function μ is negligible if for every c>0, μ(n)≤n^{-c} for all sufficiently large n. A permutation family consists of a uniform probabilistic polynomial-time key generator Gen(1ⁿ) and deterministic polynomial-time evaluation Eval(1ⁿ,pk,x), with a fixed polynomially bounded, polynomial-time computable integer m(n)≥n. For every pk in the support of Gen(1ⁿ), Eval defines a bijection π_pk:{0,1}^{m(n)}→{0,1}^{m(n)}. For every randomized polynomial-size adversary A_n, Pr[π_pk(A_n(1ⁿ,pk,π_pk(X)))=π_pk(X)] must be negligible, with pk←Gen(1ⁿ), independent uniform X and independent adversary coins. Malformed outputs fail. The public key is available to the attacker; no trapdoor is required or given. All security is classical. “Full-domain” fixes the input set to the whole Boolean cube; the valid public-key set need not be all bit strings of its length. The implication is an ordinary existence implication, without restrictions to black-box constructions and without extra assumptions such as obfuscation or subexponential security.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the stated existence implication, allowing any mathematical construction or proof technique, or refute that implication in the ordinary computational model. Proving that one-way functions do not exist would make the implication vacuously true. An oracle separation or a theorem excluding a restricted class of reductions is a construction barrier, not a refutation of the unrestricted implication. A permutation family on special sparse domains does not meet the full-domain convention fixed here; an additional trapdoor property would be a stronger positive result.
cards.why: Determine whether basic average-case inversion hardness necessarily supports efficient bijections, a rigid primitive at the foundation of cryptographic constructions.

This card explicitly fixes the full-domain keyed convention.

context_blocks.text: A one-way function is easy to evaluate but hard to invert on a random input. It may identify many different inputs and need not cover its output space. A one-way permutation has exactly one preimage for every output in its domain. The extra requirement is structural: nothing is lost mathematically, yet efficiently recovering the uniquely determined input must remain infeasible.

This card fixes the full-domain, public-key family version because the original phrase “one-way permutation” leaves several conventions unspecified. A public key chooses a permutation of an entire Boolean cube; all input strings of that length are valid. A stronger unkeyed formulation asks for a single length-preserving permutation on all bit strings. A more permissive formulation allows key-dependent sparse domains. Results in those settings must be compared with their domain and sampling requirements visible.

Making a computation reversible is not enough. The map (x,z)↦(x,z XOR f(x)) is a bijection for any efficiently computable length-compatible f, but its inverse is obtained by applying exactly the same map. Likewise, simply attaching x to f(x) makes the output injective while revealing the desired preimage. The construction has to preserve computational difficulty while removing collisions and covering the domain, without publishing the information needed for inversion.

Many other forms of cryptographic structure can be derived from bare one-wayness. Håstad, Impagliazzo, Levin and Luby show that every one-way function yields a pseudorandom generator. That success does not enforce bijectivity. The permutation question tests whether computational hardness can always be reorganized into a particularly rigid, uniquely invertible mathematical object.

Rudich’s 1988 thesis developed the oracle-separation approach and gave a barrier for this implication conditional on a combinatorial conjecture. The thesis abstract states that qualification explicitly. It is misleading to describe the original thesis alone as an unconditional separation of the ordinary existence assumptions. An oracle world changes what algorithms can access, so it diagnoses limitations of proof techniques rather than settling the actual implication.

Matsuda and Matsuura subsequently prove a fully black-box barrier even when the starting function is injective, increases length by only one bit, and satisfies their stronger adaptive one-wayness condition. Thus an apparently tiny departure from a permutation already defeats a broad class of generic constructions. Their result concerns constructions that treat the supplied primitive and adversary through specified interfaces; it does not exclude exploiting the code or other structure of a concrete function.

Asharov and Segev address another subtlety: earlier negative arguments could fail when the construction’s domains depended on the underlying primitives. They exclude black-box constructions from one-way functions even without that domain-invariance requirement. They also give a separate barrier for constructions using oracle-aided indistinguishability obfuscation, under domain-invariance conditions. The two statements have different assumptions and should not be merged into an unrestricted impossibility theorem.

There is significant progress with stronger assumptions. Shmueli and Zhandry’s July 2025 paper constructs full-domain trapdoor one-way permutations assuming subexponentially secure indistinguishability obfuscation and subexponentially secure one-way functions. It uses a new kind of pseudorandom permutation that supports controlled permutation of its outputs. The trapdoor guarantee is stronger than this card requests, but both the extra primitive and the stronger hardness assumptions prevent this from proving the target implication.

The same paper explains why its full-domain result is compatible with the earlier obfuscation barrier. Its input domain is the whole cube, but its public keys are obfuscated programs. The valid-key domain therefore depends on the building blocks. The older formal domain-invariance condition constrains both input and key domains. Keeping these two notions separate prevents an erroneous claim that a published barrier has been contradicted.

A positive answer would show that unique, length-preserving inversion hardness is available whenever basic cryptographic hardness exists. A negative answer would reveal a structural separation inside foundational cryptographic assumptions. Existing barriers make the problem especially informative: a successful construction from ordinary one-way functions would need to escape the established generic approaches, rather than merely improve their efficiency.

cards.title: Chosen-ciphertext security from ordinary public-key encryption
cards.formal: Does the existence of IND-CPA-secure public-key encryption imply the existence of IND-CCA2-secure public-key encryption in the plain model, with classical security against all nonuniform polynomial-size adversaries and no additional computational assumption?
cards.definitions: A public-key encryption scheme has uniform probabilistic polynomial-time algorithms Gen(1ⁿ)→(pk,sk) and Enc(pk,m)→c and a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm Dec(sk,c)→m or ⊥. It supports bit-string messages of any polynomially bounded length. For every polynomial p, the maximum decryption-error probability over messages |m|≤p(n) is negligible in n, with probability over key generation and honest encryption. In the IND-CPA game an adversary receives pk, chooses equal-length messages m₀,m₁ and state, receives c*=Enc(pk,m_b) for an independent uniform bit b, and guesses b. Its advantage is |Pr[guess=b]−1/2|. In the IND-CCA2 game it also has adaptive access to Dec(sk,·), both before and after choosing the challenge messages and receiving c*. After the challenge, the oracle rejects the exact bit string c*; all other ciphertext queries are allowed. Security requires negligible advantage for every nonuniform probabilistic polynomial-time adversary, allowing any polynomial number of oracle queries. Negligible means eventually smaller than n^{-a} for every a>0. Each adversary has its own polynomial resource bound, but the scheme is fixed independently of that bound. The plain model has no ideal random oracle, externally supplied common reference string, hardware or trusted setup beyond the recipient generating its own key pair. This is an unrestricted existence implication, not a requirement that a compiler treat the original scheme as a black box.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that an IND-CCA2 scheme with these guarantees exists whenever an IND-CPA scheme exists, or refute that implication in the ordinary computational model. A conversion assuming additional trapdoor functions, suitable proof systems, special pseudorandom generators or ideal random oracles does not by itself suffice. A theorem excluding a restricted class of black-box conversions is a barrier, not a negative answer to the unrestricted implication. Fixed-query bounded CCA2, pre-challenge-only CCA1 and non-malleability without adaptive decryption access are weaker targets.
cards.why: Determine whether public-key confidentiality alone can always be strengthened to resist adaptive decryption attacks, without importing another cryptographic assumption.

importance.reason: A central question about the minimal assumptions for robust public-key encryption, connecting encryption, proof systems, trapdoor structure and generic security transformations.

context_blocks.text: Public-key encryption already allows anyone, including the attacker, to create ciphertexts. Ordinary chosen-plaintext security protects the contents of an honestly generated challenge ciphertext. Chosen-ciphertext security additionally protects it while the attacker submits other ciphertexts for decryption and uses the responses to decide what to ask next. The only forbidden query is the challenge itself, because returning its plaintext would make confidentiality impossible by definition.

A simple modification illustrates the gap between definitions. Start with a secure ordinary scheme, append an unused bit to every ciphertext, and make decryption ignore that bit. The modification preserves chosen-plaintext security. A chosen-ciphertext attacker flips the challenge’s unused bit and submits the resulting different string to the oracle, which returns the challenge plaintext. This proves that a particular CPA scheme need not itself be CCA-secure; it does not rule out building another scheme from its existence.

This is why the question concerns a construction or existence implication. A successful transformation may change the ciphertext format, use many public keys, encode messages, and inspect the original algorithms’ descriptions. It must arrange that responses to every other ciphertext remain harmless. A proof faces the corresponding simulation problem: how can it answer decryption queries while relying only on a challenge from the weaker security game?

The source proposal points to Trevisan’s cryptography project list, which explicitly asks whether CCA security can be derived from CPA security by black-box techniques or by any techniques. Its bibliography juxtaposes partial negative results with positive results for non-malleability. That distinction remains important: an advance for one attack model should not silently be reported as a solution for another.

Gertner, Malkin and Myers give a black-box separation for constructions whose new decryption algorithm never calls the original encryption algorithm. This covers a substantial class of natural attempts. It still leaves constructions that re-encrypt during decryption, and does not cover arbitrary use of the source code. The scope of that restriction is central to the theorem, rather than a technical detail that can be omitted.

Choi, Dachman-Soled, Malkin and Wee construct non-malleable encryption from any semantically secure scheme and extend their approach to bounded chosen-ciphertext attacks. In the bounded version, the permitted number q of decryption queries is fixed before constructing the scheme. Full CCA2 instead asks for one scheme that withstands every polynomial-time attacker, whose query polynomial can be larger than any particular bound built into that scheme.

Another productive route adds a primitive that helps enforce ciphertext validity. Hohenberger, Koppula and Waters prove in CRYPTO 2020 that injective trapdoor functions suffice for CCA-secure public-key encryption, without requiring lossiness or correlated-product security. This removes significant earlier restrictions. An arbitrary encryption scheme is not automatically such a trapdoor function: its decryption need only recover the message, not a unique full input including encryption randomness.

Koppula and Waters obtain generic upgrades using a hinting pseudorandom generator, whose security survives a special kind of auxiliary information. Ordinary pseudorandomness does not state that guarantee. Their construction offers another way to organize the decryption proof, but applying it to arbitrary public-key encryption still requires establishing the additional hinting property from the original assumption.

Matsuda’s PKC 2025 work shows that a publicly verifiable noninteractive batch argument for NP can supply the additional ingredient. The May 2025 revision weakens the required proof-length savings: they need not be strong enough for currently known constructions of noninteractive zero knowledge. This is progress in reducing the extra structure needed for the upgrade. The paper still assumes the batch argument; it does not construct it from arbitrary CPA encryption.

A PKC 2026 paper by Brzuska, Klooß and Woo gives CPA-to-CCA transformations for threshold encryption, where several parties jointly decrypt. Its generic transform from arbitrary CPA-secure threshold encryption uses a random oracle. Its other route has additional requirements, including a stronger semi-malicious CPA notion. The July 2026 revision therefore does not establish the plain-model implication in this card.

Resolving the implication would clarify whether protection against active ciphertext manipulation is an additional foundational assumption or a consequence of ordinary public-key confidentiality. It would also explain why existing general approaches repeatedly need structure beyond the weak starting primitive. The target is a foundational security theorem; it does not ask that the resulting construction be practical or preserve the original scheme’s efficiency.

cards.title: Noninteractive zero knowledge from one-way functions
cards.formal: Does the existence of classical one-way functions imply reusable, adaptively secure noninteractive zero-knowledge arguments for circuit satisfiability in the honestly generated common-reference-string model, with computational soundness and computational zero knowledge against nonuniform polynomial-size adversaries?
cards.definitions: A one-way function is a uniformly polynomial-time computable family f_n on uniform n-bit inputs with polynomial-length outputs, such that every nonuniform randomized polynomial-size adversary given 1ⁿ and f_n(X) finds any n-bit preimage with negligible probability. Circuit satisfiability has statements x encoding Boolean circuits and witnesses w assigning their inputs, with R(x,w)=1 exactly when the circuit outputs 1. A proposed argument consists of uniform algorithms Setup(1^λ,1^B)→crs, Prove(crs,x,w)→π, and Verify(crs,x,π)→{0,1}; their time and output length are polynomial in λ+B, where B bounds statement and witness lengths. Setup is independent of the later statements; its private coins are not published. For every polynomial B=B(λ), completeness error is negligible uniformly over valid (x,w) of length at most B. Adaptive computational soundness means that every nonuniform polynomial-time adversary given crs has negligible probability of outputting an unsatisfiable x and an accepted π. Reusable computational zero knowledge means there exist uniform polynomial-time SimSetup and SimProve such that no nonuniform polynomial-time distinguisher separates these experiments: (i) it receives honest crs and can adaptively request Prove(crs,x,w) for polynomially many valid pairs; (ii) it receives simulated crs from SimSetup, and each valid query is answered by SimProve using the simulation trapdoor and x, without receiving w. Both experiments reject invalid queries, and the distinguisher retains arbitrary polynomial-size auxiliary information. All negligible bounds are in λ: for each a>0 the error is eventually below λ^{-a}. Only crs is public in the real system, and one proof message is sent for each statement. No random oracle, extra cryptographic assumption, online verifier challenge, proof of knowledge or succinctness requirement is included. Circuit satisfiability covers every NP language through witness-preserving polynomial reductions.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the stated existence implication, or refute it in the ordinary computational model. The result may use the code of the one-way function and need not be black-box. A construction adding LWE, an appropriate batch argument, trapdoor hashing, or strong extra complexity assumptions does not suffice unless those ingredients are themselves derived from the same ordinary OWF premise. An interactive proof, a witness-indistinguishable argument, or a single-theorem result without a justified reusable upgrade is not the specified conclusion.
cards.why: Determine whether the minimal assumption supporting basic cryptography is sufficient for reusable, publicly verifiable proofs that reveal no witness and require no online interaction.

importance.reason: A fundamental boundary between interactive and noninteractive zero knowledge, with implications for the assumptions behind privacy-preserving proof systems and cryptographic transformations.

cards.status_note: No construction of reusable adaptive NIZK arguments from ordinary OWFs alone, or refutation of that unrestricted implication, was found through 11 September 2026. The cited BARG, trapdoor-hash and derandomization constructions retain extra assumptions; recent OWF-only succinct proofs are interactive, and high-error characterizations run in the reverse direction.

context_blocks.text: An NP witness can be easy to check and sensitive to reveal. For circuit satisfiability, publishing a satisfying assignment gives a verifier complete evidence, but also exposes every bit of that assignment. Zero knowledge asks for convincing evidence whose visible distribution can instead be simulated without the assignment. It formalizes the requirement that verification disclose no additional information beyond the statement’s truth.

The common reference string is an explicit resource. An honest setup algorithm produces public parameters before any statements are selected. After that setup, a prover sends one message that anyone can verify. The setup may retain randomness while generating the string, but that randomness is not handed to users. The simulation trapdoor exists only in the security experiment. This model differs from asking for a noninteractive system with no setup at all.

The card allows computational soundness: a computationally unbounded attacker might find a false accepted proof, but efficient attackers must not. Such a system is called an argument. It also asks for a reusable reference string, with statements chosen after seeing the string and earlier proofs. These choices make the target precise without requiring short proofs or a way to extract a witness from a successful prover.

The classical Goldreich–Micali–Wigderson theorem already supplies interactive zero-knowledge proofs for NP from one-way functions. Interaction gives the verifier a role in challenging what the prover has prepared. The inherited Damgård–Nielsen survey explicitly asks whether one-way functions suffice in the noninteractive setting. That survey discusses a proof-system version with stronger soundness; the argument target here asks for protection only against efficient cheating.

Known positive constructions use more structure. Peikert and Shiehian construct NIZK for NP from ordinary LWE in 2019. Their method builds hash families whose correlation-intractability property supports a sound Fiat–Shamir transformation. The point is a proved property of a specially constructed family, not simply substituting an arbitrary hash function for a verifier’s random challenge. LWE is a sufficient assumption, but it has not thereby been derived from arbitrary one-way functions.

Bradley, Waters and Wu show that an adaptively sound noninteractive batch argument for NP, together with a one-way function, yields NIZK. Their TCC 2024 result also studies how to obtain the needed adaptive soundness from other batch-argument guarantees. The title “Batch Arguments to NIZKs from One-Way Functions” must be read with its starting resource intact: the batch argument is an additional primitive, rather than something their theorem constructs from a bare one-way function.

Branco and coauthors develop a vector-trapdoor-hash approach, with an updated version in March 2026. Their constructions use either LWE or a combination of DDH and LPN assumptions. The initial black-box constructions provide single-theorem zero knowledge, and their multi-theorem upgrade uses cryptography in a non-black-box way. This distinction is compatible with the target here, which allows any construction technique but requires the OWF-only assumption and reusable security.

Chen, Rothblum and Tell pursue a different route through derandomization and strong computational hardness. Their construction combines a subexponentially secure one-way function with an additional complexity assumption and obtains computational soundness against uniform adversaries. It is progress toward avoiding highly structured cryptographic primitives, but the extra hardness and the adversary convention both differ from this card.

Recent results in the reverse direction should not be read as a construction. Chakraborty, Hulett, Khurana and Tomer show in February 2026 that nontrivial NIZK arguments imply one-way functions under the hypothesis that NP is not contained in ioP/poly, even in a broad high-error regime. Their amplification consequences improve existing weak NIZK systems. Neither direction starts with an ordinary OWF alone and produces the desired NIZK system.

Another 2026 result gives succinct zero-knowledge proofs using one-way functions as black boxes. Florentz–Konopnicki and Rothblum’s protocol is interactive: its theorem explicitly bounds a number of public-coin rounds that depends on the relation’s parameters. Its noninteractive commitment component does not make the whole protocol noninteractive. A resolution of this card would isolate exactly how much cryptographic structure is needed to remove that interaction after a single reusable setup.

cards.title: Exponential lower bounds for unrestricted perfect secret sharing
cards.formal: Do constants c>0 and n₀ exist such that, for every n≥n₀, some monotone access structure Γ on [n] requires max_i log₂|S_i|/log₂|S|≥2^(cn) in every perfect secret-sharing scheme for a uniform secret in an arbitrary finite alphabet S with |S|≥2?
cards.definitions: Γ⊆2^[n] is upward closed, excludes ∅ and includes [n]. A scheme is a joint distribution of a uniformly distributed secret over a finite alphabet S and shares X_i in finite alphabets S_i. For every A∈Γ a deterministic function of (X_i)_{i∈A} equals S with probability one. For every A∉Γ the share vector (X_i)_{i∈A} is statistically independent of S. There is no linearity, efficiency or restriction on reconstruction functions. Share size counts the logarithm of its alphabet size, not its entropy or the total size of all shares. The structure may depend on n and need not be explicitly constructed.

context_blocks.text: Perfect secret sharing implements an arbitrary policy specifying which coalitions may recover a secret. General constructions use exponentially long shares, while unconditional lower bounds for unrestricted schemes are much smaller.

The cited work proves an exponential alternative involving share length or the description of reconstruction. That does not prove an exponential share lower bound when reconstruction is unrestricted. The existing upper-bound card asks whether every access structure has smaller shares; this conjecture asks for genuinely difficult structures with a different quantitative target.

cards.title: Average-case RSA inversion versus factoring for exponent 65537
cards.formal: Does polynomial-time inversion of RSA with public exponent 65537 on random valid moduli and random ciphertexts imply polynomial-time factoring of those random moduli?
cards.definitions: A valid modulus is N=pq for distinct primes p,q with gcd(65537,(p−1)(q−1))=1. RSA maps x∈ℤ_N^* to x^65537 mod N. cards.title: Does perfect zero knowledge equal statistical zero knowledge?
cards.formal: Does PZK=SZK for classical single-prover interactive proofs of promise problems, with polynomial-time verifiers and simulators, negligible proof error, and zero knowledge against every polynomial-time verifier?
cards.definitions: A promise problem is a pair (Y,N) of disjoint sets of finite binary strings. An interactive proof consists of a computationally unbounded prover P and a uniform probabilistic polynomial-time verifier V exchanging polynomially many bits on common input x. There is a negligible function ε such that on x∈Y the honest interaction accepts with probability at least 1−ε(|x|), and on x∈N every prover strategy is accepted with probability at most ε(|x|). Negligible means smaller than |x|^{−d} for every fixed d>0 at all sufficiently large lengths. No condition is imposed outside Y∪N. The view of a verifier consists of its random bits and exchanged messages. SZK requires that for every uniform probabilistic polynomial-time verifier V* there is a uniform probabilistic polynomial-time simulator S* which, on x alone, produces a distribution within negligible total variation distance of the view of (P,V*)(x), for every x∈Y. Total variation distance is one half of the sum of absolute probability differences over possible views. PZK instead permits S* to output a failure symbol ⊥ with probability at most 1/2; conditioned on nonfailure, its output distribution must equal that view exactly. Every runtime bound is a strict polynomial bound over all random outcomes, with a polynomial allowed to depend on the fixed verifier or simulator. This is the ordinary input-only simulation convention of the cited definitions, without a shared random string, an oracle, a setup assumption, or a restriction to honest verifiers.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that every promise problem admitting the stated statistical proof also admits a perfect one in this model, or exhibit a promise problem in SZK and prove that it has no PZK proof. The protocol may change completely in a positive result. An oracle separation, a failure of one proposed compiler, a perfect-zero-knowledge PCP, or an honest-verifier-only theorem does not resolve this unrelativized class equality.

context_blocks.text: Zero knowledge formalizes the idea that a verifier can reproduce what it sees without receiving help from the prover. Statistical simulation permits a negligible discrepancy between distributions. Perfect simulation requires exact agreement after the allowed failure event. Goldreich’s textbook asks whether this difference changes which statements can be proved.

The failure convention is part of the model. A strict polynomial-time perfect simulator that never fails is a different requirement, often called super-perfect zero knowledge. Allowing an expected polynomial runtime is also a separate definitional issue discussed in the source. Neither convention is silently substituted here.

PZK is contained in SZK: repeat the bounded-failure perfect simulator polynomially many times until it succeeds, and use an arbitrary output if every attempt fails. The remaining probability of failure is negligible, while successful outputs retain the exact distribution. The open direction asks whether negligible simulation error can always be eliminated by some proof system.

Bouland, Chen, Holden, Thaler and Vasudevan construct an oracle relative to which SZK is not contained in PZK. This supplies evidence against equality and rules out a proof that relativizes in the corresponding way. It does not separate the classes in the ordinary model specified here.

Gur, O’Connor and Spooner explicitly retain PZK versus SZK as open in their 2024 paper. Their perfect-zero-knowledge construction is for probabilistically checkable proofs, where a verifier queries a proof oracle. That achievement concerns a different access model from ordinary interactive proofs and leaves this equality unresolved.

The target asks for a class equality, not a quantitative improvement in a particular cryptographic protocol. Its resolution would determine whether exact distributional privacy has an intrinsic expressive cost. TCS-1929 instead concerns zero knowledge for streaming interactive proofs with a memory restriction.

cards.title: Does worst-case Nearest Codeword hardness imply low-noise LPN hardness?
cards.formal: Does the following implication hold? If binary Nearest Codeword is not in BPP, then no uniform probabilistic polynomial-time distinguisher D has advantage at least $n^{-c}$, for any fixed $c>0$ and all sufficiently large square n, between $(A,As+e)$ and $(A,u)$. Here $A\in\mathbb F_2^{n^2\times n}$, $s\in\mathbb F_2^n$, and $u\in\mathbb F_2^{n^2}$ are independent uniform random variables, and the coordinates of e are independent Bernoulli variables with rate $1/\sqrt n$. Advantage is the absolute difference of D’s acceptance probabilities in the two experiments.
cards.why: A basic security assumption would obtain an explanation through independently studied hardness. The extra assumption in the new reduction makes the remaining target concrete.

progress.text: The revision gives a reduction for $\eta=n^{-\alpha}$, any constant $\alpha<1$, from simultaneous worst-case hardness of two tasks on a code and its dual. This advances beyond earlier near-half-noise reductions; the single-assumption target remains stronger.

cards.review_note: Editorial specialization of the NCP-only direction in Section 1.2 of the September 2026 revision. It fixes the starting problem, decision-LPN distribution, sample count, noise, uniformity, and asymptotic advantage, replacing the vague phrase natural worst-case problem. The source does not state this exact parameter specialization as a numbered conjecture.

context_blocks.text: LWE has strong connections to worst-case lattice problems. Establishing comparable foundations for LPN at cryptographically useful noise rates is more difficult.

Without noise, enough independent parity equations reveal the secret by linear algebra. Flipping some answers breaks that direct procedure: the learner must cope with equations whose right-hand sides may be wrong. At a low noise rate, most equations remain correct, which makes the precise source of hardness especially important.

A worst-case-to-average-case reduction would start with an arbitrary hard coding instance and turn it into the random samples used by LPN. It must preserve a usable noise regime and show how an LPN solver would solve the original task. Requiring two different coding tasks to be hard simultaneously is a stronger premise than deriving the guarantee from one standard worst-case problem.

cards.definitions: Binary Nearest Codeword receives a binary matrix G, a binary target y with the same number of rows, and an integer t, and asks whether $\min_z\operatorname{wt}(Gz-y)\le t$, with arithmetic over F_2 and Hamming weight wt. BPP means a uniform randomized polynomial-time decider correct with probability at least 2/3 on every instance. The LPN side here is a decision problem with n-squared samples, random secret, and inverse-square-root noise. Restricting n to squares makes the noise parameter an exact rational; this is an explicit specialization of the source’s broader low-noise direction.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the displayed complexity-theoretic implication, for example by a reduction turning such an LPN distinguisher into a BPP algorithm for Nearest Codeword, or prove that the implication is false. Invoking simultaneous hardness of an additional problem on the dual code does not establish this implication.

cards.title: Do arbitrary one-way functions imply one-way functions in NC⁰?
cards.formal: Does the existence of a classical one-way function imply the existence of a classical one-way function computed by a polynomial-time uniform NC⁰ circuit family?
cards.definitions: The security parameter λ is supplied in unary. Algorithms are uniform probabilistic polynomial-time machines; security is against nonuniform polynomial-size classical circuit families. A function ν(λ) is negligible if for every c>0, ν(λ)≤λ^(−c) for all sufficiently large λ. Probabilities include setup, algorithm and adversary coins. No ideal oracle or additional trusted setup is supplied unless explicitly stated; arbitrary non-black-box implications are allowed. A one-way function is a deterministic polynomial-time map f:{0,1}*→{0,1}* of polynomially bounded, length-dependent output size, such that every allowed inverter on (1^n,f(U_n)) finds any n-bit preimage with negligible probability, for uniform U_n. A polynomial-time uniform NC⁰ family is generated from 1^n in poly(n) time, has polynomial size and a universal constant depth, and uses fan-in-two AND/OR and unary NOT gates. Inversion security quantifies over all polynomial-size adversaries, not just shallow ones.

context_blocks.text: Local evaluation and global inversion difficulty are strikingly different requirements. An NC⁰ one-way function has each output bit depend on only a constant number of input bits, while inverting the full output must defeat every polynomial-size adversary.

Known locality transformations start from stronger assumptions such as one-way functions in NC¹. Those constructions establish plausible NC⁰ cryptography, but they do not derive it from an arbitrary sequentially computable one-way function. The implication therefore asks whether cryptographic hardness can always be made local.

sentences: Cryptographic hardness must occur on instances that honest users can efficiently generate, rather than only on a difficult exceptional input.
The cited question asks whether P ≠ NP, or a suitable average-case separation between distributional classes, already implies one-way functions.
It also asks about the stronger possibility of trapdoor functions, where secret information enables inversion that remains hard publicly.
These targets add progressively more structure to a bare claim that efficient algorithms cannot solve everything.
Establishing the implications would connect cryptographic foundations to broad complexity assumptions instead of relying on individual number-theoretic or algebraic candidates.

cards.title: Quantum PCP: a constant promise gap for local Hamiltonians
cards.formal: Do there exist integers k,d≥1 and a rational constant ε∈(0,1) such that the following promise problem is QMA-hard under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions? Input is a list of m≤(n+1)^d k-local Hermitian terms H_i on n≥1 qubits and rational a<b in [0,1], with 0⪯H_i⪯I and b−a≥ε. For H=(1/m)Σ_i H_i, distinguish λ_min(H)≤a from λ_min(H)≥b.
cards.why: This asks whether approximating a quantum system’s energy captures the full difficulty of quantum witness verification. It connects complexity, quantum codes, and local testing.

progress.text: The survey develops the Hamiltonian conjecture and obstacles to quantum PCP constructions.

Bafna–Vyas explicitly describe the general conjecture as open. Their classical private PCP uses $O(\sqrt n)$ queries; stronger parameters depend on a product-expansion conjecture. This does not prove Quantum PCP.

context_blocks.text: The classical PCP theorem replaces full verification by inspecting a small part of a proof with a constant gap. Entanglement and local indistinguishability obstruct a direct quantum analogue.

Normalization makes the target meaningful. Multiplying a Hamiltonian by a large number could enlarge its energy gap, but would also violate the bound on individual terms. The conjecture asks for a constant gap in average local energy while every constraint retains bounded strength.

A useful way to read the two cases is that one input admits a low-energy global state, while in the other every state has appreciably higher average energy. The challenge is to preserve computational hardness at that coarse resolution. Checking a few local terms can detect a constant average discrepancy, but constructing a reduction with that discrepancy is the unresolved step.

cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.definitions: Here 1≤m; each term is specified by at most k distinct qubit indices and the complete matrix on those qubits, with rational real and imaginary parts encoded by signed binary numerators and positive denominators. It is tensored with identity on the other qubits. n is written in unary, thresholds in binary rational notation; N counts every supplied bit. λ_min is the smallest eigenvalue. M⪯N means that N−M is positive semidefinite, equivalently z*(N−M)z≥0 for every complex vector z. Inputs violating the matrix promises or with a<λ_min(H)<b are outside the promise. QMA consists of disjoint pairs (Y,N₀) of sets of binary strings with a polynomial-time uniform quantum verifier: on x it uses polynomially many qubits and gates over {H,T,CNOT}, an arbitrary polynomial-qubit witness, and auxiliary qubits initialized to |0⟩. H=2^(−1/2)((1,1),(1,−1)) is the Hadamard matrix, T=diag(1,exp(iπ/4)), and CNOT flips its target when its control is 1. A designated final qubit is measured. For x∈Y some witness gives acceptance probability ≥2/3; for x∈N₀ every witness gives probability ≤1/3. A deterministic machine produces the verifier circuit from x in polynomial time. QMA-hard means that for every such pair there is a deterministic polynomial-time map sending Y into the low-energy case and N₀ into the high-energy case, always producing legal instances on promised inputs. Constants k,d,ε are shared by the target problem; reduction polynomials may depend on the source promise problem.

cards.title: Does BPP differ from BQP?
cards.formal: Is $\mathrm{BPP}\subsetneq\mathrm{BQP}$? Equivalently, is there a total decision language L⊆{0,1}* with a uniform polynomial-time quantum algorithm that is correct with probability at least 2/3 on every input, but no uniform probabilistic polynomial-time classical algorithm with the same per-input correctness guarantee?
cards.definitions: BPP uses a single classical probabilistic Turing machine with independent unbiased coins, worst-case time C(n+1)^k on n-bit inputs, and error probability at most 1/3 separately for every input. BQP uses a polynomial-time uniform family of polynomial-size quantum circuits: a deterministic classical machine on 1ⁿ generates the circuit description in polynomial time. Fix gates H, T, and CNOT, where H is the Hadamard gate, T=diag(1,exp(iπ/4)), and CNOT is controlled bit-flip. Gates may act on any addressed qubits. The input register starts in |x⟩, polynomially many auxiliary qubits start in |0⟩, and one designated qubit is measured in the computational basis at the end. Its output must equal the membership bit with probability at least 2/3 for every x. The family has no advice, oracle gates, postselection, or arbitrary real-number gate parameters. Size and register bounds use fixed polynomial exponents independent of n. Equivalent standard uniform quantum-machine definitions give the same class. The problem concerns one-bit decisions on all binary strings, with no promise on the input. It does not ask for exact amplitudes, full output distributions, or a separation restricted to shallow classical circuits.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: This is the basic complexity-theoretic question of whether quantum computation expands the set of efficiently decidable problems beyond classical randomization. It gives a precise target behind the broader phrase quantum advantage and distinguishes unrestricted computational power from experimentally or structurally restricted demonstrations.

importance.reason: A central foundational separation between classical and quantum efficient computation, with consequences for algorithms, simulation, and the computational interpretation of quantum mechanics.

progress.text: Uniform bounded-error quantum computation is formalized, with BPP⊆BQP. Wigderson’s Definition 11.1 and Theorem 11.2 state the model and inclusion.
Shor gives polynomial-time quantum algorithms for prime factorization and discrete logarithms. No unconditional classical polynomial-time lower bound for those tasks follows.
Raz and Tal prove an oracle separation BQP⊄PH. This also separates BQP from BPP relative to that oracle, but not in ordinary unrelativized computation.
Bene Watts and Parham publish an unconditional shallow-circuit sampling separation. Its classical resource restrictions and sampling output differ from the unrestricted decision model fixed here.

cards.status_note: Wigderson’s Conjecture 11.4 explicitly asks for strict containment. Primary literature was checked through 10 September 2026; no unrelativized separation of these bounded-error decision classes was located. Oracle and shallow-circuit sampling advantages are recorded with their model restrictions.

context_blocks.text: Quantum computation uses interference between amplitudes, while a randomized classical algorithm evolves a probability distribution. Both models on this card ultimately output one ordinary bit with bounded error. Efficient classical random computation can be embedded in a quantum circuit, so the question is whether interference provides a strict advantage for some decision problem when both sides receive unrestricted polynomial time.

Shor’s algorithms give polynomial-time quantum factoring and discrete logarithms. They are compelling candidate advantages because efficient classical algorithms for these tasks are not known. Their classical intractability has not been proved, so the quantum algorithms alone do not separate BPP from BQP. Moreover, these are naturally function problems; a class separation still needs an appropriate decision language and a classical lower bound.

Oracle results demonstrate a stronger separation in a different setting. Raz and Tal construct an oracle relative to which BQP is not contained even in the polynomial hierarchy. In that model, an oracle call accesses a specially chosen function at unit cost, including coherently for the quantum machine. Replacing that oracle by an explicit efficiently implemented input computation is an additional requirement, not part of the oracle theorem.

There are also unconditional advantages against restricted classical circuits. Bene Watts and Parham’s August 2026 publication separates constant-depth quantum sampling from specified bounded-fan-in classical sampling models, including a restriction on available random inputs in its uniform result. This establishes an actual lower bound in that model. It leaves open arbitrary-depth polynomial-time classical decision procedures.

Even the equality BPP=BQP would assert efficient simulation only of the decision tasks defining these classes. A demand to reproduce every quantum output distribution or calculate every amplitude to high precision can be computationally stronger. Keeping the output requirement explicit prevents those simulation problems from being mistaken for this one.

cards.title: An entanglement entropy area law for general gapped two-dimensional Hamiltonians
cards.formal: For every fixed local dimension q≥2, interaction range r≥1, interaction incidence bound g≥1, norm bound J>0, and spectral gap Δ>0, is there a finite constant C=C(q,r,g,J,Δ) such that every Hamiltonian H described below, on every square lattice Λ_L, has unique ground state ψ satisfying S(ρ_A)≤C|∂A| for every A⊆Λ_L?
cards.definitions: Let L≥1 be an integer, Λ_L={1,…,L}² with open boundaries, and the Hilbert space be the tensor product of C^q over its sites. Write H=Σ_a h_a, where each h_a is Hermitian and acts only on a nonempty support X_a⊆Λ_L of diameter at most r in the maximum-coordinate metric. Each site belongs to at most g supports, counting terms with the same support separately, and the operator norm of every h_a is at most J. Suppose H has a unique normalized lowest-energy eigenvector ψ and its next eigenvalue is at least Δ above the lowest eigenvalue. This is a gap of the entire Hamiltonian; no spectral-gap condition is imposed on subregions or subsets of terms. For A⊆Λ_L, let A^c be its complement in Λ_L and ρ_A=Tr_(A^c)(|ψ⟩⟨ψ|) and S(ρ_A)=−Tr(ρ_A log_2 ρ_A), with 0 log_2 0=0. The boundary ∂A is the set of nearest-neighbor lattice edges with exactly one endpoint in A; its cardinality is the boundary length in lattice units. Empty and full regions have entropy zero. The local parameters and C must be independent of L, A, and the actual interaction matrices. Interactions may vary from site to site and with L. They need not commute or share a simultaneous minimum-energy state; translation invariance and frustration freeness are not assumed. No approximation or state-preparation algorithm is requested.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: A central problem in quantum Hamiltonian complexity: whether locality plus a uniform gap controls the quantum information in ground states in two dimensions. It would sharpen the structural foundations of tensor-network methods and separate the task of bounding entanglement from the further task of computing the state.

importance.reason: A fundamental unresolved link between spectral gaps, geometric locality, entanglement, and the resources needed to describe quantum many-body ground states.

progress.text: Hastings proves the area law for gapped one-dimensional quantum systems; the bound depends on fixed local parameters.
Huang establishes QMA-completeness of two-dimensional local Hamiltonian problems even when ground states satisfy area laws, without claiming a uniform spectral gap.
Anshu, Harrow, and Soleimanifar publish an area law for entanglement spread, rather than von Neumann entropy.

Anshu, Arad, and Gosset give a nearly linear entropy bound for vertical cuts in locally gapped frustration-free systems. In arXiv version 3, the explicit bound is n^(1+O((log n)^(−1/5))) at the end of §4.
Arad, Firanko, and Jain extend approximate-projector methods to mutual information of maximally mixed ground states; their theorem still requires a good approximate ground-space projector.
Garratt and Abanin derive entropy bounds from thermodynamic information and area laws for frustration-free systems with suitably bounded subsystem ground-space degeneracies.

cards.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The February and April 2026 results retain extra hypotheses; the general globally gapped 2D entropy area law remains unresolved. The formulation explicitly requires a size-independent constant and fixes the geometric boundary, interaction norms, local dimension, uniqueness, and global gap.

context_blocks.text: A region with m spins has enough Hilbert-space dimension for entropy m log_2 q. For a square block of side length ℓ, that is proportional to ℓ², whereas this conjecture allows only a constant times ℓ. The physical idea is that finite-range interactions and a gap should constrain how much quantum information crosses the boundary. Fixing both interaction strength and the gap prevents an artificial rescaling from making a gapless family appear uniformly gapped.

In one dimension, Hastings proves the corresponding entropy bound for gapped local systems. Since an interval has only a constant number of boundary points, its entropy remains bounded as the chain grows. Matrix-product-state approximations then connect this structure to classical numerical methods. Grouping columns of a two-dimensional lattice into single one-dimensional sites does not directly extend the theorem: each new site has dimension q^L, which grows exponentially with the width.

Anshu, Arad, and Gosset make major progress for frustration-free systems with a local gap. Frustration freeness means one state minimizes every local term; the local-gap assumption controls Hamiltonians obtained from subsets of terms, and is stronger than the global gap here. Their cited version proves a vertical-cut entropy bound n^(1+O((log n)^(−1/5))) for cut length n. It is asymptotically almost linear, but the remaining factor is not a constant and neither extra assumption follows from the statement in this card.

Anshu, Harrow, and Soleimanifar prove an area law for entanglement spread, a measure of variation among the Schmidt coefficients after an appropriate smoothing. This controls a different feature of entanglement from its entropy. For intuition, a maximally entangled state can have arbitrarily many equal Schmidt coefficients: its spread is zero while its entropy is the logarithm of their number. A spread bound therefore does not by itself answer the entropy question.

Arad, Firanko, and Jain’s February 2026 theorem treats mutual information of the maximally mixed ground state. It assumes a sufficiently accurate approximation to the ground-space projector whose operator Schmidt rank is suitably small. Constructing such an approximation for general gapped two-dimensional Hamiltonians remains a missing ingredient; the general wording of the title does not remove this hypothesis.

Garratt and Abanin’s April 2026 preprint provides thermodynamic upper bounds and proves area laws for frustration-free systems when ground-space degeneracies of the relevant subsystem Hamiltonians have suitable boundary scaling. A unique ground state for the full system does not impose that condition on each subsystem. These results retain additional assumptions.

The computational significance also needs care. Huang proves that two-dimensional local Hamiltonian instances whose ground states satisfy area laws can still be QMA-complete. Those instances are not claimed to have the uniform gap fixed here. The result nevertheless shows why an entropy bound alone should not be advertised as a general efficient classical algorithm for finding or manipulating two-dimensional ground states.

cards.title: Information-theoretic classical verification of quantum computation
cards.formal: Does there exist a uniform interactive protocol (P,V) for the following promise problem? Input is an explicit quantum circuit C over {H,T,CNOT}, starting on all-zero qubits, with one designated output bit and binary description length N. Let p(C) be the probability of output 1. YES instances have p(C)≥2/3 and NO instances have p(C)≤1/3. V is a classical probabilistic polynomial-time algorithm and the honest P is a quantum polynomial-time algorithm; they exchange only classical messages. On every YES instance, Pr[V accepts after interacting with P]≥2/3. On every NO instance, for every computationally unbounded cheating prover P*, Pr[V accepts after interacting with P*]≤1/3. Both honest running times, the number of rounds and total communication must be polynomial in N.
cards.definitions: H is the Hadamard gate, T=diag(1,exp(iπ/4)), and CNOT is controlled NOT. The circuit explicitly specifies its qubits and gates, with at most N qubits. The promise excludes intermediate acceptance probabilities; no answer is required there. The two parties know C. The verifier may use private classical random coins, but has no trusted quantum memory, operations or measurements. The honest prover starts without an input-dependent advice state and uses a uniform polynomial-size quantum computation with classical control. All communication is through a single classical interface to one prover. Soundness quantifies over arbitrary adaptive response strategies with no computational bound; probabilities include the verifier’s coins and any prover randomness or measurements. There is no trusted setup, shared secret, second noncommunicating prover or cryptographic assumption. Fixed constant completeness and soundness gaps are the target; no constant-round requirement is imposed. This circuit promise problem expresses verification for arbitrary BQP computations. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: This asks whether efficient quantum computation has an equally efficient, purely classical way to establish trust without computational hardness assumptions or isolated extra devices. A resolution would identify a basic boundary between producing quantum answers and certifying them.

importance.reason: A central quantum-complexity question connecting interactive proofs, delegation and the minimum resources needed to verify computations beyond classical simulation.

progress.text: Shamir proves IP=PSPACE. Combined with BQP⊆PSPACE this gives interactive proofs, without guaranteeing quantum-polynomial-time honest provers.
Reichardt, Unger and Vazirani release their detailed classical-control protocol using separated entangled quantum devices.
Aharonov, Ben-Or, Eban and Mahadev release the completed treatment of interactive proofs with a verifier holding a few qubits; the original work dates to 2008.
Mahadev introduces classical single-prover verification whose soundness relies on quantum hardness of LWE; presented at FOCS 2018.
Kalai, Khurana and Raizes construct witness-preserving classical verification with negligible errors under post-quantum LWE.
Aaronson, Natarajan, Tal and Villányi prove a relativizing multiprover containment and explicitly retain unconditional, efficient single-prover verification as open.
Kashefi, Leichtle, Music and Ollivier publish verification using trusted gates without trusted preparation or measurement; the preprint first appeared in March 2024.

cards.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The April 2026 primary paper explicitly leaves this single-prover, information-theoretic question open. The May 2026 trusted-gate result changes verifier resources, and the February 2026 witness-preserving protocol retains LWE. Neither meets this card’s classical-verifier and unbounded-cheater requirements.

context_blocks.text: A user who can run only classical computations would like to check the answer returned by a quantum computer. Repeating the same claimed computation on the same untrusted device gives no independent reason to trust it. Interactive verification instead lets the user issue challenges whose answers constrain whether the reported result is correct. The survey by Gheorghiu, Kapourniotis and Kashefi organizes approaches according to what the verifier can do and which resources or assumptions establish trust. This card fixes the most restrictive physical verifier: entirely classical.

The usual inclusion BQP⊆IP does not settle the question. Since quantum polynomial time is contained in polynomial space, Shamir’s IP=PSPACE theorem supplies a classical interactive proof with an unrestricted prover. However, a proof system whose honest prover must carry out much harder auxiliary computations cannot be implemented merely by running the quantum computation being certified. Requiring the honest prover to be quantum polynomial time is therefore substantive.

Aharonov, Ben-Or, Eban and Mahadev show that a verifier with a small quantum register can verify arbitrary efficient quantum computations. Quantum authentication lets a weak client protect data while delegating its processing. This demonstrates that a very limited quantum capability can be enough, but its communication and trusted operations do not satisfy the all-classical interface specified here. Their 2017 paper supplies the completed journal treatment of work first reported in 2008.

Reichardt, Unger and Vazirani provide another route: a classical verifier interacts with separated quantum devices sharing entanglement. Correlations in nonlocal games can force the devices to implement the required states and measurements. Isolation is crucial because it prevents the devices from coordinating arbitrary answers during the test. Combining both devices into one freely communicating prover removes that constraint, so the multiprover result cannot simply be reused for this card.

Mahadev’s 2018 breakthrough gives classical verification with one efficient quantum prover under the hardness of Learning With Errors for quantum algorithms. Cryptographic structure conceals information needed to cheat in the measurement tests. Its soundness is computational: the theorem protects against efficiently implementable attacks under the assumption. The present question deliberately quantifies over unbounded cheating strategies, which may break the underlying cryptography.

Recent work continues to refine these neighboring models. Kalai, Khurana and Raizes’s February 2026 construction verifies computations using one reusable QMA witness without destroying it, with negligible errors under post-quantum LWE. This is useful when the input quantum state cannot be copied. It retains the computational soundness assumption and therefore does not supply an unconditional protocol for the simpler BQP target here.

Kashefi, Leichtle, Music and Ollivier’s May 2026 journal article achieves information-theoretic verification without trusted state preparations or measurements. Its client still applies trusted quantum gates: one construction uses single-qubit Z rotations and bit flips. Removing two particular hardware requirements is meaningful progress, but a client performing these gates is not a purely classical verifier.

Aaronson, Natarajan, Tal and Villányi explicitly retain the single-prover question in April 2026. They prove BQP^O⊆MIP^O for every classical oracle O using an exponentially long classical proof queried in polynomially many locations. Their theorem concerns multiple classical provers and does not establish efficient honest provers. Relativization is proposed as a way to investigate the difficulty, rather than as an equivalence that resolves it.

cards.title: Does NPT bound entanglement exist?
cards.formal: Do there exist finite integers a,b≥2 and a bipartite density matrix ρ on ℂᵃ⊗ℂᵇ such that ρ has negative partial transpose, but ⟨ψ|(ρ^{Γ_B})^{⊗k}|ψ⟩≥0 for every integer k≥1 and every unit vector ψ of Schmidt rank at most two across (ℂᵃ)^{⊗k}:(ℂᵇ)^{⊗k}?
cards.definitions: A density matrix is a positive semidefinite Hermitian matrix with trace one. In fixed local orthonormal bases, partial transpose on B is defined by (ρ^{Γ_B})_{ij,kℓ}=ρ_{iℓ,kj}. Negative partial transpose (NPT) means that ρ^{Γ_B} has at least one negative eigenvalue; it does not mean that the whole matrix is negative semidefinite. Schmidt rank is the minimum number of product vectors whose sum is ψ. Tensor powers represent independent copies of the same fixed state. A state is k-copy distillable exactly when a Schmidt-rank-at-most-two vector makes the displayed expectation strictly negative. Thus the proposed state is undistillable for every finite number of copies. Operationally, Alice and Bob may use arbitrary local quantum operations, local auxiliary systems and unlimited classical communication in both directions, but no quantum communication or additional shared entanglement. Distillability means that they can asymptotically obtain Bell pairs (|00⟩+|11⟩)/√2 at a positive rate with error tending to zero. The finite-copy criterion above is equivalent to positive distillability in this model.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: A defining question about whether partial-transpose negativity completely captures the possibility of converting bipartite entanglement into useful Bell pairs. Its precise all-copy quantifier connects quantum resource theory to tensor-stable matrix inequalities.

importance.reason: A central structural boundary in entanglement theory, with canonical finite-dimensional candidates and consequences for what quantum correlations can accomplish under local operations.

cards.status_note: The all-copy NPT bound-entanglement question remains explicitly open in the July 2026 primary sources. New two-copy solutions and restricted three-copy progress do not settle this formulation. Reviewed through 11 September 2026.

context_blocks.text: Entanglement is a property of a state, whereas distillation is an operational ability to turn many noisy shared states into nearly perfect Bell pairs. These pairs are useful because a pair, together with classical communication, can transfer an unknown qubit by teleportation. The question asks whether there is a form of entanglement that passes the necessary negative-partial-transpose test for distillation but is nevertheless permanently unusable for this particular conversion.

The Horodeckis established that entangled states with positive partial transpose can be bound entangled. Their obstruction survives every tensor power: a positive semidefinite partial transpose remains positive semidefinite after tensoring, so no test vector can have negative expectation. This card concerns the complementary regime, where some negative eigenvector exists already, but its Schmidt rank may be too large to provide the rank-two witness needed for a distillation protocol.

Low local dimension explains why a spectral test alone can be misleading in larger systems. If one party has dimension two, every vector has Schmidt rank at most two. A negative eigenvector then immediately certifies one-copy distillability. In higher dimensions, a negative eigenvector can require three or more product terms. Combining copies enlarges both local spaces and permits collective operations, creating additional opportunities to extract a useful two-dimensional entangled subsystem.

The systematic search for NPT bound entanglement dates at least to the families studied by DiVincenzo, Shor, Smolin, Terhal and Thapliyal. Their work provides evidence and reductions to structured states rather than a proof of an all-copy counterexample. Such reductions matter because the original statement quantifies over all finite dimensions and all density matrices; symmetry can expose a tractable algebraic problem inside that enormous search space.

A canonical family is ρ_W(d,α)=(I+αF)/(d²+αd), where d≥3, −1≤α≤1 and F swaps the two d-dimensional systems. These Werner states are NPT exactly when α<−1/d, and one-copy distillable exactly when α<−1/2. Consequently the interval −1/2≤α<−1/d consists of particularly important candidates. It is nonempty for d≥3. The endpoint α=−1/2 is NPT even though its minimum expectation on rank-two vectors is zero.

Several July 2026 papers prove that the one-copy and two-copy thresholds for Werner states coincide. Fraser and coauthors obtain this from a rank-constrained partial-trace inequality, with no Hermiticity or positivity assumption on the coefficient matrix. These results include the formerly open two-ququart example ρ_W(4,−1/2). They remove a major finite-copy obstacle, but do not prove that any particular NPT Werner state is undistillable for every number of copies.

A two-copy proof cannot simply be iterated. In the corresponding matrix formulation, taking a partial trace can increase rank; tensor products also need not preserve the relevant positivity property. Bharti, Gajjala and Haug make these obstacles explicit while giving restricted many-copy extensions. Likewise, a sequence of examples that resists progressively larger numbers of copies can approach the PPT boundary without yielding one fixed NPT state that resists all of them.

Wu and Zou’s subsequent three-copy analysis proves endpoint nonnegativity for the normal rank-two coefficient sector, among other restricted sectors, and studies genuinely nonnormal cases separately. It does not settle the unrestricted three-copy question, much less the all-copy target. The distinction makes the remaining challenge concrete: control every admissible rank-two witness across the full collection of copies, rather than only witnesses with a convenient internal structure.

cards.title: Asymptotically good quantum locally testable stabilizer codes
cards.formal: Do there exist constants r,δ,s>0 and integers w,b≥1, and stabilizer codes Q on unbounded numbers n of qubits, such that Q encodes at least rn logical qubits, has distance at least δn, every listed check has weight at most w, every qubit occurs in at most b checks, and the normalized check Hamiltonian satisfies H⪰(s/n)D_Q?
cards.definitions: Use the Hilbert space (ℂ²)⊗n. On a computational basis bit, X flips the bit and Z multiplies |1⟩ by −1 while fixing |0⟩; Y=iXZ. A Pauli operator is a tensor product of I,X,Y,Z, up to phase, and its weight is the number of nonidentity tensor factors. A listed check Sⱼ is a nonidentity Hermitian Pauli operator with eigenvalues ±1. The m≥1 checks commute, and the group they generate must not contain −I. Their joint +1 eigenspace Q has dimension 2ᵏ, where k is the number of encoded logical qubits. Code distance d is the minimum weight of a Pauli operator that preserves Q but whose restriction to Q is not a scalar multiple of the identity. Checks may be redundant; both the weight bound and the per-qubit incidence bound refer to the listed checks. Define H=(1/m)Σⱼ₌₁ᵐ(I−Sⱼ)/2. For 0≤t≤n, let Q_t be the linear span of E|ψ⟩ over all |ψ⟩∈Q and Pauli errors E of weight at most t, and let Π_t be the orthogonal projector onto Q_t. Define D_Q=Σₜ₌₀ⁿ⁻¹(I−Π_t). The operator inequality H⪰(s/n)D_Q means that its difference is positive semidefinite, or equivalently that the corresponding expectation inequality holds for every quantum state. All five constants are fixed independently of n, and k≥rn and d≥δn must hold throughout an infinite family with n→∞. This card uses the bounded-degree stabilizer version of qLTC existence. Checks need not be geometrically local, and no efficient construction algorithm is required.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct or prove existence of an infinite family satisfying all the stated conditions with fixed constants, or prove that every family of stabilizer presentations fails at least one of them. The target requires maximum check weight and qubit incidence to be bounded, not merely their averages. Inverse-polylogarithmic soundness or relative distance does not qualify. Verifying soundness only for some low-weight errors is insufficient: the operator inequality must hold on the entire Hilbert space.
cards.why: A central missing object connecting quantum error correction to robust verification. It asks whether sparse quantum constraints can simultaneously protect a linear amount of information and detect global corruption with constant normalized soundness.

importance.reason: A defining construction problem beyond good quantum LDPC codes, with direct links to local testing, Hamiltonian complexity, fault tolerance and the quantum PCP program.
