cards.status_note: Checked through 11 September 2026. No bounded-degree stabilizer family with constant rate, relative distance and normalized soundness was located. The corrected 2025 and July 2026 constructions retain inverse-polylogarithmic losses, while constant-soundness variants increase locality or sacrifice other parameters.

context_blocks.text: A quantum code is the common accepting space of many checks. Measuring a uniformly selected check rejects a state with probability equal to its expected normalized energy under H. Local testability asks for a robust version of exact membership: a state that requires many local changes to reach the code must violate a noticeable fraction of checks. Constant check weight then makes this a test involving only a constant number of qubits.

Distance from the code must account for quantum degeneracy. A large Pauli operator can be a stabilizer and leave every encoded state unchanged; another can implement a logical operation while still remaining inside the code space. Neither should be called far from the code merely because its written support is large. The spaces Q_t and the operator D_Q measure how many physical qubits are needed to leave the entire code space in each orthogonal error sector. The soundness condition also covers superpositions and mixed states.

A simple classical analogy illustrates the missing property. Consider a chain of equality checks requiring adjacent bits to agree. A string consisting of a long zero block followed by a long one block can be far from either valid repetition-code word while violating only one check. Local constraints and even a large code distance therefore do not by themselves imply robust local testing. The quantum target additionally requires storing a linear number of logical qubits.

Panteleev and Kalachev resolved the existence of asymptotically good quantum LDPC codes: constant check size can coexist with constant rate and linear distance. Their work also establishes good locally testable classical codes. These are two different conclusions. Quantum local testability with constant soundness does not follow by combining the words in the paper’s title; it is the extra property sought here.

Cross and coauthors obtain constant-soundness qLTC constructions with other parameter compromises. One approach has distance growing with check locality; another has constant average locality while some checks and qubit incidences grow. Wills, Lin and Hsieh analyze distance balancing with more general classical ingredients, quantifying the accompanying soundness loss. Such tradeoffs make it important to track the maximum locality, normalized soundness, rate and distance simultaneously.

Dinur, Lin and Vidick’s construction comes much closer: it has k=Ω(n), distance Ω(n/log³n), soundness Ω(1/log³n), and constant check size. Its September 2025 revision corrects the rate analysis by shifting the chain complex. The paper also describes ways to obtain constant soundness, and then linear distance, at the cost of polylogarithmic check size. These variants do not provide all the constants required by this card at once.

The NLTS theorem is another nearby achievement with a distinct conclusion. Anshu, Breuckmann and Nirkhe show that certain good quantum codes yield Hamiltonians whose low-energy states require nontrivial circuit depth to prepare. That theorem resolves a major quantum-complexity conjecture without establishing constant-soundness local testability. A qLTC would give a stronger relation between energy and distance from a code, and could support further work toward quantum PCP; it would not by itself prove the full quantum PCP conjecture.

Li, Li and Liu’s July 2026 revision adds transversal non-Clifford operations to almost-good constructions. For example, their three-qubit controlled-controlled-Z case retains logarithmic losses in distance and soundness. The revision replaces an invalid cap-product argument from April with a substantially different proof using product-expanding local codes. This adds computational functionality while leaving the constant-parameter qLTC question open.

Sun and Vidick’s June 2026 work uses qLTCs in interactive oracle proofs for QMA, with polynomial communication and polylogarithmically many queried qubits. It illustrates the value of the available approximate parameters. Interaction and a polylogarithmic query budget remain part of that result; it is not a constant-query static quantum PCP or a construction meeting the stronger code parameters here.

The spaces Q_t and the operator D_Q measure how many physical qubits are needed to leave the entire code space in each orthogonal error sector. The soundness condition also covers superpositions and mixed states.

A simple classical analogy illustrates the missing property. Consider a chain of equality checks requiring adjacent bits to agree. A string consisting of a long zero block followed by a long one block can be far from either valid repetition-code word while violating only one check. Local constraints and even a large code distance therefore do not by themselves imply robust local testing. The quantum target additionally requires storing a linear number of logical qubits.

Panteleev and Kalachev resolved the existence of asymptotically good quantum LDPC codes: constant check size can coexist with constant rate and linear distance. Their work also establishes good locally testable classical codes. These are two different conclusions. Quantum local testability with constant soundness does not follow by combining the words in the paper’s title; it is the extra property sought here.

Cross and coauthors obtain constant-soundness qLTC constructions with other parameter compromises. One approach has distance growing with check locality; another has constant average locality while some checks and qubit incidences grow. Wills, Lin and Hsieh analyze distance balancing with more general classical ingredients, quantifying the accompanying soundness loss. Such tradeoffs make it important to track the maximum locality, normalized soundness, rate and distance simultaneously.

Dinur, Lin and Vidick’s construction comes much closer: it has k=Ω(n), distance Ω(n/log³n), soundness Ω(1/log³n), and constant check size. Its September 2025 revision corrects the rate analysis by shifting the chain complex. The paper also describes ways to obtain constant soundness, and then linear distance, at the cost of polylogarithmic check size. These variants do not provide all the constants required by this card at once.

The NLTS theorem is another nearby achievement with a distinct conclusion. Anshu, Breuckmann and Nirkhe show that certain good quantum codes yield Hamiltonians whose low-energy states require nontrivial circuit depth to prepare. That theorem resolves a major quantum-complexity conjecture without establishing constant-soundness local testability. A qLTC would give a stronger relation between energy and distance from a code, and could support further work toward quantum PCP; it would not by itself prove the full quantum PCP conjecture.

Li, Li and Liu’s July 2026 revision adds transversal non-Clifford operations to almost-good constructions. For example, their three-qubit controlled-controlled-Z case retains logarithmic losses in distance and soundness. The revision replaces an invalid cap-product argument from April with a substantially different proof using product-expanding local codes. This adds computational functionality while leaving the constant-parameter qLTC question open.

Sun and Vidick’s June 2026 work uses qLTCs in interactive oracle proofs for QMA, with polynomial communication and polylogarithmically many queried qubits. It illustrates the value of the available approximate parameters. Interaction and a polylogarithmic query budget remain part of that result; it is not a constant-query static quantum PCP or a construction meeting the stronger code parameters here.

cards.title: Passive quantum memory in three dimensions — claimed resolution
cards.formal: Does there exist a family of three-dimensional, bounded-density local Pauli stabilizer Hamiltonians Hₙ and a fixed inverse temperature 0<β<∞ for which the lifetime τₙ(β) of one encoded qubit, under the thermal dynamics below and without intervention during storage, tends to infinity as n→∞?
cards.definitions: The family may use an unbounded subsequence of qubit counts n. Place the qubits in ℝ³, with at most B qubits in each unit ball. Let Hₙ=Σⱼ(I−Sⱼ)/2, where the Sⱼ are commuting nonidentity Hermitian Pauli checks, each supported in a ball of radius R, each qubit belongs to at most B checks, and their joint +1 eigenspace has dimension two. B and R are constants independent of n. A Pauli check is a signed tensor product of I,X,Y,Z; X flips |0⟩ and |1⟩, Z changes the sign of |1⟩, and Y=iXZ. Use the following fixed Davies-type thermal generator, in units with ℏ=k_B=1. If Π_E is the energy-E spectral projector of Hₙ, define A_{i,P,ω}=Σ_{E′−E=ω}Π_{E′}PᵢΠ_E for every qubit i, P∈{X,Y,Z}, and energy difference ω. Put gβ(ω)=min{1,exp(−βω)} and Lₙ,β(ρ)=−i[Hₙ,ρ]+Σ_{i,P,ω}gβ(ω)[AρA†−(A†Aρ+ρA†A)/2], with A=A_{i,P,ω} in each summand. Its evolution is Φₙ,β,t=exp(tLₙ,β). Every single-qubit Pauli error is coupled to the bath; energy-raising rates are positive, and attempt rates do not shrink with system size. Choose a completely positive trace-preserving encoding map Encₙ,β from one-qubit states to n-qubit states, with a completely positive trace-preserving left inverse at t=0. It may use a thermal auxiliary state and need not be efficiently preparable. For this fixed encoding, let εₙ,β(t)=inf_D sup_ρ ∥D∘Φₙ,β,t∘Encₙ,β(ρ)−ρ∥₁, where ρ ranges over all one-qubit density matrices, D over recovery channels from n qubits to one, and ∥A∥₁=Tr√(A†A). Define τₙ(β)=inf{t≥0:εₙ,β(t)>1/10}, with infimum of the empty set equal to infinity. Encoding happens before storage and recovery only at the end. This card fixes a stabilizer and thermal-bath model for the broader physical existence question; it imposes neither translation invariance nor a symmetry restriction on allowed errors.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove existence of a family, one fixed finite β, and encodings with τₙ(β)→∞, or prove that no family in this stated model has that property. A bound exp(Ω(n^η)) for a fixed η>0 would be stronger than required. A lifetime improving only up to a temperature-dependent maximum system size does not suffice. Cooling the bath as n grows, increasing local interaction strengths, slowing error rates with n, enforcing an error-forbidding symmetry, or applying active correction during storage changes the target.
cards.why: A foundational question about whether quantum information can enjoy passive thermal protection in physical three-dimensional space. The recent claimed solution makes careful separation of storage, initialization, bath restrictions and stability especially important.

importance.reason: A defining problem at the intersection of quantum information and many-body physics; retained with an explicit claimed-resolution flag to preserve its history and prevent misleading open-status selection.

cards.status_note: Claimed affirmative resolution in arXiv:2605.10943, 11 May 2026, for passive storage with thermal encoding. Its assumptions and stated theorems were checked, but the full proof was not independently verified. This is not labelled confirmed open. Review cutoff: 11 September 2026.

context_blocks.text: This record now has a claimed affirmative resolution. Balasubramanian, Davydova and Lin’s May 2026 preprint presents local three-dimensional stabilizer Hamiltonians with lifetime exp(Ω(n^η)) at sufficiently low fixed temperature, for some η>0. Its initialization is a thermal encoding. The catalogue flags this as a recent proof claim whose complete argument has not been independently verified here, rather than continuing to present the broad existence problem as confidently open.

A passive memory asks the Hamiltonian and its thermal environment to preserve information between an initial encoding and a final recovery. No repeated syndrome measurements or corrections are performed during storage. Quantum information requires preserving arbitrary superpositions, not only two distinguishable classical states. A material can preserve whether it is mostly magnetized up or down while rapidly losing the phase between those two possibilities; such a material is a classical memory, not a qubit memory.

The bath must be part of the mathematical specification. If errors that change the logical information are simply forbidden, a long lifetime may reflect that restriction. If every local transition is slowed as the device grows, a divergent lifetime can be manufactured by changing the clock. The generator above fixes the time scale and includes all single-qubit Pauli couplings, with ordinary positive-temperature suppression of energy-raising transitions.

An energy barrier is informative but does not alone determine memory time. A logical error may require crossing a high-energy configuration, yet the number of routes and intermediate configurations can be so large that entropy offsets the energetic suppression. Thermodynamic stability criteria therefore use both the bath dynamics and the thermal probability of configurations on which a recovery rule becomes unstable. A recovery map used to analyze the information is compatible with passive storage when it is applied only at readout.

The order of limits matters. Williamson’s layer-code result, published in August 2026, proves a regime in which lifetime grows exponentially with linear system size, but only up to a length scale exponential in inverse temperature. The lifetime at that crossover is very large as temperature falls. For the present question, however, temperature is fixed while system size goes to infinity, so an improvement restricted to a finite crossover regime is partial self-correction.

Roberts, Koh, Tan and Yao’s cored product codes take a different route using disordered geometry. Their January 2026 revision reports finite-temperature simulations of a pinwheel-based three-dimensional memory with up to 60,000 qubits, finding evidence that lifetime increases with size below a critical temperature. Those numerical results motivate a candidate construction but cannot by themselves establish the infinite-family limit required here.

Stahl and Nandkishore obtain protection in three dimensions by enforcing a one-form symmetry on the dynamics, even when enforcement is confined to a subvolume of vanishing relative size. This is a meaningful mechanism, but it restricts which local errors the environment may produce. The present model permits every single-qubit X, Y and Z coupling, so symmetry-protected results must be distinguished from this target.

The May construction’s proven version uses a randomized geometric embedding; its separate explicit variant lacks a complete lifetime proof. Efficient passive preparation and stability under arbitrary local Hamiltonian perturbations are also left for further work. These are additional requirements, beyond the fixed-Hamiltonian storage question formulated here.

The status distinction is useful for selecting research projects: the original existence target now requires assessment of the new theorem, while initialization, perturbation stability and alternative constructions remain separate directions. They should receive their own precise statements if added to the catalogue, rather than silently replacing the question under this identifier.

cards.title: Exact quantum capacity of the qubit depolarizing channel
cards.formal: Determine Q(q), the unassisted asymptotic quantum capacity of D_q(ρ)=(1−q)ρ+(q/3)(XρX+YρY+ZρZ), for every real q∈[0,1]. Capacity is measured in reliably transmitted qubits per independent channel use, under the coding definition below.
cards.definitions: ρ is a one-qubit density matrix. The Pauli operators satisfy X|0⟩=|1⟩, X|1⟩=|0⟩, Z|0⟩=|0⟩, Z|1⟩=−|1⟩ and Y=iXZ. Thus q is the total probability of a nonidentity Pauli error, each type having probability q/3. For block length n, choose an integer kₙ≥0 and completely positive trace-preserving maps Eₙ from kₙ qubits to n qubits and Rₙ from n qubits to kₙ qubits. Let |Φₖ⟩=2^{−k/2}Σ_{x∈{0,1}ᵏ}|x⟩_A|x⟩_B, and define Fₙ=⟨Φ_{kₙ}|[id_A⊗(Rₙ∘D_q^{⊗n}∘Eₙ)](|Φ_{kₙ}⟩⟨Φ_{kₙ}|)|Φ_{kₙ}⟩. A rate r≥0 is achievable if there is a sequence of such codes with liminfₙ kₙ/n≥r and Fₙ→1. Q(q) is the supremum of achievable rates. Sender and receiver have no initially shared entanglement, classical side channel, feedback, or auxiliary quantum channel. Encoding and recovery may be computationally unrestricted and jointly process an entire block. The same q is used independently on every channel use. This definition concerns transmission of quantum states, not merely classical bits through a quantum device.
cards.answer_criterion: Give an explicit determination of the function Q(q) and prove matching achievability and converse bounds: every rate below the proposed value is achievable and no rate above it is achievable, for each q. Evaluating only a fixed block length, identifying only where capacity becomes zero, giving an approximation of unspecified accuracy, or restating the existing unbounded coherent-information optimization does not determine the requested function. The already known endpoints and zero-capacity region must be consistent with the answer.
cards.why: The unresolved communication limit of a canonical quantum-noise model. It tests whether quantum coding theory can turn regularized existence formulas into sharp quantitative limits despite degeneracy and multi-copy advantages.

importance.reason: A benchmark capacity problem connecting quantum error correction, information-theoretic converses and the operational effect of entangled encodings.

cards.status_note: Exact unassisted capacity remains open in the 2026 primary literature. The August certificate improves a positive-capacity lower bound, without claiming an exact threshold or capacity formula. All displayed thresholds use total Pauli error q. Review cutoff: 11 September 2026.

context_blocks.text: This channel is a basic model of unbiased qubit noise: a bit flip, a phase flip, or both occur with equal probabilities. Its one-parameter definition hides a hard coding problem. A quantum code must preserve superpositions and correlations with a reference system, which is why the fidelity test in the definition uses half of a maximally entangled state. Correctly transmitting only computational-basis strings would test a weaker, classical task.

Noise conventions differ substantially between papers. In this card q is the total Pauli error probability. A paper writing probabilities (1−3p,p,p,p) uses p=q/3. A paper writing (1−λ)ρ+λI/2 uses λ=4q/3 on the usual mixture range q≤3/4. For example, q=3/4 completely erases the input, even though the channel formula remains a valid quantum channel for all q≤1. The 2026 threshold values below have been converted to q once.

Quantum coding theorems give an exact but unbounded optimization: Q(q)=supₙ max_σ I_c(σ,D_q^{⊗n})/n. Here I_c is the output entropy minus the entropy jointly held by the output and a purifying reference, with entropy S(τ)=−Tr(τ log₂τ). This regularization permits inputs entangled across channel uses. It identifies the mathematical quantity, but does not by itself evaluate this particular function.

Using a maximally mixed one-qubit input gives the hashing lower bound max{0,1−h₂(q)−q log₂3}, where h₂ is binary entropy and 0 log₂0 is interpreted as zero. The expression becomes zero near q=0.1893. Degenerate quantum codes can surpass this benchmark because multiple physical errors can have the same effect on the encoded information. Consequently counting error types as if each required separate correction can underestimate achievable rates.

Agarwal and coauthors’ May 2026 paper searches rank-two input states inside the permutation-symmetric subspace, using representation theory to evaluate many-copy coherent information. It reports a 45-copy numerical positivity threshold p=0.064657, or q=0.193971 here, and explains how degeneracy suppresses the effective environment entropy. This is evidence for better codes and a lower bound on the true threshold, not an optimization over all possible block lengths and states.

Krohn-Grimberghe’s August revision provides an explicit 45-copy state with exact-arithmetic certificates for positive coherent information at q=48717/250000=0.194868. The result extends positivity to smaller q by channel composition and data processing. The preprint distinguishes the threshold printed in the May paper from a stronger state in its authors’ public repository, and bounds both that state and the new witness using certified arithmetic. The certificates are supplied by the author; this review checked the stated bounds and conventions but did not independently rerun the verification artifact.

On the upper-bound side, Q(0)=1 and Q(q)=0 for every q≥1/4. In the latter range the channel is antidegradable: the environment can simulate the receiver’s output. Reliable positive-rate transmission would then permit incompatible copies of unknown quantum information. Between the current positive-capacity lower bound and q=1/4, even the location where capacity vanishes remains unsettled. Determining that location would still leave the exact positive-rate curve to be found.

There are also finer results away from the threshold. Leditzky, Leung and Smith control the gap between single-letter coherent information and capacity at low noise through approximate degradability. Zhu and coauthors optimize channel extensions to obtain tighter upper bounds, with their work presented at TQC 2026. These techniques reduce the gap without proving that a proposed family of codes is optimal at every noise value.

Kondra and coauthors’ August 2026 strong-converse result concerns fidelity decay above capacity for degradable and antidegradable channels. Such a theorem strengthens the operational meaning of an upper bound, but does not supply the unknown capacity curve of the depolarizing channel in its intermediate regime. A full resolution here must match the best achievable rates with upper bounds that apply to arbitrary encodings and arbitrary block lengths.

cards.title: NP outside BQP
cards.formal: Is NP⊈BQP? Equivalently, is there no uniform polynomial-time quantum algorithm that decides satisfiability of every Boolean 3-CNF formula with error probability at most 1/3 on each input?
cards.definitions: NP is the class of languages L⊆{0,1}* for which there exist a deterministic polynomial-time verifier V and a polynomial p such that x∈L exactly when some binary string y of length at most p(|x|) satisfies V(x,y)=1. BQP consists of languages decided by polynomial-size quantum circuit families {C_n} that a deterministic classical algorithm generates from 1ⁿ in polynomial time. The circuits use a fixed finite universal gate set, for example Hadamard, T and controlled-NOT, polynomially many qubits initialized with the input x and zero ancillas, and a final measured output bit. Acceptance probability is at least 2/3 when x∈L and at most 1/3 when x∉L. The size bound counts all elementary gates, not only calls to a selected subroutine. There is no advice, postselection, oracle or supplied witness. A 3-CNF formula is a conjunction of clauses, each a disjunction of at most three literals, with a literal being a variable or its negation. The input length is the length of a conventional explicit binary encoding; malformed encodings are rejected. NP⊈BQP asserts the existence of at least one language in NP outside BQP, rather than merely inequality of the two classes.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove an unconditional separation NP⊈BQP, or refute it by establishing NP⊆BQP. By NP-completeness and closure under classical polynomial-time reductions, the latter is equivalent to putting 3-SAT in BQP. An oracle separation, a lower bound only on unstructured search, an algorithm for a restricted family of formulas, or a conditional hardness statement does not settle the question. context_blocks.text: An NP witness gives a short, classically checkable reason for a yes answer. For satisfiability, that witness is an assignment to the variables. The question is whether the existence of such a witness can always be decided efficiently using quantum computation, even when the witness itself is not supplied. Wigderson lists the noncontainment as Conjecture 11.5 in the inherited 2018 draft.

The distinction between verification and discovery is essential. A quantum computer can certainly evaluate a Boolean formula on a proposed assignment. It can also place assignments into superposition. But a measurement does not reveal a list of the values computed on every assignment. An efficient algorithm must arrange interference so that the eventual measurement supplies the desired decision with bounded error.

Shor’s factoring and discrete-logarithm algorithms show that quantum computation can exploit special mathematical structure to solve important problems in polynomial time. Their speed comes from extracting periodic information, not from a general procedure for every efficiently checkable witness relation. Factoring is not known to be NP-complete, so its quantum algorithm does not imply that 3-SAT or all of NP belongs to BQP.

Grover’s search algorithm gives a different kind of advantage: a quadratic improvement for an unstructured search space. Applied to N Boolean variables, the space has 2ᴺ assignments, so the generic search scale becomes 2^{N/2}, with additional polynomial work to evaluate the formula. This is a substantial speedup and remains exponential in N. The distinction is about asymptotic resources, even if that reduction could be valuable on concrete instances.

Bennett, Bernstein, Brassard and Vazirani prove a matching black-box obstruction and an oracle separation of NP from quantum polynomial time. Their result excludes a universal shortcut that treats the witness verifier only as an unknown function. An explicit formula reveals more than black-box evaluations: an algorithm can inspect shared variables, clauses and every feature of its encoding. Thus the oracle theorem does not establish the unrelativized separation asked for here.

There is a useful elementary implication. Since deterministic polynomial-time computation is contained in BQP, P=NP would put all of NP in BQP. Therefore a positive answer to this card would also prove P≠NP. The converse implication is unavailable: P≠NP alone does not rule out quantum polynomial-time algorithms for NP-complete problems. This helps explain why proving an unrestricted quantum lower bound is such an ambitious target.

The decision version already captures efficient witness finding for SAT. If a bounded-error quantum SAT decider existed, one could repeatedly fix a variable, ask whether the remaining formula is satisfiable, and retain a satisfiable branch. Amplifying the decision success probability makes the probability of any mistake across the polynomially many calls small. Finally, the resulting assignment can be checked classically. This is a consequence of SAT’s self-reduction, not an assumption that a quantum algorithm hands over all possible witnesses at once.

The conjecture also supports hardness results for tasks whose inputs and outputs are intrinsically quantum. In June 2026, Cifuentes proves that an efficient quantum algorithm for detecting a large nonidentity Pauli coefficient of a circuit-prepared state would imply NP⊆BQP. The reduction holds even for pure states and a constant threshold with a promised gap. It transfers the conjecture to a tomography-related task; it does not prove the conjecture itself.

Several nearby questions should remain distinct. BPP versus BQP asks whether quantum computation adds power beyond classical randomization. NP versus BQP asks whether quantum computation can solve every classically verifiable decision problem. Allowing a quantum witness changes the verifier class again, to QMA. Establishing a separation or a speedup involving one pair does not automatically establish the relation between the others.

A resolution would locate a fundamental boundary of quantum computation. If NP⊆BQP, quantum algorithms would provide a universal efficient route to classical constraint satisfaction and its many reductions. If NP⊈BQP, some efficiently verifiable problems would resist even ideal fault-tolerant quantum computers. Neither answer is about today’s hardware capacity: the model already grants arbitrarily scalable, accurate quantum computation with polynomial resources.

context_blocks.text: A quantum state may encode a proof that has no short classical description. Oracle separations test this idea but do not separate the standard classes.

The same quantum verifier is used on both sides of the comparison. What changes is the proof supplied by a prover: either a classical string or a quantum state. To prove a separation, one needs a verification task whose positive instances admit useful quantum proofs but no comparably short classical proofs for any efficient quantum verifier. cards.title: Computability of quantum channel capacity
cards.formal: Does there exist a single classical Turing algorithm that, given any effectively described finite-dimensional memoryless quantum channel Φ and a positive rational ε, halts and outputs a rational r satisfying |r−Q(Φ)|≤ε, where Q is the unassisted quantum capacity in qubits per channel use?
cards.definitions: The input includes positive integers d_A,d_B and a program describing the unnormalized Choi matrix J(Φ)=Σᵢⱼ |i⟩⟨j|⊗Φ(|i⟩⟨j|), a matrix of order d_A d_B. On input k≥1, that program must halt and output a rational complex matrix whose real and imaginary entries approximate the corresponding entries of J(Φ) within 2⁻ᵏ. It is promised that the limiting matrix is positive semidefinite and Tr_B J(Φ)=I_A, so it defines a completely positive trace-preserving linear map from d_A-dimensional input states to d_B-dimensional output states. This explicitly specifies “effective description”; finite algebraic matrix descriptions are included. The requested algorithm need only meet its guarantees on inputs satisfying these promises. Memorylessness means n uses implement Φ^{⊗n}, allowing arbitrary joint encoding and decoding across those uses. No preshared entanglement, additional classical communication, feedback or auxiliary channel is free. Operationally Q(Φ) is the supremum of asymptotically achievable quantum transmission rates with error tending to zero. Equivalently, Q(Φ)=sup_{n≥1} n⁻¹ max_ρ I_c(ρ,Φ^{⊗n}). Here ρ ranges over density matrices on A^{⊗n}; if ψ_{RAⁿ} is any purification and ω=(id_R⊗Φ^{⊗n})(ψ), then I_c=S(ω_{Bⁿ})−S(ω_{RBⁿ}), with S(τ)=−Tr(τ log₂τ) and 0 log₂0=0. There is no running-time bound beyond eventual halting for every valid channel description and every ε>0.
cards.answer_criterion: A positive answer requires a uniform algorithm with a proved finite stopping rule and additive error guarantee for every promised input. A negative answer must prove that no such approximation algorithm exists in this specified representation. An asymptotic formula without an effective convergence bound, hardness only for polynomial-time computation, or undecidability of a different assisted, zero-error or memoryful capacity is insufficient. Undecidability of testing the exact equality Q(Φ)=0 alone would also not disprove computable additive approximation.

cards.status_note: No uniform computability theorem or impossibility proof for this finite-dimensional memoryless unassisted capacity found through 11 September 2026. The corrected 2026 paper explicitly leaves the general question open: its quantum-capacity result is QMA-hardness, while its undecidability result concerns a restricted assisted zero-error classical capacity.

context_blocks.text: Capacity is the best rate at which a noisy channel can transmit information reliably after coding over many uses. For quantum transmission, the object being preserved is an arbitrary quantum state, including its entanglement with a reference system. A channel may badly corrupt each individual input and still support a positive asymptotic rate through suitable coding. This card asks whether that optimal rate can always be computed to requested precision at all.

The quantum coding theorem expresses capacity through regularized coherent information: optimize over a block of n uses, divide by n, and take the supremum over every block length. Devetak’s coding theorem gives an operational justification for this expression. It is an exact mathematical characterization, but it involves infinitely many optimization problems. A numerical procedure needs an additional way to know when unexamined block lengths cannot improve the answer by more than ε.

For each fixed block length, the input dimension is finite and the coherent-information objective can be approximated on the compact space of density matrices. Exhaustive computation can therefore produce successively better certified lower bounds on Q. This can be absurdly expensive and still count as computation here. The obstruction is that increasing lower bounds need not come with a computable certificate of how far they remain below their limit.

Cubitt, Elkouss, Matthews, Ozols, Pérez-García and Strelchuk show that no universal constant number of channel uses suffices even to expose positive coherent information. For every chosen block length, they construct a channel whose optimized coherent information is zero there, but becomes positive at a larger block length. These are different channels as the chosen length changes. The theorem does not rule out an algorithm whose stopping time depends on the channel description and requested precision.

The input convention is important because a quantum channel is described by real and complex numbers. A finite program that supplies certified rational approximations gives an algorithm meaningful access to those numbers without granting exact tests of arbitrary computable-real equality. It also includes ordinary finite circuit descriptions over computable gates. The validity of the channel and approximation program is promised; solving the separate problem of recognizing all valid descriptions is not required.

Leung and Smith prove continuity of unassisted quantum capacity in finite output dimension, with an explicit bound in terms of channel distance and dimension. Thus small errors in specifying a fixed-dimensional channel change its capacity by a controlled amount. This prevents a simple discontinuity argument from settling this approximation question. Continuity controls perturbations of the channel, while the missing stopping rule concerns convergence over code block lengths.

The 2025 review Undecidability in Physics distinguishes this question from established undecidability results for other information-theoretic quantities. Channels with memory can carry an evolving hidden state across uses; that is different from repeating Φ independently. Zero-error capacities demand perfect distinguishability at finite stages, unlike an error that tends to zero under asymptotic coding. Neither change can be imported silently into the present problem.

Bhattacharyya, Mehta and Zhao prove in 2026 that approximating quantum capacity is QMA-hard for channels specified succinctly by circuits. Their promise distinguishes capacity at least 3/4 from capacity at most 1/4, even for degradable channels. This is strong evidence against efficient computation, but it leaves unrestricted computability untouched: a QMA-hard problem can still have an exhaustive terminating algorithm. Circuit size also differs substantially from the length of a fully expanded channel matrix.

Their corrected March 2026 version proves undecidability for a separate restricted capacity: one-shot, entanglement-assisted, zero-error classical communication through a classical-to-quantum channel, with maximally entangled assistance and projective decoding measurements. Those restrictions are part of the theorem. The paper explicitly says it does not resolve general quantum-capacity computability. Its revision history records a correction to the earlier treatment of the assisted zero-error result.

It is also necessary to separate approximation from deciding whether the answer is exactly zero. Even when a nonnegative real quantity is computable to arbitrary error, every finite approximation can leave open whether it is zero or merely very small. Conversely, identifying some zero-capacity families does not provide approximations for every channel. The requested output and tolerance make this card an unambiguous uniform approximation problem.

A positive resolution would supply a general certification procedure for quantum communication rates, however slow. A negative resolution would show that no universal procedure can always certify the optimal rate to a chosen tolerance, despite finite input and output dimensions and independent repeated noise. Either outcome would clarify whether regularized formulas describe quantities that are algorithmically accessible or can exceed the reach of computation.

cards.definitions: Let G be a finite group with identity e and H≤G a subgroup. Its left cosets are gH={gh:h∈H}. A hiding function f:G→S is strictly H-periodic when f(g)=f(g′) if and only if gH=g′H, equivalently g⁻¹g′∈H. The codomain labels distinguish different cosets but have no promised algebraic meaning. The output is a finite list h₁,…,h_r whose generated subgroup equals H, not merely its order or a membership test. Every finite subgroup has a generating set of at most ⌈log₂|G|⌉ elements, so a short output is possible when group elements have short encodings. The standard hiding oracle coherently maps |g⟩|0⟩ to |g⟩|f(g)⟩; with a fixed binary output encoding it can be implemented as |g⟩|z⟩↦|g⟩|z XOR f(g)⟩. Bounded error means that the entire output generates exactly H with probability at least 2/3 on each promised instance. The desired resource bound concerns all computation, including classical preprocessing, group operations, non-oracle quantum gates, measurements and output processing, rather than just calls to f. The precise finite encoding and uniform access to arbitrary G remain unspecified in the source import, as recorded in statement_review.
cards.answer_criterion: The intended positive answer is a uniform bounded-error quantum algorithm with polynomial total cost in log|G|, valid for every group and hiding function in one specified efficient group-access model. A query upper bound alone does not qualify. A negative answer would exclude such algorithms in that same fixed model. The current card retains the missing group-representation specification instead of silently choosing a narrower group family or a stronger oracle.

context_blocks.title: A subgroup hidden by equal values
context_blocks.text: The oracle groups elements together by assigning the same label exactly on each coset of H. Consider addition modulo 12 and H={0,4,8}. The function f(x)=x mod 4 is constant on the four cosets and different between them. Outputting the single generator 4 identifies H; listing all twelve inputs or reconstructing the oracle’s labels is unnecessary. In a non-Abelian group, the distinction between left and right cosets matters, so the left-coset convention is explicit.

context_blocks.title: Easy membership does not give a short description
context_blocks.text: An element g belongs to H exactly when f(g)=f(e), so a single comparison with the identity’s label tests membership. That test does not by itself find generators quickly: a small hidden subgroup may contain only a tiny fraction of G. The objective is to recover its structure with cost polynomial in the number of bits needed to describe a group element, rather than by scanning every group element.

context_blocks.title: The query problem is already solved
context_blocks.text: Ettinger, Høyer and Knill prove that a polynomial number of hiding-function queries suffices for an arbitrary finite group. Their Theorem 1 gives an O((log|G|)^4) bound and also discusses an exact version with arbitrary one-qubit gates. The same paper explicitly says that its classical preprocessing and quantum networks are inefficient. Thus the title’s polynomial query complexity does not settle the total-running-time question. The bounded-error target here does not require the exact gate model from their additional exactness result.

context_blocks.title: Progress depends on the group family
context_blocks.text: Efficient quantum algorithms solve the Abelian hidden subgroup problem and explain several classic quantum speedups. In August 2026, Morales obtains additional non-Abelian cases: certain semidirect products under bounded-rank and exponent conditions, and quasi-Hamiltonian groups under an input-structure assumption. Those hypotheses do not cover arbitrary finite groups. The dihedral case remains an independently important specialization recorded elsewhere in the atlas.

context_blocks.title: What still needs specification
context_blocks.text: A multiplication table has roughly |G|² entries, far larger than a polynomial in log|G|. A short generating set with coherent group-operation access is a different input model. Unique element names, knowledge of the group order, and access to uniform superpositions can also change the available operations. The original import names a standard model without spelling these choices out, while its principal reference is designed to count only hiding-oracle queries. The common mathematical task and current research boundary are now stated, but the card remains unfinished until its group representation and cost conventions are fixed.

cards.title: A polynomial-time quantum algorithm for the dihedral hidden subgroup problem
cards.formal: Does there exist one uniform bounded-error quantum algorithm and constants C,c>0 such that, for every N≥2 and every oracle f hiding a subgroup H of D_N, the algorithm outputs generators of H with probability at least 2/3 using at most C(⌈log₂N⌉+ℓ+2)ᶜ total operations, where ℓ is the bit length of an oracle value?
cards.definitions: The dihedral group D_N has 2N elements represented as pairs (x,b) with x∈ℤ/Nℤ and b∈{0,1}, and multiplication (x,b)(y,d)=(x+(−1)ᵇy mod N,b+d mod 2). Its identity is (0,0). The classical input is N in binary and the positive integer ℓ specifying the output-register width. An arbitrary subgroup H≤D_N is hidden by f:D_N→{0,1}^ℓ when f(g)=f(g′) if and only if gH=g′H, equivalently g⁻¹g′∈H. Thus distinct left cosets have distinct labels, whose bit patterns carry no promised structure. Quantum access is the reversible XOR oracle U_f|g,z⟩=|g,z⊕f(g)⟩, usable on superpositions; it acts as the identity on invalid group encodings. Each call costs one oracle operation. Count all other elementary quantum gates, measurements and classical bit operations as well, using a fixed universal gate set such as Clifford+T. Uniformity requires an effective polynomial-time classical controller, with no advice depending on N, H or f. There is no input truth table for f and no additional subset-sum, state-preparation or memory-access oracle. The output is a finite list of encoded group elements whose generated subgroup equals H; the empty list is allowed for H={1}. The success probability is over the algorithm’s internal randomness and measurements, for every legal hiding function separately. The displayed bound is a worst-case bound on total work, not merely query count or parallel depth. When ℓ is polynomial in log N, as in the usual oracle model, the target is polynomial time in log N.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct and prove correct a quantum algorithm with the stated uniform polynomial total-work guarantee, or prove that no such algorithm exists. A polynomial number of oracle queries with superpolynomial postprocessing, a speedup using uncounted parallel hardware, or an algorithm requiring an additional subset-sum oracle does not suffice. Failure of one family of measurements or sieves is not a negative solution for all quantum algorithms.
cards.why: A central test for quantum algorithms beyond abelian Fourier sampling. The information can be acquired with few queries, but extracting the subgroup efficiently remains a fundamental computational challenge with lattice-related consequences under the appropriate reductions.

importance.reason: A basic nonabelian hidden-structure problem with a long-standing gap between polynomial information requirements and subexponential known algorithms.

cards.status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. No verified polynomial-time solution is recorded. Simon’s August 2026 coset-algorithm claim is disputed: the September 1 Gupte–Ragavan–Zhandry response proves failure of the proposed template, and Guo–Yang identify an unsupported independence hypothesis. context_blocks.text: Hidden subgroup problems ask a quantum algorithm to recover symmetry from equality patterns in a function. In an abelian group, Fourier sampling can turn those patterns into usable constraints, providing the framework for familiar quantum period-finding algorithms. The dihedral group adds a reflection to a cyclic rotation group and is among the simplest noncommutative settings in which the general polynomial-time method remains unresolved.

A representative hard case has H=H_s={(0,0),(s,1)}, with an unknown s∈ℤ/Nℤ. The hiding promise says f(x,0)=f(x+s,1), and each restriction to b=0 or b=1 is injective. Recovering the subgroup is therefore recovering a cyclic hidden shift. The unrestricted subgroup problem reduces to this reflection case after handling its rotational part; the inherited Kuperberg paper uses the hidden-shift formulation for its main algorithm.

A coherent oracle query followed by discarding the function value yields a coset state. In the reflection case it has the form (|0,x⟩+|1,x+s⟩)/√2 for an unknown random x. Fourier transformation of the cyclic coordinate produces a known random label k and a qubit with relative phase exp(2πiks/N). The phase contains information about s, but measuring that qubit does not simply reveal the modular product ks as a classical number.

This is already enough information in a statistical sense: polynomially many queries suffice if computationally expensive processing is allowed. The main obstacle is implementing an effective collective extraction of the hidden shift with polynomial total work. A bound on oracle calls therefore cannot be substituted for a bound on running time. The card deliberately counts both quantum gates and classical postprocessing.

Kuperberg’s first sieve gives time and query complexity 2^{O(√log N)}. It repeatedly combines phase states so that their labels become more useful for recovering the shift. This is a substantial speedup over generic classical approaches, yet it is superpolynomial in the input length n≈log N: the target here is n^{O(1)}, not 2^{O(√n)}.

The resource picture improved further. Regev obtains subexponential time with polynomial space, at a larger exponent involving √(log N log log N). Kuperberg’s later collimation sieve restores exp(O(√log N)) time while using only O(log N) quantum space, although classical storage remains subexponential. Small quantum memory and polynomial overall running time are different achievements.

The lattice connection is important but needs its access-model qualification. Regev reduces a unique-shortest-vector problem to solving dihedral coset samples. Thus a polynomial algorithm that works from those samples would have consequences for lattice algorithms. An arbitrary hiding-function oracle provides a different interface, so one should not silently claim that every conceivable oracle-HSP algorithm automatically implements the coset solver required by that reduction.

An older positive claim remains visible in search results. Moore and Young’s February 2022 preprint claimed polynomial time for dihedral groups of power-of-two size, but was withdrawn on February 23. The withdrawal states that Lemma 4.3 is wrong and that the main algorithm needs the states asserted by that lemma. It is retained here as a documented withdrawn attempt, not a known algorithm.

A much more recent claim requires a separate status entry. Daniel Simon’s August 2026 preprint claims a polynomial-time dihedral coset algorithm, replacing a subset-sum step with a different erasure procedure. Its latest listed revision is August 17 and acknowledges a correction to the analysis as well as a new critical response. A valid coset algorithm of the claimed generality would settle the reflection case, making this directly relevant to the present question.

Gupte, Ragavan and Zhandry’s response, revised September 1, gives an information-theoretic obstruction to the proposed algorithm. They show that its use of only a truncated portion of the classical Fourier labels leaves negligible advantage in guessing the secret’s least-significant bit. Their theorem covers a broader template containing the proposed procedure; it does not exclude all algorithms for the dihedral problem. The authors also supply a Lean formalization. This catalogue review checked the primary statements and repository description, but did not independently rerun that formalization.

Guo and Yang independently analyze the supporting lemmas. Their August 17 paper proves corrected statements while identifying a remaining independence assumption that the proposed choice of a partition does not supply. They explicitly conclude that establishing those lemmas does not establish correctness of the algorithm. The card therefore flags the recent claim as disputed rather than presenting polynomial time as established.

Positive results elsewhere among nonabelian groups continue to refine the boundary. Morales’ August 2026 algorithm handles certain scalar-action semidirect products with bounded generator rank and exponent-to-prime ratio polylogarithmic in group size, and another family with modular subgroup structure. For the ordinary dihedral family, the relevant ratio would be N/2, which does not meet that condition as N grows. These structural advances leave the unrestricted dihedral target intact.

A solution would identify a new way to convert nonabelian quantum information into efficiently recoverable classical structure. A negative result would be equally consequential because polynomial query complexity is already available: it would isolate a genuine computational obstruction in processing the information. The significance comes from that algorithmic boundary, alongside the precise reductions to coset and lattice problems.

cards.title: Graph isomorphism in BQP
cards.formal: Is GI∈BQP? Equivalently, does a uniform quantum algorithm decide, on every pair of finite simple graphs on n vertices given by their adjacency matrices, whether they are isomorphic, with error probability at most 1/3 and worst-case total running time n^{O(1)}?
cards.definitions: A graph is finite, undirected, loopless and has no parallel edges. For equally sized vertex sets [n]={1,…,n}, an isomorphism from G to H is a bijection π:[n]→[n] satisfying {u,v}∈E(G) if and only if {π(u),π(v)}∈E(H) for every u≠v. The input consists of the two explicitly written binary adjacency matrices; unequal vertex counts are rejected immediately and empty graphs are handled trivially. There are no promises of rigidity, bounded degree, typicality, or a particular input distribution. BQP means a polynomial-time uniform family of quantum circuits over a fixed universal gate set such as Clifford+T, acting on computational-basis encodings of the classical input and initialized ancillas, with a measured output bit. There must be fixed constants C,c such that all gates, measurements and classical control can be implemented within C(n+2)ᶜ total elementary operations. The algorithm accepts each isomorphic pair with probability at least 2/3 and each nonisomorphic pair with probability at most 1/3. It receives no nonuniform advice, witness, graph-orbit state, isomorphism oracle or uncounted memory-preparation service. The target is the decision problem for an ordinary vertex permutation; it is not the distinct relation called quantum graph isomorphism in nonlocal-game theory.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove membership by giving a correct uniform quantum algorithm with the stated worst-case polynomial total cost, or prove GI∉BQP. A classical polynomial-time algorithm would also answer yes. A separation for a specified Fourier-sampling or sieve model is not a negative answer for unrestricted BQP; an invariant that distinguishes only some nonisomorphic pairs is not a complete positive answer.
cards.why: A canonical test of whether quantum computation can efficiently recognize equivalence of explicit combinatorial structures, beyond the algebraic problems already handled by standard period finding.

cards.status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. No uniform polynomial-time quantum algorithm for ordinary graph isomorphism, or proof of GI∉BQP, was found in the checked primary sources. The 2026 correlation tests, state-isomorphism classifications and NPA hierarchy results do not settle this question.

context_blocks.text: Graph isomorphism asks whether two descriptions encode the same finite relational structure after renaming the vertices. It is an exact equivalence problem, rather than a search for approximately similar networks. A proposed permutation is easy to verify by comparing all adjacency entries, but finding a successful permutation or ruling out every permutation can require reasoning about highly symmetric graphs.

Elementary invariants help without settling the problem. For instance, a six-cycle and two disjoint triangles both have six vertices, six edges and degree two at every vertex, but cannot be isomorphic because one is connected and the other is not. More elaborate invariants must likewise be assessed by whether they distinguish every required pair, not just by how well they perform on a test set.

Aaronson’s 2005 challenge list identifies graph isomorphism among the natural targets for quantum algorithms beyond Shor and Grover. The formulation on this card turns that broad research motivation into one exact complexity-class membership question. It imposes no particular algorithmic approach and permits a classical algorithm as a special case of a quantum one.

Babai’s classical breakthrough gives a quasipolynomial-time algorithm, with bound exp((log n)^{O(1)}). The original argument required a correction in January 2017, after which the quasipolynomial claim was restored. This is the relevant general classical benchmark, rather than brute-force examination of n! permutations. Quasipolynomial time is still larger than the polynomial bound asked for here.

One tempting quantum approach uses the action of permutations on graphs. The state that is a uniform superposition over all distinct labeled copies of G would be identical for isomorphic graphs and orthogonal for nonisomorphic ones. If such states could always be prepared efficiently, an overlap test would help. The state-preparation step is the difficulty: preparing a superposition of pairs |π⟩|πG⟩ is easy, but coherently removing the permutation register does not follow from that construction. Simply discarding the register gives a mixed state, not the desired pure superposition.

The established hidden-subgroup approach makes this difficulty precise in another form. Graph isomorphism can be reduced to finding hidden symmetry in permutation groups, and the standard procedure generates quantum coset states. Hallgren, Roetteler and Sen, independently of Moore and Russell and later in joint work, prove that measurements on too few such states reveal insufficient information in the relevant hard cases. Their bound requires joint access to Ω(n log n) states to obtain useful information.

That lower bound is a restriction on information extraction in a particular representation. The number of required states is itself polynomial. It does not say that every measurement on that many states needs superpolynomial computation, and it does not forbid an algorithm that uses the explicit input graphs in a different way. A negative solution to GI∈BQP would have to rule out those broader possibilities as well.

The inherited quantum-inspired reference has a substantive June 2026 revision. Maxwell, van den Hoven and Renema analyze correlations in Gaussian boson samplers and derive a classical test for a necessary condition of graph isomorphism. At restricted correlation order it can certify that some graph pairs are different. At the maximum order their condition becomes sufficient, but their method is no longer efficient. The authors explicitly separate these two regimes.

This illustrates why a photonic sampling procedure is not automatically a polynomial-time decision algorithm for all graphs. One must account for how many samples or correlations are required to distinguish a worst-case pair, how accurately they must be estimated, and the classical work used to interpret them. Efficiently generating individual samples does not by itself establish a uniform bound for the complete decision task.

May 2026 work by Gheorghiu, Jacobs, Mehraban and Motamedi studies isomorphism of quantum states under group actions. They show, among other results, that a Clifford-group state problem is at least as hard as ordinary graph isomorphism, while a Pauli-group variant is BQP-complete. The direction and the group matter: the BQP algorithm for the Pauli problem is not thereby an algorithm for the GI-hard Clifford problem.

A further naming distinction appears in the 2026 paper on the NPA hierarchy by Kar, Roberson, Seppelt and Zeman. It studies a quantum isomorphism relation and its noncommutative semidefinite relaxations, with polynomial-time algorithms at each fixed level. Those statements concern a different relation on graphs and fixed relaxations; they do not establish a quantum algorithm deciding whether an ordinary vertex bijection exists.

A positive answer would enlarge the collection of important exact structure problems known to admit efficient quantum algorithms, unless a classical polynomial algorithm arrived at the same time. A negative answer would be exceptionally strong: GI has efficiently verifiable permutation witnesses and hence belongs to NP, so GI∉BQP would in particular imply P≠NP. The question is fundamental on both sides, independently of any particular physical implementation.

cards.context:
Graph isomorphism asks whether two descriptions encode the same finite relational structure after renaming the vertices. It is an exact equivalence problem, rather than a search for approximately similar networks. A proposed permutation is easy to verify by comparing all adjacency entries, but finding a successful permutation or ruling out every permutation can require reasoning about highly symmetric graphs.

Elementary invariants help without settling the problem. For instance, a six-cycle and two disjoint triangles both have six vertices, six edges and degree two at every vertex, but cannot be isomorphic because one is connected and the other is not. More elaborate invariants must likewise be assessed by whether they distinguish every required pair, not just by how well they perform on a test set.

Aaronson’s 2005 challenge list identifies graph isomorphism among the natural targets for quantum algorithms beyond Shor and Grover. The formulation on this card turns that broad research motivation into one exact complexity-class membership question. It imposes no particular algorithmic approach and permits a classical algorithm as a special case of a quantum one.

Babai’s classical breakthrough gives a quasipolynomial-time algorithm, with bound exp((log n)^{O(1)}). The original argument required a correction in January 2017, after which the quasipolynomial claim was restored. This is the relevant general classical benchmark, rather than brute-force examination of n! permutations. Quasipolynomial time is still larger than the polynomial bound asked for here.

One tempting quantum approach uses the action of permutations on graphs. The state that is a uniform superposition over all distinct labeled copies of G would be identical for isomorphic graphs and orthogonal for nonisomorphic ones. If such states could always be prepared efficiently, an overlap test would help. The state-preparation step is the difficulty: preparing a superposition of pairs |π⟩|πG⟩ is easy, but coherently removing the permutation register does not follow from that construction. Simply discarding the register gives a mixed state, not the desired pure superposition.

The established hidden-subgroup approach makes this difficulty precise in another form. Graph isomorphism can be reduced to finding hidden symmetry in permutation groups, and the standard procedure generates quantum coset states. Hallgren, Roetteler and Sen, independently of Moore and Russell and later in joint work, prove that measurements on too few such states reveal insufficient information in the relevant hard cases. Their bound requires joint access to Ω(n log n) states to obtain useful information.

That lower bound is a restriction on information extraction in a particular representation. The number of required states is itself polynomial. It does not say that every measurement on that many states needs superpolynomial computation, and it does not forbid an algorithm that uses the explicit input graphs in a different way. A negative solution to GI∈BQP would have to rule out those broader possibilities as well.

The inherited quantum-inspired reference has a substantive June 2026 revision. Maxwell, van den Hoven and Renema analyze correlations in Gaussian boson samplers and derive a classical test for a necessary condition of graph isomorphism. At restricted correlation order it can certify that some graph pairs are different. At the maximum order their condition becomes sufficient, but their method is no longer efficient. The authors explicitly separate these two regimes.

cards.definitions: An n-qubit pure state is a unit vector u∈ℂ^(2^n), indexed by binary strings x∈{0,1}^n. A Hamiltonian is a Hermitian matrix; its energy in u is u†Hu, its ground energy λ_min(H) is its least eigenvalue, and ||H|| is its operator norm. A k-local Hamiltonian is a sum of polynomially many terms, each acting nontrivially on at most k qubits and as the identity on the rest. The constant k and the polynomial bound are independent of n. No geometric locality or efficient uniform construction of the Hamiltonian family is added to the source’s existence target. The norm bound fixes the energy scale, so multiplying all terms cannot create the required constant gap artificially. For a family F of nonzero finite complex vectors, a succinct representation consists of an injective map rep:F→{0,1}*, one polynomial q and one polynomial-time compiler A. Every u∈F has |rep(u)|≤q(log₂ dim u). On a valid representation A outputs descriptions of a coordinate-query procedure Q_u, a randomized sampler S_u, and m=||u||; on every string outside the image of rep it must reject. For any coordinate x, Q_u returns the complex amplitude u_x, including its phase, in time polynomial in log dim u. S_u produces x with probability exactly |u_x|²/||u||² in polynomial time. The resulting circuit descriptions have polynomial size in log dim u. This is the source’s perfect, ζ=0 access, with no approximation to the distribution or norm. The representation map itself need not be computable from an explicitly listed vector. The same polynomial bounds and compiler apply throughout F; the eventual threshold n₀ may depend on this entire representation family. The assertion tests every unit vector in F_n, not one preselected sequence of easy states. The source counts exact complex additions, subtractions, multiplications and divisions at unit cost; this is not automatically a bit-cost sampling model.
cards.answer_criterion: Resolve the stated source-model existence proposition with its ∃Hamiltonian family, ∃ε, ∀representation family, ∃n₀ quantifiers and perfect-sampling plus amplitude-query requirements. Before treating the card as a standalone machine-level benchmark, resolve the numerical conventions recorded in statement_review. Excluding only stabilizer states, Gaussian states or constant-depth quantum preparation does not exclude every family allowed by Definition 5.1.

context_blocks.title: Sampling outcomes loses phase information
context_blocks.text: The states |+⟩=(|0⟩+|1⟩)/√2 and |−⟩=(|0⟩−|1⟩)/√2 both produce a uniformly random bit when measured in the computational basis. Yet for H=(I−X)/2, where X exchanges |0⟩ and |1⟩, their energies are 0 and 1. Their measurement distributions agree while their energies differ. This is why the source also requires access to each complex amplitude.

context_blocks.title: What a succinct description must do
context_blocks.text: Listing all 2^n amplitudes would be exponentially long. A permitted description instead has length polynomial in n and supports the prescribed efficient queries and samples. cards.formal: Is multiplicative approximation of the permanent of an independent complex Gaussian matrix, on a sufficiently large fraction of instances, #P-hard under randomized polynomial-time reductions as in the Permanent-of-Gaussians Conjecture?

cards.title: Bell nonlocality from finitely many copies of every entangled state
cards.formal: For every entangled finite-dimensional bipartite state ρ, do finitely many copies ρ^⊗k and local filters suffice to produce correlations violating a Bell inequality, without an auxiliary entangled state?
cards.definitions: A state is a positive semidefinite trace-one operator on H_A⊗H_B. It is entangled when it is not a convex combination of product states. Local filters are trace-nonincreasing completely positive maps F_A,F_B applied to the respective k-fold systems before measurement questions are selected; the joint success probability must be positive. Normalize the successful filtered state. Each party then chooses a local measurement from a finite set of positive-operator-valued measurements. The resulting conditional distribution p(a,b|x,y) is Bell-nonlocal when it has no representation Σ_λ q_λ p_A(a|x,λ)p_B(b|y,λ), with nonnegative q_λ summing to one. Such a representation is precisely a local hidden-variable model for finite questions and answers. Local ancillary states and shared randomness are allowed, but no additional shared entangled state is supplied.

context_blocks.text: Entanglement and observable Bell nonlocality are related but distinct resources. This question asks whether repeated access to the same entanglement always reveals nonlocal behavior after local preprocessing.

Liang, Masanes and Rosset prove an activation result using a suitable auxiliary state. That resource is stronger than additional copies of the given state and is expressly excluded here. Direct one-copy Bell tests also do not settle the finite-copy filtered target.

cards.title: Classical simulation of polynomial-gap local stoquastic adiabatic computation
cards.formal: Can every polynomial-time adiabatic computation described by explicit local stoquastic Hamiltonians with an inverse-polynomial global spectral gap be sampled classically in polynomial time to inverse-polynomial total-variation error?
cards.definitions: A Hamiltonian is stoquastic in the computational basis when every off-diagonal matrix entry is real and nonpositive. The intended input describes a smoothly varying sum of terms acting on a constant number of qubits, an efficiently preparable initial ground state and computational-basis measurement at the end. The gap is the separation of the lowest two eigenvalues of the full Hamiltonian, not only a symmetry-restricted subspace. The intended simulator is uniform randomized classical computation.

context_blocks.text: Stoquasticity removes a sign obstruction that often complicates classical statistical simulation. Whether that suffices for efficient simulation of general explicit local adiabatic computations remains a basic question about the source of quantum computational power.

Their result does not establish a general polynomial-time simulation theorem. Oracle-model separations also require care before being transferred to explicitly supplied local interactions.

references.title: Separating Quantum and Classical Advice with Good Codes
references.authors: John Bostanci; Andrew Huang; Vinod Vaikuntanathan
references.locator: Introduction

cards.review_note: The statement and listed results were individually checked against the cited sources. New proofs were not independently verified. The assessment of importance is editorial.

context_blocks.text: Advice is not a witness chosen for an individual input. It is one nonuniform information resource shared by an entire input-length class.

For a fixed input length, the advice must support all inputs of that length. It cannot be tailored after seeing the particular instance. This makes it different from a witness, which is chosen to establish a claim about one input. A fresh copy of the same quantum advice state can be supplied for each computation.

The possible advantage is not that a measurement reveals an arbitrary amount of classical information from a few qubits. cards.title: Strong quantum IOPs with polynomial communication
cards.formal: Does every QMA promise problem admit a constant-round strong quantum interactive oracle proof with a uniform polynomial-time verifier, total prover-message length polynomial in the input length n, total query complexity O(1), completeness at least 2/3, and soundness at most 1/3? progress.text: The general qIOP has polynomial communication but uses a polynomial private quantum resource. The strong construction operates on constantly many qubits but communicates $\exp(\operatorname{poly}(n))$ qubits. Question 1.9 asks for polynomial communication.

references.locator: Definitions 1.1–1.2; Theorems 1.5, 1.7; Question 1.9

cards.status_note: Literature checked on 10 September 2026; dates and review scope are recorded below.
cards.review_note: The statement and listed results were individually checked against the cited sources. New proofs were not independently verified. The assessment of importance is editorial.

context_blocks.text: A quantum proof can be much larger than the portion a verifier actually inspects. An interactive oracle proof lets a prover supply such messages over several rounds, with the verifier charged for the qubits it touches. Communication volume and access complexity are therefore different resources.

The strong model requires the verifier to hand each received quantum message back in full and forbids sending an additional quantum message of its own. It still has private workspace. Returning a message does not mean undoing the measurement or channel applied to the queried qubits; the resulting state can be returned.

For example, a protocol might inspect only two qubits from an enormous register. That has constant query complexity but still transmits the enormous register. Conversely, allowing the verifier to retain part of a received message changes the protocol model even if the amount of communication is small.

The existing constructions meet different combinations of the desired bounds: general qIOPs have polynomial communication, while the strong construction has exponential communication. The question asks for polynomial communication in the strong model itself. The constant-round requirement and constant total query budget must hold together.

cards.definitions: In each round the prover supplies a quantum register W. The verifier chooses queried positions through a measurement and applies a quantum channel only to those qubits and its private register; query cost counts accessed message qubits, summed over rounds. It returns the entire W register, may send additional classical information, and sends no additional quantum register. It can retain its own private workspace, but cannot retain any part of a prover-message register. The parties have no initial shared entanglement. Total prover-message length counts the full incoming registers, not only queried qubits. This restates the strong model of Definitions 5.1–5.2 and 5.13–5.15.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct such a protocol for every QMA promise problem, or prove that at least one QMA promise problem has no protocol meeting all these bounds. Polynomial communication in the weaker general qIOP model does not suffice.

importance.reason: Tests how far succinct interactive verification can extend to quantum proofs with explicit communication restrictions; affects a broad proof-system design space.

sentences: In a nonlocal XOR game, separated players try to satisfy a parity condition without communicating after receiving their inputs.

Constructing a robust separation would turn a large relative advantage into a reliably detectable quantum advantage.

cards.title: Martin’s full conjecture for Turing-invariant functions under determinacy
cards.formal: Assume ZF+DC+AD. Do both assertions hold? (I) Every Turing-invariant function f:2^ω→2^ω is either constant in Turing degree on a cone or satisfies x≤_T f(x) on a cone. (II) Cone-wise Turing reducibility prewellorders all such functions that are above the identity on a cone, and the pointwise jump f′ has rank exactly rank(f)+1 in this prewellorder.
cards.definitions: A real x∈2^ω is an infinite binary sequence, identified with a subset of the natural numbers. Write x≤_T y if an oracle Turing machine with oracle y computes x, and x≡_T y for mutual reducibility. A function f is Turing-invariant when x≡_T y implies f(x)≡_T f(y). A cone above a real a is {x:a≤_T x}. Being constant on a cone means ∃a,b ∀x≥_T a, f(x)≡_T b; the output sequences need not be literally equal. Define f≤_M g by ∃a ∀x≥_T a, f(x)≤_T g(x), and f≡_M g by mutual ≤_M. Let F be the set of all Turing-invariant f for which id≤_M f, where id(x)=x. The prewellorder assertion says that ≤_M is total on F and its quotient by ≡_M is well-ordered. The rank of f is the ordinal order type of the quotient classes strictly preceding [f]. The jump of a real y is y′={e: the e-th oracle program with oracle y halts on input e}; f′(x)=f(x)′. ZF is Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory without the axiom of choice. DC is dependent choice: every serial binary relation on a nonempty set admits an infinite successive chain. AD says every infinite game in which two players alternately choose natural numbers, with an arbitrary specified set of winning sequences, is determined. Functions are not assumed computable, Borel, order-preserving, or uniformly Turing-invariant. Cone bases may depend on the functions being compared.

cards.status_note: Explicitly open in Walsh’s March 2026 survey; checked through 10 September 2026. The saved draft’s already-settled regressive subcase has been replaced by the full quantified Part I, together with Part II. Determinacy, degree-wise constancy, and restrictions in the partial results are stated explicitly.

context_blocks.text: The Turing degrees form a complicated partial order, with many incomparable and specially constructed degrees. Yet operations arising naturally by relativizing mathematical definitions often produce a much more organized hierarchy. Martin’s conjecture attempts to make that phenomenon precise through invariance under Turing equivalence and comparison on cones, rather than through an undefined requirement that a construction be “natural.”

The two parts have different jobs. Part I rules out a function that remains nonconstant on every cone but never uniformly reaches the input degree on any cone. Part II concerns functions already above the identity. It asserts comparability and well-foundedness of their cone-equivalence classes, and says that taking an oracle halting problem moves exactly one level up, leaving no intervening class.

Cone-wise comparison ignores behaviour below a fixed computational base. This is meaningful under determinacy: every Turing-invariant set either contains a cone or is disjoint from one, giving Martin’s zero-one measure on degree-invariant sets. Thus “almost everywhere” in the literature means on a cone, not outside a null set for ordinary Lebesgue measure on binary sequences.

Restricting to functions below the identity gives a strictly narrower case with a known theorem: Slaman and Steel show that a Turing-invariant function satisfying f(x)≤_T x on a cone must be constant there or equivalent to the identity on a smaller cone. The unresolved Part I quantifies over all invariant functions, including ones not initially comparable with the identity.

Uniform invariance is another substantial restriction. It requires a single map that turns indices witnessing x≡_T y into indices witnessing f(x)≡_T f(y), independently of the actual reals. Steel and Slaman–Steel establish the conjecture for this subclass. Merely preserving equivalence classes, as the question requires, does not supply that uniform map.

Lutz and Siskind prove Part I for all order-preserving functions and more generally for measure-preserving invariant functions. Here measure-preserving means that for every fixed degree a there is a cone on which f(x) computes a. Their theorem supplies major new cases.
The March 2026 survey by Walsh still presents the full conjecture as open and keeps the Borel restriction on the earlier Part II result for order-preserving functions.

cards.title: Kolmogorov–Loveland randomness versus Martin-Löf randomness
cards.formal: Is every Kolmogorov–Loveland random infinite binary sequence Martin-Löf random with respect to the fair-coin product measure?
cards.definitions: Work in Cantor space 2^N, with coordinates numbered 0,1,… and fair-coin product measure μ. For a finite binary string σ, the cylinder [σ]={X:σ is a prefix of X} has measure 2^{−|σ|}. A Martin-Löf test is a sequence (U_k)_{k≥1} of open sets obtained by one algorithm enumerating pairs (k,σ), with U_k equal to the union of its enumerated cylinders for index k and μ(U_k)≤2^{−k}. A sequence X is Martin-Löf random if for every such test X∉⋂_k U_k. A Kolmogorov–Loveland betting strategy starts with capital 1. From the finite history h of bits already revealed, a partial computable procedure outputs a previously unqueried coordinate j and a rational multiplier q∈[0,2], before seeing X(j). The selected coordinates can be reconstructed from the earlier history and the same procedure; no coordinate may be selected twice along any run. After X(j) is revealed, the capital is multiplied by q if the bit is 0 and by 2−q if it is 1, and that bit is appended to h. Thus each bet preserves expected capital under a fresh unbiased bit and cannot create debt. q=1 allows reading a bit without risking capital. The next coordinate may depend on all revealed values and need not exceed previous coordinates. If the procedure fails to produce its next action, no further capital is earned. There are no oracle, running-time or space allowances beyond ordinary partial computability. A strategy succeeds on X if its capital at completed bets has unbounded supremum. X is Kolmogorov–Loveland random if every such strategy has bounded capital on X; the bound may depend on both X and the strategy. Rational multipliers suffice for the standard notion, and allowing partial rather than total computable strategies does not change the resulting class.
