cards.status_note: Efficient recovery above the threshold and information-theoretic recovery below it in suitable fixed-q assortative regimes are proved. The checked fixed-community computational lower bound remains conditional on an unproved low-degree conjecture. Growing-community algorithms in the August 2026 revision concern a different quantifier regime. No unconditional settlement of this precise fixed-q question found through 11 September 2026.

context_blocks.text: Community detection asks whether the edges of a network reveal an underlying partition. Here every vertex has the same expected degree, regardless of its group. Consequently, sorting vertices by degree cannot directly identify their communities. The signal is in the pattern of connections between vertices, and each vertex has only a constant expected number of observations even as the network grows.

The target is deliberately much weaker than recovering every label. A constant-degree graph has many isolated vertices, whose memberships cannot be inferred from their incident edges. Weak recovery asks only for a fixed improvement over random guessing on average. Permuting all community names must be allowed: renaming the hidden groups changes neither the graph distribution nor the quality of an inferred partition.

The quantity dθ² compares the growth in the number of observed neighbours with the decay of label information along an edge. In a local tree approximation, d describes branching and θ describes how much a child’s label remembers its parent’s label. This explains why the value one is a natural boundary for algorithms based on propagation of small correlations. It does not by itself prove an impossibility result for algorithms that use the whole graph.

Abbe and Sandon prove efficient recovery above this boundary for every fixed number of communities. Their method uses an acyclic form of belief propagation and addresses the effect of cycles in the finite graph. This supplies the algorithmic side of the proposed threshold. The question asks whether a qualitatively different method can succeed strictly below it in the assortative case a>b.

There really are parameters for which the graph contains useful information below the Kesten–Stigum threshold. Banks, Moore, Neeman and Netrapalli establish such regimes for at least eleven groups in the assortative model. Their recovery argument permits exponential computation, searching over sufficiently plausible partitions. Their five-group statement concerns the disassortative case, where between-group edges are more likely; that is a different parameter range from this card.

This produces a concrete computational-versus-statistical puzzle. The missing labels are not intrinsically unidentifiable everywhere below the boundary, yet known efficient methods do not recover them throughout the information-theoretically possible region. An affirmative answer to this card would refute the universal fixed-community barrier with a single parameter example. A negative answer would establish that the obstruction is computational wherever recovery is statistically possible.

Ding, Hua, Slot and Steurer give conditional evidence in 2025. In their parameterized symmetric model, a low-degree conjecture implies a strong computational lower bound for recovery below the threshold by a fixed margin. Their recovery definition uses correlation with the centred membership matrix. The result is a reduction from a conjecture about testing to recovery hardness, not an unconditional exclusion of polynomial-time algorithms. Its model and hypothesis restrictions matter when applying it to a particular choice of a,b.

The precise conjecture in that paper also matters. Its bounded test functions must have expectation bounded below under the planted distribution. The authors explain that a broader earlier version was refuted using rare events. Thus citing a generic “low-degree conjecture” without stating that a hypothesis remains unproved would erase both the conditional nature of the result and an actual correction in the underlying evidence.

A 2026 revision of work by Chin, Mossel, Sohn and Wein gives efficient recovery below the usual boundary when the number of communities grows sufficiently quickly, in particular in a regime above √n. This is an important warning against treating the threshold as universal over every block model. Here q is fixed before n tends to infinity. Even a very large fixed q eventually lies below √n, so the growing-community algorithm does not supply the fixed-parameter example requested.

Settling this problem would test whether a threshold suggested by local propagation describes all efficient global algorithms in a basic random graph model. A new algorithm would identify exploitable structure missed by the familiar threshold calculation. A rigorous barrier would give a particularly clean example in which unlimited inference and efficient inference have different capabilities, with the data distribution specified by only three constants.

cards.title: Can random 3-SAT at constant density be refuted in polynomial time?
cards.formal: Do there exist an integer C≥6 and a uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithm A such that A never outputs UNSAT on any satisfiable 3-CNF formula, and Pr[A(F)=UNSAT]→1 as n→∞ for F drawn from R_3(n,Cn)? The probability is over both the formula and A’s independent random bits.
cards.definitions: For n≥3, R_3(n,m) is the distribution on ordered lists of m clauses obtained independently with replacement. Each clause selects a uniformly random three-element subset of {1,…,n} and independently negates each of its three variables with probability 1/2. Each clause is their disjunction; the formula is the conjunction of the list, with duplicate clauses permitted. On every input A outputs UNSAT or UNKNOWN. Soundness is exact: for every satisfiable formula and every random tape A returns UNKNOWN. Its time is bounded by a fixed polynomial in the explicit binary input length on every input and every random tape, including adversarial formulas; variable names are binary integers and n is part of the encoding. A may use only fresh independent fair random bits and has no advice or external oracle. The constant C, the machine, and the time polynomial are chosen before n. The probability limit means that for every η>0 there is n0 such that the probability is at least 1−η for all n≥n0. There is no requirement to use a specified refutation proof system: a sound decision procedure certifying unsatisfiability suffices. Restricting the existential choice to integers C≥6 loses no larger constant-density regime, since an algorithm at a smaller density can run on the corresponding prefix of the random clause list.

context_blocks.text: At a sufficiently large fixed clause density, a random 3-CNF formula is unsatisfiable with probability approaching one. That fact alone does not give a sound algorithm for a particular input: a procedure that always announces unsatisfiability would incorrectly reject satisfiable adversarial formulas. The question is whether an efficient algorithm can recognize almost all random instances while retaining exact soundness on every satisfiable instance.

The random distribution and the algorithmic quantifiers have different roles. A is constrained on all inputs, but its success guarantee applies to the stated distribution. C is an absolute constant, so success only at a density growing with n does not meet the target. Likewise, proving that short certificates exist does not automatically yield an algorithm that finds them.

Allen, O’Donnell and Witmer define refutation as a sound UNSAT-or-fail procedure and develop refutation algorithms for random constraint satisfaction problems. They distinguish this task from planted-instance detection and from strong refutation, which certifies that every assignment violates a positive fraction of constraints. These distinctions determine which hardness assumptions and consequences apply.

Feige’s random-3-SAT hypothesis is often presented in a stronger gap formulation. For example, Barak’s formulation requires soundness even on nearly satisfiable formulas. This card records the exact-satisfiability, constant-density refutation question requested in the proposal; it does not identify that formulation with every version called Feige’s hypothesis. The gap formulation is documented as related context.

Chan, d’Orsi and Xu’s 2026 work generalizes density, sum-of-squares degree and refutation-strength tradeoffs for random CSPs. Its broader predicate model is not a polynomial-time, constant-density solution of this random-3-SAT target. The question remains a distinct counterpart to the catalogue’s planted-clique detection problem.

cards.why: Separate the typical absence of satisfying assignments from the computational ability to certify that absence soundly.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation, with the stated model, domains, promises and quantifiers. A conditional theorem settles only its conditional version. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-verified proof matching the full target.

importance.reason: A foundational average-case refutation problem with documented connections to proof complexity, learning and approximation. It supplies a different average-case task from planted recovery or detection. The exact-satisfiability variant is recorded without importing consequences of stronger gap hypotheses.

cards.title: Does average-case NP hardness imply infinitely-often one-way functions?
cards.formal: Does $\mathrm{DistNP}\not\subseteq\mathrm{HeurBPP}$ imply the existence of a polynomial-time computable function f with the following property? For every probabilistic polynomial-time inverter I and every constant c>0, infinitely many lengths n satisfy $\Pr[|z|=n\ \land\ f(z)=f(x)]<n^{-c}$, where $x\sim U(\{0,1\}^n)$ and $z\leftarrow I(1^n,f(x))$. The probability includes inverter randomness. This card fixes the infinitely-often security convention used by the cited characterization.
cards.why: It asks whether distributional hardness alone suffices for basic cryptography: a central connection between average-case complexity and cryptographic constructions.

progress.text: The revised paper characterizes the remaining obstruction by the gap between approximation factors $\ell^{1-o(1)}$ and $O(\ell)$ for minimum-description-length agnostic learning. Here $\ell$ is advice complexity of sampling. The original April version states a different quantitative claim.

context_blocks.text: Hardness of deciding typical instances and hardness of finding preimages are different requirements. The assumption P ≠ NP alone is weaker and belongs to a separate existing question.

An average-case decision problem asks an algorithm to classify instances drawn from a specified distribution. A one-way function creates a different experiment: sample an input, reveal its efficiently computed image, and ask an adversary to find any valid preimage. The sampling process and the form of the required answer both matter.

A reduction has to turn the first kind of difficulty into the second while preserving efficient generation and a meaningful success probability. It cannot simply use a hard yes/no question as a function and assume its inverse is hard. The question is whether some average-case hardness can exist without yielding the basic inversion obstacle on which one-way-function cryptography is built.

cards.definitions: DistNP consists of pairs (L,D) with L in NP and D_n a polynomial-time samplable distribution on n-bit inputs. Such a pair is in HeurBPP if a single randomized algorithm A runs in time polynomial in n and 1/delta and, for every n and $0<\delta<1$, at least a $1-\delta$ fraction of x drawn from D_n have $\Pr[A(x,\delta)=L(x)]\ge2/3$. The output is a decision bit. Infinitely-often security is weaker than requiring negligible inversion probability at all sufficiently large lengths; the latter is a distinct stronger target.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the implication under the two explicit distributional and security definitions, or prove that average-case NP hardness can hold while every polynomial-time function fails that infinitely-often inversion guarantee. A result only about an oracle world does not settle the unrelativized implication.

importance.reason: Links average-case NP hardness to the existence of a basic cryptographic primitive; resolving it would clarify the foundations of complexity-based cryptography.

cards.title: Polynomial smoothed complexity of FLIP for Max-Cut
cards.formal: Are there absolute constants C,a,b>0 such that, for every n≥1, every simple undirected graph G on n vertices, every φ≥1/2 and every collection of independent edge-weight distributions supported on [−1,1] with probability densities bounded by φ, the expected length of the longest strictly improving single-vertex-flip path is at most C(n+1)^a(1+φ)^b?
cards.why: A flagship unresolved explanation of why a canonical PLS local-search algorithm works efficiently on perturbed inputs.
cards.status_note: The ESA 2024 source explicitly retains the arbitrary-graph problem. Searches for subsequent work through 11 September 2026 found no resolution of this expected longest-path target. The general high-probability upper bound and the smoothed 3-FLIP lower bound were separated from the required guarantee. Proofs have not been independently audited.
cards.review_note: Fixed the source’s signed [-1,1] bounded-density model and one-shot independent sampling. Made expectation of the longest path, arbitrary initial cuts, strict improvement and iteration cost explicit. Preserved the expected-time target; did not replace it by a tail bound or a choice of pivot rule.

cards.definitions: The graph and one Lebesgue-measurable density f_e for each edge are chosen adversarially before the random weights. Each f_e is nonnegative, integrates to 1 on [−1,1], and is at most φ almost everywhere; weights w_e are sampled independently once from these densities and then held fixed. They may be negative and need not be identically distributed. A cut is a subset S⊆V, with value W_w(S)=Σ_{uv∈E: exactly one of u,v lies in S} w_uv. A legal step replaces S by S△{v} for one vertex v, and requires a strictly larger cut value. Define L(G,w) as the largest number of steps in any such path, maximized over all starting cuts and all choices of improving vertices after w is known; set L=0 if there is no step. There are finitely many cuts and strict improvement prevents revisiting one, so L≤2^n−1 and its expectation is well-defined. The expectation is over w alone, with the maximum over paths inside it. The resource counted is improving steps, not the bit cost of exact real arithmetic or of sampling distributions. The target concerns all graphs and all allowed densities with one common polynomial. A run ends at a single-flip local maximum, which need not maximize cut value globally.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the displayed universal polynomial bound on E_w[L(G,w)], or prove its logical negation by exhibiting admissible families that exceed every such polynomial. A bound for selected graph classes or for one favorable pivot rule does not establish the proposition. A rare long path or an unperturbed worst-case instance alone does not refute an expected bound under these density constraints.

context_blocks.title: What FLIP improves
context_blocks.text: The procedure repeatedly moves a vertex to the opposite side when this increases the weight crossing the cut. Different choices can produce different paths, so the question controls the longest one. This includes starting cuts and choices made after seeing the sampled weights, rather than relying on a particular implementation to avoid a bad path.

context_blocks.title: Local optimality has a different goal
context_blocks.text: Consider a four-cycle 1–2–3–4–1 with weights 0.9 on edges 12 and 34 and weights 1 on edges 23 and 41. The cut {1,2} has weight 2, and moving any single vertex decreases it by 0.1. Nevertheless, the alternating cut {1,3} has weight 3.8. Fast termination here would mean finding a state with no improving single move, without asserting that FLIP finds a global maximum.

context_blocks.title: What the smoothing parameter permits
context_blocks.text: The adversary chooses the graph and the distributions, while independent draws supply the randomness. Density bounded by φ prevents a distribution from putting too much probability in an arbitrarily short interval: an interval of length h has probability at most φh. cards.title: Constant adaptivity gap for influence maximization with full feedback
cards.formal: Is there a universal constant C such that OPT_adaptive(G,p,k)≤C·OPT_nonadaptive(G,p,k) for every independent-cascade influence instance under full-adoption feedback?
cards.definitions: The input is any finite directed graph, an independent retention probability p_e∈[0,1] for each edge, and a budget 1≤k≤|V|. Sample a live-edge subgraph once. A seed activates all vertices reachable from it along live edges. A nonadaptive strategy selects at most k seeds before observing the subgraph. An adaptive strategy selects seeds sequentially, observing after each choice the resulting activated set and the outcomes of edges explored by its completed cascade. Both objectives maximize the expected total number of activated vertices over strategies with no computational restriction. The expectation is over the live-edge graph and strategy coins. Failed transmissions into vertices already active reveal no additional state.

cards.title: Rapid mixing of Glauber dynamics with Δ+2 colours
cards.formal: Do absolute constants C,c>0 exist such that, for every finite simple n-vertex graph G with maximum degree Δ and every integer q≥Δ+2, the single-vertex heat-bath Glauber chain on proper q-colourings has total-variation mixing time t_mix(1/4)≤Cn^c?
cards.definitions: Let n≥1 and Ω={σ:V(G)→[q] : σ(u)≠σ(v) for every edge uv}. Colours are labelled; unused colours are allowed. At each discrete step choose v uniformly from V(G), then choose a colour uniformly from [q]\{σ(u):u∈N(v)} and assign it to v, leaving all other vertices unchanged. The current colour is among the available choices. Let P be this transition matrix and π the uniform distribution on Ω. Define t_mix(1/4)=min{t∈Z_{≥0}: max_{σ∈Ω} (1/2)Σ_{τ∈Ω}|P^t(σ,τ)−π(τ)|≤1/4}. This counts individual vertex updates, not sweeps or bit operations. The constants C,c must be independent of n, Δ, q and G. The initial proper colouring is arbitrary, and the graph has no girth, treewidth or randomness promise. This card fixes a uniform polynomial bound across degrees, rather than leaving the exponent’s parameter dependence implicit.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: A central boundary question for Markov-chain sampling: does the simplest local recolouring process mix efficiently whenever the universal ergodicity threshold is met?

cards.status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. The general-graph Δ+2 conjecture remains open in the checked sources. August 2026 results improve restricted-girth regimes with fixed relative slack; they do not establish the universal additive-two bound.

context_blocks.text: A proper colouring is easy to construct greedily with this many colours. Sampling one nearly uniformly is a different task: a deterministic rule can strongly favour a small part of the solution space. Glauber dynamics is an appealing candidate because every update uses only a vertex and its neighbours, yet repeated local changes must reproduce the global distribution. The inherited paper states the conjecture and proves it for particular graph classes.

The threshold Δ+2 has a concrete role. On a clique with Δ+1 vertices and exactly Δ+1 colours, every vertex sees all other colours in its neighbourhood. No vertex can change colour, so each proper colouring is a separate absorbing state. With at least Δ+2 colours, the single-vertex chain is irreducible on every graph and converges to the uniform distribution. The unresolved issue is how long this convergence takes.

Connectivity of the recolouring graph is insufficient to control that time. A walk may need to cross a narrow passage between two large collections of colourings. Even short paths between every pair do not show that a random walk finds the appropriate passages often enough. The card therefore asks for a distributional guarantee from the worst starting colouring, rather than a bound on the number of recolourings in an intelligently chosen path.

The update convention matters when comparing sources. A second standard version proposes a colour uniformly from the entire palette and rejects it if a neighbour uses it. This is the Metropolis version used in several cited papers. Its off-diagonal transition probabilities and the heat-bath probabilities differ by a factor between 1 and q/(q−Δ). That factor is at most 1+Δ/2 in the present range, so the distinction is relevant to sharp runtime statements but does not create an exponential gap between their polynomial-mixing questions.

The early general-graph milestones were Jerrum’s q>2Δ regime and Vigoda’s improvement to roughly 11Δ/6. Graph structure can bring the colour threshold much closer to the target. Heinrich proves n^{O(tw(G)^3)} mixing with q≥Δ+2, so bounded treewidth is covered even when maximum degree is unbounded. There was further progress during 2026. Both the girth restriction and the dependence on δ matter. Taking δ=2/Δ is not justified by a theorem that first fixes δ and then requires sufficiently large Δ.

The other inherited 2026 source studies an additional constraint: prescribed colour-class sizes. Such a condition changes the sample space, and a single-vertex update generally cannot preserve it. Its algorithms for equitable or mildly skewed colourings therefore address a separate sampling problem. They provide useful context for why global constraints complicate local sampling, while explicitly leaving the unconstrained Δ+2 conjecture open.

This is fundamental because it tests whether the basic local sampler remains efficient throughout the universally ergodic range. A proof would connect a simple combinatorial availability condition with global probabilistic convergence. A negative answer would identify an obstruction to efficient local sampling that survives despite spare colours at every vertex and connectivity of the entire state space.

cards.definitions: Ω(a,b) is the set of matrices M∈{0,1}^{r×s} with Σ_j M_ij=a_i and Σ_i M_ij=b_j. The state space is promised nonempty; no restriction on density or balance is imposed. At each discrete step, stay put with probability 1/2. Otherwise choose uniformly an unordered pair of distinct rows and independently an unordered pair of distinct columns. If their 2×2 submatrix is ((1,0),(0,1)) or ((0,1),(1,0)), replace it by the other pattern; otherwise stay put. If r<2 or s<2, the state space is a singleton and each step stays put. P denotes this transition matrix and π the uniform measure on Ω. Define t_mix(1/4)=min{t∈ℕ: max_{M∈Ω} (1/2)Σ_{N∈Ω}|P^t(M,N)−1/|Ω||≤1/4}, with value +∞ if the set is empty. Time counts attempted transitions, including stays. The maximum is over every initial state. The constants are independent of r,s and all margins; preprocessing, bit costs and sampling algorithms using other transitions are not part of this mixing-time question.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove one universal bound K(r+s)^c for all feasible margins in the specified lazy chain, or prove that its worst-case mixing time is not bounded by any polynomial in r+s. A proof confined to regular or stable margins, a different chain, or average initial states does not settle the full target.

context_blocks.text: Status update: Fu, Qin and Wang’s July 2026 revision claims a solution for this exact lazy binary-matrix chain. Theorem 2.2 gives t_mix(1/4)≤binom(r,2)binom(s,2)(rs ln 2+ln 4), which implies a universal polynomial bound in r+s. The transition probabilities and scope were compared with this card. The proof was not independently verified here, so the card records an uncertain claimed resolution.

A binary matrix can describe which species occur at which sites, or which vertices are adjacent across the two sides of a bipartite graph. Fixing its row and column sums preserves the activity of every individual row and column. Sampling uniformly from all matrices with those same margins provides a baseline for asking whether additional patterns are unusual, without confusing them with the already-fixed totals.

The elementary move preserves every margin. Replacing [[1,0],[0,1]] by [[0,1],[1,0]] changes where four entries lie while leaving each involved row sum and column sum unchanged. For a 2×2 matrix with all margins equal to one there are exactly two states. The chain stays or switches with equal probability, so one attempted transition already gives the uniform distribution. Larger instances may have many possible rectangles, most of which are not switchable.

Every allowed transition has the same probability as its reverse, making the uniform distribution stationary. Feasible binary matrices with the same margins are connected by switches, and the explicit probability of staying removes periodicity. These facts establish eventual convergence. Rapid mixing asks for a bound on how long the worst initial state can remain far from uniform; connectivity alone need not give a small bound.

Earlier theorems establish rapid mixing under additional structure. The unified approach handles P-stable degree-sequence families: roughly, small perturbations of the prescribed degrees do not create more than polynomially many times as many realizations. Such results cover broad families while retaining a hypothesis absent from the universal question. An efficient algorithm that merely finds one feasible realization would address a different task.

The inherited 2018 reference compares the switch chain with Curveball, which resamples relationships across a pair of rows using a larger move. Faster practical movement does not by itself prove a polynomial worst-case bound. A theorem about another transition rule must include the appropriate chain comparison before it can answer this card’s fixed-chain question.

The authors also supply a Lean formalization repository and identify its closed main theorem. This review checked that the artifact is linked by the paper and author, but did not build it or audit the correspondence of its definitions and theorem dependencies. The presence of a formalization is recorded as evidence, not as an independent machine verification performed by this catalogue.

The question is specifically the bipartite, zero-one matrix case. Integer-valued contingency tables, forbidden positions and general nonbipartite graphs have different state spaces or moves. A theorem for arbitrary feasible binary margins is broad enough here, while its consequences for those other sampling questions must be assessed separately.

cards.title: An FPRAS for perfect matchings in general graphs
cards.formal: Does there exist a fully polynomial randomized approximation scheme for the number Z(G) of perfect matchings in every finite undirected simple graph G? More precisely, is there one randomized algorithm A and one polynomial p such that, for every explicitly encoded graph G and rational 0<ε<1, A halts within p(L,⌈1/ε⌉) bit operations and outputs a nonnegative rational Ẑ satisfying Pr[(1−ε)Z(G)≤Ẑ≤(1+ε)Z(G)]≥3/4, where L is the total binary input length?
cards.definitions: A matching is a set of edges with no shared endpoints. It is perfect if every vertex is incident to exactly one selected edge. Z(G) is the number of distinct such edge sets; edges and vertices are unweighted. The graph is specified by a labeled vertex set and its full edge list, without bipartiteness, density, degree, expansion or planarity promises. For an odd number of vertices Z(G)=0; for the empty graph Z(G)=1. The random bits are independent fair bits, all computational and output costs are counted, and the time bound holds for every random tape. When Z(G)=0, require output zero with probability one; this causes no loss of generality because existence of a perfect matching can be decided deterministically in polynomial time before approximation begins. The fixed success probability 3/4 can be amplified to 1−δ by independent repetitions and a median, with an O(log(1/δ)) multiplicative overhead. The same polynomial p must work for all graphs and all requested accuracies. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: A canonical unresolved problem in approximate counting, separating efficient existence testing from estimating the number of solutions. It also controls the approximability of other counting and partition-function problems through reductions.

importance.reason: The major missing generalization of the permanent FPRAS, with an established obstruction to the direct Markov-chain approach and consequences beyond matchings.

context_blocks.text: Finding a perfect matching and estimating how many exist are different tasks. Edmonds’ algorithm handles existence and maximum cardinality in general graphs, whereas exact counting is #P-complete even in bipartite graphs. Approximation avoids asking for every digit of a potentially exponential count, but still requires a reliable multiplicative estimate. The 2018 paper of Štefankovič, Vigoda and Wilmes places this gap at the center of general matching-counting research.

Jerrum, Sinclair and Vigoda resolve the bipartite case through an FPRAS for the permanent of any nonnegative matrix. A square bipartite adjacency matrix records allowed pairs between two fixed vertex classes; a permutation chooses one partner for every vertex. The algorithm combines a Markov chain on perfect and near-perfect matchings with simulated annealing and weights that balance different pairs of unmatched vertices.

Applying that theorem to the ordinary adjacency matrix of a nonbipartite graph does not count its perfect matchings. For example, K₄ has three perfect matchings, but its adjacency matrix has permanent nine: the latter also counts directed cycle-cover patterns. The corresponding general-graph quantity is a hafnian, a sum over partitions of the vertex set into unordered pairs. The distinction is combinatorial, not a matter of merely changing the matrix dimensions.

Counting all matchings is another solved neighboring problem: Jerrum and Sinclair give an FPRAS for the monomer–dimer partition function. The desired perfect matchings may form a very small fraction of that distribution. A disjoint union of k edges already has 2ᵏ matchings and just one perfect matching. Thus approximate uniform sampling from all matchings, followed by waiting for a perfect one, need not run in polynomial time. This example concerns that proposed reduction, not hardness of counting on the example graph.

Štefankovič, Vigoda and Wilmes show that the straightforward extension of the JSV chain encounters exponential mixing bottlenecks on general graphs; changing weights based only on the unmatched-vertex pattern does not give a universal remedy. They also use the Gallai–Edmonds decomposition to obtain algorithms for structurally restricted graphs. A factor-critical component is one whose deletion of any one vertex leaves a perfect matching. Their parameter concerns the number of ears in such a component’s ear decomposition, not simply its vertex count.

The problem matters beyond matching counts themselves. Fei, Goldberg and Lu’s 2025 journal paper classifies approximation of several two-state spin-system partition functions. Some parameter settings are linked by approximation-preserving reductions to perfect-matching counting in general graphs, and the paper explicitly retains that task as a central open question. A resolution would therefore determine tractability for related counting models as well.

On 27 August 2026, Chen, Vigoda and Yang post an improved permanent FPRAS. For an r×r zero–one matrix their stated bound is O(r⁶ ε⁻² log⁵ r log(2/δ)), improving the previous leading dependence at fixed accuracy and success probability. Their analysis controls mixing of observables describing unmatched-vertex patterns through a restricted Poincaré inequality and coupled flows. The state space remains bipartite; the new theorem does not remove the general-graph obstruction.

The central issue is whether the extra structure available in bipartite graphs is essential for efficient approximate counting. A positive result would extend one of the landmark successes of randomized counting to all graphs. A negative result would establish a striking boundary: even though perfect matching existence remains efficiently decidable on both sides, relative counting would become computationally harder once arbitrary odd-cycle structure is permitted.

cards.title: Does #BIS admit an FPRAS?
cards.formal: Does there exist one probabilistic Turing algorithm A and one polynomial p such that, for every finite simple bipartite graph G and rational ε∈(0,1), A(G,ε) halts within p(L,⌈1/ε⌉) steps on every random tape and returns a nonnegative rational Ẑ with Pr[(1−ε)Z(G)≤Ẑ≤(1+ε)Z(G)]≥3/4? L is the full input bit length, including ε; Z(G) is the number of independent sets.
cards.definitions: The input lists the vertices, their bipartition U,V and all edges, with no loops or repeated edges; ε is supplied as a positive binary numerator and denominator. An independent set I⊆U∪V contains no edge’s two endpoints. Z(G) counts all such subsets, including ∅, so Z(G)≥1 and the empty graph has Z=1. The output is a signed binary numerator and positive binary denominator representing Ẑ≥0. A uses independent fair coin bits, with no advice or oracle. All input reading, computation, random-bit access and output writing count toward the bound. The success probability is separately required on every input and is over A’s coins. The same program and polynomial work for all bipartitions, degrees, graph sizes and accuracies.

context_blocks.text: #BIS asks for the number of independent sets in an arbitrary bipartite graph. Exact counting is already difficult, while approximate counting places the problem in a widely studied intermediate regime: it is a canonical complete problem for the class #RHΠ₁ under approximation-preserving reductions, and many spin-system and combinatorial counting problems are equivalent to it. The main unresolved issue is whether this intermediate status hides a fully polynomial randomized approximation scheme.

The relative-error requirement matters when the graph has few independent sets as well as when it has exponentially many. The algorithm must work for every explicitly encoded graph and every requested accuracy, with no structural promise that would make local sampling mix rapidly. A polynomial bound in |V| alone, an additive approximation, or an algorithm whose polynomial degree depends on the graph family would be a different statement.

Several restricted classes do admit efficient approximation schemes. For example, results for almost every sufficiently regular bipartite graph and for dense regular bipartite graphs exploit expansion or spectral structure. These theorems demonstrate that the target is achievable on substantial subclasses, but they do not provide a worst-case FPRAS for arbitrary bipartite inputs.

The conjectured difficulty is deliberately weaker than #P-hardness of approximation. #BIS is believed not to have an FPRAS, yet it is also believed not to be NP-hard under the usual approximation-preserving reductions. Resolving the card would therefore locate a central intermediate point between problems with known FPRASes and problems with robust hardness barriers.

The earlier catalogue pointer TCS-6225 came from a paper on independent sets in random regular bipartite graphs and preserved only a truncated source excerpt. This card states the general #BIS question explicitly and keeps the restricted-family results as progress rather than treating them as a solution.

cards.title: A deterministic FPTAS for the nonnegative permanent
cards.formal: Is there a uniform deterministic algorithm that, for every explicitly given nonnegative rational n×n matrix A and every rational ε∈(0,1), outputs a rational Z satisfying (1−ε)per(A)≤Z≤(1+ε)per(A) in time polynomial in the input bit length and 1/ε?
cards.definitions: For n≥1, per(A)=Σ_{π∈S_n}∏_{i=1}^n A_{i,π(i)}, where S_n is the set of permutations of [n]. Each entry is represented by a nonnegative integer numerator and positive integer denominator in binary. Let L be the total binary description length of A and ε. There must be one fixed polynomial P such that the algorithm uses at most P(L,1/ε) bit operations on every input. Ordinary deterministic Turing computation is intended, with output bits and arithmetic costs counted; there are no random bits, nonuniform advice, counting oracles or exact-real unit-cost operations. No density, expansion, lower-bound-on-positive-entries, bounded-degree or matrix-scaling promise is imposed. Zero entries are allowed. If per(A)=0, the algorithm must return Z=0 exactly. This zero case is decidable in polynomial time by checking whether the bipartite support graph has a perfect matching. FPTAS means fully polynomial-time approximation scheme: the running-time exponent must be independent of ε, and the error is relative to per(A), not additive relative to n!, a matrix norm, or another normalization.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct such a deterministic approximation scheme or prove that none exists. A randomized FPRAS does not settle the deterministic question. An approximation within a factor depending superconstantly on n, or a scheme with running time n^{g(1/ε)}, does not meet the stated guarantee. Exact #P-hardness alone is not a refutation, since using exponentially small ε is allowed to take exponential time under the FPTAS bound.
cards.why: A landmark derandomization problem: match the accuracy and efficiency of the permanent FPRAS using deterministic computation on every nonnegative rational matrix.

importance.reason: One of the central explicit tests of derandomization in approximate counting, with broad connections to matchings, sampling, convex optimization and correlation decay.

context_blocks.text: For a zero–one matrix, the permanent counts perfect matchings in its bipartite support graph: rows and columns are the two vertex classes, and a permutation chooses one allowed partner for every row. With nonnegative weights it sums the products of edge weights over these matchings. Finding one perfect matching is efficient, but estimating how much total weight all perfect matchings contribute is a different task.

Unlike the determinant, the permanent has no alternating signs in its permutation sum. Nonnegativity makes multiplicative approximation meaningful even when the total is very small. It also makes zero detection easy: a positive permanent is equivalent to existence of a perfect matching using positive entries. The hard part is accurate quantitative estimation on positive instances, not distinguishing an arbitrary exponentially tiny value from zero by floating-point tolerance.

Jerrum, Sinclair and Vigoda provide a randomized fully polynomial approximation scheme for every nonnegative matrix. Their method combines weighted perfect and near-perfect matchings, sampling and simulated annealing. Thus a solution need not discover that approximate counting is possible; it must remove randomness while retaining arbitrary relative accuracy and polynomial dependence on the requested inverse accuracy.

The randomized side continues to improve. Chen, Vigoda and Yang’s August 2026 preprint reduces the reported running time for zero–one matrices to O(n⁶ log⁵ n) when the relative accuracy and success probability are fixed, with an extension to general nonnegative matrices. The better analysis concerns a restricted Poincaré inequality for the Markov chain. It remains a sampling-based randomized algorithm.

A major deterministic approach is the Bethe permanent, obtained from a variational optimization over doubly stochastic matrices. Anari and Rezaei prove that it lower-bounds the permanent and loses at most a factor 2^{n/2}. This factor is attained on block-diagonal matrices built from two-by-two all-ones blocks. The tight example limits the unmodified Bethe estimate, rather than proving that every deterministic approximation algorithm must lose that much.

In late August 2026, Anari and independently Narang and Perkins go beyond the canonical Bethe estimate. Both approaches exploit structure near the bad two-by-two blocks and achieve a factor c^n for some absolute c<√2. This improves the exponential base. A fixed positive base above one, however, still gives an error factor growing exponentially with the matrix dimension.

The September 9 preprint of Kudria, Luo and Majid improves the general deterministic polynomial-time guarantee to exp(O(n(log log n)²/log n))=exp(o(n)). Its algorithm uses convex optimization of weighted matching sums, together with deterministic correlation-decay estimates. The theorem explicitly handles arbitrary nonnegative rational matrices in the bit model, so it applies to this card’s input class. Its approximation factor is still much larger than 1+ε.

There is a useful amplification threshold. Make a block-diagonal matrix containing r copies of A; its permanent is per(A)^r. If a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm approximated an N by N permanent within exp(O(N^{1−γ})) for one fixed γ>0, applying it at N=rn and taking an rth root would reduce the logarithmic error to O(n^{1−γ}/r^γ). Polynomially many copies in n and 1/ε would then suffice for an FPTAS.

The September theorem’s logarithmic saving does not cross that threshold: polynomially many copies increase log(rn) by only a constant-factor scale, leaving a large logarithmic error after root extraction. Consequently, subexponential approximation and arbitrary relative accuracy remain distinct milestones. A solution would remove one of the most prominent uses of randomness in approximate counting while clarifying how much global matching information deterministic optimization can recover.

Its algorithm uses convex optimization of weighted matching sums, together with deterministic correlation-decay estimates. The theorem explicitly handles arbitrary nonnegative rational matrices in the bit model, so it applies to this card’s input class. Its approximation factor is still much larger than 1+ε.

There is a useful amplification threshold. Make a block-diagonal matrix containing r copies of A; its permanent is per(A)^r. If a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm approximated an N by N permanent within exp(O(N^{1−γ})) for one fixed γ>0, applying it at N=rn and taking an rth root would reduce the logarithmic error to O(n^{1−γ}/r^γ). Polynomially many copies in n and 1/ε would then suffice for an FPTAS.

The September theorem’s logarithmic saving does not cross that threshold: polynomially many copies increase log(rn) by only a constant-factor scale, leaving a large logarithmic error after root extraction. Consequently, subexponential approximation and arbitrary relative accuracy remain distinct milestones. A solution would remove one of the most prominent uses of randomness in approximate counting while clarifying how much global matching information deterministic optimization can recover.

cards.title: Can all vertices of a rational polytope be enumerated in output-polynomial time?
cards.formal: Do there exist a deterministic Turing machine A and a polynomial p such that, for every rational matrix M and rational vector b with P={x∈R^d:Mx≤b} bounded, A lists each vertex of P exactly once and halts within p(L+S) bit operations, where L is the binary input length and S is the total binary length of the required vertex list? The dimension d is part of the input.
cards.definitions: The input specifies integers m,d≥1, M∈Q^(m×d), and b∈Q^m. Every rational is written as a reduced signed integer numerator and positive integer denominator in binary, with delimiters; L includes this entire explicit representation. P may be empty or lower-dimensional, and redundant inequalities and degeneracy are allowed. A vertex is an extreme point: v∈P such that v=(x+y)/2 with x,y∈P implies x=y=v. Every vertex is rational. The output is a finite list in arbitrary order of these vectors, with each coordinate in the same reduced rational encoding, followed by an end marker. S includes separators and the end marker; it is determined independently of the algorithm, so padding or duplicate outputs cannot enlarge the permitted bound. The empty polytope has an empty vertex list. The bound concerns total running time, including writing the output, without a polynomial-delay or polynomial-workspace requirement. Correctness and the bound are required on the bounded-polyhedron promise; behavior outside that promise is immaterial.

context_blocks.text: A finite system of inequalities describes a convex region implicitly, while a vertex list describes its extremal feasible points explicitly. Linear programming can optimize one linear objective without producing that list. Enumerating the list asks whether the entire conversion can be performed with only polynomial overhead relative to the information that must actually be returned.

The number of vertices can be exponential in the input length, so a running-time bound polynomial in the input alone would be inappropriate. Output-polynomial time allows that unavoidable cost. It still excludes an algorithm that examines exponentially many intermediate objects when the final list is short. Degeneracy is particularly relevant because many collections of tight inequalities can describe the same vertex.

Reimers and Stougie explicitly identify total-polynomial vertex enumeration for bounded polyhedra as a longstanding open question. They obtain such an algorithm under a bounded branch-width condition. Their paper also distinguishes the general unbounded-polyhedron problem, for which output-polynomial enumeration would imply P=NP. That hardness statement does not resolve the bounded target here.

Dong, Fan, Xiong and Zeng study vertices of hyperplane arrangements. An arrangement includes intersections that may lie outside the feasible region selected by a system of inequalities. Consequently, an output-sensitive bound for the entire arrangement is measured against a different output and does not establish the required bound in the number of vertices of this polytope.

This card adds geometric enumeration to a category that already contains counting and hypergraph-transversal questions. Its target is the exact finite output of an algorithm in variable dimension. Neither approximate vertices nor a fast method restricted to simple polytopes meets that target.

cards.definitions: H=([n],E), n≥0, is supplied as the explicit vertex list and a finite list of edges e⊆[n], each edge an increasing list of binary vertex identifiers. Repeated edges have no effect. L(H) is the bit length of this input including delimiters. A transversal is a set T⊆[n] intersecting every e∈E; it is inclusion-minimal when no proper subset has this property. Output each such T as an increasing list of its binary vertex identifiers with a delimiter, in arbitrary order; no duplicate, nonminimal or incomplete output is allowed. L_out(H) is the sum of the bit lengths of these records, counting one delimiter even for T=∅. If E is empty, the unique minimal transversal is ∅. If E contains ∅, there is no transversal and L_out=0. Time includes all computation, output and termination detection. The polynomial and algorithm are independent of n, E, edge size and output size; there is no separate delay or workspace bound, advice, oracle or randomization. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.

cards.title: Hadwiger’s conjecture: high chromatic number forces a clique minor
cards.formal: For every integer t≥1 and every finite nonempty simple undirected graph G, does χ(G)≥t imply that G contains K_t as a graph minor? Equivalently, is every K_t-minor-free graph (t−1)-colorable?
cards.definitions: A simple graph has no loops or parallel edges. A proper coloring assigns colors to vertices so that adjacent vertices receive different colors; χ(G) is the minimum number of colors. K_t is the complete graph on t vertices. A K_t minor is witnessed by t pairwise disjoint nonempty vertex sets B_1,…,B_t such that each induced subgraph G[B_i] is connected and every pair B_i,B_j has at least one edge between it. These branch sets can be contracted and all unwanted vertices or edges deleted. They may have arbitrary sizes; the minor need not be induced and no parity condition is imposed. Equivalently, the Hadwiger number h(G), the largest t for which G has a K_t minor, must satisfy h(G)≥χ(G). The statement concerns existence, with no running-time requirement on finding the coloring or branch sets.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: A flagship structural graph problem connecting coloring, contractions, and excluded-minor classes. A resolution would identify the exact universal coloring obstruction in every minor-closed setting; improvements also develop structural tools relevant to graph algorithms and approximation.

importance.reason: One of the central graph-theoretic conjectures, with an exact extremal target and consequences across coloring and minor structure.

context_blocks.text: A graph can have very few large complete subgraphs and still need many colors. Hadwiger asks whether contracting connected pieces always reveals a complete graph as large as the number of colors originally needed. This would make a global obstruction to coloring visible through a precise structural certificate: disjoint connected regions linked in every pair. The complete graph K_(t−1) shows that the proposed upper bound for K_t-minor-free graphs cannot be reduced.

The conjecture encompasses the Four-Color Theorem because planar graphs exclude K_5 minors. Wagner’s structure theorem makes the t=5 case equivalent to four-colorability of planar graphs. Robertson, Seymour, and Thomas extended this equivalence to t=6 by proving that a minimal counterexample in that case would be apex: deleting one vertex leaves a planar graph. Thus the known exact cases extend through K_6 minors; the first unresolved case is t=7.

The earlier general approach forced clique minors from high average degree. The resulting O(t√log t) degeneracy bound gives a coloring bound of the same order by repeatedly removing a low-degree vertex and coloring in reverse. That density threshold is sharp, so simply improving its numerical constant cannot yield Hadwiger’s linear target. The chromatic-number question requires using structure beyond this degree argument.

Delcourt and Postle obtain O(t log log t) colors through a reduction to coloring much smaller minor-free subgraphs, on roughly t times a polylogarithmic number of vertices. Their reduction also shows that proving a linear bound on these small graphs would imply a linear bound without a size restriction. It narrows where a genuinely new coloring argument is needed, without imposing the small-size hypothesis on the conjecture itself.

Liu and Luo’s September 2026 preprint builds on that reduction and claims O(t log log log t). Its proof combines contractions that reduce degeneracy with fractional colorings, which distribute weight across independent sets. Even this extra logarithm removed leaves both the O(t) weakening and the sharp coefficient in the original conjecture unresolved. The result is recorded as a new preprint claim, not as an independently verified proof.

An odd clique minor imposes additional compatibility conditions on two-colorings inside its branch trees. Kühn, Sauermann, Steiner, and Wigderson construct graphs with no odd K_t minor and chromatic number approximately 1.5t, disproving the odd Hadwiger conjecture. Their graphs are not counterexamples to the ordinary-minor assertion asked here: forbidding odd minors permits more graphs than forbidding all clique minors.

cards.title: Deterministic linear-time minimum spanning tree
cards.formal: Is there one deterministic comparison-based algorithm that, on every connected simple undirected graph with n vertices, m edges and arbitrary real edge weights, outputs a minimum spanning tree in O(m+n) worst-case time in the comparison RAM model below?
cards.definitions: The graph is explicitly supplied as vertex and edge records, with vertices numbered 1,…,n and edges given distinct identifiers. An edge record contains its two endpoints and a weight key representing an arbitrary real number. A spanning tree is a set T of n−1 edges connecting all vertices without a cycle; it is minimum when Σ_{e∈T}w(e) is smallest among all spanning trees. For n=1 the output is empty. Equal and negative weights are permitted, and any minimum tree is acceptable. Weight keys may be copied and compared, but their bit representations cannot be inspected, and arithmetic on their numerical values is unavailable. Each comparison has unit cost. Nonweight data, addresses and indices use O(log(m+n+2))-bit words on a random-access machine, with unit-cost reads, writes, comparisons, standard word arithmetic, bitwise Boolean operations and shifts; arithmetic is restricted to these words. All ordinary operations count in the running time, not just weight comparisons. The algorithm has a fixed finite description and no input-length-dependent advice or free precomputed tables. Any tables it constructs, as well as writing the output, are charged to its time. The hidden linear-time constant must be independent of graph topology, n,m and the weights. This fixes a conventional uniform sequential comparison model. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: A central unresolved boundary between deterministic and randomized algorithms for a classical graph optimization problem, and a rare case where a provably optimal algorithm exists before its exact asymptotic complexity is understood.

cards.status_note: The deterministic linear-time comparison problem remains open in the primary-author material checked through 11 September 2026. Integer-word algorithms, high-girth results and the optimal-decision-tree theorem do not settle this formulation.

context_blocks.text: A minimum spanning tree connects a graph as cheaply as possible without redundant cycles. It is among the basic examples where a local greedy rule produces a global optimum, and it appears in network design and clustering. The optimization objective is well understood; the unsettled issue is how much computation is fundamentally needed to identify the right n−1 edges when the input already contains m edge records.

Sorting every edge is sufficient for Kruskal’s algorithm, but sorting is a stronger task than the required output. On a graph that is itself a tree, every edge belongs to the answer regardless of their relative weights. On a triangle, only the identity of a largest-weight edge is needed: discard it. Thus the familiar comparison lower bound for sorting all keys does not automatically become a lower bound for finding an MST. A faster algorithm must exploit the graph’s structure to avoid unnecessary ordering information.

The cut and cycle rules make this possible. A lightest edge across a cut can be selected safely, and a strictly heaviest edge on a cycle can be discarded. Equal weights can be handled consistently by comparing pairs consisting of the weight and the edge identifier. These rules avoid numerical arithmetic on weights, so the problem is meaningful for arbitrary real keys even though the objective is expressed as a sum.

Karger, Klein and Tarjan combine random sampling with linear-time MST verification to obtain a Las Vegas algorithm with expected O(m+n) running time. It always returns a correct tree; randomness controls the work spent on recursive filtering. The target here is a deterministic guarantee for every input, so fixing an arbitrary random seed does not inherit the expected-time theorem.

Chazelle’s deterministic algorithm achieves O(mα(m,n)) time, where α is a slowly growing inverse-Ackermann function. Its soft-heap machinery deliberately permits a controlled set of key increases inside an auxiliary data structure while the surrounding algorithm preserves the exact MST answer. The extra factor is tiny for practical input sizes, yet unbounded asymptotically. Removing it asks for an exact structural understanding of the problem’s complexity, not merely an implementation improvement.

Pettie and Ramachandran establish a different kind of optimality: total algorithmic running time can match, within a constant factor, the optimal worst-case number of edge comparisons for MST. Their algorithm is uniform; it constructs the small optimal decision trees it needs within the time analysis. But the asymptotic size of that optimum is itself unknown. Consequently a proof that linear-size comparison decision trees always suffice would settle the algorithmic question through their theorem.

The graph family also matters. Eisenstat and coauthors show that it is enough to solve graphs with at most 3n/2 edges, and separately relate the general problem to graphs with any fixed lower bound on girth, the length of a shortest cycle. Their available high-girth algorithm requires a lower bound that grows with n. That difference between a fixed girth threshold and a slowly growing threshold leaves the general deterministic question open.

Changing the access model can remove the obstacle. Fredman and Willard give a deterministic linear-time algorithm using integer-word operations on the weights. That theorem can exploit their binary representation, which the real-key comparison model deliberately withholds. Similarly, an algorithm that is fast for a random graph topology has an average-instance guarantee, even if the algorithm itself is deterministic; it does not bound the work on every graph.

The remaining challenge can therefore be stated without ambiguity: retain exactness, arbitrary real-key weights and all graph topologies, and make every part of the computation linear without random choices. A negative answer would be equally significant, by establishing an intrinsic cost for deterministic comparison-based optimization that expected-time random sampling avoids.

cards.title: The Erdős–Hajnal conjecture for every forbidden induced graph
cards.formal: For every finite undirected simple graph H with at least two vertices, does there exist a real constant c(H)>0 such that every n-vertex undirected simple graph G with n≥1 and no induced copy of H satisfies max{α(G),ω(G)}≥n^{c(H)}?
cards.definitions: An induced copy of H is an injective map f:V(H)→V(G) such that distinct u,v are adjacent in H if and only if f(u),f(v) are adjacent in G. Thus both edges and nonedges must match. α(G) is the maximum size of a set of pairwise nonadjacent vertices, and ω(G) is the maximum size of a set of pairwise adjacent vertices. The constant c(H) may depend arbitrarily on the entire fixed graph H, but not on G or n. No density, degree, dimension or algorithmic promise is imposed on G. The claim concerns existence of a clique or independent set, without requiring a polynomial-time construction. A hereditary graph class is one closed under taking induced subgraphs; the class of H-free graphs is hereditary.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: A foundational prediction that forbidding any fixed induced pattern forces polynomial-size order inside a graph. Its links to hereditary classes, neighborhood complexity and sparse/dense decompositions make it a central structural question with connections to algorithmic graph theory.

importance.reason: A major unifying conjecture for hereditary graph classes, with a sharp qualitative gap between general bounds and the target and substantial recent progress on special cases.

cards.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The 2026 primary literature explicitly retains the full conjecture as open. Sági’s historical revised claim is recorded separately and is not treated as a verified solution; the withdrawal of its earlier version does not itself refute the revision. New six-vertex and bounded-VC-dimension results have restricted scope.

context_blocks.text: Ramsey’s theorem guarantees a clique or independent set of logarithmic size in every sufficiently large graph, and random graphs show that this order of magnitude is unavoidable without further restrictions. Erdős–Hajnal predicts a dramatic change after forbidding even one fixed induced pattern: the guaranteed set should grow as a positive power of the number of vertices. The conjecture therefore asks how much global organization a single local structural exclusion forces.

For a simple example, a graph with no induced three-vertex path is a disjoint union of cliques. If it has t components, choosing one vertex from each gives an independent set of size t, while the largest component has at least n/t vertices and is a clique. One of these sets has size at least √n. This proves the conjecture for that forbidden graph and illustrates the desired polynomial gain through a structural decomposition.

The general theorem of Erdős and Hajnal gives a lower bound exp(c_H√log n). Bucić, Nguyen, Scott and Seymour improve it to exp(c_H√(log n·log log n)) for a positive constant depending on H. Their 2024 journal paper is the first improvement of this general bound. It is still smaller than nᵟ for every fixed δ>0 as n grows, so the extra logarithmic factor does not reach the conjectured scale.

Closure under complementation and vertex substitution lets proofs for a few building blocks settle many further forbidden graphs. Substitution replaces one vertex by a graph whose vertices all have the same neighbors outside the replacement. The remaining five-vertex building blocks were the bull, the five-cycle and the five-vertex path, together with its complement. Nguyen, Scott and Seymour’s proof for the path, published in March 2026, completes all forbidden graphs on at most five vertices.

For longer fixed paths, their separate all-path theorem gives homogeneous sets of size 2^{(log n)^{1−o(1)}}. This is close to the polynomial scale in its exponent but still does not assert n^c for any fixed positive c. In particular, the five-vertex result should not be described as resolving the conjecture for paths of arbitrary length.

Huang, Ju and Zhou’s August 2026 revision proves two additional six-vertex cases using an extension of iterative sparsification. The E-graph is a five-vertex path with a new leaf attached to its middle vertex. The Bird starts from a triangle with leaves attached to two different triangle vertices, then extends one of those leaves by one more edge. Both contain an induced five-vertex path, so excluding either permits a larger class than excluding the path itself.

A 28 August 2026 preprint by Tran and Nguyen reports another six-vertex case, specified without a drawing by vertex set {a,b,c,d,e,f} and edge set {ab,bc,cd,de,af,bf,df}. It develops the comb and sparsification framework further. This is an individual new forbidden pattern, rather than a proof for every six-vertex graph.

Another strand connects the conjecture with finding large nearly empty or nearly complete induced subgraphs. Bucić, Fox and Pham prove equivalence with polynomial quantitative versions of the Rödl and Nikiforov statements. This makes the problem relevant to structural decompositions and induced-pattern density, beyond locating a single clique or independent set.

There are also stronger quantitative results under additional hypotheses. Sun, Wang and Zeng’s July 2026 preprint gives exponent at least (Cd)⁻ᵈ for graphs of neighborhood VC-dimension at most d. This dimension bounds the size of a vertex set on which neighborhoods realize every possible subset. Such a restriction controls neighborhood complexity; arbitrary H-free graphs are not assumed to satisfy a fixed VC-dimension bound.

sentences: Forbidding one fixed induced graph excludes both its edge pattern and its nonedge pattern.
The Erdős–Hajnal conjecture predicts that every graph with this restriction has a clique or independent set of polynomial size.
The exponent may depend on the forbidden graph but must stay positive as the host graph grows.
This would show that every proper hereditary restriction forces much stronger homogeneous structure than arbitrary graphs guarantee.
The saved review records special-case advances and unvalidated full-solution claims separately, and a near-polynomial bound with a vanishing exponent does not establish the required fixed exponent.

cards.context:
Ramsey’s theorem guarantees a clique or independent set of logarithmic size in every sufficiently large graph, and random graphs show that this order of magnitude is unavoidable without further restrictions. Erdős–Hajnal predicts a dramatic change after forbidding even one fixed induced pattern: the guaranteed set should grow as a positive power of the number of vertices. The conjecture therefore asks how much global organization a single local structural exclusion forces.

For a simple example, a graph with no induced three-vertex path is a disjoint union of cliques. If it has t components, choosing one vertex from each gives an independent set of size t, while the largest component has at least n/t vertices and is a clique. One of these sets has size at least √n. This proves the conjecture for that forbidden graph and illustrates the desired polynomial gain through a structural decomposition.

The general theorem of Erdős and Hajnal gives a lower bound exp(c_H√log n). Bucić, Nguyen, Scott and Seymour improve it to exp(c_H√(log n·log log n)) for a positive constant depending on H. Their 2024 journal paper is the first improvement of this general bound. It is still smaller than nᵟ for every fixed δ>0 as n grows, so the extra logarithmic factor does not reach the conjectured scale.

Closure under complementation and vertex substitution lets proofs for a few building blocks settle many further forbidden graphs. Substitution replaces one vertex by a graph whose vertices all have the same neighbors outside the replacement. The remaining five-vertex building blocks were the bull, the five-cycle and the five-vertex path, together with its complement. Nguyen, Scott and Seymour’s proof for the path, published in March 2026, completes all forbidden graphs on at most five vertices.

For longer fixed paths, their separate all-path theorem gives homogeneous sets of size 2^{(log n)^{1−o(1)}}. This is close to the polynomial scale in its exponent but still does not assert n^c for any fixed positive c. In particular, the five-vertex result should not be described as resolving the conjecture for paths of arbitrary length.

Huang, Ju and Zhou’s August 2026 revision proves two additional six-vertex cases using an extension of iterative sparsification. The E-graph is a five-vertex path with a new leaf attached to its middle vertex. The Bird starts from a triangle with leaves attached to two different triangle vertices, then extends one of those leaves by one more edge. Both contain an induced five-vertex path, so excluding either permits a larger class than excluding the path itself.

A 28 August 2026 preprint by Tran and Nguyen reports another six-vertex case, specified without a drawing by vertex set {a,b,c,d,e,f} and edge set {ab,bc,cd,de,af,bf,df}. It develops the comb and sparsification framework further. This is an individual new forbidden pattern, rather than a proof for every six-vertex graph.

Another strand connects the conjecture with finding large nearly empty or nearly complete induced subgraphs. Bucić, Fox and Pham prove equivalence with polynomial quantitative versions of the Rödl and Nikiforov statements. This makes the problem relevant to structural decompositions and induced-pattern density, beyond locating a single clique or independent set.

There are also stronger quantitative results under additional hypotheses. Sun, Wang and Zeng’s July 2026 preprint gives exponent at least (Cd)⁻ᵈ for graphs of neighborhood VC-dimension at most d. This dimension bounds the size of a vertex set on which neighborhoods realize every possible subset. Such a restriction controls neighborhood complexity; arbitrary H-free graphs are not assumed to satisfy a fixed VC-dimension bound.

cards.title: Reed’s χ–ω–Δ conjecture
cards.formal: Does every nonempty finite simple undirected graph G satisfy χ(G)≤⌈(Δ(G)+1+ω(G))/2⌉?
cards.definitions: A graph is simple when it has neither loops nor parallel edges. A proper k-colouring is a map from V(G) to {1,…,k} assigning different colours to endpoints of every edge; χ(G) is the minimum such k. The degree of a vertex is its number of neighbours, and Δ(G) is the maximum degree. A clique is a vertex set whose distinct vertices are all adjacent, and ω(G) is its largest possible size. The ceiling ⌈x⌉ is the least integer at least x. The statement concerns all such graphs, including disconnected graphs and graphs with isolated vertices. For an edgeless nonempty graph, χ=ω=1 and Δ=0. The empty graph can be included with χ=ω=Δ=0, without changing the question. There are no restrictions on graph size, maximum degree, forbidden subgraphs or the method used to obtain a colouring.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the stated inequality for every finite simple graph, or give a finite graph and a proof that its chromatic number exceeds the displayed ceiling. The target is an existence theorem, so a polynomial-time colouring algorithm is not required. An asymptotic bound with an additive error, a convex combination with clique coefficient less than 1/2, or a theorem restricted to sufficiently large maximum degree is partial progress unless the remaining cases are also covered.
cards.why: A central structural colouring problem with an exact, best-possible target. It asks how much the absence of a large clique must reduce the number of colours, and guides probabilistic, structural and algorithmic approaches to colouring.

importance.reason: A defining universal conjecture linking three basic graph parameters, with sharp examples and broad influence on colouring theory and its algorithmic methods.

cards.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The September 8 primary revision explicitly retains the exact undirected inequality as open. Small-clique estimates, sufficiently-large-degree interpolation bounds, and the recolouring and directed variants do not settle the full statement. The published 0.119 bound’s stated dependency is preserved in the context.

context_blocks.text: Two elementary bounds frame graph colouring. A clique needs a distinct colour for every vertex, so χ≥ω. On the other hand, greedily colouring vertices in any order uses at most Δ+1 colours: at most Δ colours are forbidden by already coloured neighbours. Reed asks whether an upper bound halfway between these two numbers always suffices, after rounding up. This would sharply connect a local obstruction, the size of a clique, to the global task of partitioning all vertices into independent sets.

The rounding is essential even for a five-cycle. It has maximum degree two and clique number two, but it needs three colours because an odd cycle is not bipartite. The unrounded average is 5/2. Complete graphs also meet the proposed upper bound exactly. These examples show that the question is about a precise universal inequality, rather than merely reducing the leading constant in a loose estimate.

There is also a useful family explaining the coefficient 1/2. Replace each vertex of a five-cycle by a clique of size t, joining every vertex of two replacement cliques whenever their cycle vertices were adjacent. The resulting graph has 5t vertices, maximum degree 3t−1 and clique number 2t. An independent set contains at most two vertices, so at least ⌈5t/2⌉ colours are necessary. A universal bound ⌈(1−ε)(Δ+1)+εω⌉ with ε>1/2 would give fewer colours for large t. Thus the conjectured interpolation coefficient cannot be increased.

Reed established a weaker universal interpolation with some fixed positive coefficient ε in place of 1/2. This already gives a saving proportional to the gap between maximum degree and clique number. Proving such a saving is difficult because high degree need not mean that a neighbourhood resembles a clique, and local savings must coexist across many overlapping neighbourhoods.

Hurley, de Joannis de Verclos and Kang report ε=0.119 for sufficiently large maximum degree, using a refined random colouring procedure and local sparsity estimates. Their published paper explicitly records a dependency: the 0.119 calculation uses a then-unreviewed result of Delcourt and Postle. Remark 3.1 gives ε=0.113 using an alternative published ingredient. The September 2026 digraph paper continues to cite the 0.119 bound. Both constants remain far below the conjectured 1/2.

A different advance handles graphs with much smaller cliques. Bonamy, Kelly, Nelson and Postle bound the chromatic number by O(Δ√(log ω/log Δ)), with related list and correspondence colouring results. For suitable relations between ω and Δ this is much stronger than a small fixed improvement on the greedy bound. It does not prove the desired average bound across the full range of clique sizes.

Recent related work also changes the task. The 2025 recolouring paper studies whether proper colourings can be connected by Kempe changes: swap two colours on a connected component induced by those colours. Its general conjectured interpolation coefficient is 1/3 because reconfiguration has obstructions beyond the existence of one colouring. Its positive results on odd-hole-free graphs therefore need to be read in that separate model.

Kawarabayashi and Picasarri-Arrieta extend the framework to directed graphs, where each colour class must induce an acyclic digraph. Their SODA 2025 work, revised in September 2026, proves a positive-ε interpolation and proposes the exact half-average analogue. Replacing each undirected edge by arcs in both directions recovers ordinary colouring, so the proposed directed statement would imply Reed’s conjecture. The directed partial theorem does not supply the missing coefficient.

cards.title: Is graph isomorphism solvable in polynomial time?
cards.formal: Does there exist one deterministic classical algorithm that, for every pair of finite simple undirected graphs G and H given by explicit adjacency matrices, decides whether G and H are isomorphic in time polynomial in the total input length?
cards.definitions: Two graphs on equally many vertices are isomorphic if a bijection of their vertex sets preserves adjacency in both directions. The input contains the complete graph descriptions; unequal vertex counts are rejected immediately. The algorithm must be uniform, deterministic and correct on every graph pair, with no promise of bounded degree, rigidity, expansion, or random input. Polynomial time is measured in the binary input length, so the Θ(n²) adjacency data may be read in full. The question concerns ordinary vertex-permutation isomorphism, not quantum isomorphism, graph canonization under a different output requirement, or isomorphism of groups or tensors. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: Tests whether the central equivalence problem for finite combinatorial structures can be recognized in deterministic polynomial time after the quasipolynomial barrier was broken.

importance.reason: A canonical unresolved problem at the intersection of algorithms, permutation groups and complexity theory, with a precise best-known general upper bound.

context_blocks.text: Graph isomorphism asks whether two finite graphs differ only by a relabelling of their vertices. A proposed relabelling is easy to verify, so the problem lies in NP, but ruling out all relabellings can be difficult for highly symmetric graphs.

Many special cases have polynomial-time algorithms, including bounded-degree graphs and several classes with strong structural restrictions. These results do not automatically combine into an algorithm for arbitrary graphs, whose automorphism groups can have a much richer structure.

Babai’s breakthrough gives a deterministic quasipolynomial-time algorithm, with running time exp((log n)^{O(1)}), improving the earlier subexponential bound. Quasipolynomial time is still asymptotically larger than every fixed polynomial, so the final gap to P remains exactly the question on this card.

Graph canonization is closely related: producing a canonical labelled representative is at least as demanding as deciding isomorphism in many standard reductions, but a theorem about one output formulation must preserve the required runtime and uniformity before it answers the decision problem. Quantum graph-isomorphism relations and BQP algorithms likewise concern different computational problems.

No general polynomial-time algorithm or unconditional lower bound excluding one was found in the checked literature through 11 September 2026. The problem remains a clean benchmark for the boundary between efficiently verifiable symmetry and efficient recognition of symmetry.
