cards.title: Tutte’s 5-flow conjecture
cards.formal: Does every finite loopless bridgeless undirected multigraph G admit an orientation of every edge and an assignment f:E(G)→{1,2,3,4} such that, at each vertex, the sum of f on incoming edges equals the sum on outgoing edges as integers?
cards.definitions: A finite loopless undirected multigraph consists of a finite vertex set and a finite set of distinct edge identities, each with two different endpoints. Several edges may have the same endpoint pair. An edge is a bridge if deleting that edge increases the number of connected components. Bridgeless means there are no such edges; disconnected graphs and isolated vertices are allowed. An orientation chooses a tail and head for each edge independently. At vertex v, integer flow conservation is Σ_{e:head(e)=v}f(e)=Σ_{e:tail(e)=v}f(e), with empty sums zero. A nowhere-zero k-flow is such an orientation and assignment with values 1,...,k−1. The statement is an existence assertion, not a bound on construction time, and does not impose an embedding or a vertex-degree bound.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation with the stated model, hypotheses and quantifier order. The proof must settle the entire target. A result conditional on an additional assumption settles only that conditional version. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof checked by a proof assistant and matching this statement.

cards.title: Almost-linear-time exact maximum matching in general graphs
cards.formal: Is there one randomized sequential algorithm that, on every explicitly represented finite simple undirected graph G with n vertices and m edges, outputs an exact maximum-cardinality matching with probability at least 2/3 and has expected running time (n+m+2)^{1+o(1)} in the word-RAM model below?
cards.definitions: A matching M⊆E(G) is a set of edges no two of which share an endpoint. Its size is |M|, and ν(G)=max{|M|:M is a matching in G}. The algorithm must output valid edge identifiers forming a matching on every terminating execution, and |M|=ν(G) with probability at least 2/3 on each input. It must terminate with probability one. Vertices are labelled 1,…,n and the input is an adjacency-list or edge-list representation of size O(n+m); isolated vertices are included in n. Put N=n+m+2. Use a random-access machine with Θ(log N)-bit words, supporting constant-cost reads, writes, comparisons, addition, subtraction, multiplication, integer division with nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations and shifts on words, and fresh uniform random words. Intermediate larger integers require multiple words and their processing is charged. Preprocessing and output writing are included. The program is uniform, with no advice or free precomputed tables. The time statement means that this same algorithm satisfies: for every real ε>0 there are constants Cε and Nε such that for every input with N≥Nε, its expected number of operations is at most Cε N^{1+ε}. The expectation is over its own random choices, not a distribution on graph inputs. No edge weights, degree restriction, bipartiteness promise, approximation slack or auxiliary communication model is assumed. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.

context_blocks.text: Maximum matching is a basic model of pairing compatible objects while using each object at most once. General graphs allow compatibility patterns that cannot be separated into two sides. Edmonds’ blossom method established that this optimization is polynomial-time solvable. The remaining question is how close its exact computational cost can come to the size of the graph that must be read.

Maximum and maximal have different meanings. A maximal matching merely cannot be extended by adding a single edge. On a four-vertex path, the middle edge alone is maximal, while the two outside edges form a maximum matching of size two. A greedy linear-time procedure can therefore solve maximal matching and still fail the exact task on a tiny input. The card requires the global optimum, with no allowed loss of even one matched pair.

Alternating paths explain how a nonmaximum matching can improve. Such a path alternates edges outside and inside the matching and starts and ends at unmatched vertices. Flipping its edge membership increases the matching size by one. In general graphs, odd cycles complicate the search for shortest augmenting paths; contracted structures called blossoms keep track of these possibilities. Micali and Vazirani’s classical algorithm achieves O(m√n) time, with later work developing its proof and presentation.

Bipartite graphs have a particularly effective flow formulation. Direct each edge from the left side to the right, join a source to left vertices and right vertices to a sink, and give every edge capacity one. Integral maximum flow gives a maximum matching. Almost-linear exact flow algorithms therefore solve bipartite matching within the desired time scale. There is no supplied bipartition in the present question, and the same construction does not automatically encode odd-cycle constraints.

A triangle illustrates the polyhedral obstacle without requiring a large example. If a fractional variable of one half is placed on each edge, every vertex has total incident value one, but the total value is 3/2 while an integral matching has size at most one. For any odd vertex set S, an integral matching uses at most (|S|−1)/2 edges entirely inside S. Handling these additional odd-set restrictions efficiently is part of what distinguishes general matching from its bipartite counterpart.

Algebraic algorithms offer another route. Mucha and Sankowski use Gaussian elimination to construct maximum matchings in randomized time governed by matrix multiplication, conventionally written O(n^ω) for an available exponent ω>2. This is a major improvement over combinatorial bounds on dense graphs. It still does not yield input-size almost-linear time on all sparse graphs, where a dense n-by-n matrix representation can itself exceed the input size by a large factor.

Approximation also behaves differently. Duan, Pettie and Su obtain a (1−δ)-approximation for maximum weight matching in O(mδ⁻¹ log δ⁻¹) time, hence linear time for fixed δ; unit weights cover cardinality. To force exact cardinality purely by rounding this guarantee, one would need δ small enough that the possible loss is below one edge. When the optimum is Θ(n), that requires δ=O(1/n), so substituting it into the approximation running time loses the desired almost-linear bound.

Ansaripour, Danaei and Mehlhorn’s 2024 implementation study is useful for interpreting experiments: the observed behaviour on random graphs can be close to linear, while specially constructed inputs expose substantial differences between algorithms. Empirical speed and average graph behaviour therefore cannot establish the bound quantified over every input here. Their paper also keeps the distinction between the faster bipartite results and general matching explicit.

A June 2026 revision by Chakraborty and coauthors places construction of a general maximum matching in polynomial-time catalytic logspace. This model permits a large auxiliary tape with arbitrary initial contents, provided those contents are restored. It is progress on space and reversible use of auxiliary memory. The polynomial-time statement is not an almost-linear running-time theorem, so it does not resolve this card.

cards.title: The Gyárfás–Sumner conjecture
cards.formal: For every finite nonempty tree T and every integer r≥1, does there exist a finite integer B(T,r) such that every finite simple undirected graph G with clique number at most r and no induced subgraph isomorphic to T has chromatic number at most B(T,r)?
cards.definitions: A tree is a connected graph with no cycle. All graphs here are finite, simple and undirected. The clique number ω(G) is the largest number of pairwise adjacent vertices, and the chromatic number χ(G) is the least number of colours in a proper vertex colouring, in which adjacent vertices receive distinct colours. Both parameters are zero for the empty graph. For S⊆V(G), the induced graph G[S] retains all edges of G with both endpoints in S. Saying that G contains an induced T means there is an injective map φ:V(T)→V(G) such that xy is an edge of T if and only if φ(x)φ(y) is an edge of G. Extra edges between image vertices are forbidden. The quantifier order is ∀T ∀r ∃B ∀G: the integer B may depend arbitrarily on T and r, but not on |V(G)|, maximum degree or any additional parameter of G. Equivalently, for each T there is a function f_T:N→N with χ(G)≤f_T(ω(G)) for every induced-T-free graph G. No prescribed polynomial growth, computability requirement for f_T, or efficient colouring algorithm is part of the target. The statement concerns ordinary chromatic number, not fractional, list, oriented or domatic colouring parameters.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the stated bound for all finite trees and all fixed clique bounds, or exhibit one fixed tree T and one fixed integer r together with induced-T-free graphs G_k satisfying ω(G_k)≤r and χ(G_k)→∞. A single finite graph can disprove a proposed numerical bound but cannot refute the existence of some larger bound. A bound that still grows with |V(G)|, or a theorem with a different excluded object or extra host-graph promise, is not a full resolution.
cards.why: Determine whether every fixed induced tree is an unavoidable pattern in graphs whose chromatic number grows while their clique number stays bounded.

context_blocks.text: A clique explains one elementary reason for needing many colours: its vertices must all receive different colours. But graphs can require arbitrarily many colours even when every clique has size at most two. The conjecture proposes that forbidding any one fixed induced tree eliminates this unbounded gap. Once the tree and clique bound are fixed, the same finite palette should suffice no matter how many vertices the graph has.

The induced condition is essential. A copy of a tree as an ordinary subgraph can ignore unwanted edges between its vertices. An induced copy must reproduce both adjacency and nonadjacency. Complete graphs contain every sufficiently small tree as an ordinary subgraph, while most of those trees do not occur as induced subgraphs. The difficult step in building the desired tree is therefore arranging its branches without creating extra edges among them.

Trees are the natural boundary for this kind of one-forbidden-pattern statement. High-girth graphs can have arbitrarily large chromatic number while containing no short cycles. If a fixed forbidden graph contains a cycle, choosing larger girth avoids that graph while retaining an unbounded chromatic number and a bounded clique number. The corresponding obstruction is absent for forests. This is why the conjecture is a proposed classification, rather than an arbitrary choice of forbidden shape.

There are substantial positive cases. Kierstead and Penrice proved the conjecture for every tree of radius at most two: some central vertex is within distance two of every other vertex. Paths and further tree families are also known. Scott and Seymour subsequently strengthen the radius-two result under exclusion of a fixed complete multipartite subgraph, with polynomial bounds in its part size. Such results exploit restrictions on how branches can interact.

Nguyen, Scott and Seymour’s 2023 preprint, published in 2024, obtains a copy of any fixed rooted tree under the conjecture’s high-chromatic-number hypotheses, with every path from the root induced. This controls unwanted edges along ancestor–descendant paths. It still permits edges between different branches, and those edges may prevent the whole vertex set from inducing a tree. The distinction isolates one of the remaining obstacles.

Their later work on near-linear stable sets applies to every fixed excluded forest and fixed clique bound. It proves an independent set of size n^{1−o(1)}, and consequently a chromatic bound n^{o(1)}, where n is the number of vertices. Thus every fixed positive power n^ε eventually exceeds the available upper bound. Nevertheless, a function such as log n is also n^{o(1)} and is unbounded, so subpolynomial growth does not establish the constant B(T,r) sought here.

That work also proves a bounded fractional chromatic number for multibrooms, formed by identifying the roots of several paths that have additional leaves at their far ends. Fractional colouring covers vertices by weighted independent sets and minimizes the total weight. Ordinary colouring requires an actual partition into colour classes. The paper retains the full conjecture for general multibrooms despite its stronger fractional conclusion.

Davies and Yuditsky establish the conjecture, with a polynomial bound in the clique number, for intersection graphs of axis-aligned boxes in every fixed dimension d. Their result first appeared in 2024 and was published in April 2026. Both the excluded forest and dimension are fixed parameters. Allowing the dimension to grow with the input would let the bound vary with an extra parameter, so the theorem does not cover arbitrary graphs with the uniform bound required here.

For algorithms, this conjecture identifies a structural source of bounded colouring complexity and large independent sets. It does not itself promise that a suitable colouring can be found efficiently. A proof with an effective construction would offer additional algorithmic information; a counterexample would reveal a family of sparse-clique graphs whose chromatic obstruction survives exclusion of one fixed induced tree. The size-independent existence statement is already fundamental.

cards.title: The optimal quantitative Excluded Grid Theorem
cards.formal: For each integer r≥2, let f(r) be the least nonnegative integer t such that every finite simple undirected graph of treewidth at least t contains the r×r square grid as a minor. Determine the asymptotic order of f(r) up to universal constant factors, including the correct logarithmic dependence.
cards.definitions: The r×r grid has vertex set {1,…,r}², with an edge between (i,j) and (i′,j′) exactly when |i−i′|+|j−j′|=1. It has r² vertices; r denotes side length. A graph H is a minor of G if H can be obtained by deleting vertices, deleting edges and contracting edges, after removing loops and merging parallel edges. Equivalently, a model of H consists of one nonempty connected vertex set in G for each vertex of H, all pairwise disjoint, with an edge of G joining the corresponding sets for every edge of H. Additional edges are permitted. A tree decomposition of G is a tree T with bags B_t⊆V(G), such that every vertex belongs to some bag, the endpoints of every edge belong together to some bag, and the bags containing any given vertex form a connected subtree of T. Its width is max_t |B_t|−1; treewidth tw(G) is the minimum such width. Robertson–Seymour’s Grid-Minor Theorem guarantees that f(r) is finite. The quantifier over G includes graphs of arbitrary size, degree and genus. This is an extremal existence threshold; no efficiency requirement for finding the grid model is imposed. Polylogarithmic factors mean (log r)^c for a fixed constant c, and matching bounds here must resolve such factors rather than suppress them.
cards.answer_criterion: Identify an explicit asymptotic function h(r) and universal constants a,b>0 such that a h(r)≤f(r)≤b h(r) for all sufficiently large r. The upper bound must force a grid minor in every graph above the stated threshold; the lower bound must give graphs of comparable treewidth that exclude it. In particular, this determines whether f(r)=O(r²(log r)^c) for some fixed c. Merely improving a nonmatching polynomial exponent, solving the planar-host case, or replacing minors by a different containment relation is progress rather than a complete answer.

context_blocks.text: Treewidth measures how large the interacting pieces of a graph must be when organized along a tree. Many algorithms work by dynamic programming across the bags of a tree decomposition, with a strong dependence on bag size. A grid provides a canonical obstruction to small treewidth: its rows and columns create many overlapping connections that cannot be separated into very small bags. The Excluded Grid Theorem states that every graph of sufficiently large treewidth contains such an obstruction as a minor.

The unknown quantity is how much treewidth must be spent to force a grid of a given side length. The qualitative theorem only says that some finite threshold exists. A sharp quantitative bound would explain how efficiently general tangled connectivity can be organized into a planar grid. This is not a statement that the graph itself is planar, or that a grid must appear as an induced subgraph.

A vertex-count example already rules out a linear threshold. The complete graph on r²−1 vertices has treewidth r²−2, but cannot contain an r×r grid minor because taking a minor cannot increase the number of vertices. Thus f(r)≥r²−1. Its many edges cannot replace the need for r² disjoint nonempty branch sets in a minor model. This is why the fact that the r×r grid itself has treewidth r does not imply a linear bound for arbitrary host graphs.

The known lower bound is stronger: f(r)=Ω(r² log r). Robertson, Seymour and Thomas obtain it using bounded-degree expanders of logarithmic girth. Such graphs have treewidth proportional to their number of vertices, while every cycle is long. A large grid contains quadratically many vertex-disjoint small cycles; lifting those cycles through a minor model requires quadratically many disjoint long cycles in the host. This consumes a logarithmic factor of additional vertices.

Chekuri and Chuzhoy obtain the first polynomial upper bound, replacing an enormous quantitative gap by a polynomial relationship between treewidth and grid size. Their proof is constructive: a randomized polynomial-time algorithm finds a grid model at the scale established by their theorem. This makes the result useful both as a structural guarantee and as a subroutine, although this card asks only for the optimal existence threshold.

Chuzhoy and Tan improve the general upper bound to O(r⁹(log r)^c) for an absolute constant c. Their SODA 2019 paper, published in journal form in 2021, builds on well-linked sets and paths of connected clusters. Well-linkedness supplies many disjoint connections; the challenge is arranging them into the grid’s particular pattern without losing too much width at successive stages. The lower and upper bounds still differ by a large power of r.

The same paper records competing predictions: Robertson–Seymour–Thomas conjectured that the r² log r lower bound is tight, while Demaine and coauthors proposed a cubic threshold. Consequently, the catalogue target is the actual asymptotic order. A near-quadratic upper bound would be a major result, but should not be described as the only conjectured answer. Even r² times an unspecified power of log r would leave part of the present target unresolved.

The 2025 paper The Grid-Minor Theorem Revisited strengthens the structural description of graphs excluding a fixed planar minor. It represents them inside clique blow-ups of graphs whose treewidth is controlled by the excluded graph’s treedepth. The blow-up size is an unspecified function of the excluded graph. This gives useful product structure and colouring applications, while leaving the optimal numerical threshold f(r) undetermined.

Catching Rats in H-minor-free Graphs, presented at SODA 2026, makes another substantial refinement under an extra host-graph restriction. For a fixed excluded graph H with t vertices and Euler genus g, a graph excluding both H and the r×r grid has treewidth O(gr+t^{2304}), hence O(t²r+t^{2304}). This is linear in r when H is fixed. General graphs in our question need not exclude any fixed H, so that additional parameter cannot be treated as a universal constant.

The threshold influences the quantitative strength of grid-based routing arguments, packing-versus-covering theorems and parameterized algorithms. Better bounds can improve how a large-treewidth case yields useful structure, or how a no-grid case bounds the state space for dynamic programming. A matching lower bound would be equally informative: it would identify an unavoidable loss in converting unrestricted graph connectivity into a planar obstruction.

Their SODA 2019 paper, published in journal form in 2021, builds on well-linked sets and paths of connected clusters. Well-linkedness supplies many disjoint connections; the challenge is arranging them into the grid’s particular pattern without losing too much width at successive stages. The lower and upper bounds still differ by a large power of r.

The same paper records competing predictions: Robertson–Seymour–Thomas conjectured that the r² log r lower bound is tight, while Demaine and coauthors proposed a cubic threshold. Consequently, the catalogue target is the actual asymptotic order. A near-quadratic upper bound would be a major result, but should not be described as the only conjectured answer. Even r² times an unspecified power of log r would leave part of the present target unresolved.

The 2025 paper The Grid-Minor Theorem Revisited strengthens the structural description of graphs excluding a fixed planar minor. It represents them inside clique blow-ups of graphs whose treewidth is controlled by the excluded graph’s treedepth. The blow-up size is an unspecified function of the excluded graph. This gives useful product structure and colouring applications, while leaving the optimal numerical threshold f(r) undetermined.

Catching Rats in H-minor-free Graphs, presented at SODA 2026, makes another substantial refinement under an extra host-graph restriction. For a fixed excluded graph H with t vertices and Euler genus g, a graph excluding both H and the r×r grid has treewidth O(gr+t^{2304}), hence O(t²r+t^{2304}). This is linear in r when H is fixed. General graphs in our question need not exclude any fixed H, so that additional parameter cannot be treated as a universal constant.

The threshold influences the quantitative strength of grid-based routing arguments, packing-versus-covering theorems and parameterized algorithms. Better bounds can improve how a large-treewidth case yields useful structure, or how a no-grid case bounds the state space for dynamic programming. A matching lower bound would be equally informative: it would identify an unavoidable loss in converting unrestricted graph connectivity into a planar obstruction.

cards.title: Caccetta–Häggkvist: minimum outdegree forces a short directed cycle
cards.formal: For every pair of integers n≥2 and 1≤r≤n−1, does every simple loopless digraph D on n vertices with minimum outdegree at least r contain a directed cycle of length at most ceil(n/r)?
cards.definitions: A simple loopless digraph has a finite vertex set V and an arc set A⊆{(u,v)∈V×V:u≠v}; each ordered pair occurs at most once. Both (u,v) and (v,u) are allowed. The outdegree d⁺(v) is |{u:(v,u)∈A}| and minimum outdegree is min_(v∈V)d⁺(v). A directed cycle of length ℓ≥2 is a sequence of pairwise distinct vertices v_1,...,v_ℓ with (v_i,v_(i+1))∈A for every i and v_(ℓ+1)=v_1. Thus an opposite pair of arcs is a directed 2-cycle. ceil(n/r) is the least integer not smaller than n/r. There is no planarity, regularity, connectivity or algorithmic assumption.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation with the stated model, hypotheses and quantifier order. The proof must settle the entire target. A result conditional on an additional assumption settles only that conditional version. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof checked by a proof assistant and matching this statement.

cards.title: Almost-linear triangle detection
cards.formal: Does there exist one uniform randomized word-RAM algorithm that, on every finite simple undirected graph with n vertices and m edges given by adjacency lists, decides whether a triangle exists with success probability at least 2/3 and worst-case running time (n+m+2)^{1+o(1)}?
cards.definitions: A triangle is a set of three distinct vertices u,v,w for which all three unordered edges {u,v},{v,w},{w,u} are present. The input gives labelled vertices 1,…,n and explicit adjacency lists; it is promised to describe a simple undirected graph, and can be disconnected or contain isolated vertices. The RAM has words of w=⌈4 log₂(n+2)⌉ bits, random-access memory, and unit-cost word reads/writes, comparisons, Boolean operations, shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo 2ʷ, and integer division by a nonzero word. Independent random words may be generated at unit cost. Input reading and all preprocessing count toward time. The running-time bound holds for every graph and every random tape, while correctness probability is over the algorithm’s internal randomness. The o(1) is a function tending to zero as n+m tends to infinity, for this one fixed algorithm; equivalently, for every ε>0 the same algorithm eventually uses at most (n+m+2)^{1+ε} operations. There is no promise on density, degree, arboricity or triangle count. Matrix multiplication and other algebraic techniques are allowed if their implementation fits this machine model. Only one yes/no answer is required.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct and analyze an algorithm meeting the stated all-input time and probability guarantees, or prove that no such algorithm exists. A deterministic O(n+m) algorithm would be an even stronger positive answer. A fixed exponent above one, an O(n²) bound that is only input-linear on dense graphs, output-sensitive listing, or an algorithm restricted to bounded-arboricity graphs does not settle the question. The target fixes the original draft’s “linear or at least almost-linear” alternative at the precise almost-linear threshold.

context_blocks.text: Triangle detection is among the smallest nontrivial pattern-finding tasks in a graph. The pattern has only three vertices, but a graph may contain an enormous number of possible triples. The question asks whether all the relevant combinations can be handled in essentially the time required to read the graph. It must also handle triangle-free instances, where an algorithm cannot stop upon finding a convenient local witness.

Detection is different from listing. A complete graph has Θ(n²) input edges and Θ(n³) triangles, so explicitly listing every triangle cannot take linear time in the input size. A yes/no answer has constant output size and faces no such output-size obstruction. Likewise, approximate counting or finding triangles in a distribution of random inputs does not supply an exact decision guarantee on every adversarial graph.

Chiba and Nishizeki give triangle listing in O(m·a(G)) time, apart from reading isolated vertices, where arboricity a(G) is the minimum number of forests needed to cover the graph’s edges. This gives linear time on any family of bounded arboricity, including planar graphs. General graphs can have arboricity of order √m, so this approach has a superlinear worst-case cost. A sparse graph can still contain a dense, difficult region.

Alon, Yuster and Zwick improve the general sparse-graph bound using a degree threshold. Handle triangles touching a low-degree vertex by local enumeration, and use matrix multiplication on the smaller set of high-degree vertices. For an available square matrix-multiplication exponent τ, the resulting standard bound is O(n+m^{2τ/(τ+1)}), roughly O(n+m^{1.407}) at familiar current exponents. The optimization balances the cost of the two parts.

Even setting the matrix-multiplication exponent to two in this particular reduction leaves exponent 4/3 in m. Thus faster dense multiplication alone, inserted into the same degree-splitting argument, would not make the sparse algorithm almost linear. This is an observation about the upper-bound method, not a proof that a different graph algorithm cannot do better.

Abboud and Vassilevska Williams formulate a no-almost-linear triangle hypothesis and use it to derive conditional lower bounds for dynamic problems. The conjecture concerns general algorithms on logarithmic-word RAMs. Their separate combinatorial Boolean-matrix-multiplication conjecture restricts the kinds of techniques used; it should not be substituted for the unrestricted question here. Reductions transfer assumed hardness, rather than establish an unconditional superlinear lower bound.

The distinction remains useful in current work. Kumabe and Uezato’s ICALP 2026 paper reduces triangle detection to matching certain fixed regular expressions with two backreference uses. Consequently, an almost-linear algorithm for that matching task would also give an almost-linear triangle algorithm. This illustrates why a small graph pattern can govern complexity in a seemingly unrelated setting.

Search results require source checks. Dumitrescu’s March 2024 claim of faster combinatorial triangle algorithms was withdrawn three days after posting; the author states that the algorithm may fail and identifies an invalid case analysis. It is not an established improvement.

I also checked the parent-edge rule in Vega’s August 2025 linear-time proposal. Consider the path 0–1–2–3–4–5–6 plus edges 0–3, 3–6 and 0–6. A legal DFS follows the whole path. Its unique triangle is {0,3,6}, consisting entirely of back edges. No test restricted to a DFS parent, its child and a common neighbour can find it. A local simulation and exhaustive triple check confirm this counterexample to the stated rule; this is not a test of later replacement implementations.

A separate September 2026 Aegypti revision claims O(n²) time via bucket reduction. That claimed bound is not almost linear for every sparse input, even if its correctness were established. I have not adjudicated its different proof. An all-density statement must keep both n and m visible: a dense-case breakthrough and an input-linear sparse algorithm are distinct achievements.

A resolution would identify whether a basic three-way adjacency condition inherently requires substantial work beyond scanning an explicit graph. A positive algorithm would affect graph-pattern routines and invalidate hardness assumptions used by many reductions. A negative result would provide a major unconditional lower bound for a simple polynomial-time graph problem on a strong, standard machine model.

cards.title: Seese’s conjecture for MSO₁ and clique-width
cards.formal: For every isomorphism-closed class C of finite simple undirected graphs, does decidability of its MSO₁ satisfiability problem imply that some constant k bounds the clique-width of every graph in C?
cards.definitions: An MSO₁ sentence is built from vertex equality, adjacency E(x,y), membership x∈X in vertex sets, Boolean connectives, and quantification over individual vertices and subsets of the vertex set. There is no built-in vertex order, edge-set quantification, parity predicate or other counting extension. For a fixed class C, Sat_MSO₁(C) consists of all finite encoded MSO₁ sentences φ for which some G∈C satisfies φ. Decidable means that one Turing machine, allowed to depend on C, halts and answers correctly for every input sentence. C itself is not an input to that machine; no complexity bound is required. By negating sentences this is equivalent to deciding the theory Th_MSO₁(C)={φ: every G∈C satisfies φ}. A k-expression builds a labeled graph from single vertices with labels in [k], disjoint union, relabeling every vertex of one label to another, and adding all edges between two distinct labels. The clique-width cw(G) is the smallest k permitting such an expression after labels are forgotten; set cw(∅)=0. The conclusion is ∃k∀G∈C cw(G)≤k, with k depending on C. No hereditary, minor-closed, bounded-degree or finite-forbidden-subgraph assumption is imposed.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the implication for every such graph class, or give one class of unbounded clique-width together with a correct terminating algorithm for its entire MSO₁ satisfiability problem. A single finite graph cannot refute a uniform width bound for a class. Model checking on a supplied graph, or decidability with a promise about sentence size, is not the premise. Results requiring parity predicates or restricted graph classes do not prove the full statement.
cards.why: A major proposed structural necessity for logical decidability, connecting graph decompositions, finite model theory and algorithms over infinite families of finite inputs.

importance.reason: A foundational conjecture asking whether bounded clique-width is unavoidable whenever an entire graph class has decidable vertex-set monadic logic.

references.title: Hereditary 2-WQO Graph Classes Have Bounded Clique-Width
references.authors: Julien Duron; Nikolas Mählmann; Szymon Toruńczyk
references.locator: Posted 12 July 2026; v2 dated 26 July; hereditary two-label well-quasi-ordering hypothesis

cards.status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. Seese’s MSO₁ decidability implication remains unresolved in the checked primary literature. The parity extension, the shrub-depth expressiveness characterization and the July 2026 2-WQO result have distinct hypotheses or conclusions.

context_blocks.text: An MSO₁ sentence can describe a graph property by quantifying over sets of vertices. Three-colorability, for example, can be expressed by choosing three sets that partition the vertices and requiring each set to be independent. Checking such a sentence on one finite graph is always decidable by exhaustive search. The premise here is much stronger: from a sentence alone, decide whether it holds in at least one member of an entire, potentially infinite graph class.

Clique-width measures how many vertex labels are needed to construct a graph using a small repertoire of operations. Labels identify groups of vertices that receive the same future edge additions. Dense graphs can have small clique-width: a complete graph can be built with two labels by inserting one vertex, joining it to all previous vertices, and merging its label. Thus the conjectured structural restriction is not a sparsity condition.

The classical treewidth theorem provides the motivation. Seese proves structural restrictions from decidability of monadic theories, and the version allowing quantification over edge sets forces bounded treewidth. Grid-minor machinery supports that argument. The MSO₁ conjecture replaces edge-set quantification by vertex-set quantification and asks for bounded clique-width instead. Transferring the proof requires a logical way of recovering the appropriate obstruction.

Bounded-width descriptions support decidability because graph properties can be translated into properties of construction trees. In particular, for each fixed k the full class of graphs of clique-width at most k has decidable MSO₁ satisfiability. But the conjecture is only a necessary-condition statement for an arbitrary class C. One cannot infer that every subclass of a bounded-width class has decidable theory.

For a simple reason, such a converse would be false. Choose an undecidable set S of positive integers, and let C contain exactly the edgeless graphs whose numbers of vertices belong to S. All those graphs have clique-width one. A sentence specifying exactly n vertices would decide whether n∈S if satisfiability over C were decidable. Restricting which sizes occur can encode undecidability even when each individual graph has trivial structure.

Courcelle–Oum prove the implication after extending MSO₁ with the predicate Even(X), saying that a vertex set has even cardinality. Their vertex-minor and isotropic-system machinery establishes bounded clique-width from decidability of this stronger logic. This strengthens the premise: a decision procedure for ordinary MSO₁ sentences need not handle parity sentences. Therefore their theorem supplies substantial progress while leaving the exact statement here open.

Hereditary classes, which are closed under taking induced subgraphs, are a useful focus even though the card quantifies over all classes. If satisfiability is decidable on C, it is also decidable on its hereditary closure: ask whether some vertex subset induces a graph satisfying the input sentence, using a relativized MSO₁ formula. Unbounded clique-width is preserved on passing to that larger class. Thus a proof covering all hereditary classes would suffice.

Dawar–Sankaran develop a stronger route through interpreting arbitrarily large grids. Their Theorem 3.2 reduces that stronger assertion to two settings: antichains of unbounded clique-width under induced-subgraph containment, and minimal hereditary classes of unbounded clique-width. They verify the grid interpretation for the known minimal families studied in their paper. This is a research program and collection of cases, not a completed classification of all such families.

The inherited ICALP 2025 paper by Mählmann settles a different boundary: on hereditary classes, bounded shrub-depth characterizes coincidence of first-order and monadic second-order expressive power. Its conclusion formulates a stronger conjectural relationship between clique-width and MSO dependence, explaining how parts of that conjecture would imply Seese’s. Shrub-depth and clique-width are distinct parameters, and a theorem about expressive power does not by itself decide satisfiability.

Duron–Mählmann–Toruńczyk’s July 2026 preprint proves that every hereditary 2-WQO class has bounded clique-width. Here 2-WQO means that every infinite sequence of graphs with two possible vertex labels contains an earlier graph embedding as a label-preserving induced subgraph of a later one. This resolves a related structural conjecture, but it starts from a well-quasi-ordering hypothesis. It does not turn an arbitrary MSO₁ decision procedure into such an ordering property.

The unresolved implication asks whether decidable graph theories always have bounded constructional complexity. A proof would show that broad logical decidability cannot arise from some entirely different mechanism on classes of unbounded clique-width. A counterexample would reveal precisely such a mechanism. Either outcome would change how structural graph theory explains the limits of automated reasoning over whole families of finite structures.

Hereditary classes, which are closed under taking induced subgraphs, are a useful focus even though the card quantifies over all classes. If satisfiability is decidable on C, it is also decidable on its hereditary closure: ask whether some vertex subset induces a graph satisfying the input sentence, using a relativized MSO₁ formula. Unbounded clique-width is preserved on passing to that larger class. Thus a proof covering all hereditary classes would suffice.

Dawar–Sankaran develop a stronger route through interpreting arbitrarily large grids. Their Theorem 3.2 reduces that stronger assertion to two settings: antichains of unbounded clique-width under induced-subgraph containment, and minimal hereditary classes of unbounded clique-width. They verify the grid interpretation for the known minimal families studied in their paper. This is a research program and collection of cases, not a completed classification of all such families.

The inherited ICALP 2025 paper by Mählmann settles a different boundary: on hereditary classes, bounded shrub-depth characterizes coincidence of first-order and monadic second-order expressive power. Its conclusion formulates a stronger conjectural relationship between clique-width and MSO dependence, explaining how parts of that conjecture would imply Seese’s. Shrub-depth and clique-width are distinct parameters, and a theorem about expressive power does not by itself decide satisfiability.

Duron–Mählmann–Toruńczyk’s July 2026 preprint proves that every hereditary 2-WQO class has bounded clique-width. Here 2-WQO means that every infinite sequence of graphs with two possible vertex labels contains an earlier graph embedding as a label-preserving induced subgraph of a later one. This resolves a related structural conjecture, but it starts from a well-quasi-ordering hypothesis. It does not turn an arbitrary MSO₁ decision procedure into such an ordering property.

The unresolved implication asks whether decidable graph theories always have bounded constructional complexity. A proof would show that broad logical decidability cannot arise from some entirely different mechanism on classes of unbounded clique-width. A counterexample would reveal precisely such a mechanism. Either outcome would change how structural graph theory explains the limits of automated reasoning over whole families of finite structures.

cards.title: Exact directed maximum flow in O((m+n) polylog n) time
cards.formal: For every fixed integer a≥1, do there exist a constant k≥0 and a uniform classical randomized algorithm A_a that, on every directed graph with n≥2 vertices, m arcs, distinguished distinct vertices s,t and integer capacities in {0,…,n^a}, outputs an exact maximum s–t flow with probability at least 2/3 in worst-case time O((m+n)(log(n+2))^k)?
cards.definitions: The graph is explicitly given by its labelled vertex set {1,…,n} and an arc list, with no loops and at most one arc per ordered vertex pair; opposite arcs are allowed. A flow assigns an integer f_e to each arc, with 0≤f_e≤u_e and equal incoming and outgoing sums at every vertex other than s,t. Its value is the outgoing sum at s minus the incoming sum at s; maximum refers to the largest such value. Output the m flow values, not only an approximate value. Use a word RAM with word length B_a⌈log₂(n+2)⌉ for a fixed integer B_a large enough to store capacities, total flow and memory addresses. Unit-cost operations are random-access word reads/writes, comparisons, Boolean operations, shifts, addition, subtraction, multiplication modulo 2^w and integer division of nonzero divisors. Multiword computations are charged for their component operations. Independent fair random bits are allowed, with each generated word charged. All preprocessing and output are included, and the time bound holds on every random execution. There are no oracles or input-dependent advice. A_a, k, B_a and the hidden constant may depend on a, but not on the graph. The m+n convention includes explicitly listed isolated vertices.

context_blocks.text: Maximum flow is a basic model for routing through capacity constraints. A feasible solution must obey conservation at intermediate vertices, and optimality measures the largest transferable amount between two terminals. Even a graph with small integer capacities can require globally coordinated changes to a feasible routing. The question asks whether finding the exact optimum can cost only a polylogarithmic factor more than reading the graph.

Almost-linear algorithms already represent a major qualitative advance. Chen and coauthors obtained exact maximum flow and minimum-cost flow in m^(1+o(1)) time for polynomially bounded integral data. Li and Wice’s August 2026 preprint obtains an almost-linear maximum-flow bound through a different framework. Neither stated asymptotic guarantee is O(m polylog n).

The distinction concerns the remaining overhead. For example, exp(√log n) is subpolynomial in n but exceeds every fixed power of log n. A running time containing that factor can be almost linear without satisfying this card. Removing the residual gap would identify a sharper computational cost for a central graph optimization primitive.

Exactness is also a substantive part of the target. A flow whose value is within a fixed relative error of optimum does not determine the optimum integer value when that value is large. Conversely, restricting capacities to polynomial magnitude means their binary encodings occupy logarithmically many bits each. The question is therefore not asking an algorithm to read arbitrarily long capacities in a graph-size-only time bound.

The primary topic is a static graph algorithm, so the current catalogue places the question in Structural graph theory and graph algorithms. Dynamic maintenance, parallel computation and strong polynomiality for unbounded-bit linear programming impose different requirements. No existing maximum-matching or dynamic-connectivity card represents this flow target.

cards.definitions: A finite simple undirected graph G=(V,E) has a finite vertex set V and an edge set E consisting of unordered two-element subsets of V; there are no loops or parallel edges. An isomorphism from G to H is a bijection f:V(G)→V(H) such that {u,v} is an edge of G if and only if {f(u),f(v)} is an edge of H. Write [G] for its isomorphism class. For v∈V(G), G−v is the induced graph on V(G)∖{v}: remove v and exactly the edges incident with v. Define D(G) to be the multiset {[G−v]:v∈V(G)}, with one entry for every deleted vertex. Thus D(G)=D(H) means that for each isomorphism class K of graphs on n−1 vertices, the number of vertices v with [G−v]=K equals the corresponding number for H. Each entry forgets all original vertex labels, including the identity of the deleted vertex; repeated isomorphism classes retain their multiplicities. All graphs, including disconnected graphs and graphs with isolated vertices, are included. The question is a structural uniqueness statement and imposes no running-time requirement on an algorithm.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that equal vertex decks imply isomorphism for every n≥3, or refute the conjecture by exhibiting two nonisomorphic finite simple undirected graphs with n≥3 and identical decks, with proofs of those properties.

context_blocks.text: Imagine receiving every graph obtained by deleting one vertex from an unknown graph, with the vertex labels erased in each view. Different deletions can yield identical-looking graphs, and their number of occurrences remains part of the data. The conjecture says this complete collection determines the original graph uniquely up to relabeling.

For a path on three vertices, deleting either endpoint leaves a single edge, while deleting the middle vertex leaves two isolated vertices. Its deck therefore consists of two copies of the edge and one edgeless two-vertex graph. The triangle instead has three copies of the edge. The lower limit of three vertices is necessary: an edge and an edgeless graph on two vertices both have a deck of two isolated single vertices.

Some global information survives deletion automatically. If n≥3, every original edge appears in exactly n−2 members of the deck, so the total number of edges is the sum of the edge counts in the deck divided by n−2. Comparing each member’s edge count with that total also recovers the multiset of vertex degrees. These counts do not specify how all vertices fit together; that missing arrangement is the substance of the question.

Uniqueness has a different meaning from efficient recovery. There are finitely many graphs of a fixed order, so one can always enumerate those whose decks match the input. The conjecture says there is just one matching isomorphism class whenever the input is the deck of a graph with at least three vertices. It does not require that this enumeration be replaced by a polynomial-time algorithm.

McKay reports exhaustive verification through 13 vertices, and the 2026 revision by Heinrich and coauthors proves reconstruction for every interval graph with at least three vertices. Neither a finite range nor this particular graph class covers all finite graphs. The computations and proofs were not independently reproduced in this review.

A 2026 AI-assisted result concerns a structured bipartite incidence-deletion analogue: it retains the deleted vertex as an isolated vertex, preserves a given bipartition in isomorphisms, and assumes 2-connectivity and pairwise distinct vertex types. Its theorem is not the unrestricted vertex reconstruction conjecture.

The status record also preserves a 2024 general proof claim by O’Shea and Wilkins. Its publisher abstract was checked, but the full argument was inaccessible and is not validated here. Later specialist sources still formulate the general conjecture as open, so this review does not label it resolved.

cards.title: Berge–Fulkerson: six perfect matchings covering each edge twice
cards.formal: Does every finite loopless bridgeless cubic multigraph G have an ordered list (M_1,...,M_6) of perfect matchings such that for every edge e∈E(G), |{i∈{1,...,6}:e∈M_i}|=2?
cards.definitions: Edges of a multigraph have distinct identities and may share their unordered pair of endpoints; loops are forbidden. Cubic means every vertex has degree three, counting incident edge identities with multiplicity. A bridge is an edge whose deletion increases the number of connected components, and bridgeless graphs have none. Disconnected graphs are allowed. A matching is a subset of edges no two of which share an endpoint. It is perfect if every vertex is incident with exactly one of its edges. The six matchings may repeat; membership counts positions in the list, not just distinct subsets. The conclusion requires every edge to occur exactly twice, with no omitted edge and no extra coverage. No algorithmic bound is required.

cards.title: Barnette’s Hamiltonicity conjecture
cards.formal: Is every finite simple undirected graph that is 3-connected, cubic, bipartite and planar Hamiltonian?
cards.definitions: A simple graph has neither loops nor parallel edges. It is 3-connected if it has at least four vertices and deleting any set of at most two vertices leaves a connected graph. Cubic means every vertex has degree exactly three. Bipartite means its vertices admit a partition into two sets with no edge having both endpoints in the same set. Planar means it has a drawing in the plane whose edge interiors do not intersect and contain no vertices; different edges may meet only at shared endpoints. A Hamiltonian cycle is a cyclic ordering v_1,...,v_n of all vertices, each appearing exactly once, such that {v_i,v_(i+1)} is an edge for every i, with v_(n+1)=v_1. The cycle must use only edges already present in the graph. No algorithmic running-time guarantee is requested.

cards.title: Seymour’s second-neighborhood conjecture
cards.formal: Does every finite nonempty oriented graph D contain a vertex v for which |N⁺⁺(v)|≥|N⁺(v)|, where N⁺(v) consists of vertices at directed distance one from v and N⁺⁺(v) consists of vertices at directed distance exactly two?
cards.definitions: An oriented graph is a finite vertex set V and an arc set A⊆V×V with no loops and with at most one of (u,v),(v,u) present for each distinct pair. Arc multiplicities are not allowed. N⁺(v)={u:(v,u)∈A}. N⁺⁺(v)={w∈V∖(N⁺(v)∪{v}): there exists u with (v,u)∈A and (u,w)∈A}. Thus a vertex already in the first neighborhood is not counted in the second, even if it is also reachable by a length-two walk. Cardinalities count vertices rather than paths or arcs. A sink has both sets empty and satisfies the inequality. No lower bound on outdegree, connectivity or planarity is imposed.

cards.title: Erdős girth conjecture: is the classical spanner size bound tight?
cards.formal: For every fixed integer $k\ge 2$, do there exist a constant $c_k>0$ and arbitrarily large simple undirected graphs $G$ with $n$ vertices, at least $c_k n^{1+1/k}$ edges, and no cycle of length at most $2k$? Equivalently, can the $O_k(n^{1+1/k})$ extremal upper bound for girth greater than $2k$ be attained up to a constant factor for every $k$? The first unsettled value is $k=4$: girth at least nine and $\Omega(n^{5/4})$ edges.
cards.why: This is a structural problem with a short, rigorous reduction to an algorithmic limit. I include it because many claims that a distance-preserving graph representation is optimal depend on precisely this unproved construction. A proof would establish those lower bounds; a counterexample would force a re-examination of the expected stretch–space tradeoff.
cards.definitions: The girth is the length of a shortest cycle, with infinite girth for a forest. A $t$-spanner is a spanning subgraph $H\subseteq G$ satisfying $d_G(u,v)\le d_H(u,v)\le t\,d_G(u,v)$ for every reachable pair. The parameter $k$ is fixed as $n$ grows, and constants may depend on $k$. The question asks for existence; an efficient explicit construction would be a stronger result.

progress.text: Althöfer, Das, Dobkin, Joseph, and Soares give sparse multiplicative spanners: every weighted $n$-vertex graph admits stretch $2k-1$ with $O_k(n^{1+1/k})$ edges. High-girth graphs give the corresponding obstruction to improving size.

Bodwin and Lopez review the remaining girth conjecture in Section 1.1. Their degree-fault-tolerant spanner lower bound is unconditional, separating a new algorithmic result from the still-open underlying conjecture.

context_blocks.text: High degree tries to make short cycles unavoidable. In a graph whose small neighborhoods contain no cycles, a breadth-first search keeps discovering new vertices rather than revisiting old ones. Sustaining large branching for several levels consumes the available vertices rapidly. This is the reason a ban on short cycles forces an upper bound on density; the conjecture asks whether graphs can pack edges as efficiently as that counting argument permits.

The algorithmic connection is direct. Suppose a unit-weight graph has girth greater than $2k$. If a subgraph omits an edge $uv$, every remaining $u$–$v$ path has at least $2k$ edges: a shorter path together with $uv$ would create a forbidden cycle. Thus any $(2k-1)$-spanner must keep every edge. A dense graph of this kind is a certificate that no smaller spanner can preserve the required distances.

For example, a triangle-free graph alone is not enough for the $k=2$ application: a four-cycle allows one edge to be replaced by a three-edge detour. Excluding both triangles and four-cycles makes every edge indispensable for stretch three. This example explains why the exact girth threshold appears in the conjecture.

The conjecture is not an established law of graph sparsification. The 2026 source records that only the parameters 1, 2, 3, and 5 are known and discusses reasons to question the general statement. Its new fault-tolerant lower bound bypasses the conjecture for that model; it does not construct the missing high-girth families.

cards.title: Tuza’s triangle packing–covering conjecture
cards.formal: For every finite simple undirected graph G, is τ_△(G)≤2ν_△(G), where τ_△(G) is the minimum size of an edge set meeting every triangle and ν_△(G) is the maximum number of pairwise edge-disjoint triangles?
cards.definitions: A simple graph has no loops or parallel edges. A triangle is a set of three distinct vertices together with all three edges between them. An edge set F meets every triangle if each triangle contains at least one edge of F; equivalently, deleting F makes G triangle-free. Define τ_△ as the minimum cardinality of such F⊆E(G). A packing is a family of triangles whose three-edge sets are pairwise disjoint; triangles in a packing may share vertices. Define ν_△ as the maximum cardinality of a packing. Both values are zero when G has no triangles, including the empty graph. The inequality concerns integral edge sets and integral packings, with no fractional weights and no running-time requirement.

cards.title: Is Exact Matching on general graphs in deterministic polynomial time?
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic algorithm, polynomial in the input bit length, that decides the following problem? Given a simple undirected graph G on an even number n of vertices, each edge colored red or blue, and an integer $0\le k\le n/2$, determine whether G has a perfect matching containing exactly k red edges. The algorithm must be correct on every input. No bipartition is promised, and no randomness or computational hardness assumption is allowed.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that this decision problem belongs to P, or prove that it does not. A randomized polynomial-time algorithm, an approximation to the red count, or an algorithm restricted to bipartite graphs does not establish the positive answer.
cards.why: I include this because it is a concrete combinatorial derandomization target with a short, checkable definition. It asks whether randomness is necessary for an exact constraint on top of an otherwise tractable optimization problem, connecting matching algorithms to algebraic identity testing.
cards.definitions: P denotes languages decidable by a uniform deterministic Turing machine in time polynomial in the ordinary adjacency-list encoding and the binary encoding of k. A perfect matching is a set of disjoint edges covering every vertex. If a polynomial-time decision algorithm exists, a matching can also be recovered by polynomially many decisions on residual instances. This target concerns sequential polynomial time, not deterministic NC.

progress.text: Mulmuley, U. Vazirani, and V. Vazirani provide the randomized algebraic matching framework underlying polynomial-time Exact Matching algorithms.
El Maalouly surveys algorithms and related problems while retaining general deterministic polynomial-time Exact Matching as open.
Du claims a deterministic bipartite algorithm. Version 3 states eight explicit hypotheses in its Lean formalization. That paper does not claim a general-graph solution.

Sato and Yamaguchi’s revised preprint tests all possible red counts simultaneously with high probability using O(n^ω) finite-field operations, where ω denotes the matrix-multiplication exponent used by their algebraic routines. The algorithm remains randomized; the introduction explicitly retains deterministic polynomial-time Exact Matching as open.

context_blocks.text: Perfect matching already has efficient deterministic algorithms on general graphs. Requiring a prescribed number of red edges adds an exact constraint that the ordinary matching objective does not express. A minimum-red matching and a maximum-red matching only identify two ends of the attainable range; intermediate counts can be missing.

For example, color a six-cycle alternately red and blue. Its two perfect matchings have respectively three and zero red edges. Neither one nor two is attainable. This obstruction appears even in a bipartite graph; allowing odd cycles adds further structure that a general algorithm must handle.

A yes answer is easy to verify once a matching is supplied: check that every vertex is covered once and count the red edges. The difficulty is finding a deterministic procedure that also certifies no instances in polynomial time. The existing algebraic route uses random choices to prevent the cancellation that can hide a feasible matching.

The graph class is essential. A 2026 preprint claims a deterministic solution for bipartite Exact Matching, and the separate catalogue entry records that claim and its formalization limits. This card concerns all graphs. Even a validated bipartite theorem would need another argument before it could settle the proposition here.

cards.title: Neumann–Lara’s planar two-color conjecture
cards.formal: For every finite oriented graph D whose underlying undirected graph is planar, is there a coloring c:V(D)→{0,1} such that neither color class induces a directed cycle?
cards.definitions: An oriented graph has no loops or parallel arcs and contains at most one of (u,v) and (v,u) for each unordered pair of distinct vertices. Its underlying simple undirected graph joins u,v exactly when one of these arcs is present. Planarity means that graph admits a drawing in the plane with edges intersecting only at common endpoints. For a vertex set X, the induced subdigraph D[X] retains every arc of D whose two endpoints lie in X. A directed cycle is a cyclic sequence of distinct vertices with all successive arcs oriented forward. A digraph is acyclic if it has no directed cycle. Color classes may be empty. This is not proper coloring: an arc may have endpoints of the same color provided no monochromatic directed cycle results. The assertion asks only for existence, without an algorithmic running-time bound.

cards.title: Can subcubic subgraphs preserve treewidth within a constant factor?
cards.formal: Does there exist a real constant C≥1 such that every finite nonempty simple undirected graph G contains a nonempty subgraph H with maximum degree at most 3 and tw(H)≥tw(G)/C?
cards.definitions: A subgraph H=(V_H,E_H) satisfies V_H⊆V(G) and E_H⊆E(G)∩{{u,v}:u,v∈V_H,u≠v}. Edges and vertices may be deleted, but no edge is contracted and no new vertex or edge is introduced. H need not be induced, connected or spanning. Its maximum degree is max_(v∈V_H)|{u:{u,v}∈E_H}|. A tree decomposition of a nonempty graph F consists of a finite tree T with vertex bags B_t⊆V(F), such that every vertex lies in a bag, both endpoints of each edge lie in a common bag, and the nodes whose bags contain a fixed vertex induce a nonempty connected subtree. Its width is max_t|B_t|−1. Treewidth tw(F) is the minimum width over all such decompositions; nonempty edgeless graphs have treewidth zero. C is independent of G and its treewidth. No bound on the number of vertices of H and no construction-time requirement is imposed.

cards.title: Linear-time directed shortest paths with positive integer weights
cards.formal: Is there a uniform deterministic word-RAM algorithm which computes all single-source distances in every directed graph with positive integer edge weights in O(m+n) worst-case time?
cards.definitions: Use a uniform word-RAM with word length w, addressed word memory, addition and subtraction modulo 2^w, multiplication modulo 2^w, Boolean bit operations, shifts by less than w, comparisons and conditional branches, each costing one step. No nonuniform tables are supplied; initialization and preprocessing are charged. The graph has vertex set [n], m explicitly listed directed edges, a designated source s, and weights in {1,…,2^w−1}, with w≥⌈log₂(n+m+2)⌉. Parallel edges and loops are allowed. A distance is the minimum sum of weights on a directed s-to-v path, or infinity if no such path exists. Finite distances can be represented in at most two words; output costs count. The algorithm must work for every w with a universal constant in O(m+n).

context_blocks.text: Positive weights make directed shortest paths a fundamental optimization primitive, yet direction obstructs the classical linear-time result for undirected integer-weighted graphs. The target removes all superlinear overhead in the integer RAM model.

Recent algorithms break the sorting barrier for directed real-weighted shortest paths. Their sublogarithmic overhead and the later almost-linear results are substantial advances, but neither “almost linear” nor “nearly linear” means O(m+n). This card fixes the weight representation and charges preprocessing.

cards.why: Settle whether directed weighted reachability has the same input-linear cost as its basic unweighted counterpart in the integer model.

cards.title: Is Boolean dimension bounded for posets with planar cover graphs?
cards.formal: Does there exist an integer d≥1 such that every finite poset P=(V,<) with a planar undirected cover graph admits strict total orders L_1,...,L_d on V and a Boolean function φ:{0,1}^d→{0,1} satisfying, for all distinct x,y∈V, x<y if and only if φ(1[x<_(L_1)y],...,1[x<_(L_d)y])=1?
cards.definitions: A finite poset is specified by an irreflexive transitive relation < on a finite set V. The undirected cover graph has vertex set V and an edge {x,y} when x<y with no z satisfying x<z<y, or the reverse relation. Planarity means that this undirected graph has a drawing in the plane whose edge interiors do not intersect; an upward planar drawing of the order is not required. A strict total order compares every distinct pair in exactly one direction and is transitive. The orders L_i need not extend the partial order. Each indicator 1[x<_(L_i)y] is a bit. Both the d orders and φ may depend on P, but the bound d is universal and independent of |V| and the height of P. The least possible number of orders is Boolean dimension. The claim is purely existential, with no algorithmic requirement.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation with the stated model, hypotheses and quantifier order. The proof must settle the entire target. A result conditional on an additional assumption settles only that conditional version. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof checked by a proof assistant and matching this statement.

cards.title: Hamiltonian paths in all connected vertex-transitive graphs
cards.formal: Does every finite nonempty connected vertex-transitive simple undirected graph have a Hamiltonian path?
cards.definitions: A graph is vertex-transitive if for every u,v there is a bijection of its vertex set preserving adjacency and sending u to v. A Hamiltonian path is an ordering of all vertices without repetition in which consecutive vertices are adjacent; the one-vertex graph is allowed. The target asks for existence, with no requirement to compute the path efficiently. It asks for a path rather than a cycle, and is not restricted to Cayley graphs.

context_blocks.text: Vertex transitivity expresses complete local symmetry, but does not give an obvious global route visiting each vertex once. The Hamiltonian-path conjecture is a classical structural question connecting graph symmetry with spanning paths.

It lies within the atlas’s accepted graph-structure and path scope. Positive results for particular group actions or graph families do not settle the universal statement. The cycle variant has exceptional behavior and is not substituted for the path question.

cards.title: Strongly explicit Ramanujan families for every degree
cards.formal: For every integer d≥3, is there an infinite family of connected d-regular Ramanujan graphs whose neighbor function is computable deterministically in poly(log n) bit operations?
cards.definitions: A d-regular graph is Ramanujan if every adjacency eigenvalue other than the trivial eigenvalues d and, in the bipartite case, −d has absolute value at most 2√(d−1). Strong explicitness means a vertex and a port index specify a neighbor without writing down the whole graph. The target permits a family of selected unbounded sizes rather than every admissible size; no positive additive slack in the eigenvalue bound is allowed.

context_blocks.text: Ramanujan graphs achieve the optimal asymptotic spectral expansion bound for a fixed degree. Strong explicitness makes their local connectivity available with work polynomial in the vertex-label length.

Explicit and strongly explicit almost-Ramanujan constructions are different from attaining the exact bound at every fixed degree. Alon’s paper carefully separates these guarantees. cards.title: Is minimum-color cycle solvable in polynomial time under ETH?
cards.formal: Assuming the deterministic Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH) specified below, does there exist one deterministic Turing machine A and constants C,c≥1 such that, for every explicitly edge-colored finite simple undirected graph G, A finds a simple cycle using the fewest distinct colors, or correctly reports that G is acyclic, within C(L+1)^c bit operations, where L is the total input length?
cards.definitions: The graph has vertices 1,...,n, with n≥1. Its explicit encoding lists n and m=|E(G)| in binary, followed by the m distinct unordered endpoint pairs and a color κ(e)∈{1,...,max(1,m)} for every edge, all in binary with delimiters. The coloring need not be proper. A simple cycle is a sequence of distinct vertices v_1,...,v_t, with t≥3, whose consecutive pairs and {v_t,v_1} are edges. Its cost is the cardinality of {κ(e):e lies on the cycle}. The output is such a vertex sequence attaining the minimum cost, or an acyclic marker if no cycle exists. L includes every endpoint and color label, rather than an oracle for an arbitrary set function. Here ETH asserts that there is ε>0 for which no deterministic algorithm decides satisfiability of all 3-CNF formulas with N variables in time 2^(εN) times a polynomial in their binary encoding length. A 3-CNF formula is a conjunction of clauses with at most three Boolean literals. This hypothesis is part of the mathematical setting of the target.
cards.answer_criterion: Working under the stated ETH hypothesis, prove that the required polynomial-time algorithm exists or prove that none exists. An unconditional algorithm with correctness and polynomial bit-cost proof answers positively. A proof that any such algorithm would contradict ETH answers negatively. An obstruction relying only on a stronger unlisted hardness conjecture does not settle this target. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-checked proof of the full conditional statement.

cards.title: Bipartite Exact Matching: deterministic polynomial time
cards.formal: Given a bipartite graph $G=(L\cup R,E)$ with $|L|=|R|=n$, a red/blue coloring of its edges, and $k\in\{0,\ldots,n\}$, decide whether $G$ has a perfect matching containing exactly $k$ red edges. The historical question asks for a deterministic algorithm polynomial in the ordinary bit encoding of $(G,k)$. An April 2026 preprint claims such an algorithm. This entry records that claimed resolution and its verification limits; it is no longer labeled as a confirmed open problem.
cards.why: I retain and expand this entry because exact cardinality constraints can remain difficult even when unconstrained optimization is easy. It is also a useful status correction: a research catalogue should preserve the problem and the claimed advance, while distinguishing an attributed preprint theorem from a proof that has been independently checked.
cards.definitions: A perfect matching consists of pairwise vertex-disjoint edges covering every vertex. Exactly k is an equality constraint, not an upper bound or an approximation target. This card concerns sequential deterministic polynomial time. Ordinary bipartite perfect matching in NC and Exact Matching on general graphs are separate questions.

progress.text: El Maalouly’s survey develops algorithms and reductions around Exact Matching while describing deterministic polynomial time as unresolved.
Du’s first preprint version claims a deterministic $O(n^6)$ algorithm for all bipartite graphs and describes its proof as formally verified.

Version 3 states $O(n^6)$ arithmetic complexity and qualifies the Lean result: the main theorem is reduced to eight explicit hypotheses. The claimed mathematical resolution and the formalization scope must be assessed separately.

cards.status_note: Claimed resolution, verification pending. Reviewed 10 September 2026 using version 3. The preprint and its eight formalization hypotheses have not been independently proved or audited here.

context_blocks.text: An ordinary perfect matching assigns every left vertex to a different right vertex. Here an additional equality constraint counts how many selected edges are red. Minimizing or maximizing the red-edge count does not decide whether a particular intermediate count is attainable.

Consider two left vertices and two right vertices, with every possible edge present. Color the two diagonal edges red and the two off-diagonal edges blue. The only perfect matchings have either two red edges or none. There is no perfect matching with exactly one red edge, although one lies between the minimum and maximum attainable counts. Even this small example defeats an interval-based feasibility test.

The randomized algebraic approach encodes matchings in a polynomial and tests whether a relevant coefficient vanishes. Finding a deterministic replacement has made the problem a particularly concrete meeting point of graph algorithms and polynomial identity testing. Approximation results relax the equality constraint and therefore answer a different question.

Du’s April 2026 preprint claims a deterministic solution for every bipartite graph. Version 3 describes its Lean formalization as reducing the main theorem to eight explicit hypotheses, rather than independently checking all ingredients. The paper states that these hypotheses correspond to mathematical results proved there or in prior work. That qualification matters when assessing the original version’s stronger formal-verification wording.

cards.title: Two anticomplete paths with unrestricted terminal pairing
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, given a finite simple undirected graph G and four distinct pairwise nonadjacent vertices a,b,c,d, decides whether G contains two vertex-disjoint paths with no edge between their vertex sets, whose four endpoints are exactly a,b,c,d? Any of the three pairings of the four terminals is accepted.
cards.definitions: The input is an n×n adjacency matrix together with four vertex indices. A path is a sequence of distinct vertices with an edge between each consecutive pair. The two paths must have disjoint vertex sets P and Q and satisfy E(G)∩(P×Q)=∅. Each terminal is the endpoint of exactly one path; none is an internal vertex. The accepted endpoint pairings are {ab,cd}, {ac,bd}, and {ad,bc}, with no prescribed source/sink partition. Paths can equivalently be required to be induced: replace either path by a shortest path between its endpoints in its own vertex set. This does not create an edge to the other path. Polynomial time means that one uniform deterministic Turing machine answers correctly on every valid input in at most C(n+1)^k steps for fixed constants C,k. Invalid encodings or nonindependent terminal sets are rejected by this formulation. There are no restrictions on the degree, genus, or connectivity of G.
cards.answer_criterion: Give such a polynomial-time algorithm with a proof, or prove that none exists. An NP-hardness proof for this exact unrestricted-pairing language would establish a negative answer under P≠NP, and must be labelled conditional accordingly. Hardness for a single prescribed pairing or for a prescribed source/sink partition is insufficient.
cards.why: This isolates a basic difference between specifying two routes and merely asking for two separated connections among four terminals. It is a compact test of how much freedom in terminal assignment can change the complexity of induced graph structure detection.

importance.reason: A concrete four-terminal primitive at the boundary of tractable routing and induced-containment hardness. Its importance comes from a missing basic complexity classification and its role in induced-minor detection, rather than from a large parameter range.

progress.text: The problem is in NP: the two vertex sequences form a certificate of length O(n log n), and adjacency, disjointness, terminal coverage, and absence of cross edges can all be checked in polynomial time. This is an immediate consequence of the stated definition, not a polynomial-time decision algorithm.

Trotignon explicitly asks for the complexity of the four-terminal problem with no prescribed pairing in Section 4.5 of the Dagstuhl report, printed page 140. The card makes its polynomial-time membership question explicit.

Aboulker, Bonnet, Picavet, and Trotignon prove NP-completeness for induced two-path routing even in a restricted class of string graphs. Their stronger flow theorem fixes two source terminals and two sink terminals. It does not automatically classify the language accepting all three perfect pairings.

The exact unrestricted-pairing question remains supported by its 2019 open-problem source. The checked recent theorem concerns different terminal constraints; no subsequent primary-source resolution of this exact question was located.

references.title: Induced Disjoint Paths Without an Induced Minor
references.authors: Pierre Aboulker; Édouard Bonnet; Timothé Picavet; Nicolas Trotignon
references.locator: ICALP 2025, Article 4; Section 1 defines linkage and S–T flow separately; Theorems 1–2. Full preprint: arXiv:2502.05289v1, 7 February 2025.

cards.status_note: Explicitly open in the 2019 problem source. Primary literature checked through 10 September 2026 did not provide a resolution for all three terminal pairings. The 2025 hardness results for prescribed pairs and S–T flow are kept separate; the evidence date of the original open statement is retained.

context_blocks.text: Ordinary disjoint routing prevents the paths from sharing vertices. Here even an unused graph edge between the two routes is forbidden. Thus one path must avoid the entire neighborhood of the other, and deciding which vertices to reserve can constrain a distant part of the graph.

The freedom to choose partners is the point of the question. Four terminals have three perfect pairings. A graph is accepted if at least one pairing works. A hard instance for a prescribed pairing may have an easy solution using another pairing; therefore simply invoking the hardness of any individual pairing does not classify their union.

The stable-terminal restriction isolates the unresolved case in Trotignon’s question. To see why an edge between two terminals helps, its endpoints would have to lie on the same solution path. That path can be shortened to the edge itself, leaving a reachability test for the remaining two terminals after deleting the closed neighborhoods of the first pair. Testing terminal edges handles these nonindependent cases.

This is a small routing primitive relevant to detecting induced minors, where a model must preserve both adjacency and nonadjacency between its connected pieces. An algorithm would allow a search to postpone the choice of which terminal belongs with which other terminal. A hardness proof would show that this flexibility still cannot overcome the anticompleteness constraint.

There are useful tractable restrictions. For graphs of any fixed bounded genus, polynomial algorithms for prescribed induced paths also solve this question by trying the three pairings. Conversely, the 2025 hardness theorem even for string graphs concerns prescribed pairs or a source/sink partition. The latter permits only two of our three pairings.
