cards.status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. No uniform algorithm or undecidability theorem for isomorphism of arbitrary one-relator group presentations was found in the checked sources. The 2026 generic algorithms and Diophantine undecidability result do not settle this all-input isomorphism question.

context_blocks.text: A group presentation is a finite description of an often infinite algebraic object. The same group can have quite different descriptions: for example, ⟨a,b | b=a²⟩ and ⟨x | empty relator⟩ both describe an infinite cyclic group. The question is whether one defining relation leaves enough structure to recognize abstract equality of group types algorithmically, even when the supplied generators and words look unrelated.

This is the third of Dehn’s classical decision problems. Word equality compares elements within one fixed presentation; conjugacy asks for a particular kind of equivalence between elements; isomorphism compares the entire groups. Linton and Nyberg-Brodda’s survey records the general one-relator isomorphism problem as open, despite broad positive results for subclasses.

The known uniform word algorithm gives a useful positive semidecision procedure. Enumerate possible word images u₁,…,u_k for the generators of G in H and v₁,…,v_ℓ for the generators of H in G. Check that the images satisfy each defining relation and that the two compositions fix every generator. Every check is a finite collection of word-equality tests. If mutual inverse homomorphisms exist, their finite descriptions eventually appear.

The missing part is termination on nonisomorphic inputs. Searching longer for generator images cannot certify that none exist. Equivalently, an effective bound on the lengths of some pair of mutually inverse generator-image tuples, depending only on the input length, would permit a finite search. Conversely, a total isomorphism algorithm would allow such a computable bound to be assembled by checking the finitely many inputs of bounded length and finding witnesses for the positive cases.

Easily computable invariants can reject some pairs. Abelianization, for example, takes the exponent sums of the relator and gives a finitely generated abelian quotient whose isomorphism type can be computed by integer linear algebra. But it is incomplete: the free group on two generators and ℤ² have the same abelianization, whereas one is nonabelian and the other is abelian. The free group is represented here using the allowed empty relator, and ℤ² by the commutator relation.

Another tempting simplification is to ask whether an automorphism of the free group carries one relator to the other, allowing inversion. Whitehead’s algorithm handles the corresponding orbit question. The survey explains that this sufficient condition is not necessary for isomorphism of the quotient groups: the Magnus conjecture asserting such a converse was disproved, and some groups have infinitely many inequivalent one-relator descriptions.

Hyperbolic groups form a large positive case. Dahmani and Guirardel solve isomorphism uniformly for all hyperbolic groups, including those with torsion. Their result also handles peripheral structures and automorphism computations, reflecting how geometric decompositions can organize otherwise unbounded searches. It is a decision theorem, not merely a heuristic for finding likely isomorphisms.

All one-relator groups with torsion are hyperbolic, so this theorem covers that entire subclass. The survey also records decidability for one-relator groups with nontrivial center and other structured families. General torsion-free one-relator groups remain beyond these combined results. Even elementary examples such as ℤ² show that the one-relator condition does not imply hyperbolicity.

Generic-case results explain why many randomly generated instances may nevertheless be tractable. Kapovich, Schupp and Shpilrain establish rigidity for large classes of random one-relator presentations: isomorphism can be forced by simple transformations of the displayed generators and relator. The exceptional inputs are small in a specified distributional sense, but an undecidable set of inputs could still lie among such exceptions.

Kapovich’s August 18, 2026 preprint extends a generic rigidity program to fixed numbers of generators and relators. It gives an algorithmically recognizable generic family and a quadratic-time generic isomorphism algorithm, using small-cancellation stability and rigidity under free-group automorphisms. Its one-relator specialization is relevant progress, while its guarantee remains a generic one rather than a terminating decision procedure for every input.

A different August 2026 result by Nyberg-Brodda proves undecidability of the Diophantine problem for certain one-relator Baumslag–Gersten groups. That task asks whether arbitrary systems of equations with coefficients have solutions. It demonstrates that one relation does not ensure decidability of every natural algebraic question. However, it supplies no automatic reduction to isomorphism between two one-relator presentations, so the present problem remains distinct.

A resolution would clarify whether this very economical presentation format has an effective classification in principle. The positive answer could be extremely slow and still be decisive. The negative answer would require encoding undecidable information into abstract group type while retaining a single defining relator—a much more specific construction than demonstrating difficult equations inside one fixed group.

cards.title: The optimal bit complexity of integer multiplication
cards.formal: Determine, up to constant factors as n→∞, the optimal worst-case running time for exactly multiplying two n-bit nonnegative binary integers by one uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine. The target is an attainable asymptotic upper bound with a matching lower bound for every correct machine in this model.
cards.why: One of the most basic unresolved limits of exact computation, affecting fast arithmetic throughout algorithms.

A conjectured optimal matrix-transposition lower bound is shown to imply the corresponding multiplication lower bound.
New OBDD-width bounds concern a restricted branching-program model and do not close the multitape time gap.

cards.definitions: For every integer n≥1 the input consists of two length-n binary strings encoding integers a,b with 0≤a,b<2^n; leading zeroes are allowed. The required output is the ordinary binary representation of ab, padded to length 2n. The machine has a fixed finite program, a fixed finite tape alphabet, and a fixed finite number of one-dimensional tapes with one head per tape. Input strings and end markers occupy designated tapes initially, other tapes are blank, and the output must be written explicitly on a designated output tape. In one transition the machine reads and writes at most one cell per tape and moves each head by at most one cell. The cost is the number of transitions, including access, data movement and output. The same machine must halt correctly for every n and every input pair; its tape count and alphabet cannot grow with n. For a fixed correct machine M, let t_M(n) be its maximum running time over the 2^(2n) pairs of n-bit strings. Bounds concern these fixed-machine functions as n tends to infinity. A matching rate g(n)>0 means some correct M has t_M(n)=O(g(n)), while every correct M has t_M(n)=Ω(g(n)); constants and thresholds may depend on M. A fresh hardcoded machine for each n is not allowed. No random access, unit-cost arithmetic on arbitrarily long integers, advice, oracle or quantum operations are part of the model. Changing the padded output convention to ordinary unpadded binary changes the cost by only O(n).
cards.answer_criterion: Give an asymptotic rate g(n) and prove both the existence of a single correct deterministic multitape machine running in O(g(n)) worst-case time and an Ω(g(n)) worst-case lower bound for every correct machine. This asks for matching bounds up to multiplicative constants, not necessarily the particular rate n log n. An upper bound without a matching universal lower bound, or a lower bound for a restricted computational model, is a partial result.

context_blocks.title: A familiar operation with an unknown limit
context_blocks.text: For example, 11₂ multiplied by 11₂ is 1001₂: the input integers are 3 and 3, and the exact product is 9. The question asks how the cost grows when each input contains millions or many more bits. The school multiplication procedure performs quadratically many elementary digit operations. That describes one procedure, not a lower bound on every possible algorithm.

context_blocks.title: Bits and data movement are charged
context_blocks.text: A machine instruction that multiplies two arbitrarily large integers in one step would make the question trivial by placing the entire task inside the instruction set. Here each tape head accesses one cell at a time. Arithmetic on long numbers and rearranging their bits therefore take time. The explicit output alone gives a linear lower bound. It does not establish the additional logarithmic factor in the best known upper bound.

context_blocks.title: What the O(n log n) theorem settles
context_blocks.text: Harvey and van der Hoeven proved that binary integer multiplication takes O(n log n) time in this multitape model. Their 2021 theorem settles the upper-bound conjecture associated with Schönhage and Strassen. It does not prove that all algorithms require this much time. The 2025 paper by the same authors states that even a superlinear lower bound remains unknown in the unrestricted multitape model. The gap is between a linear lower bound and an n log n upper bound.

context_blocks.title: The matrix-transposition connection
context_blocks.text: A 2025 theorem relates multiplication to moving data: transposing an s×s binary matrix written row by row. Even a 2×2 matrix with entries a,b,c,d changes its row-order encoding from abcd to acbd. If every multitape machine needs Ω(s² log s) time for the general transposition task, their theorem implies Ω(n log n) time for multiplication. The transposition premise is itself unproved, so this is a conditional relationship between lower bounds, not an unconditional proof of multiplication’s optimality.

context_blocks.title: Which later results concern this question
context_blocks.text: Qin’s August 2026 result bounds the width of ordered binary decision diagrams computing a middle product bit on restricted inputs. Width in that model does not bound the running time of every multitape machine. Likewise, arithmetic-operation counts and performance on typical or small inputs answer other questions. This card concerns exact products, the worst input at each length, and one fixed algorithm working at all lengths.

cards.title: Strassen’s asymptotic rank conjecture for concise cubic tensors
cards.formal: For every n≥1 and every tensor T∈ℂ^n⊗ℂ^n⊗ℂ^n whose three flattenings all have rank n, is lim_{k→∞} R(T^⊗k)^(1/k)=n?
cards.definitions: R(T) is the least r such that T=Σ_{i=1}^r a_i⊗b_i⊗c_i with a_i,b_i,c_i∈ℂ^n. Each flattening views the tensor as a linear map from the dual of one factor into the tensor product of the other two. In T^⊗k the first, second and third tensor factors are respectively grouped, producing a tensor with three factors ℂ^(n^k). Submultiplicativity of rank makes the displayed limit equal to inf_{k≥1} R(T^⊗k)^(1/k). This is exact rank over ℂ, not border rank, and there is no explicitness or computational requirement on T.

context_blocks.text: Matrix rank has a simple algebraic characterization, whereas tensor rank changes substantially when many independent copies are considered jointly. Strassen’s conjecture says that in the asymptotic setting the three flattening dimensions already determine the answer.

The cubic concise formulation is the target proposed in the personal list. It includes matrix-multiplication tensors, so a positive resolution would imply matrix multiplication exponent two; the reverse implication is not claimed. The 2024–2026 source studies structural properties of asymptotic rank without proving this equality.

cards.why: A structural conjecture about the cost of all bilinear computations, extending well beyond one matrix-multiplication algorithm.

cards.title: Unrestricted arithmetic lower bounds for the discrete Fourier transform
cards.formal: Let S(n) be the minimum size of a complex arithmetic straight-line program that computes all n coordinates of the discrete Fourier transform (DFT) exactly, in the model below. cards.definitions: For n≥1 set ω_n=exp(−2πi/n), and define DFT_n(x)_j=Σ_{k=0}^{n−1}ω_n^{jk}x_k for j=0,…,n−1 and x∈ℂ^n. This is the unnormalized cyclic DFT. A straight-line program is a finite acyclic list of scalar instructions. Each instruction either adds, subtracts or multiplies two previously available values, or multiplies one value by a fixed complex scalar. Input coordinates and any fixed complex constants are available initially. Values may be reused without limit, and all n required output coordinates must occur among the computed values. Size is the number of instructions; each complex scalar operation costs one, regardless of operand magnitude. The sequence and all constants may depend on n but not on x. Constants need not be efficiently generated or have a bounded bit representation. There is no restriction on circuit depth, reuse, storage, intermediate magnitudes or numerical conditioning. Operations are exact and must compute the required polynomial identities for every complex input. This is the standard division-free arithmetic-circuit formulation used to make the imported model precise; subtraction and multiplication by any reciprocal constant are allowed. No comparison, branching, floor, bit extraction, approximation or quantum operation is present. For this linear output map, allowing products of input-dependent intermediate values changes minimum size by at most a constant factor compared with linear circuits using only addition, subtraction and scalar multiplication, as stated in the cited circuit reference. Counting a two-input linear combination as one instruction instead of at most three also changes cost only by a constant factor.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the uniform lower bound for every sufficiently large power-of-two length and every program in the stated model, or refute it. Precisely, a refutation must show that for every c>0 and every threshold N there is a power of two n≥N and a program of size less than c n log₂n. A family using o(n log n) operations would suffice, but the full logical negation does not require a uniformly generated family or such a bound at every length. A lower bound requiring bounded coefficients, unitary gates, limited storage or numerical stability does not establish the target.

context_blocks.title: A fast transform reuses intermediate values
context_blocks.text: For four inputs, form a=x₀+x₂, b=x₁+x₃, c=x₀−x₂ and d=x₁−x₃. The four Fourier outputs are a+b, c−id, a−b and c+id. Shared sums let the same work serve several output coordinates. The classical FFT extends this reuse to obtain O(n log n) operations; the question is whether a different unrestricted program can do asymptotically better.

context_blocks.title: Normalization should not decide this question
context_blocks.text: Dividing all outputs by √n gives the normalized DFT. In the unbounded-scalar model, converting either normalization to the other costs at most n extra operations, so the conjectured asymptotic lower bound is equivalent for the two. A lower-bound argument tied to one normalization may nevertheless fail for the other when its coefficients are restricted.

context_blocks.title: What the classical lower bound assumes
context_blocks.text: Morgenstern’s lower bound, recalled in both full sources, gives order n log n for the unnormalized transform when scalar magnitudes have a fixed bound. The determinant magnitude of that transform is n^{n/2}, whereas the normalized matrix has determinant magnitude one. Arbitrarily large scalars invalidate the bounded per-operation growth used by that result. Thus the known theorem does not already settle this card.

context_blocks.title: Unitary and well-conditioned models
context_blocks.text: Ailon proves an n log n bound for normalized Fourier computation with two-coordinate unitary gates and no extra storage. Subsequent results relate possible speedup to numerical ill-conditioning. These are meaningful restrictions on computations; the present model permits general arithmetic, arbitrary reuse and large intermediate values, so those lower bounds have a narrower scope.

context_blocks.title: Related tasks use different cost measures
context_blocks.text: The 2026 source studies necessary divisions in Toom-Cook interpolation at integer evaluation points and division-aware costs. It does not give an unrestricted DFT operation lower bound. Counting only multiplications, approximating Fourier outputs at fixed precision, or applying a quantum Fourier transform to state amplitudes also asks a different question from computing this entire classical complex output vector.

cards.title: Do single-pair shortest paths require cubic-size min-plus circuits?
cards.formal: For n >= 2, assign an arbitrary nonnegative real weight x_{ij} to every unordered edge {i,j} of the complete undirected graph on vertices 1,...,n. Define $f_n(x)=\min_{P:1\leadsto n}\sum_{e\in P}x_e$, where P ranges over simple paths. A circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with input gates x_{ij} and optional constants 0 and infinity, binary gates min(a,b) or a+b, unrestricted reuse of gate outputs, and one designated output. Its topology depends on n but not on x, and it must compute f_n exactly for every permitted weight assignment. Let s(n) be the minimum number of binary gates in such a circuit. Is s(n)=Omega(n^3)? Equivalently, do there exist constants c>0 and n0 such that every such circuit has at least c n^3 gates for every n>=n0?
cards.definitions: A simple path visits no vertex twice. The two occurrences x_{ij} and x_{ji} denote the same input, because the graph is undirected. Infinity is an optional internal constant with min(a,infinity)=a and a+infinity=infinity; all input edge weights are finite and nonnegative. The circuit has no subtraction, tests with separate Boolean outputs, conditional routing, or input-dependent memory access. A min gate directly returns the smaller of its two numerical arguments. Input gates, wires, and reuse of an already computed value are free; binary arithmetic gates are counted. Circuits need not be generated uniformly by an efficient algorithm, so the proposed lower bound is nonuniform and imposes no depth restriction.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the quantified cubic lower bound, or refute it by proving its negation: for every c>0 and every n0 there is an n>=n0 with a correct circuit using fewer than c n^3 gates. An o(n^3)-size circuit family for all sufficiently large n would suffice for a negative answer. A lower bound for a more restricted circuit class, for all-pairs output, or for shortest paths allowing negative input weights does not establish this statement.
cards.why: This is a basic unconditional lower-bound question for dynamic programming. A resolution would clarify whether the standard cubic relaxation computation is intrinsically necessary even for one distance when computation is restricted to minimum and addition, and would illuminate why monotone lower-bound methods struggle with paths of varying lengths.

context_blocks.text: The numerical task is elementary to state: return one shortest-path distance. The difficulty is understanding what can be done by a fixed network of minimum and addition operations. An algorithm that chooses which vertex to process next using comparisons may use information to control its future computation. This circuit model cannot turn the identity of a minimum into arbitrary control flow. Consequently, a fast implementation of a graph-search algorithm does not automatically supply a circuit of comparable size.

A concrete upper bound comes from repeated relaxation. Initialize d_0(1)=0 and d_0(v)=infinity otherwise, and compute d_k(v)=min(d_{k-1}(v), min over u distinct from v of d_{k-1}(u)+x_{uv}). Every edge can influence the answer: choose a simple source-to-target path through that edge, make its other edges cheap, and all edges outside the path expensive. Thus dependence on the quadratic number of inputs gives a quadratic lower bound, but does not charge separately for repeated reuse of intermediate computations. The missing factor n is the substantive issue.

Its many required outputs are essential to the usual argument; requesting only the distance from 1 to n leaves room for different sharing. The database formulation places the question in absorptive semirings, where adding an unnecessary detour is absorbed. This card fixes the nonnegative tropical instance so that its allowed operations and output are unambiguous.

cards.title: Does integer multiplication have linear-size Boolean circuits?
cards.formal: Do there exist constants C>0 and n₀≥1 such that, for every integer n≥n₀, a Boolean circuit of at most Cn gates maps every pair of n-bit unsigned integers to all 2n bits of their exact product?
cards.definitions: The circuit has input bits a₀,…,a_{n−1},b₀,…,b_{n−1}, representing a=Σᵢaᵢ2ⁱ and b=Σᵢbᵢ2ⁱ, and output bits c₀,…,c_{2n−1} satisfying Σⱼcⱼ2ʲ=ab. Gates are two-input AND and OR and one-input NOT; constants 0 and 1 are allowed. Size counts gates, excluding input nodes and output wires. Fan-out and depth are unrestricted. There is one circuit for each n, with no uniformity requirement on how these circuits are generated. Every input must be answered exactly, with no randomness. Leading zeros are permitted. Let M(n) be the minimum gate count in this model; the proposition is M(n)=O(n). Changing to any other fixed functionally complete bounded-fan-in Boolean basis changes size by only a constant factor.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the quantified linear-size upper bound, or prove its negation: for every C and every n₀ there is n≥n₀ with M(n)>Cn. A lower bound c·n with fixed c, a lower bound for bounded depth or restricted wiring, or a limitation of a particular multiplication algorithm does not give the required negative answer. A uniform linear-bit-time algorithm would imply the upper bound, but is a stronger demand than the existence of these nonuniform circuits.

context_blocks.text: Addition admits circuits whose gate count grows linearly with the input width. Multiplication is another elementary arithmetic operation, but the corresponding linear-size bound remains unknown. Goldreich singles it out immediately after the general challenge of proving a superlinear Boolean-circuit lower bound for an explicit function.

The circuit computes every output bit, including carries and the most significant half of the product. Treating a multiplication instruction on a whole machine word as one operation would hide the work being measured. The target concerns exact Boolean computation at individual-bit granularity.

Viola’s author manuscript, carrying a 2023–2026 revision notice, explicitly retains the linear-size multiplication question in Section 4.2. It also proves that multiplication and squaring are equivalent for this linear-size threshold: multiplication gives squaring immediately, and the converse uses squares together with linear-size addition and subtraction.

A negative answer would give a superlinear lower bound for a particularly concrete, efficiently computable family of multi-output Boolean functions. It would apply even to circuits tailored separately to each input length. A positive answer would show that the familiar logarithmic overhead of fast multiplication constructions is not necessary in this circuit model.

The existing TCS-7174 asks for optimal time on a deterministic multitape Turing machine. This card asks only about nonuniform gate count. The archived Karatsuba entry TCS-5168 concerns a reversible pebbling tradeoff, and TCS-6494 asks for a particular reduction from matrix transposition; neither is this unrestricted linear-size question.

cards.title: Exponential multilinear-formula lower bounds for the permanent
cards.formal: Does there exist c>0 such that, for every sufficiently large n, every multilinear arithmetic formula over ℂ computing perm_n has at least 2^(cn) gates?
cards.definitions: The permanent is perm_n(X)=Σ_{π∈S_n}∏_{i=1}^n x_{i,π(i)}. An arithmetic formula is a finite rooted tree with variable or complex-constant leaves and binary addition or multiplication gates, evaluated as a commutative polynomial. Every gate must compute a multilinear polynomial: every variable has degree at most one in every monomial after cancellation. The formula must agree identically with perm_n on ℂ^(n²), not merely on Boolean inputs. Size counts all gates, including leaves. No restriction on the numerical complexity of complex constants is imposed.

context_blocks.text: Multilinear formulas give a restricted but important setting in which superpolynomial lower bounds are known for an explicit central polynomial. The exponential target asks how far that separation can be taken even after substantial algebraic structure is imposed.

Raz’s lower bound grows as n^{Ω(log n)}, which is superpolynomial but not exponential in n. The broader permanent circuit problem permits sharing subcomputations and intermediate nonmultilinear polynomials, so these are not interchangeable targets. The survey records the unresolved exponential strengthening.

cards.title: Can the shortest addition-chain length be computed in polynomial time?
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic algorithm that, given an integer n≥1 in binary, outputs its exact shortest addition-chain length ℓ(n) in time polynomial in the binary input length?
cards.definitions: An addition chain for n is a strictly increasing sequence of integers 1=a₀<a₁<⋯<aᵣ=n such that, for every i≥1, there are j,k<i with aᵢ=aⱼ+aₖ; j=k is allowed. Its length is r, the number of additions, so ℓ(1)=0. The input is the ordinary binary expansion without leading zeros, of length b=⌊log₂n⌋+1. The output is ℓ(n) in binary. One fixed deterministic multitape Turing machine must halt within p(b) steps on every input, for one fixed polynomial p. All bit operations and output writing count. Subtraction, arbitrary constants other than the initial 1, and multiplication of previously formed exponents are not allowed chain operations. Chain entries can be reused arbitrarily. The cost of finding ℓ(n) is distinct from the number ℓ(n) of steps in the chain itself.
cards.answer_criterion: Give such an exact algorithm with one polynomial bound, or prove that no such algorithm exists. An approximation to ℓ(n), a fast heuristic, polynomial time in n rather than log n, or exact results for a restricted family of exponents do not resolve the question. NP-hardness of a multiple-target variant does not establish hardness for this single-target problem. Conditional hardness must retain its assumption.

context_blocks.text: Exponentiation can reuse powers: multiplying aʲ and aᵏ produces a^{j+k}. Thus a chain specifies a multiplication-only program for an arbitrary formal power aⁿ. Erickson’s notes explain why repeated squaring uses O(log n) multiplications and then ask whether the absolute minimum count can be computed efficiently.

For example, 1,2,3,5,10,15 gives five multiplications for a¹⁵. A convenient repeated-squaring implementation can use six. This small difference illustrates the exact optimization target: the asymptotic order of the chain length is already understood, while selecting its optimal integer value can require much more search.

Each chain step can at most double its largest entry, giving ℓ(n)≥⌈log₂n⌉. Reading the binary digits of n gives a chain with at most 2⌊log₂n⌋ steps. Consequently a shortest chain has O(b) entries of at most b bits. Exhaustive enumeration is finite and yields an exact algorithm, but not a polynomial bound in b.

The decision problem “ℓ(n)≤k?” is in NP: a short chain, together with its predecessor indices, is a polynomial-size certificate. Computing the exact length is equivalent to deciding these thresholds in polynomial time, by searching between the elementary bounds. This observation does not establish NP-completeness.

Koziel and coauthors explicitly distinguish the single-target problem from the generalized task of forming several specified values, for which NP-completeness is known. Their work develops efficient chains for cryptographic arithmetic. The 2025 primary article by Kempes and coauthors likewise describes the exact complexity of the single-target problem as unknown.

The Scholz–Brauer conjecture already appears as TCS-7170. It bounds ℓ(2ⁿ−1) in terms of ℓ(n); even its resolution would not supply a polynomial-time method for finding ℓ(n) on arbitrary binary input. The present algorithmic question has a different conclusion and computational significance.

cards.why: Locate the exact computational difficulty of optimizing multiplication-only exponentiation, a basic reusable arithmetic program with short certificates but no known efficient exact optimizer.

importance.reason: A longstanding exact optimization problem at the intersection of arithmetic algorithms, circuit reuse and cryptographic exponentiation. Its single-target complexity is repeatedly distinguished from the solved hardness of the generalized problem; it is not a numerical special case of Scholz–Brauer.

cards.title: Is rational solvability of polynomial equations decidable?
cards.formal: Does there exist a Turing machine that, given any integer-coefficient polynomial f(X₁,…,Xₘ), always halts and correctly decides whether $\exists (q_1,\ldots,q_m)\in\mathbb Q^m:f(q_1,\ldots,q_m)=0$? The number of variables and polynomial degree are unrestricted parts of the finite input.
cards.definitions: Encode m≥1 and a finite list of monomials, each with a signed binary integer coefficient and an m-tuple of nonnegative binary exponents. Repeated monomials may be combined effectively; zero polynomials are allowed. A rational solution consists of exact fractions qᵢ=aᵢ/bᵢ, where aᵢ∈ℤ and bᵢ is a positive integer, with no prescribed bound on numerators or denominators. The required algorithm is one finite deterministic program, independent of m, degree, and coefficients. It must return yes exactly when a rational zero exists and no otherwise; it may use any finite amount of time and space on each input. Malformed encodings are rejected. The task supplies no oracle, height inequalities, integrality constraints on the unknowns, or promise of a solution. Rational coefficients would give an equivalent problem by clearing coefficient denominators. A finite system f₁=⋯=fᵣ=0 is equivalent over ℚ to the single equation f₁²+⋯+fᵣ²=0.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: This is a fundamental boundary between algorithmic arithmetic and undecidability. It asks whether exact rational polynomial constraints admit any general terminating solver, connecting computation, logical definability, and the arithmetic geometry of rational points.

importance.reason: A central unsolved decidability problem for an elementary, pervasive constraint language. A resolution would locate the computability boundary for rational polynomial feasibility.

progress.text: The Davis–Putnam–Robinson–Matiyasevich theorem settles the integer-solution problem negatively. The rational-solution analogue remains distinct.
Koenigsmann gives a universal first-order definition of ℤ in ℚ and related low-quantifier undecidability results. This does not supply an existential definition.
Anscombe and coauthors survey local-global methods and explicitly identify Hilbert’s tenth problem over number fields, including ℚ, as open.
Garcia-Fritz, Pasten, and Vidaux prove undecidability after adjoining finitely many height-comparison conditions. Those extra conditions are not part of ordinary rational solvability.

Rank-stability advances imply undecidability over rings of integers of all number fields. Poonen’s account dated 3 July 2026 reviews the proof and gives an alternative Diophantine-definability argument; the domains remain rings of integers.

cards.status_note: Explicitly open in the cited rational-solvability and local-global sources. Research through 10 September 2026 found no resolution over ℚ. The recent results for rings of integers and for additional height predicates do not answer this formulation.

context_blocks.text: Rational tuples can be enumerated by increasing bounds on their numerators and denominators, and substitution into an integer polynomial is exact and computable. Thus yes-instances can already be recognized eventually. The difficulty is knowing when to stop searching and certify that no rational point exists. The question asks about computability itself, before any requirement of efficiency.

Hilbert’s original problem required integer solutions. Matiyasevich’s completion of the Davis–Putnam–Robinson program proves that version undecidable. Permitting fractions changes the problem: a polynomial can have a rational zero and no integer zero, so applying a rational solver directly to the same equation would not decide the integer problem. A reduction must encode the missing integrality restriction using only the allowed rational polynomial equations.

An existential definition of ℤ inside ℚ would provide such an encoding and imply undecidability. In particular the ring of integers of ℚ is ℤ, so this breakthrough does not decide the question on this card. cards.context:

cards.title: Polynomial-time, polynomial-factor approximation of Euclidean SVP
cards.formal: Does there exist a constant C>0 and a classical randomized algorithm A running in polynomial time such that, for every rank-n rational lattice basis B, A outputs a nonzero integer vector z satisfying ∥Bz∥₂≤n^C λ₁(L(B)) with probability at least 2/3?
cards.definitions: The input is an explicitly encoded matrix B∈ℚ^{d×n}, d≥n≥1, with linearly independent columns. Each rational entry is given by a binary numerator and positive binary denominator. L(B)={Bz:z∈ℤⁿ} is the lattice, and λ₁(L)=min{∥v∥₂:0≠v∈L} is the length of a shortest nonzero vector in the Euclidean norm ∥v∥₂=(Σᵢvᵢ²)^{1/2}. Rank n, rather than ambient dimension d or coefficient magnitude, controls the approximation factor. There must be one polynomial P such that every run halts in at most P(L) bit operations, where L is the input’s total bit length; output bits and random bits are counted. Randomness consists of independent fair bits. Require z to be a nonzero integer vector on every run, while the length guarantee may fail with probability at most 1/3. Both P and C are independent of all input parameters. There are no distributional, uniqueness, conditioning, ideal-lattice or basis-quality promises. A deterministic algorithm would also qualify. The one-dimensional case is exactly solvable by a basis vector. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: A central algorithmic gap in lattice complexity: known polynomial-time methods give superpolynomial approximation factors, while key computational and cryptographic questions lie in the polynomial-factor regime.

importance.reason: A fundamental worst-case algorithm question at the heart of lattice reduction, with a wide gap between current methods and the target and connections to cryptographic hardness.

cards.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. No classical polynomial-time algorithm with any fixed polynomial approximation factor was found for unrestricted Euclidean search SVP. context_blocks.text: A lattice basis can disguise very short vectors as cancellations between long columns. For example, b₁=(N,1) and b₂=(N+1,1) both have length about N, while b₂−b₁=(1,0) has length one. Simply selecting the shortest input column therefore has no dimension-only approximation guarantee. Basis reduction changes the representation without changing the lattice, aiming to expose short integer combinations.

The LLL algorithm solves a major version of this task in polynomial bit time: with the standard reduction parameter, it finds a nonzero vector within 2^{(n−1)/2} of the shortest length. The factor is exponential in rank, even though the running time is polynomial. This was enough to transform computational number theory and enable applications such as factoring rational polynomials, but it leaves the much stronger approximation asked for here open.

Block reduction improves the quality by solving shorter-vector problems in projected sublattices of limited rank. The best general polynomial-time guarantees summarized by Bennett have approximation factor 2^{O(n log log n/log n)}. That is smaller than the basic LLL factor but still grows faster than every fixed power of n. Larger blocks improve approximation at the cost of more expensive local computations; a polynomial number of calls to an expensive subroutine does not imply polynomial total time.

Known hardness results approach, but do not reach, the polynomial-factor regime. Haviv and Regev show that approximation within 2^{(log n)^{1−δ}}, for fixed δ>0, cannot be polynomial time unless NP has randomized quasipolynomial-time algorithms. Stronger assumptions give further nearly polynomial factors. Every such factor must be read with its quantifiers: hardness for a smaller approximation factor concerns a more demanding task and does not eliminate the possibility of a much looser nᶜ approximation.

Decision and search also need care. GapSVP distinguishes λ₁≤r from λ₁>γr, with no requirement on intermediate inputs. Aharonov and Regev place the decision problem with γ=O(√n) in NP∩coNP, using short certificates on both sides. This is strong evidence about its structural complexity and a barrier to certain NP-hardness proofs. It is not a polynomial-time search algorithm that finds a short lattice vector.

The intermediate approximation regime is central to lattice cryptography. Worst-case to average-case reductions relate particular polynomial-factor lattice problems to problems such as SIS and LWE at specified parameters. These implications have a direction: an efficient worst-case algorithm would invalidate the corresponding hardness premise, but the existence of a security reduction alone would not prove that every deployed cryptosystem is broken. The exponent, problem variant and cryptographic parameters all matter.

Sato and Yasuda’s May 2026 PotBKZ algorithm guarantees termination after a polynomial number of calls to its potential-reducing enumeration routine. This improves control of the reduction process, including a self-dual variant. It does not give a polynomial-time polynomial-factor approximation for arbitrary rank, because the cost and quality of the block enumeration must still be accounted for.

Hirahara and Ogitsuka’s August 2026 preprint improves the randomness properties of lattice hardness reductions. Under a stated exponential lower-bound assumption for nondeterministic circuits, they obtain deterministic NP-hardness reductions for every constant Euclidean approximation factor. Both qualifications matter: the derandomization is conditional, and the approximation factors are constants, rather than all polynomial factors. Their separate parameterized hardness results also use a different resource measure.

The question isolates the large gap between useful reduction algorithms and the approximation range used in fundamental hardness assumptions. Even an algorithm with a very large fixed exponent C would be a major qualitative advance; the target does not demand exact SVP or a small approximation constant.

cards.title: Can a classical randomized algorithm factor every integer in polynomial time?
cards.formal: Do there exist constants C,c and a uniform classical randomized algorithm that, on every positive integer N given in binary, outputs its complete prime factorization with probability at least 2/3 and always halts within C(n+1)ᶜ bit operations, where n=⌊log₂N⌋+1?
cards.definitions: For N≥2, the required output is the ordered list (p₁,e₁),…,(pᵣ,eᵣ), with distinct primes p₁<⋯<pᵣ, positive integer exponents eᵢ, and N=∏ᵢpᵢ^{eᵢ}. All output integers are encoded in binary. The factorization of N=1 is the empty list; zero and malformed encodings are outside the positive-integer domain and are rejected. The same finite probabilistic Turing machine must work for all N. Its random tape contains independent fair bits, and the success probability is over these bits separately for each fixed input. The polynomial time bound holds on every random tape. An incorrect output or a failure symbol counts as failure. There are no quantum operations, input-dependent advice, factoring or order-finding oracles, promises of a special form for N, or supplied factors of nearby integers. In particular n is the bit length of N, not its numerical value.
cards.answer_criterion: Answer yes with a proved algorithm meeting the worst-case polynomial running time and per-input success guarantee. Answer no by proving that every uniform classical randomized algorithm fails one of these requirements for some inputs, regardless of its polynomial exponent. Deterministic factoring would suffice for yes, but a deterministic lower bound alone would not suffice for no. Experiments or algorithms for a restricted class of integers do not settle the statement.
cards.why: Integer factorization is a basic inverse problem in arithmetic and a central test case for the potential power of quantum computation. Its classical complexity has direct consequences for factoring-based cryptography and for algorithms that currently require access to a factoring subroutine.

importance.reason: A defining open problem of computational number theory, with broad consequences for cryptography, arithmetic algorithms, and classical-versus-quantum computation.

progress.text: Sieve methods establish powerful subexponential classical approaches. The standard general number field sieve estimate remains a heuristic expected-time analysis, as summarized in the current large-order paper.
Shor gives polynomial-time quantum algorithms for factorization and discrete logarithms. Quantum computation is outside the classical model fixed here.
Agrawal, Kayal, and Saxena prove deterministic polynomial-time primality testing. The result does not give a polynomial-time factoring algorithm.
Harvey and Hittmeir rigorously factor N in O(N^{1/5}(log N)^{16/5}/(log log N)^{3/5}) deterministic bit operations, improving the preceding exponent-one-fifth bound by a logarithmic factor.

Harvey and Hittmeir’s revised large-order algorithm removes earlier power-of-N lower restrictions on its target order parameter. Their introduction still explicitly identifies polynomial-time integer factorization as unknown; the improved subroutine does not provide such a factoring algorithm.

context_blocks.text: Multiplying the prime factors is easy, and the factors themselves fit in a polynomial-size output. Discovering them is the unresolved step. Trial division up to √N is polynomial in the number’s value but exponential in its binary input length. The distinction between N and log N is essential even when a newer algorithm improves the power of N substantially.

Primality testing and factorization are different tasks. The Agrawal–Kayal–Saxena algorithm decides in deterministic polynomial time whether a number is prime, without necessarily exhibiting a divisor when the answer is composite. It also makes a proposed full factorization efficiently checkable: verify that every listed base is prime and that the product is N.

Because an output can be checked, a bounded-error polynomial-time factoring algorithm can be repeated until a valid factorization is obtained, giving an always-correct algorithm with polynomial expected time. Conversely, a polynomial expected-time always-correct algorithm can be truncated at a suitable constant multiple of its expected bound to obtain the formulation above. This equivalence concerns performance on every input; success on a sampled family of integers alone is weaker.

The general number field sieve has the familiar heuristic expected-time estimate exp(((64/9)^{1/3}+o(1))(ln N)^{1/3}(ln ln N)^{2/3}). This is subexponential but still superpolynomial in the bit length. Rigorous deterministic bounds of N^{1/5+o(1)} make a different tradeoff and remain exponential in that length. Neither bound is a proof that faster classical factoring is impossible.

Shor’s quantum algorithm factors in polynomial time, using quantum order finding. It provides an upper bound in a more powerful computational model; it does not establish a classical lower bound. A classical polynomial-time algorithm would undermine factoring-based cryptographic assumptions, but the absence of such an algorithm has not been proved from P≠NP or from the efficiency of multiplication.

cards.title: Are discrete logarithms in prime fields in randomized polynomial time?
cards.formal: Is there a uniform classical randomized algorithm that, for every prime p, every generator g of the multiplicative group Fₚ*, and every h∈Fₚ*, returns the unique integer x∈{0,…,p−2} satisfying gˣ≡h (mod p), with probability at least 2/3 and worst-case running time polynomial in log₂p?
cards.definitions: The input consists of ordinary binary integers (p,g,h), with p prime and 1≤g,h≤p−1, promised that g has multiplicative order p−1. Set n=⌈log₂(p+1)⌉; the total input length is Θ(n). A single probabilistic Turing machine must use at most C(n+1)^c bit operations on every random tape, for fixed constants C,c independent of p,g,h. It may output failure on unsuccessful runs. Success probability is over its own independent fair random bits and must be at least 2/3 separately on every promised input. Its only input is (p,g,h): no factorization of p−1, precomputed logarithm table, advice, special-form description of p, or oracle is supplied. Any preprocessing it performs counts in its runtime. The algorithm may exploit the ordinary integer encoding and all efficiently computable arithmetic modulo p; it is not restricted to generic group operations. The group is multiplication of nonzero residues, not an elliptic-curve group or the additive group. For p=2 the only logarithm is x=0.
cards.answer_criterion: Give and prove a classical algorithm with the specified uniform polynomial worst-case time and per-instance success guarantee, or prove that no such algorithm exists. A generic-group lower bound, a fast algorithm for a restricted family of primes, a quantum algorithm, or a polynomial bound in p rather than log p does not settle the question.
cards.why: A fundamental inversion problem in computational number theory and a central candidate for separating efficient classical from quantum computation. Its resolution would clarify which arithmetic structure can overcome generic group barriers and would reshape finite-field cryptographic assumptions.

importance.reason: One of the principal unresolved number-theoretic algorithmic problems, with direct connections to cryptography, index calculus, and quantum speedups.

The card keeps heuristic sieve analyses, fixed-characteristic extension fields, reusable preprocessing, and quantum algorithms separate.

context_blocks.text: Computing gˣ mod p is efficient by repeated squaring, even when x is given in binary and is as large as p−2. The inverse problem asks which exponent produced a residue. A polynomial-time solution would remove the computational asymmetry used in finite-field discrete-logarithm cryptography. It would also solve the corresponding computational Diffie–Hellman problem by recovering an exponent, although hardness of discrete logarithms alone does not establish every stronger security assumption.

A proposed answer is easy to verify: check the exponent range and compute gˣ mod p. Consequently a bounded-error polynomial algorithm could be repeated until a verified answer is obtained, giving expected polynomial time with no incorrect output. Conversely, a verified expected-polynomial-time solver can be truncated and repeated to obtain constant success within a polynomial budget. This makes the fixed runtime convention compatible with the usual Las Vegas formulation.

The number field sieve exploits arithmetic structure that generic group algorithms cannot see. It gathers multiplicative relations among suitably smooth objects, solves a large linear system, and reduces an individual target to the resulting logarithms. Its usual large-characteristic complexity estimates have the heuristic subexponential form exp(O((ln p)^{1/3}(ln ln p)^{2/3})). This grows faster than every polynomial in the bit length.

Generic lower bounds do not settle the concrete prime-field problem. Shoup proves a square-root barrier in the size of the largest prime factor of a group’s order when elements are accessed through an abstract random encoding. The present algorithm receives actual residues and can use their number-theoretic structure, as the sieve already does. A proof against the oracle model cannot simply be transferred to this richer interface.

The field regime is crucial. Kleinjung and Wesolowski give a rigorous expected-time bound (p·d)^{2log₂d+O(1)} for discrete logarithms in F_{p^d}. For fixed p and growing extension degree d this is quasipolynomial in the input size. For prime fields d=1 and growing p, that expression is merely polynomial in p, which is exponential in its binary length. Their breakthrough therefore leaves this question open.

Later sieve work also studies how preprocessing can be shared across targets and across fields. The Discrete Logarithm Factory paper develops such improvements, especially for non-prime fields, and distinguishes the cost of a target logarithm from the cost of building reusable data. sentences: A discrete logarithm in a prime field asks which exponent of a supplied generator produces a target nonzero residue.
The question seeks a classical randomized algorithm with running time polynomial in log p for every promised input.
Exponentiation is efficient, but reversing it requires identifying one exponent among p−1 possibilities.
A solution would remove a foundational computational asymmetry used in finite-field cryptography.

The saved review distinguishes prime fields from fixed-characteristic extension fields and explains why generic-group lower bounds do not rule out algorithms exploiting the concrete arithmetic of residues.

cards.context:
Computing gˣ mod p is efficient by repeated squaring, even when x is given in binary and is as large as p−2. The inverse problem asks which exponent produced a residue. A polynomial-time solution would remove the computational asymmetry used in finite-field discrete-logarithm cryptography. It would also solve the corresponding computational Diffie–Hellman problem by recovering an exponent, although hardness of discrete logarithms alone does not establish every stronger security assumption.

A proposed answer is easy to verify: check the exponent range and compute gˣ mod p. Consequently a bounded-error polynomial algorithm could be repeated until a verified answer is obtained, giving expected polynomial time with no incorrect output. Conversely, a verified expected-polynomial-time solver can be truncated and repeated to obtain constant success within a polynomial budget. This makes the fixed runtime convention compatible with the usual Las Vegas formulation.

The number field sieve exploits arithmetic structure that generic group algorithms cannot see. It gathers multiplicative relations among suitably smooth objects, solves a large linear system, and reduces an individual target to the resulting logarithms. Its usual large-characteristic complexity estimates have the heuristic subexponential form exp(O((ln p)^{1/3}(ln ln p)^{2/3})). This grows faster than every polynomial in the bit length.

Generic lower bounds do not settle the concrete prime-field problem. Shoup proves a square-root barrier in the size of the largest prime factor of a group’s order when elements are accessed through an abstract random encoding. The present algorithm receives actual residues and can use their number-theoretic structure, as the sieve already does. A proof against the oracle model cannot simply be transferred to this richer interface.

The field regime is crucial. Kleinjung and Wesolowski give a rigorous expected-time bound (p·d)^{2log₂d+O(1)} for discrete logarithms in F_{p^d}. For fixed p and growing extension degree d this is quasipolynomial in the input size. For prime fields d=1 and growing p, that expression is merely polynomial in p, which is exponential in its binary length. Their breakthrough therefore leaves this question open.

Later sieve work also studies how preprocessing can be shared across targets and across fields. The Discrete Logarithm Factory paper develops such improvements, especially for non-prime fields, and distinguishes the cost of a target logarithm from the cost of building reusable data. Here all preprocessing is charged to the algorithm on a single input, so a cheap online lookup after a very expensive table construction is insufficient.

cards.title: Can a quantum algorithm approximate Euclidean SVP within a polynomial factor in polynomial time?
cards.formal: Do there exist a constant C>0 and a uniform quantum algorithm A with polynomial running time such that, for every rational matrix B∈Q^(d×n) with d≥n≥1 and linearly independent columns, A outputs a nonzero z∈Z^n satisfying ∥Bz∥₂≤n^C λ₁(L(B)) with probability at least 2/3?
cards.definitions: The full matrix, dimensions and every rational entry are given classically; rationals use signed binary numerators and positive binary denominators. Let N be the total encoding length. L(B)={Bz:z∈Z^n}, λ₁(L)=min{∥v∥₂:0≠v∈L}, and ∥v∥₂=(Σ_i v_i²)^(1/2). Approximation depends on rank n rather than the ambient dimension d or N. Use a uniform quantum circuit computation with classical polynomial-time control, polynomially many qubits initially in computational basis states, gates H=2^(−1/2)[[1,1],[1,−1]], T=diag(1,exp(iπ/4)) and CNOT, and computational-basis measurements with classical feed-forward. The classical input bits may be copied into input qubits. One polynomial p(N) bounds total classical bit operations, gate applications, measurements and output bits on every branch. Classical control and circuit generation are uniform in the input length and use no advice or oracle; a unit-cost quantum random-access oracle for the input is not supplied. The output is a binary-encoded integer coefficient vector, required to be nonzero on every branch; the norm guarantee may fail with probability at most 1/3. The constants C and p are independent of all inputs. There is no uniqueness, average-case, ideal-lattice, modular or conditioning promise.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation, with all definitions, promises, resource bounds and quantifiers as stated. A conditional result establishes only the explicitly conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-verified proof of the full target.

context_blocks.text: A short lattice vector may be hidden by cancellation among much longer basis columns. The task is to find an integer combination with length bounded relative to the shortest possible nonzero combination. Allowing a factor n^C is a substantial relaxation of exact shortest-vector search, yet remains far stronger than the guarantees of basic polynomial-time lattice reduction.

The existing TCS-6667 asks the same approximate search question for a classical randomized algorithm. TCS-7169 instead asks about a quantum algorithm for exact SVP. This card distinguishes the missing intermediate combination: quantum computation with a polynomial approximation factor. A classical solution of the matching approximation target would qualify here, but a quantum solution would not automatically give a classical one.

Regev’s worst-case to average-case reduction connects specified GapSVP and SIVP tasks to Learning With Errors. Its consequence has a direction: a suitable efficient LWE solver yields quantum algorithms for the lattice tasks in the theorem. It does not establish an unrestricted equivalence between arbitrary polynomial-factor search SVP and every LWE parameter family.

The distinction matters for interpretation of a breakthrough. An algorithm satisfying this card would substantially change our understanding of quantum lattice reduction. Its effect on a particular cryptographic assumption would still depend on the approximation exponent, the exact lattice problem and the reduction parameters. Merely naming LWE is insufficient to infer that every parameter choice has been broken.

Rank and bit length are separate variables. Increasing coefficients must not be mistaken for increasing the allowed approximation factor, and a polynomial algorithm must include the cost of reading and manipulating their binary representations. The specified gate model permits ordinary quantum computation while excluding an additional oracle resource hidden in a data-access convention.

cards.title: Exact Euclidean SVP in single-exponential time and polynomial space
cards.formal: Do absolute constants C,d>0 and a randomized classical algorithm exist that, given any rational rank-n lattice basis B of bit length L, find a shortest nonzero Euclidean lattice vector with probability at least 2/3 using at most 2^{Cn}L^d bit operations and L^d bits of working space?
cards.definitions: The input is B∈Q^{m×n}, with m≥n≥1 and linearly independent columns; each rational entry is encoded by a signed binary numerator and a positive binary denominator. L includes the matrix dimensions and all entry encodings. The lattice is Λ(B)={Bz:z∈Zⁿ}, and λ₁(Λ)=min_{z∈Zⁿ\{0}}‖Bz‖₂, with the ordinary Euclidean norm in R^m. Output a nonzero integer coordinate vector z satisfying ‖Bz‖₂=λ₁(Λ); any minimizer is acceptable. The algorithm is a uniform probabilistic Turing machine with read-only input, write-only output and a stream of independent random bits. Every stored bit, including retained randomness and intermediate lattice vectors, counts toward space; external writable storage and preprocessing oracles are unavailable. The time and space limits must hold on every execution, and the success probability must hold separately for every valid input. The exponent n is lattice rank, not ambient dimension or coefficient precision. All preprocessing and precision management count. There is no promise of a unique shortest vector, a random lattice, a reduced input basis or approximation slack.
cards.answer_criterion: An affirmative answer gives an algorithm satisfying both bounds simultaneously with a proof of exact success on every lattice. A negative answer proves that every randomized polynomial-space algorithm fails some single-exponential-time requirement, or establishes an appropriate time-space lower bound excluding the stated constants. An example defeating one enumeration or sieving method is not enough. Exponential-space algorithms and polynomial-space algorithms taking 2^{Θ(n log n)} time leave the question open.
cards.why: A canonical time-space tradeoff question in exact algorithms: can the single-exponential speed of lattice sieving and Voronoi methods be achieved with only polynomial memory?

importance.reason: A longstanding resource boundary for exact lattice algorithms, central to enumeration versus sieving and increasingly relevant to lattice time-space hardness assumptions.

cards.status_note: Open for exact Euclidean SVP with the simultaneous worst-case time and space bounds stated here, following primary literature checked through 11 September 2026. The 2026 sheaf-based proposal discusses a memory-saving regime but does not establish the required uniform exact-success and runtime theorem. Cryptographic time-space hardness is an assumption, not an unconditional negative resolution.

context_blocks.text: The familiar exact algorithms offer two different resource profiles. Enumeration explores candidate lattice vectors while retaining a relatively small search state, but its proved worst-case time is n^{O(n)}. Sieving and Voronoi methods achieve 2^{O(n)} time by retaining exponentially many vectors or geometric constraints. The question asks whether one can obtain the faster asymptotic time without the exponential memory.

These time scales differ by more than a constant in the exponent: n^{cn}=2^{cn log₂n}. For any fixed C, the factor log₂n eventually makes n^{cn} exceed 2^{Cn}. Conversely, this card permits a large constant C. A polynomial-memory algorithm with time 2^{100n} would resolve the existence question affirmatively even if it were unusable in practice and slower than current exponential-memory algorithms at moderate ranks.

The output is exact, and the zero vector is excluded. Returning a vector whose length is within a fixed or polynomial factor of optimum solves a different task. Ties create no ambiguity: if several shortest vectors exist, any one is valid. Rational input also allows exact comparison of squared lengths, so the definition does not rely on floating-point tolerance or an unspecified geometric oracle.

The standard basis illustrates why practical performance alone says little about the general bound. For B=I, a shortest vector is immediately visible. A basis with long, strongly correlated columns may describe a lattice with much shorter integer combinations. Preprocessing can improve the basis substantially, but its own running time and memory must be charged. Supplying an already ideal basis would remove part of the problem.

Kannan’s enumeration method uses recursive preprocessing to control the search region. Hanrot–Stehlé’s analysis gives the more precise n^{n/(2e)+o(n)} time benchmark, up to polynomial input-size factors, and later work reduces preprocessing overhead. This refines the constant multiplying n log n; it does not change that scale to O(n). The bound is about the method, not an unconditional lower bound on every polynomial-space algorithm.

The inherited Micciancio–Voulgaris paper proves a different landmark: deterministic single-exponential algorithms using Voronoi-cell computations. Its March 2012 revision improves the bound to roughly 2^{2n} time and 2^n space, suppressing polynomial factors. The paper explicitly leaves single-exponential time with polynomial space as an open direction. Reading only the phrase deterministic single exponential in its title would miss the resource that remains unresolved.

Exponential memory can encode reusable relationships among many short vectors. Recomputing a discarded value may save space, but repeated recomputation can increase the running time beyond the allowed bound. A valid positive solution must control this global cost as well as the size of each local calculation. Streaming a large list through a small buffer is not sufficient if later steps require repeatedly reconstructing most of the list.

Theoretical and heuristic guarantees also need separation. Pruning an enumeration tree or keeping a smaller sieve pool may work well on tested lattices. A proof for the present question must additionally show that the retained search process reaches an exact minimizer with probability at least 2/3 on every input within the stated time. Successful benchmark instances cannot supply that universal guarantee.

A January 2026 paper by Koyuncu–Linker–Ozel proposes a sheaf-based sieving framework and discusses polynomial memory under coarse graining. Its §4 initially gives storage O((M+K)n) for M initial vectors and K iterations, then suggests reducing memory when most new vectors replace old ones. It does not provide a uniform proof that this replacement regime retains the exact-success guarantee and a 2^{O(n)} iteration bound on every lattice. It is therefore recorded as a related proposal rather than a resolution of this precise question.

The resource gap is also used in current cryptographic research. Albrecht–Lai–Postlethwaite’s CRYPTO 2026 work derives consequences from hypothetical algorithms for hinted inhomogeneous short-integer solutions, connecting them to single-exponential algorithms with polynomial memory for broader worst-case lattice tasks. Its hardness conclusions rely on a time-space assumption; they do not prove that such algorithms are impossible.

The importance of the problem is that it isolates memory as a potential source of exponential speedups in exact geometry. A solution could change the theoretical basis for choosing between enumeration and large-pool methods. Its cryptographic consequences would still have to be assessed through the relevant reductions and concrete parameters; the existence of some 2^{Cn}-time exact solver is not itself a polynomial-time attack.

cards.definitions: The lattice generated by B is Λ(B)={Bz:z∈ℤ^d}; d is its rank and m its ambient dimension. Its first minimum λ₁(Λ) is the minimum Euclidean length of a nonzero lattice vector. Full column rank makes this minimum positive and attained. The output is the signed binary coefficient vector z, so lattice membership and the corresponding integer vector Bz can be recovered without a real-number encoding. Any shortest vector is acceptable, with no uniqueness promise; the zero vector is excluded. Exactness means squared length equals λ₁², rather than being within a multiplicative factor greater than one. Use the standard uniform quantum circuit model: a classical polynomial-time machine generates, from 1^L, a circuit on an L-bit input register, zero-initialized ancillary qubits and output qubits, using the fixed universal gates H, T and CNOT, followed by computational-basis measurement and polynomial-time classical decoding. H is the Hadamard gate, T=diag(1,exp(iπ/4)), and CNOT maps |a,b⟩ to |a,a⊕b⟩. Circuit size, qubit count, input processing and output writing are polynomial in L. No advice, oracle, pre-supplied quantum state or unit-cost access to an exponentially large memory is provided. Failure is allowed on at most one third of runs for each valid input; it is not an average over randomly chosen lattices. Malformed encodings and rank-deficient matrices can be rejected classically. Integer bases are the imported target; clearing rational denominators preserves shortest vectors up to a common scale and increases encoding length only polynomially.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove existence of the algorithm with the stated worst-case polynomial cost and exact-search success on every valid basis, or prove that no such algorithm exists. Classical NP-hardness alone does not establish the negative answer for quantum computation. A polynomial-factor approximation, an algorithm for a promised special family, or an exponential-time speedup does not establish the positive answer.

context_blocks.title: The basis can hide a short vector
context_blocks.text: The vectors (100,1) and (101,1) are both long, but their difference is (1,0). Since every nonzero integer vector has length at least one, this difference is shortest in their lattice. SVP searches all integer combinations of the supplied basis, rather than choosing its shortest column.

context_blocks.title: Exactness is a separate demand from probability
context_blocks.text: A successful run must output a genuinely shortest vector. Bounded error permits some runs to fail; it does not permit every run to return a slightly longer vector. Similarly, a quantum state encoding many candidate vectors is not the requested classical answer until a shortest coefficient vector can be extracted with the required probability.

context_blocks.title: Why classical hardness does not settle the quantum question
context_blocks.text: Micciancio proves randomized NP-hardness even for some constant-factor Euclidean approximations, hence also for exact search. A polynomial-time quantum exact solver would therefore put all NP decision problems in BQP, the class with bounded-error polynomial-time quantum algorithms. This is a complexity consequence of the reduction, not a proved impossibility: NP⊆BQP is not known to be false.

context_blocks.title: Faster exponential algorithms still leave the target open
context_blocks.text: The 2025 paper gives exact quantum algorithms with exponential dependence on rank and explicitly separates QRAM access. Hhan’s August 2026 preprint states expected classical time about 2^{0.6039d} and quantum time about 2^{0.5411d}, up to lower-order exponential and polynomial factors; the quantum bound uses exponentially large QRAM. Kim’s concurrent sampling preprint also gives an exponential exact-SVP consequence. These recent claims were checked for scope, not independently proved. None gives polynomial time in L.

context_blocks.title: The recent coset claim has a different lattice consequence
context_blocks.text: Simon’s August 2026 DCP preprint claims polynomial-factor approximate SVP, which would not provide exact shortest vectors even if the algorithm were correct. Gupte, Ragavan and Zhandry’s response, revised on 1 September, claims a direct impossibility result for that proposed algorithm. The claim and response therefore do not supply a resolution of the exact-search problem on this card.

cards.title: Deterministic polynomial-time construction of a prime of a given bit length
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic algorithm and constants C,c>0 which, on input 1^n for every n≥2, output a prime p with 2^(n−1)≤p<2^n in at most Cn^c bit operations?
cards.definitions: Use uniform classical deterministic Turing computation, with no advice or oracle. Integers and rational numerators and denominators are encoded in binary; L denotes the total input bit length. A polynomial bound has constants independent of the input. The unary input parameter requests an n-bit output. A prime is an integer greater than one with no positive divisors other than one and itself. Correctness and the bound must hold for every n≥2; neither randomization, an oracle, a prime table supplied as advice, nor an unproved number-theoretic hypothesis is allowed.

context_blocks.text: Primality testing and finding a prime are different algorithmic tasks. A quickly checkable certificate for a candidate does not by itself identify a candidate in a prescribed bit-length interval.

Random sampling efficiently finds primes, while deterministic generation is a classical explicit-construction problem tied to derandomization and time-bounded information. The source uses the sequence of primes produced by deterministic search to explain that connection. Pseudodeterministic randomized generation also leaves this all-input deterministic target unresolved.

cards.formal: Determine the capacity region C(a,b,P₁,P₂) of the memoryless real channel Y₁,t=X₁,t+aX₂,t+Z₁,t and Y₂,t=bX₁,t+X₂,t+Z₂,t for every fixed a,b∈ℝ and finite P₁,P₂≥0, with independent messages, average power constraints, no feedback or cooperation, and vanishing average decoding error. Equivalently, determine the exact function F(a,b,P₁,P₂,λ)=sup_{(R₁,R₂)∈C}[λR₁+(1−λ)R₂] for every λ∈[0,1], under the operational definitions below.
cards.definitions: For a block of n uses, messages M_i are independent and uniform on {1,…,K_{i,n}}. Transmitter i applies a deterministic encoder f_{i,n}:{1,…,K_{i,n}}→ℝⁿ depending only on its own message. Its codebook satisfies (nK_{i,n})⁻¹∑_{m=1}^{K_{i,n}}∑_{t=1}ⁿ f_{i,n}(m)_t²≤P_i. All Z_{i,t} are mutually independent N(0,1) random variables independent of the messages. Receiver i applies a measurable decoder g_{i,n}:ℝⁿ→{1,…,K_{i,n}} to its own received vector. The probability that either decoded message is wrong is averaged over both messages and all noise. A nonnegative pair (R₁,R₂) is achievable if there is a sequence of such codes with this error tending to zero and liminf_{n→∞} n⁻¹ log₂ K_{i,n}≥R_i for i=1,2. C is the closure of achievable pairs, measured in bits per real channel use. Gains, powers and both codebooks are known to all terminals. Arbitrary encoding across time and predetermined time sharing with power allocation are permitted; transmitters have no messages in common, output feedback, or communication between them. C is compact, convex and downward closed, so the nonnegative supporting function F uniquely determines it.
cards.answer_criterion: Formulation unfinished. The operational capacity region and supporting function are defined. The accepted finite-dimensional characterization has no specified syntax, allowed auxiliary distributions, dimension bound or evaluation requirement. Excluding a restatement informally is not a mathematical acceptance predicate; no new representation restriction is invented here.
cards.why: A defining problem in network information theory: even two interfering sender–receiver pairs expose limits of our ability to characterize optimal communication. An exact solution would distinguish which forms of message splitting, interference decoding and power allocation are fundamentally necessary.

importance.reason: A foundational multi-user capacity frontier with a simple channel model, strong approximate results and unresolved exact tradeoffs. Recent disputed claims make the precise formulation and status record especially valuable.

cards.status_note: Status checked on 10 September 2026. Khandani arXiv:2501.14941v12 (7 September) claims capacity throughout weak interference. Nair–Zhao’s January manuscript questions parts of an earlier version and disproves a restricted Gaussian-optimality statement without power control; that is not an adjudication of v12. This review has not established the correctness of the latest claim or a complete arbitrary-parameter characterization. Established partial results are separated from the claim. The original proposal’s arXiv:1508.05726 reference was withdrawn in 2018.

context_blocks.text: Two independent conversations share the same medium: each receiver sees its desired signal, a scaled version of the other sender’s signal, and Gaussian noise. With only one sender, Shannon’s formula gives the rate ½ log₂(1+P). With two senders, improving one link can make the other harder to decode. The mathematical object is therefore a two-dimensional region of feasible rate pairs. Knowing its largest total rate does not identify all tradeoffs between the users.

Han–Kobayashi coding splits each message into a part decoded by both receivers and a private part decoded only by its intended receiver. It includes treating interference as noise and decoding interference as special strategies. Time sharing can also allocate different powers to different phases while meeting the average constraints. Shang and Chen’s monograph organizes these inner bounds and the exact results in particular regimes, including the distinction between full regions and sum-rate capacity.

Strong interference is a solved benchmark. When |a|≥1 and |b|≥1, the capacity region consists of R₁≤½log₂(1+P₁), R₂≤½log₂(1+P₂), and R₁+R₂≤min{½log₂(1+P₁+a²P₂),½log₂(1+b²P₁+P₂)}. Both receivers can decode both messages. With a=b=0, the region is the rectangle given by the two individual bounds. These exact cases anchor the question but do not characterize arbitrary interference strengths.

Etkin, Tse and Wang show that a simple Han–Kobayashi strategy and new converse bounds locate the general region within a universal additive gap. Their celebrated one-bit theorem also gives high-signal-to-noise insights. A fixed gap can be extremely useful for system design while leaving the exact boundary unknown: it does not shrink merely because longer codes are allowed.

Recent work separates several different Gaussian-optimality questions. Nair and Zhao’s ISIT 2025 result identifies a substantial parameter range in the one-sided, or Z, channel where the optimized Gaussian-signaling region needs no multiplexing. This optimizes a particular achievable region; it does not prove that no other signaling distribution or coding strategy can do better.

Their January 2026 manuscript then shows that Gaussian distributions can be suboptimal within a single-phase Han–Kobayashi region when power control is disallowed. Its Conjecture 1 still asks whether Gaussian signaling with power control achieves full Z-channel capacity. Remark 2 reports difficulty verifying parts of an earlier Khandani proof claim. The counterexamples concern the restricted single-phase statement and do not disprove optimality after the allowed power allocation and time sharing.

Gohari, Nair and Zhao’s February 2026 work combines auxiliary-receiver and genie-aided converse techniques. Its Gaussian specialization captures known corner and sum-rate behavior, including associated changes in boundary slope. The theorem supplies an outer region rather than a general equality with an achievable region, so it advances the converse side without itself resolving the full target.

Khandani’s preprint, revised on 7 September 2026, makes a stronger claim: Gaussian Han–Kobayashi coding attains capacity throughout weak interference, with at most two time-sharing phases. This would settle a major part of the problem if established. The current revision has not been independently validated in this review. The earlier Nair–Zhao criticism predates it and cannot automatically be applied to every revised argument. This card therefore marks the present status as uncertain and records the claim explicitly.

The original short proposal cited a withdrawn paper by Huleihel and Merhav. Its claimed improvement using codewords with Gaussian memory was withdrawn in April 2018. Nair and Ng subsequently establish that temporally correlated Gaussian inputs do not enlarge the Gaussian Han–Kobayashi region once the comparison includes the appropriate scalar time sharing. The withdrawn result is retained only as a status correction, not as evidence of progress.
