context_blocks.text: A marginal measures the fraction of records matching a pattern on selected coordinates. Low-order marginals describe small groups of attributes, while all marginals permit every such pattern. The family contains exponentially many queries even though one query has a short description. A synopsis is therefore an efficiently evaluable representation, rather than a literal list of exponentially many answers.

Privacy and accuracy quantify different objects. The privacy guarantee compares the complete output distributions after changing one person’s row. Accuracy concerns all queries simultaneously on each fixed database. Once a successful synopsis has been released, its deterministic evaluation reveals no additional access to the original records. An algorithm answering only a prespecified small batch is not automatically an algorithm for this target.

Vadhan’s Open Problem 7.8 asks about polynomial-time private estimation of all higher-order marginals with vanishing error using only polynomially many rows in the dimension. The present card fixes approximate-DP parameters, replacement adjacency and a noninteractive evaluable synopsis. These choices state one concrete version of the proposal; they are not asserted to be equivalent to every interactive or fixed-order formulation.

Chandrasekaran, Thaler, Ullman and Wan give subexponential-time private algorithms for marginal queries on small databases. Their result illustrates useful progress between exponential and polynomial cost. The constant-accuracy, per-query statement in that paper does not provide the polynomial-time, vanishing-error synopsis required here.

Requiring synthetic records would impose an extra restriction. The benchmark permits any binary synopsis with an efficient evaluator, because hardness of synthetic-data generation need not rule out other ways of answering queries. The existing TCS-0506 concerns private PAC sample complexity, while TCS-6040 asks about strong approximation of coverage functions. Neither asks this computational query-release question.

cards.formal: For a finite set $Y$, public losses $\ell_y$ have sensitivity 1 under a one-record change in the database $X$. The only access to $X$ is through adaptive queries $q_i(X)+N(0,1/(2\rho_i))$, with sensitivity at most 1 and $\sum_i\rho_i\le\rho$. cards.title: Optimal private selection using only Laplace queries
cards.formal: Let $Y$ be a finite set of candidates, each with a public loss function $\ell_y$ of sensitivity one under a one-record database change. To access the database, an algorithm makes $k$ adaptive sensitivity-1 queries. Its answers are $q_i(X)+\mathrm{Lap}(k)$, where $k$ is the scale. Can it guarantee expected excess loss $O(\log|Y|)$ for arbitrary losses? The algorithm may choose the number of queries.
cards.why: The cost of pure privacy is a structural model distinction, rather than an arbitrary change of constants. It determines the reach of noise addition as a universal primitive.

progress.text: The binary-tree algorithm has error $O(\log^2|Y|)$.

context_blocks.text: This model corresponds to basic composition for pure privacy. The stronger concentration of Gaussian noise cannot simply be transferred.

Here the menu of candidates is finite and each loss changes by at most one when one database record changes. The algorithm tries to choose a candidate whose expected loss is close to the best available loss. Its only observations are sensitivity-bounded statistical queries with Laplace noise.

Taking more queries is not free in this interface: the noise scale of each answer grows with the total query count k. A method that estimates all losses can spend too much accuracy on candidates that will never be selected. A method that repeatedly eliminates candidates risks making irreversible choices from noisy comparisons. The problem asks whether a carefully organized query process can still reach logarithmic excess loss.

context_blocks.text: This question is already resolved. Nikolov’s August 2022 preprint, published at SODA 2023 and subsequently in the Journal of Privacy and Confidentiality, gives the requested pure-private normalized Euclidean guarantee. Theorem 1 explicitly identifies its conclusion as the resolution of Nikolov–Ullman Open Problem 2. The source proposal was therefore stale when imported.

A statistical query is a bounded average. For a database of categories, an indicator query asks what fraction of records belong to a selected set of categories. Several queries can ask about overlapping sets, so their answers concern the same individuals. Privacy constrains the distribution of the entire released vector under replacement of any one record. Protecting each coordinate separately with the full privacy budget would not establish the required joint guarantee.

The normalized Euclidean error is the square root of the average squared coordinate error for one output, followed by expectation over the mechanism. If the error vector is (1,0,…,0), its normalized Euclidean error is 1/√k, whereas its maximum-coordinate error is one. Thus one badly estimated query can have much less effect on the average criterion. The position of the expectation also matters: this is not the square root of the expected squared error.

The 2021 question sought a bound independent of k, the number of queries. Its shifted logarithm handles a singleton universe, and the minimum with one reflects a trivial data-independent release: outputting the zero vector has normalized error at most one. A singleton universe in fact permits exact release, because all databases have the same answer vector. These conventions do not assert a matching lower bound in every parameter regime.

Nikolov proves sample complexity O(log T/(εα²)) for normalized error α, alongside sharper alternatives for some parameters. Rearranging gives the square-root accuracy bound. His definitions use bounded real queries, replacement adjacency and the expected norm divided by √k, matching this card. The mechanism exploits a lower-dimensional representation of the feasible answer vectors and also has an efficiency guarantee beyond this card’s existence requirement.

The July 2026 version of Fitzsimons’s paper focused on the maximum-coordinate problem and retained a √log(2k) factor. Its 3 August revision adds Theorem 1.2 with the exact Euclidean rate and explicitly acknowledges Nikolov’s earlier solution. The Euclidean conclusion therefore must not be classified as still open by reading only the first version or the abstract-page summary. The newer paper’s claimed formalization was not independently built or audited here.

cards.title: Does every finite-template decision promise CSP have a P/NP-hard dichotomy?
cards.formal: For every pair of fixed finite relational structures A,B of the same finite signature, with a homomorphism A→B, is the decision promise problem of distinguishing I→A from I↛B either solvable in deterministic polynomial time or NP-hard under deterministic polynomial-time many-one promise reductions?
cards.definitions: A finite relational signature is a finite list of relation symbols R with fixed positive arities a_R. A structure A consists of a finite nonempty domain and, for each R, a relation R^A⊆A^{a_R}. A homomorphism h:I→A is a map on domains such that (v₁,…,v_a)∈R^I implies (h(v₁),…,h(v_a))∈R^A for every R and tuple. The templates A,B and their relations are fixed for each computational problem. Only I varies; its domain and relation tuples are explicitly listed in binary, of total length L. The algorithm must accept all I admitting a homomorphism to A and reject all I admitting no homomorphism to B. On I→B but I↛A, either answer is allowed. A→B makes the yes and no sets disjoint. Polynomial time means one deterministic algorithm for the fixed pair, halting on every input in O(L^c), with c and hidden constants allowed to depend on A,B. NP-hardness means a deterministic polynomial-time map from 3-SAT formulas φ to structures I_φ such that satisfiable φ yield I_φ→A and unsatisfiable φ yield I_φ↛B. The question is about deciding the promise, not producing a B-valued assignment. No uniform algorithm for classifying templates is required. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.

cards.status_note: Open classification question in the cited survey, with relevant partial results checked through 10 September 2026. The card asks for an unconditional decision dichotomy over all fixed finite template pairs; it does not assume decision/search equivalence or a complete algebraic classification.

context_blocks.text: Ordinary constraint satisfaction asks whether a collection of local requirements can all hold simultaneously. Promise CSPs keep two versions of each requirement: the input is guaranteed to admit a solution satisfying the stronger version, while the relaxed task uses the weaker one. For graph colouring, A=Kₖ and B=K_c with k≤c produces the decision task of distinguishing k-colourable graphs from graphs that are not c-colourable. Graphs in between impose no decision requirement.

When A=B, the promise disappears. Bulatov and Zhuk independently proved in 2017 that every finite-template CSP is either in P or NP-complete. The present question asks whether a comparable exclusion of intermediate complexity survives arbitrary finite promises. It does not follow merely by applying the classical theorem to A and B separately: the relaxed task can be easier than either endpoint CSP.

A concrete tractable example promises that each listed triple of Boolean variables can have exactly one 1 and asks only for a not-all-equal assignment. Solve the equations x+y+z=1 over the integers, then map positive values to 1 and nonpositive values to 0. No such triple can become all zero or all one. Barto proves that this tractability cannot be explained by sandwiching the pair through a tractable finite-domain CSP, unless P=NP. Finite templates can therefore need an infinite intermediate domain in this natural algorithmic framework.

The algebraic approach studies operations that combine several A-solutions coordinatewise into one B-solution. These polymorphisms capture useful structure for algorithms and reductions, but their input and output domains can differ, preventing the direct use of all the composition arguments available in ordinary CSP. The survey emphasizes that a full dichotomy was not yet backed by enough evidence to be asserted as a settled consensus conjecture; this card poses it as a precise open question.

Important subclasses are classified. Brakensiek and Guruswami obtain a dichotomy for symmetric Boolean promise CSPs allowing negations, with tractable cases going beyond a direct reuse of Schaefer’s classical Boolean CSP classification. That theorem does not classify all Boolean templates or all finite domains.

The 2026 work of Banakh, Barsukov, and Nakajima expands the logical viewpoint by relating Promise MMSNP to finite-domain PCSPs. It also classifies a family defined by forbidden monochromatic cliques under the Rich 2-to-1 Conjecture. Both the restricted family and the additional assumption matter: this is not an unconditional classification of every finite template pair.

cards.title: The Bodirsky–Pinsker infinite-domain CSP dichotomy
cards.formal: For every countable finitely bounded homogeneous structure A over a finite relational signature, and every finite-signature first-order reduct B of A, is CSP(B) either decidable in deterministic polynomial time or NP-complete under polynomial-time many-one reductions?
cards.definitions: A relational signature is a finite list of relation symbols with fixed finite arities. A is homogeneous if every isomorphism between two finite induced substructures extends to an automorphism of A. It is finitely bounded if there is a finite set F of finite structures in its signature such that a finite structure embeds into A exactly when none of the structures in F embeds into it; embeddings preserve both relations and their complements. Countable allows finite or countably infinite domains. B has the same domain as A, with finitely many relations each definable by a first-order formula over A without parameters; it may forget original relations and introduce definable ones. For each fixed B, an input to CSP(B) is an explicitly encoded finite structure I in B’s signature. Accept exactly when there is a map h from the domain of I to that of B preserving every relation tuple. Equivalently, a finite conjunction of atomic B-constraints must have a satisfying assignment. h need not be injective. A, B and their defining formulas are fixed, not part of the input; running times are measured in the finite instance’s bit length. context_blocks.text: The finite-domain CSP dichotomy, proved independently by Bulatov and Zhuk in 2017, says that fixing a finite collection of relations on a finite domain leaves no intermediate complexity between polynomial time and NP-completeness. The infinite-domain conjecture asks whether this organizing principle survives when variables can take rational values, positions in a countable graph, or other infinitely many possibilities, provided the template has a finite structural description.

The restrictions explain why the question is computationally meaningful. Homogeneity means that finite patterns completely determine their symmetry type. Finite boundedness gives a finite list of forbidden patterns for checking whether a proposed finite configuration can occur. For a fixed reduct, one can guess a partition of the variables representing equal values and the finite relational pattern on those values, then check the constraints and forbidden patterns. The signature and forbidden sizes are constants, so this yields polynomial-size NP certificates despite the infinite domain.

For a concrete example, the ordered rational numbers (ℚ;<) are homogeneous and finitely bounded. Constraints consisting only of strict inequalities are feasible exactly when their directed inequality graph is acyclic. Adding the definable ternary relation “y lies strictly between x and z” gives the classical NP-complete Betweenness problem. Thus the same domain can support both tractable and hard constraint languages; the choice of allowed relations is decisive.

A central method studies polymorphisms: operations which, applied coordinatewise to several satisfying tuples of any relation, produce another satisfying tuple. Such operations record ways of combining solutions and can prevent standard hardness gadgets. Barto and Pinsker identify a particular algebraic identity that characterizes the absence of the relevant hardness construction for model-complete cores. The missing general step is turning the tractable-side algebraic structure into polynomial-time algorithms. The bare P/NP-complete dichotomy asked here is weaker than proving that full algebraic classification.

Pinsker, Rydval, Schöbi, Spiess and Winkler’s May 2026 revision shows that the conjecture can be reduced to templates without algebraicity: fixing finitely many elements does not force any additional element into a finite orbit. Their construction replaces domain elements by infinite families while preserving the relevant constraint complexity. They also connect tractable infinite-domain templates to finite-domain promise CSPs through intermediate structures. These are reductions in the scope of the conjecture, rather than a general tractability algorithm.

Dorochko and Wrona’s July 2026 revision proves a different dichotomy: for first-order expansions of finitely bounded homogeneous model-complete cores, the CSP is first-order definable or hard for deterministic logarithmic space under first-order reductions. An expansion retains all original relations; this hypothesis does not cover arbitrary reducts. Moreover, L-hard problems can still be in P, so the result separates a much lower boundary and leaves the P versus NP-complete question open.

Feller and Pinsker’s August 2026 revision develops effective tools for comparing templates. In particular, a model-complete core is computable when the structure has a finitely bounded Ramsey expansion, an additional structural hypothesis. Their decidability results concern interpretability and equivalent algebraic presentations, not a complete algorithmic classification of all templates in this card.

A resolution would say whether a finite description by symmetric local patterns rules out intermediate NP complexity across a large family of logical and combinatorial problems. The difficulty is to find algorithms that exploit this description uniformly within each fixed template, without assuming that the infinitely many possible values can simply be replaced by one fixed finite domain.

cards.title: Constant-colour polynomial-time colouring of 3-colourable graphs
cards.formal: Is there a fixed integer C≥3 and a uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithm that, on every finite simple undirected graph G promised to be 3-colourable, outputs a proper vertex colouring using at most C colours with probability at least 2/3?
cards.definitions: The input is an explicitly given graph G=([n],E), n≥1, with no loops or parallel edges, encoded by its adjacency matrix. A proper k-colouring is a map c:[n]→[k] such that c(u)≠c(v) for every {u,v}∈E. The promise is existence of a proper 3-colouring; such a colouring is not supplied. There must be one C, one randomized Turing machine A, and fixed constants K,d such that A uses at most K(n+1)^d bit operations on every graph and every random tape. On each promised input, the probability, over independent unbiased internal random bits, of outputting a proper C-colouring is at least 2/3. Invalid outputs can be replaced by a failure symbol after checking all edges. No correctness requirement is imposed on non-3-colourable inputs, but the time bound still applies. The algorithm may colour such an input whenever it can; it need not recognize the promise. C is independent of n, degree, density and the input graph. No planarity, bounded-degree, expansion, forbidden-subgraph, random-input or supplied-decomposition promise is available. Randomization is explicitly permitted in this version of the inherited question; a deterministic algorithm would be a stronger positive result. The algorithm must colour every vertex and avoid every monochromatic edge on a successful run.
cards.answer_criterion: Give such an algorithm for at least one fixed C, or prove that no such C and randomized polynomial-time algorithm exist. A growing colour bound, a partial colouring of most vertices, or a guarantee only on a restricted graph family is insufficient. NP-hardness of the 3-versus-C promise for every fixed C would establish the usual complexity-theoretic obstruction; excluding randomized algorithms from that obstruction additionally uses NP≠RP. Hardness for C=5 alone leaves all larger constants unresolved. Conditional hardness results must keep their assumptions explicit.
cards.why: A defining promise-CSP problem: determine whether relaxing an NP-hard colouring task to any fixed larger palette permits efficient construction of a valid solution.

cards.status_note: No constant-colour algorithm or unrestricted all-constant hardness resolution found through 11 September 2026. The February 2026 primary paper retains the gap between five-colour NP-hardness and a growing O(n^{0.19539}) algorithmic bound. The March logic result is restricted to fixed-point logic with counting. This card explicitly allows bounded-error randomized algorithms.

context_blocks.text: The input comes with a guarantee that three colours suffice, but not with the partition into three independent sets. Allowing more colours is a relaxation of the output requirements. The question asks whether some fixed amount of this relaxation makes the problem efficiently solvable on every promised input. A mechanism for choosing 100 colours would qualify just as a mechanism for choosing six colours would; the constant need not be close to three.

This promise matters. Strong inapproximability results for the chromatic number on unrestricted graphs can use instances whose chromatic number grows with the graph size. They do not automatically establish hardness when the yes-instances must have chromatic number at most three. Conversely, an algorithm for planar graphs would use a structural assumption missing here. Three-colourable graphs can be dense and can have high-degree vertices.

The problem is a basic example of promise constraint satisfaction. An edge asks its two endpoints to receive different labels. The promise says the constraints have a solution over a three-element domain; the algorithm is allowed to use a larger fixed domain. In graph-homomorphism language, an input maps to K₃ and the output must provide a map to K_C. The associated decision promise distinguishes graphs mapping to K₃ from graphs not mapping to K_C.

Barto, Bulín, Krokhin and Opršal prove NP-hardness of finding a five-colouring of a three-colourable graph, as part of a broader algebraic framework. This is far stronger than hardness of finding the promised three-colouring, yet it excludes only particular small output domains under standard complexity assumptions. It does not rule out a successful algorithm using six, 100 or any other larger fixed number of colours.

A useful elementary observation is that the neighbours of any vertex in a three-colourable graph induce a bipartite graph: the vertex’s own colour cannot appear among its neighbours. Thus one can efficiently colour a large neighbourhood using two fresh colours. When all remaining degrees are small, greedy colouring is effective. Balancing these two procedures already gives an O(√n)-colour algorithm. The challenge is to extract much more global information than this local observation provides.

Modern algorithms combine combinatorial reductions with semidefinite relaxations. The relaxation assigns vectors that mimic the separation of colours, and rounding extracts independent sets or other useful progress. Kawarabayashi, Thorup and Yoneda’s STOC 2024 work strengthens the combinatorial side and obtains Õ(n^{0.19747}) colours after combining it with the SDP approach. The suppressed factors are polylogarithmic in n.

Bansal, Huang and Lee’s February 2026 preprint improves the SDP analysis using third-level neighbourhoods and a new vector 5/2-colouring construction. Combined with the combinatorial component, its theorem gives O(n^{0.19539}) colours. A vector 5/2-colouring is a geometric relaxation, not an ordinary assignment using a fractional number of colours. The exponent improvement is real progress, while the final number of actual colours still grows with n.

Hardness evidence also goes beyond five colours under additional assumptions. Guruswami and Sandeep show that a fixed d-to-1 Label Cover conjecture implies hardness for every constant output palette. Their premise requires perfectly satisfiable yes-instances. Replacing perfect completeness by near-perfect completeness changes what the reduction guarantees, so established results about almost-satisfiable games cannot simply be substituted into this argument.

Dawar and Molnár’s full version, revised in March 2026, proves that fixed-point logic with counting cannot separate three-colourable graphs from graphs requiring more than any fixed number of colours. This is an unconditional obstruction for that logic on unordered structures, not for all polynomial-time algorithms on explicitly encoded graphs. The card sits at the intersection of approximation algorithms, algebraic reductions and limits of relaxation methods: a resolution would tell us how much a fixed expansion of the solution domain can help.

cards.title: Search-to-decision equivalence for finite promise CSPs
cards.formal: For every fixed pair of finite relational structures A and B with the same finite signature and A→B, does polynomial-time solvability of the decision promise CSP(A,B) imply polynomial-time solvability of its search version? Decision must accept X whenever X→A and reject X whenever X↛B. Search, on every X promised to satisfy X→A, must output an explicit homomorphism X→B.
cards.definitions: A finite relational signature is a finite list of relation symbols with fixed positive integer arities. A structure A consists of a finite nonempty domain and one relation R^A⊆A^r for each r-ary symbol R; B and the input X have relations with the same symbols and arities. A homomorphism h:X→B is a map on domains such that (x₁,…,x_r)∈R^X implies (h(x₁),…,h(x_r))∈R^B for every symbol and tuple. Write X→B when some such map exists. A and B are constants defining the computational problem, and are not part of each input. The input explicitly lists X’s vertices and relation tuples; its encoding length is N. Both algorithms are deterministic Turing machines with running time polynomial in N on all inputs; their constants and exponents may depend on A and B. The decision algorithm may answer either way when X↛A but X→B. The search algorithm receives no homomorphism to A, only the promise that one exists. It must output the image of every vertex and satisfy every B-relation on promised inputs; outside that promise it may output anything or a failure symbol, but must still halt within its polynomial bound. The quantifiers are ∀(A,B): (∃ polynomial-time decider D)⇒(∃ polynomial-time search algorithm S). No uniform procedure that discovers D or S from arbitrary templates, and no requirement to use D as a black-box oracle, is included.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the implication for every fixed finite template pair, or identify one fixed pair with a polynomial-time decision algorithm and prove that its promised search problem has no polynomial-time algorithm. An impossibility for one rounding scheme, an undecidable problem with the template as part of the input, or hardness on instances lacking X→A does not refute the statement. A conditional separation is relevant progress but must retain its complexity assumption.

context_blocks.text: A promise CSP separates the conditions known to be satisfiable from the conditions a solution must meet. The structure A describes the stronger requirements; B describes the weaker ones. The fixed homomorphism A→B ensures that an A-solution can always be converted into a B-solution if it is known. The difficulty is that the input supplies only the existence promise, without the stronger solution itself.

Graph colouring is a concrete example. Take A to be the complete graph on three vertices and B the complete graph on six vertices. Search asks for an actual six-colouring of a graph known to be three-colourable. Decision merely separates three-colourable graphs from graphs that are not six-colourable. On graphs whose chromatic number is four, five or six, the decider may say anything. That unconstrained region is a central obstacle to turning its answers into a colouring.

Search immediately gives decision: run the search algorithm and check the proposed B-homomorphism. Every A-satisfiable input yields a valid output, while a graph or structure with no B-homomorphism can never pass verification. The all-input polynomial running-time requirement makes this argument valid even when the search promise fails. The unknown direction is whether a decider can always be made constructive.

For ordinary finite CSPs, where A=B, polynomial-time decision and search are equivalent. With a genuine promise, a step-by-step fixing procedure has an extra difficulty. After committing a variable to a B-value, the residual instance may still have a B-solution but cease to have an A-solution. The original decision guarantee then no longer certifies which remaining choices are safe. Adding arbitrary pinning constraints can also change the fixed constraint language.

Some positive cases are immediate. If there is a fixed finite structure C with A→C→B and a polynomial-time solver for CSP(C), solve in C and compose with the fixed map C→B. This includes the cases where CSP(A) or CSP(B) is tractable. But the general PCSP framework admits tractable examples that are not explained by an intermediate tractable finite CSP, assuming P≠NP, so this method does not cover the whole question.

There are also elementary constructive relaxations. Suppose Boolean variables occur in triples, with a promise of an assignment having exactly one 1 in every triple, and the goal is merely to make each triple nonconstant. Solve the integer linear system x+y+z=1 for the listed triples, allowing arbitrary integers. The promise makes it feasible. Map positive integers to 1 and nonpositive integers to 0. No equation can have all three integers positive, or all three nonpositive, so this map satisfies every weaker triple. This illustrates a rounding rule whose correctness can be checked directly.

Larrauri’s FOCS 2025 work proves that finding a B-solution on every instance accepted by BLP, AIP or their combination can encode any chosen TFNP problem through a suitable fixed template. TFNP consists of polynomially verifiable search problems whose solutions are guaranteed to exist. The accepted instances need not satisfy X→A. Thus the rounding task can be harder than the promised search task. The May 2026 revision explicitly corrects earlier overbroad claims and keeps the general implication open.

The same work proves undecidability of several algorithmic meta-problems, where A and B are supplied as input and one asks whether a relaxation solves their PCSP. This concerns recognizing an entire family of templates. Our question permits a different fixed algorithm for each fixed template, so undecidability of that recognition task is logically compatible with a positive answer here.

Recent constructive progress also occurs under explicit algebraic hypotheses. The SODA 2026 robust-satisfiability paper gives algorithms for Boolean PCSPs with majority polymorphisms when the stronger constraints are almost satisfiable, along with matching conditional tradeoffs in several settings. Such results identify useful rounding structure, but do not provide a transformation for an arbitrary tractable decision template.

The issue is fundamental because a feasibility guarantee is often only the beginning of an algorithmic application: one needs the assignment, colouring or schedule. cards.context:
A promise CSP separates the conditions known to be satisfiable from the conditions a solution must meet. The structure A describes the stronger requirements; B describes the weaker ones. The fixed homomorphism A→B ensures that an A-solution can always be converted into a B-solution if it is known. The difficulty is that the input supplies only the existence promise, without the stronger solution itself.

Graph colouring is a concrete example. Take A to be the complete graph on three vertices and B the complete graph on six vertices. Search asks for an actual six-colouring of a graph known to be three-colourable. Decision merely separates three-colourable graphs from graphs that are not six-colourable. On graphs whose chromatic number is four, five or six, the decider may say anything. That unconstrained region is a central obstacle to turning its answers into a colouring.

Search immediately gives decision: run the search algorithm and check the proposed B-homomorphism. Every A-satisfiable input yields a valid output, while a graph or structure with no B-homomorphism can never pass verification. The all-input polynomial running-time requirement makes this argument valid even when the search promise fails. The unknown direction is whether a decider can always be made constructive.

For ordinary finite CSPs, where A=B, polynomial-time decision and search are equivalent. With a genuine promise, a step-by-step fixing procedure has an extra difficulty. After committing a variable to a B-value, the residual instance may still have a B-solution but cease to have an A-solution. The original decision guarantee then no longer certifies which remaining choices are safe. Adding arbitrary pinning constraints can also change the fixed constraint language.

Some positive cases are immediate. If there is a fixed finite structure C with A→C→B and a polynomial-time solver for CSP(C), solve in C and compose with the fixed map C→B. This includes the cases where CSP(A) or CSP(B) is tractable. But the general PCSP framework admits tractable examples that are not explained by an intermediate tractable finite CSP, assuming P≠NP, so this method does not cover the whole question.

There are also elementary constructive relaxations. Suppose Boolean variables occur in triples, with a promise of an assignment having exactly one 1 in every triple, and the goal is merely to make each triple nonconstant. Solve the integer linear system x+y+z=1 for the listed triples, allowing arbitrary integers. The promise makes it feasible. Map positive integers to 1 and nonpositive integers to 0. No equation can have all three integers positive, or all three nonpositive, so this map satisfies every weaker triple. This illustrates a rounding rule whose correctness can be checked directly.

Larrauri’s FOCS 2025 work proves that finding a B-solution on every instance accepted by BLP, AIP or their combination can encode any chosen TFNP problem through a suitable fixed template. TFNP consists of polynomially verifiable search problems whose solutions are guaranteed to exist. The accepted instances need not satisfy X→A. Thus the rounding task can be harder than the promised search task. The May 2026 revision explicitly corrects earlier overbroad claims and keeps the general implication open.

The same work proves undecidability of several algorithmic meta-problems, where A and B are supplied as input and one asks whether a relaxation solves their PCSP. This concerns recognizing an entire family of templates. Our question permits a different fixed algorithm for each fixed template, so undecidability of that recognition task is logically compatible with a positive answer here.

Recent constructive progress also occurs under explicit algebraic hypotheses. The SODA 2026 robust-satisfiability paper gives algorithms for Boolean PCSPs with majority polymorphisms when the stronger constraints are almost satisfiable, along with matching conditional tradeoffs in several settings. Such results identify useful rounding structure, but do not provide a transformation for an arbitrary tractable decision template.

The issue is fundamental because a feasibility guarantee is often only the beginning of an algorithmic application: one needs the assignment, colouring or schedule. A positive theorem would justify moving between classification of decision problems and construction of solutions throughout finite PCSPs. A negative theorem would reveal a precise local-constraint problem where efficient recognition of the promised gap conceals a harder search task.

cards.title: Is distinguishing 3-colourable graphs from graphs needing more than six colours NP-hard?
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic polynomial-time many-one reduction R from Boolean 3-SAT to finite simple undirected graphs such that, for every 3-CNF formula F, satisfiability of F implies χ(R(F))≤3 and unsatisfiability of F implies χ(R(F))>6?
cards.definitions: A 3-CNF formula is a conjunction of clauses containing at most three literals, each literal being a Boolean variable or its negation; the formula and variable indices have a standard explicit finite binary encoding. R is a uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine that outputs a graph as a labelled vertex set {1,…,n} and a list of unordered pairs of distinct vertices, with no repeated edges. Its total running time and output length are bounded by one polynomial in the formula’s encoding length. A proper k-colouring assigns one of {1,…,k} to each vertex so that endpoints of every edge receive different colours. χ(G) is the least such k, with χ of the empty graph taken to be zero. The promise decision problem, also denoted PCSP(K₃,K₆), has yes-instances χ≤3 and no-instances χ>6; graphs with χ=4,5,6 are outside the promise. K_k is the loopless complete graph on k vertices. No colouring or satisfiability witness is supplied as input. The reduction must satisfy the two implications unconditionally, without a Unique Games or Label Cover hardness hypothesis. Because 3-SAT is NP-complete, this reduction is precisely the usual deterministic many-one NP-hardness target for the promise problem.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation, with all definitions, promises, resource bounds and quantifiers as stated. A conditional result establishes only the explicitly conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-verified proof of the full target.

context_blocks.text: The input promise says that three colours suffice, but it does not reveal the three colour classes. Allowing a larger palette relaxes the output condition. The associated gap decision task distinguishes such promised yes-instances from graphs that cannot be coloured even with six colours. This isolates a small finite-template promise CSP with a particularly clear combinatorial meaning.

Barto, Bulín, Krokhin and Opršal establish hardness for colouring k-colourable graphs with 2k−1 colours, including the 3-versus-5 case. The 3-versus-6 question remains explicitly posed in subsequent work. Increasing the permitted palette weakens the output requirement, so hardness at five colours does not imply hardness at six.

TCS-6637 asks whether some fixed constant C admits a polynomial-time colouring algorithm for every 3-colourable graph. A negative result for six colours alone does not exclude algorithms using seven, one hundred or another fixed palette. Conversely, an algorithm with a growing number of colours does not settle even the six-colour search problem. The new card is a precise frontier case, rather than a duplicate of the quantifier over arbitrary constants.

The decision and search tasks should also be kept distinct. A polynomial-time six-colouring algorithm on 3-colourable inputs would decide the gap by checking its output: on a graph requiring more than six colours, no valid output exists. This implication explains the algorithmic relevance of the decision hardness target without redefining NP-hardness as a blanket statement about every search reduction.

The six-colour case has value beyond its small numerical parameters. It tests how far promise relaxation can preserve intractability after the classical CSP dichotomy, and it provides a fixed finite object on which algebraic and combinatorial limitations can be stated. Its specialist home remains Constraint satisfaction under the catalogue’s graph-category expansion.

cards.title: Are word equations with linear length constraints decidable?
cards.formal: Is there a Turing machine that halts on every finite input consisting of a system of word equations U_i=V_i and a system of integer linear equalities and inequalities on the variable lengths, and answers YES exactly when a simultaneous solution exists in the free monoid Σ*? The alphabet, equations, variables, and arithmetic coefficients are part of the input, with the conventions below.
cards.definitions: Σ is a finite nonempty alphabet of constant symbols and X={X_1,…,X_k} is a disjoint finite set of variables. Each U_i,V_i is an explicitly written finite word over Σ∪X; repeated occurrences of a variable must receive the same substitution. A solution assigns a finite word σ(X_j)∈Σ* to each variable and extends by concatenation while fixing every letter of Σ. The empty word is allowed. Every substituted equality σ(U_i)=σ(V_i) must hold as a literal equality of words. The additional constraints are a finite conjunction of atoms sum_j a_j|σ(X_j)|≤b or sum_j a_j|σ(X_j)|=b, where all coefficients and constants are signed binary integers. Length is the number of alphabet symbols. There is no product of two variable lengths, letter-frequency counter, regular-expression predicate, string-to-integer conversion, or universal quantifier. The requested decider need not run in polynomial, elementary, or any specified computable time bound, but must terminate on satisfiable and unsatisfiable inputs alike. Nonempty-substitution requirements can be imposed using |σ(X_j)|≥1. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: A fundamental boundary for reasoning about concatenation and numerical size simultaneously. It governs whether a complete terminating solver can exist for a basic fragment of string constraints used in verification, while connecting free-monoid equations, arithmetic and reachability.

importance.reason: A longstanding decidability question at the intersection of formal languages, number-theoretic constraints and automated verification; even unrestricted termination is unknown, before asking for efficient algorithms.

progress.text: Makanin establishes decidability of plain word equations. Adding linear length constraints remains outside that theorem; the distinction is reviewed by Ciobanu.
Ciobanu’s survey explicitly separates the open length-constraint problem from undecidable letter-count and Parikh-image extensions.

Day and Konefal’s RP 2025 paper appears online, giving decidability for quadratic equations with at most two unknowns and semilinear constraints on solution lengths. The proceedings carry a 2026 copyright year.
Version 3 of Barros, Cadilhac, and Pérez claims NEXP-hardness for the nonerasing positive-Boolean formulation. Only its arithmetic-with-divisibility problem is asserted NEXP-complete.
Przybocki and Barrett’s IJCAR 2026 paper gives partial termination criteria for extended Nielsen transformations and explicitly retains general decidability as open.

references.title: NEXP-Completeness and Exponential Coefficient Growth for Existential Presburger Arithmetic with Divisibility
references.authors: Ignacio Barros; Michaël Cadilhac; Guillermo A. Pérez
references.locator: Preprint v3, 19 July 2026; Theorem 1 is EPAD NEXP-completeness; Corollary 2 is NEXP-hardness of the nonerasing positive-Boolean word-equation formulation

cards.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The IJCAR 2026 primary source explicitly leaves general word-equation satisfiability with length constraints open. The two-variable quadratic theorem is a restricted case, and the July NEXP-hardness claim is a lower bound rather than a decidability result. This card fixes existential satisfiability with concatenation and integer linear length constraints only.

context_blocks.text: The two ingredients are individually manageable: plain word equations are decidable by Makanin’s theorem, and integer linear arithmetic is decidable. Their combination is difficult because string equality constrains how letters align, while arithmetic constrains the lengths of pieces across those alignments. A decision procedure for either component does not automatically decide their interaction. Ciobanu’s survey identifies this specific combination as a major remaining question.

Taking lengths gives useful necessary conditions, but can lose decisive information. For distinct letters a and b, the equation Xa=bX yields the harmless length identity |X|+1=1+|X|. Nevertheless, it has no finite-word solution. If X is nonempty its first letter must be b, and cancelling that b leaves the same equation for a shorter word; eventually one obtains the false equality a=b. This example shows why satisfying the induced linear equations alone cannot certify a word solution.

There is an elementary way to recognize every YES instance eventually: enumerate all tuples of finite words and test the equations and length constraints. If a solution exists, this search reaches it. For a NO instance, however, there is no prescribed point at which enumeration can stop. A computable bound on the size of some solution to every satisfiable input would therefore be sufficient for decidability. The existence of large witnesses by itself does not establish undecidability.

Several nearby theories have a different status. Constraints on the numbers of individual letters, or on the full vector of letter counts, can make word-equation satisfiability undecidable. Those predicates carry information beyond total length. Similarly, results with alternating quantifiers concern a stronger logical language. Importing either kind of undecidability theorem into this purely existential length-only question would change the problem.

Day and Konefal prove decidability for quadratic word equations in at most two unknowns, using a connection with matrix-semigroup reachability. Quadratic means each unknown has at most two occurrences across the equation. The two-unknown restriction is essential to the result stated in their RP 2025 paper. Its abstract also explains that sets of possible solution-length vectors need not be semilinear, so representing every such set by ordinary Presburger arithmetic cannot simply be assumed.

Przybocki and Barrett’s IJCAR 2026 work analyzes when extended Nielsen transformations terminate. These transformations reason about prefixes of variable values while tracking partial length information. Their cut graph records dependencies between occurrences, giving a sufficient termination criterion and a partial converse. This advances a procedure used in string solvers, but neither guarantees termination for every input nor decides the unrestricted problem.

Barros, Cadilhac, and Pérez’s July 2026 preprint claims NEXP-hardness for nonerasing satisfiability of positive Boolean combinations of word equations and Presburger length constraints, already over two letters. cards.context:
The two ingredients are individually manageable: plain word equations are decidable by Makanin’s theorem, and integer linear arithmetic is decidable. Their combination is difficult because string equality constrains how letters align, while arithmetic constrains the lengths of pieces across those alignments. A decision procedure for either component does not automatically decide their interaction. Ciobanu’s survey identifies this specific combination as a major remaining question.

Taking lengths gives useful necessary conditions, but can lose decisive information. For distinct letters a and b, the equation Xa=bX yields the harmless length identity |X|+1=1+|X|. Nevertheless, it has no finite-word solution. If X is nonempty its first letter must be b, and cancelling that b leaves the same equation for a shorter word; eventually one obtains the false equality a=b. This example shows why satisfying the induced linear equations alone cannot certify a word solution.

There is an elementary way to recognize every YES instance eventually: enumerate all tuples of finite words and test the equations and length constraints. If a solution exists, this search reaches it. For a NO instance, however, there is no prescribed point at which enumeration can stop. A computable bound on the size of some solution to every satisfiable input would therefore be sufficient for decidability. The existence of large witnesses by itself does not establish undecidability.

Several nearby theories have a different status. Constraints on the numbers of individual letters, or on the full vector of letter counts, can make word-equation satisfiability undecidable. Those predicates carry information beyond total length. Similarly, results with alternating quantifiers concern a stronger logical language. Importing either kind of undecidability theorem into this purely existential length-only question would change the problem.

Day and Konefal prove decidability for quadratic word equations in at most two unknowns, using a connection with matrix-semigroup reachability. Quadratic means each unknown has at most two occurrences across the equation. The two-unknown restriction is essential to the result stated in their RP 2025 paper. Its abstract also explains that sets of possible solution-length vectors need not be semilinear, so representing every such set by ordinary Presburger arithmetic cannot simply be assumed.

Przybocki and Barrett’s IJCAR 2026 work analyzes when extended Nielsen transformations terminate. These transformations reason about prefixes of variable values while tracking partial length information. Their cut graph records dependencies between occurrences, giving a sufficient termination criterion and a partial converse. This advances a procedure used in string solvers, but neither guarantees termination for every input nor decides the unrestricted problem.

Barros, Cadilhac, and Pérez’s July 2026 preprint claims NEXP-hardness for nonerasing satisfiability of positive Boolean combinations of word equations and Presburger length constraints, already over two letters. This strengthens the PP-hardness stated in its first version. Its NEXP-completeness theorem is for arithmetic with divisibility, not for unrestricted word equations with lengths. Positive Boolean formulas can be expanded into finitely many conjunctions for purposes of decidability, but that expansion need not be polynomial. The result therefore records a substantial complexity barrier without establishing a general decider or undecidability.

cards.definitions: Formulas are finite expressions generated by variables p_i (i∈ℕ), ⊥, negation, conjunction and the unary operator □; other Boolean connectives and ◇ are abbreviations. Variable indices use binary notation and formulas are supplied as fully written syntax trees. A substitution assigns a finite formula to each variable occurring in φ, may use new propositional variables, and extends simultaneously through the connectives and □; it does not substitute recursively inside its newly inserted formulas. There are no distinguished parameters that must remain unchanged. A frame is a nonempty set W with an arbitrary relation R⊆W×W, finite or infinite. A valuation assigns a subset of W to every variable. Satisfaction uses the usual truth tables, ⊥ is false everywhere, and w⊨□ψ iff v⊨ψ for all v with wRv. Validity means satisfaction at every world in every frame with every valuation. This is the basic normal modal logic K, with no reflexivity, transitivity or seriality requirement on R. The substitution is existentially quantified without a length bound. Only its existence is decided; no running-time bound or output unifier is required. Malformed formula encodings are rejected.

upgraded_from.title: Decidability of unification in the basic modal logic K

references.title: Research reference · www.mathnet.ru

context_blocks.text: A modal formula talks about truth at a world and at worlds accessible from it. Unification asks whether its variables can be replaced by formulas so that the result becomes valid on every frame. This is a global requirement on one syntactic replacement, shared across all worlds and models. Choosing a satisfying assignment in one model is a different and weaker task.

For example, □p is unifiable: replacing p by ⊤ makes it valid. In contrast, ◇p is satisfiable in a model with an accessible world where p holds, but has no unifier in K. At a world with no successors, ◇ψ is false for every replacement ψ. Such dead ends are allowed by K’s unrestricted frame semantics. These examples distinguish satisfiability from the existence of a valid substitution instance.

For any proposed finite substitution, validity of the resulting K formula is decidable. Enumerating all finite substitutions therefore eventually finds a witness whenever one exists. The unresolved part is a procedure that also halts and answers no on every nonunifiable formula. A search that works only for positive instances does not give the requested decider. There is no time bound in this question.

Jeřábek’s theorem that K has nullary unification type concerns the organization of all unifiers, not their nonexistence. For the formula p→□p, unifiers exist, including p↦⊤, but they lack a complete irredundant family under the usual instantiation order. In that order, a unifier is more general when other unifiers arise by further substitution, modulo equivalence in K. The theorem blocks a particularly well-behaved classification of witnesses; it does not prove undecidability of whether any witness exists.

The choice of logic changes the problem. Wolter and Zakharyaschev prove undecidability after adding a universal modality, which can state that a formula holds at every world of a model. That extra operator is absent here. Their other negative results also add modalities and nominals. A decidable validity problem can thus coexist with undecidable unification, but those extension results do not settle basic K.

Positive results for stronger frame conditions likewise require care. Gougeon’s 2025 work computes most general unifiers for extensions of K5, including versions with fixed parameters. K5 imposes a Euclidean condition on accessibility: two successors of one world must be accessible from one another in the appropriate direction. K does not impose that condition. Beklemishev’s 2025 paper explicitly separates the open K case from solved transitive logics.

A resolution would locate a basic limit of automated substitution reasoning: can the simplest normal modal logic recognize when an expression can be made universally valid? The target concerns only existence. Constructing every unifier, deciding admissibility of arbitrary inference rules, or finding a most general unifier asks additional questions.

cards.title: Does greedy CDCL without restarts p-simulate resolution?
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic polynomial-time transformation which, given a CNF formula F and a resolution refutation π of F, outputs a legal greedy CDCL refutation of the same F, without restarts, in the asserting-learning model defined below? Both the transformation time and the output length are polynomial in the binary length of (F,π).
cards.definitions:
Literals are x_i or ¬x_i for i∈{1,…,n}; clauses are sets of literals and F is a finite set of clauses. A resolution inference derives (C∖{x})∪(D∖{¬x}) from clauses C containing x and D containing ¬x. A refutation is a finite sequence ending in the empty clause, each entry being an input clause or an inference from earlier entries, with parent indices and pivot recorded. Variable indices and pointers use binary notation. Clause and formula encodings explicitly list their literals.

A CDCL state consists of a database D containing F and an ordered trail of assignments to distinct variables of F. Each assignment is marked either as a decision or with its reason clause in D. Its decision level is the number of decisions up to that assignment. Initially D=F and the trail is empty. A clause is falsified if all its literals are false on the trail; it is unit if exactly one literal is unassigned and all others are false. The following priority of actions is mandatory.

If D has a falsified clause, a conflict must be processed before any other action. At decision level zero the run ends with UNSAT. Otherwise choose a falsified clause K and a trivial resolution analysis: start with K and repeatedly resolve the current clause with a reason clause recorded on the current trail, using a distinct pivot at each step. Every intermediate clause must be falsified by the current trail. Stop at a nonempty asserting clause C, meaning that exactly one of its variables has the current highest decision level. The trace records the full analysis. Add C to D and erase the suffix of the trail whose decision levels exceed a, where a is the maximum level of the other literals of C, or zero if there are none. Then perform one legal unit propagation and return to the conflict-first priority check.

If there is no conflict but a unit clause exists, choose such a clause, assign its unassigned literal to true, record that clause as the reason, and repeat the priority check. Only when neither conflicts nor units exist may a new decision assign either value to an unassigned variable. At such a stable state the run may first delete any subset of learned clauses, retaining all input clauses and all reasons appearing on the current trail, and must then make a decision. A satisfying complete trail ends with SAT, not a refutation. There is no independent operation clearing or shortening the trail: backjumping is allowed only after a conflict and only to the assertion level.

All choices of decisions, unit reasons, conflict clauses, trivial asserting analyses and permitted deletions are free components of the output trace. No fixed branching heuristic or first-UIP policy is imposed. No new variables, preprocessed replacement formula, unrecorded learned axioms or restarts are permitted. The only learned clauses are those derived by the recorded conflict analyses. The trace length counts all clauses, literals, assignments, analysis steps and pointers in an explicit binary encoding, so expensive analysis cannot be hidden in one step. This is the restart-free instantiation of the Vinyals model with arbitrary trivial asserting learning. The requested p-simulation is a uniform translation supplied with π; mere existence of a short trace, or finding one from F alone, is a different claim.

context_blocks.text: Clause learning stores consequences of encountered conflicts and reuses them during a SAT search. General resolution permits arbitrary reuse of earlier clauses, without requiring that they arise along a current partial assignment. This question asks whether the constraints of a greedy search, even with freely chosen decisions and learning, impose a superpolynomial cost when restarting is unavailable.

The operational model matters. Exhaustive unit propagation and immediate conflict processing constrain which trails are reachable. A restart discards the current trail while retaining learned information, whereas a backjump must be justified by the newly learned asserting clause. The statement specifies those actions separately rather than treating every return to decision level zero as a prohibited restart.

Vinyals gives an execution-trace proof system with explicit propagation reasons, conflict-analysis derivations, deletion rules and cost measures. The present card selects its no-restart policy and allows arbitrary trivial asserting analyses. This avoids making the question depend on a particular solver implementation, while retaining actual greedy search restrictions.

The supplied resolution proof is part of the translator’s input. An affirmative answer therefore would not give a polynomial-time SAT solver or a practical heuristic that discovers short proofs unaided. A theorem guaranteeing only polynomial-size traces, without a polynomial-time translation, would establish the corresponding size-simulation statement rather than the full p-simulation asked here.

Vinyals’ 2022 exposition distinguishes known simulations using non-greedy propagation or preprocessing from the unresolved greedy no-restart comparison. Buss and Thapen’s later work identifies candidate formulas for separating related resolution systems but does not prove that separation. These results motivate the target without establishing a resolution of the operational model on this card.

cards.title: FO model checking on hereditary monadically dependent graph classes
cards.area: Database theory and finite model theory
cards.formal: For every hereditary effectively monadically dependent class C of finite simple graphs, do there exist a deterministic algorithm A_C, a computable function f_C:N→N and a constant d_C such that A_C decides whether G satisfies a first-order sentence φ in time f_C(|φ|)(|V(G)|+1)^{d_C} for every G∈C? The precise effectiveness condition is given below; the graph is supplied without a structural decomposition.
cards.definitions: The class C is fixed, is closed under isomorphism and induced subgraphs, and is not part of each input. First-order sentences use equality, adjacency E(x,y), Boolean connectives and quantifiers over individual vertices. They do not quantify over sets, and no vertex order or arithmetic is supplied. The input is the explicitly represented graph G and the sentence φ; the parameter k=|φ| is its encoded length. The algorithm must halt on every input, and its correctness and stated time bound are required when G∈C; it need not recognize membership in C. To define monadic dependence, let θ(x,y) be any fixed first-order formula using adjacency and finitely many additional unary predicates. A graph in T_θ(G) is obtained by interpreting these predicates as arbitrary vertex subsets, putting an edge between distinct u,v whenever θ(u,v) or θ(v,u) holds, and taking any induced subgraph. C is monadically dependent when no single θ gives all finite graphs among the outputs T_θ(G), G∈C. For an explicit effective version, define P_s as the bipartite powerset graph with vertices a₁,…,a_s and b_S for every S⊆{1,…,s}, and edges a_i b_S exactly when i∈S. Require a computable function b:N→N_{≥1} such that, for every formula θ and every G∈C, P_{b(|θ|)} is absent from T_θ(G). Formula length includes its predicate symbols under a fixed effective encoding. This is the computable dependence-function convention of Mählmann’s Definition 12.24. The programs computing b and the eventual algorithm may depend on C; they are not extra per-instance certificates. The exponent d_C is independent of k. The query-evaluation problem here is for the plain graph signature; unary colours occur in the structural definition. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: Determine whether excluding arbitrary first-order graph encoding exactly supplies the structure needed for tractable logical queries on hereditary graph classes.

importance.reason: The central proposed tractability boundary for first-order model checking on hereditary graph classes, connecting database queries, model theory, sparsity and dense graph structure.

cards.status_note: Explicitly open in the July 2026 neighborhood-complexity paper. The independent-side hardness and stable-side algorithm are known; radius-one merge-width does not provide the full algorithm. This card fixes the effective dependence-function convention to require a computable FPT bound. No resolution found through 11 September 2026.

context_blocks.text: First-order logic describes many small graph queries with quantifiers over vertices. For example, the existence of a dominating set of size k can be expressed by choosing k vertices and requiring every vertex to equal or be adjacent to one of them. A direct evaluation can try n^k choices. Fixed-parameter tractability asks for the stronger form f(k)n^d: the query may be expensive, but its length must not keep increasing the exponent of the graph size.

Graph structure can make this possible. The broad research programme asks which hereditary classes support such evaluation. Hereditary means that deleting vertices keeps a graph inside the class, a natural closure property when a query examines a portion of a database or network. Sparse graph classes gave early positive results, but dense classes with controlled structure also admit efficient model checking. Thus density alone cannot describe the boundary.

Monadic dependence measures whether unrestricted graph structure can be hidden inside a class through a fixed logical interpretation. Unary predicates mark arbitrary vertex subsets. A formula then defines new edges, after which selected vertices may be retained. If this process can generate every finite graph, apparently restricted inputs still contain arbitrary graph complexity in an interpretable form. Monadic dependence forbids that possibility.

The effective hypothesis matters to the exact computational claim. A structural class can have finite obstruction bounds at every logical complexity while those bounds grow faster than any computable function. Mählmann makes the dependence condition quantitative using forbidden powerset graphs and distinguishes computable parameter bounds from weaker conventions for fixed-parameter tractability. This card adopts that explicit effective formulation, so “there exists a finite bound” is not silently substituted for an algorithmically bounded parameter function.

One direction of the broader classification has been established. Dreier, Mählmann and Toruńczyk prove that first-order model checking is AW[*]-hard on every hereditary monadically independent graph class. Under the standard assumption FPT≠AW[*], this excludes efficient model checking on the independent side. Their structural characterization uses flip-breakability, a separation property allowing controlled changes to adjacency between vertex groups. The missing direction is the algorithm for dependent classes.

A major positive theorem proves fixed-parameter tractability for monadically stable classes. Stability additionally forbids interpreting arbitrarily long linear orders; dependence forbids arbitrary graph encoding and allows more classes. The 2023 preprint by Dreier, Eleftheriadis, Mählmann, McCarty, Pilipczuk and Toruńczyk, published at FOCS 2024, settles the stable case using neighborhood complexity and suitable covers. It does not make the two structural notions equivalent.

Merge-width is a graph parameter used in existing model-checking theorems. Dreier and Toruńczyk describe a graph by a sequence of successively coarser vertex partitions, recording deviations from default adjacencies between parts. Their model-checking theorem applies to bounded merge-width when a witnessing construction sequence is supplied. This theorem assumes that a witnessing sequence is supplied and does not cover the stated input model.

The July 2026 neighborhood-complexity paper proves that, for every fixed positive η, the number of distinct sets N(v)∩A is O(|A|^{1+η}) in a monadically dependent class, with the constant depending on the class and η. It also constructs sequences witnessing radius-one merge-width n^{o(1)} in polynomial time. This supplies a concrete structural and algorithmic step. General first-order formulas require control at radii depending on the formula, so radius one does not complete the model-checking argument.

Related February 2026 work by Dreier and Kuske accelerates the construction of low-crossing orders and neighborhood covers, improving model-checking runtimes within the already tractable monadically stable setting. Such refinements are useful because they make the structural tools more practical, while leaving the dependent-versus-stable boundary in place.

A positive answer would unify several major algorithmic graph frameworks through one logical condition and explain when small declarative queries can avoid repeated high-dimensional enumeration. A counterexample satisfying the effective hypothesis would show that the absence of arbitrary logical graph encoding is insufficient for tractability. Either outcome would sharpen the connection between graph structure and query evaluation.

cards.title: The full constant-delay conjunctive-query classification
cards.area: Database theory and finite model theory
cards.formal: Is there a total algorithm that, given any conjunctive query q with self-joins allowed, decides whether q admits enumeration of all distinct answers with O_q(N) preprocessing and O_q(1) worst-case delay on every database of size N?
cards.definitions: A query is a finite formula q(x̄)=∃ȳ ∧ᵢ Rᵢ(z̄ᵢ), with no constants, negation, disequalities or aggregation. The head x̄ lists distinct variables; every variable occurs in a relational atom. Relation symbols have fixed positive finite arities within q and may occur repeatedly; repeated variables within atoms are allowed. Boolean queries have an empty head. A database D explicitly lists finite set-valued relations over a domain [n]; N=1+n+the total number of tuple entries in these lists. Each domain identifier fits in O(log(N+2)) bits. q(D) is the set of head tuples extendible to an assignment satisfying all atoms. Fix the deterministic word-RAM convention with addition, multiplication, comparison, Boolean word operations and indirect access costing one step, words of O_q(log(N+2)) bits, and a polynomial address universe of initially zero cells. Accessed cells and operations are charged; no linear-space or constant-extra-space restriction is imposed. This allows direct tuple-membership tables without charging for touching every unused address. Membership in the target class means that for this fixed q there are an enumerator and constants C_q,B_q whose preprocessing takes at most C_q N steps, whose word length is at most B_q log₂(N+2), and whose time to the first answer, between consecutive answers, and from the last answer to termination is at most C_q after preprocessing. Empty output must be reported within the same delay bound. Output order is arbitrary and each tuple appears exactly once. The classifier takes q, not D, as input and must halt on every query; it has no prescribed runtime bound and need not output the enumerator. This is an explicit effective yes/no formulation of the source’s broader request for a complete tractability classification. The word instructions are random-access reads/writes, comparisons, conditional branches, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo 2^w, integer quotient/remainder with nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, and shifts of a w-bit word; shifts by at least w yield zero. The constant in word length w=Θ(log n) (or Θ(log N) when N is the stated input size) is fixed with the algorithm. Address arithmetic has the same cost, larger integers occupy multiple words, and no instruction performs arbitrary-precision arithmetic in one step. When randomization is allowed, a fresh independent uniform w-bit word costs one operation. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: A missing general tractability boundary for relational query evaluation, connecting logical syntax, enumeration algorithms and fine-grained lower bounds.

importance.reason: A central database-theory classification question: identify exactly which fixed queries permit optimal preprocessing and delay, including the self-joins excluded by classical dichotomies.

cards.status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. The checked primary sources leave the general self-join classification unresolved. The exact target is an editorial effective formulation, with a specified RAM and permissive polynomial memory. Known negative classifications use stated fine-grained hypotheses; newer projected-query and dynamic results do not cover the whole class.

context_blocks.text: A conjunctive query combines relational lookups with shared variables, then projects away variables that are not requested in the output. For example, q(x,z)=∃y R(x,y)∧S(y,z) asks for all endpoint pairs connected through an intermediate value. It may have many witnesses y for one answer (x,z), but under the set semantics here that answer must be printed only once. A self-join occurs when several atoms use the same relation symbol.

This is data complexity: q is fixed while the database grows. Even a fixed query can produce quadratically or cubically many answers, so linear total running time is often impossible just because of output size. Linear preprocessing followed by constant delay is a more appropriate ideal. It permits total time proportional to input plus output while also controlling the wait for each answer, including the first one and the final termination signal.

The classical positive condition is free-connex acyclicity. Form the query hypergraph with a vertex for each variable and one edge for the variables of each atom. It is acyclic when its edges admit a join tree: the edges containing any particular variable form a connected subtree. Free-connex additionally requires acyclicity after adding one edge containing all output variables. Bagan–Durand–Grandjean develop constant-delay enumeration for this structure.

For the example ∃y R(x,y)∧S(y,z), the two atom edges form a path, but adding the output edge {x,z} creates a cycle. Its answers are exactly the nonzero entries in the Boolean product of the two relation matrices. This explains why projection is tied to matrix multiplication. Classical hardness for acyclic self-join-free queries relies on a Boolean-matrix-multiplication assumption, rather than an unconditional superlinear lower bound.

Carmeli–Segoufin show that the self-join-free classification does not extend merely by ignoring repeated relation names. Some cyclic queries with self-joins allow constant-delay enumeration. Their paper gives positive and negative conditions, a classification for queries with at most two output variables under stated hyperclique assumptions, and further results for queries whose Boolean cores are cyclic. A general classification remains outside these theorems.

A particularly instructive example is the full query R(x,y)∧R(y,z)∧R(x,t)∧R(t,z). A two-step path from x to z already yields an answer with t=y. When another middle vertex becomes available for those endpoints, it can be paired with previously stored middle vertices to produce further answers. The paper generalizes this symmetry through mirror queries. Its algorithms may store information proportional to the output, which is why this card explicitly allows growing memory.

Adding a predicate on only one of the two middle vertices can break that symmetry. More generally, assignments can identify several query variables with one database element. This is allowed by the syntax; injective matching would be another task. Such identifications generate extra answers that can invalidate a hardness reduction designed for independent relations. Any complete criterion has to account for the interaction between repeated symbols, variable identifications and the chosen output variables.

Rouvroy’s May 2025 research report studies acyclic queries with self-joins and projections, focusing on atoms of arity at most two. It develops a sufficient condition through a construction called patching, alongside necessary conditions and examples not captured by either side. The report explicitly says it is not yet polished. These are useful additional tractability results, but the report does not claim the full classification; relation arity at most two also differs from having at most two output variables.

The source question asks for a structural classification. To make this card a definite yes/no problem, the formal target asks whether membership in the tractable class is decidable from query syntax. This does not demand a fast classifier, nor one uniform enumerator with constants independent of q. It does demand termination for every query. A finite list of sufficient patterns is progress only if there is also a justified answer for every remaining query.

Recent dichotomies for incremental view maintenance concern another resource tradeoff. Chmielewski–Draghici–Olteanu–Zhang’s June 2026 preprint studies insertions into semiring-annotated databases and classifies a self-join-free setting using acyclicity and p-hierarchy. There the update cost and the semiring affect tractability. Such a dynamic, annotated classification does not resolve static distinct-answer enumeration with arbitrary self-joins.

A solution would explain exactly when a query can be compiled into an output stream with predictable response time after one linear scan of its data. The significance reaches beyond one faster join implementation: it would provide a general language-level boundary for a basic form of relational computation. The explicit memory, projection and duplicate conventions make proposed classifications comparable instead of allowing the target to change between examples.

cards.title: Is there a logic capturing polynomial time on unordered structures?
cards.area: Database theory and finite model theory
cards.formal: Does there exist a logic L with decidable syntax and isomorphism-invariant semantics on finite relational structures such that its sentences define exactly the polynomial-time decidable Boolean properties, and an effective compiler maps each sentence to a correct polynomial-time evaluation algorithm with a polynomial running-time bound?
cards.why: The central descriptive-complexity question of characterizing feasible computation without supplying an arbitrary order.

progress.text: Grohe surveys the general capturing question and positive results for particular classes of structures.
Grädel–Grohe make the effective compiler and decidable-syntax requirements explicit in their survey of choiceless computation.
Witnessed symmetric choice yields capture on classes with definable isomorphism in the extended formalism.
Group-order logic research retains the general question and studies restricted generating-set operations.
